Part I: Foundations — The Agentic Runtime

Chapter 1: The Agentic Harness Mental Model

"The model is not the agent. The harness is the agent. The model is just the brain."

1.1 What Is an "Agentic Harness"

Most engineers encounter Claude through the chat API: send a message, get a message back. Clean, stateless, request-response. An agentic harness is the opposite of that.

An agentic harness is the orchestration layer that sits between an LLM and the real world. It transforms a language model — something that can only produce text — into an agent that can read files, run commands, browse the web, spawn subagents, and modify state. The model stays the same. The harness is what gives it legs.

The anatomy is always the same, regardless of implementation language:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 USER INTERFACE                │
│        (terminal, API, background daemon)     │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                     │ user prompt
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────┐
│              AGENTIC HARNESS                  │
│  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌─────────┐ │
│  │ System Prompt│  │  Tool    │  │Permission│ │
│  │  Assembler  │  │ Registry │  │  Layer  │ │
│  └─────────────┘  └──────────┘  └─────────┘ │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │           Control Loop                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                     │ assembled prompt + tools
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────┐
│             CLAUDE API (claude-*)             │
│       claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-opus-4-8      │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                     │ tool_use / text response
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────┐
│               TOOL EXECUTORS                  │
│  filesystem │ shell │ web │ agents │ MCP...   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The distinction matters because the harness owns the agency. It decides which tools Claude can see, what context gets injected into the system prompt, which tool calls get executed versus blocked, and when the loop terminates. The model is powerful, but it is fundamentally reactive — it responds to what the harness presents to it. If you want to understand or build AI agents, understanding the harness is the prerequisite.

Every production harness you will encounter — Claude Code, LangChain agents, AutoGPT, OpenAI Assistants — is a variant of this same pattern. What differs is the sophistication of the control loop, the richness of the tool surface, the expressiveness of the permission model, and the quality of context management. Claude Code is currently the most complete public reference implementation of an agentic harness, and it is the primary source of ground truth for this book.

1.2 The Control Loop

The control loop is the heartbeat of every agentic harness. Understanding it precisely is not optional — it determines what the model can and cannot do, where failures occur, and how you debug them.

Here is the loop as implemented in Claude Code v2.1.220:

flowchart TD
    A([User Prompt]) --> B[Assemble System Prompt]
    B --> B1[Inject: git status]
    B --> B2[Inject: memory / CLAUDE.md]
    B --> B3[Inject: env info / working dir]
    B --> B4[Inject: tool descriptions]
    B1 & B2 & B3 & B4 --> C[Send to Claude API]
    C --> D{Response Type?}
    D -->|tool_use| E[Permission Check]
    E -->|denied| F[Return tool_result: denied]
    E -->|allowed| G[Execute Tool]
    G --> H[Return tool_result to conversation]
    H --> C
    D -->|text only| I([Final Response to User])
    F --> C

Walk through each step:

Assemble system prompt. The harness does not send a static system prompt. Before every call to the Claude API it assembles the prompt dynamically from several sources: the base instructions (tool descriptions, behavioral rules), CLAUDE.md content discovered from the filesystem, the current git status, environment variables, working directory, and any memory/context from prior turns. This assembly is where most harness complexity lives.

Send to Claude API. The assembled conversation — system prompt plus message history — goes to the API as a standard Messages request. The harness provides the tool schema list alongside it. Claude sees only what the harness chooses to show it.

Receive response. Claude returns one of two things: a tool_use block (the model wants to call a tool) or a plain text message (the model is done for this turn). A single response can contain multiple tool_use blocks, which the harness may execute in parallel.

Permission check. Before executing any tool call, the harness evaluates it against the permission layer. This is where allow/deny rules, glob patterns, and the auto-mode classifier make their decision. If denied, the harness returns a tool_result explaining the denial without executing anything. Claude then adjusts.

Execute tool. If permitted, the harness calls the tool's execute function with the parameters Claude provided. The tool can be synchronous (returns immediately) or asynchronous (background task, returns a task ID).

Return tool_result. The tool output is appended to the conversation as a tool_result message and the loop continues. The API call is made again with the full updated conversation.

Termination. The loop ends when Claude produces a text-only response — no tool_use blocks. At that point the harness has nothing left to execute and returns the final message to the user.

This loop is deceptively simple on paper. The complexity emerges from everything happening around it: context window management, permission evaluation, parallel tool execution, error recovery, and the fact that multi-turn conversations can run for hundreds of iterations.

1.3 Claude Code as Reference Implementation

Claude Code v2.1.220 is the harness this book uses as its ground truth. It is worth understanding the implementation details because they reflect deliberate architectural choices you will want to replicate or consciously deviate from.

Distribution

Claude Code ships as a native binary, not pure JavaScript. It is compiled for ten platform targets:

PlatformArch
darwinarm64, x64
linuxx64, arm64, x64-musl, arm64-musl
linux-androidx64, arm64
win32x64, arm64

This matters architecturally. The binary approach means startup time is milliseconds, memory overhead is predictable, and the harness can be invoked as a subprocess without Node.js startup cost. For a tool used in tight CI loops or spawned as subagents inside workflows, this is significant.

Installation methods:

# Recommended: curl installer
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | sh

# Homebrew (macOS)
brew install claude

# Bun (cross-platform)
bun install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# npm (deprecated but functional)
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

The npm/bun distribution wraps the native binary. When the npm postinstall script runs successfully, it copies the native binary to the appropriate bin path. When postinstall fails (restricted environments, offline installs), cli-wrapper.cjs acts as a fallback launcher — it detects the platform, locates the vendored native binary inside the package, and shells out to it. This two-path approach is how the package maintains both npm distribution compatibility and native binary performance.

Configuration Entry Point

The primary configuration file is ~/.claude/settings.json for global settings and .claude/settings.json for project-level settings. The schema is published at json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json. Every behavioral aspect of the harness — model selection, permission rules, tool availability, hook scripts — is controlled through this settings layer. Chapter 2 covers the full configuration architecture.

1.4 The 52+ Tool Surface

The tool surface is how the harness exposes capabilities to the model. Claude Code organizes tools into three tiers, each with different loading behavior.

Tier 1: Core Tools (Always Loaded)

Six tools are loaded unconditionally on startup. Their descriptions are always present in the system prompt:

ToolPurpose
BashExecute shell commands in a persistent CWD
ReadRead files (text, images, PDFs, notebooks)
EditMake exact string replacements in files
WriteCreate or overwrite files
AgentSpawn subagents (background or foreground)
AskUserQuestionPresent structured questions to the user

These six represent the minimal surface needed for the model to be useful: shell access, filesystem read/write, and the ability to delegate work. Everything else is additive.

Tier 2: Deferred Tools (ToolSearch)

Over twenty tools are not loaded at startup. They exist in a registry and are loaded on demand when the model invokes ToolSearch with a query. This is a deliberate context-budget optimization — each tool description costs tokens in the system prompt, and loading all 52+ tools unconditionally would consume meaningful context before the user's first message.

The deferred tools include:

CronCreate       CronDelete       CronList
EnterPlanMode    ExitPlanMode
EnterWorktree    ExitWorktree
LSP
NotebookEdit
ScheduleWakeup
TaskCreate       TaskGet          TaskList
TaskOutput       TaskStop         TaskUpdate
WebFetch         WebSearch
Workflow
Skill

The model learns about deferred tools through brief, token-efficient registry entries. When it needs one — say, it wants to schedule a recurring task — it calls ToolSearch("schedule task"), receives the full CronCreate schema, and proceeds. The tool is now active for the rest of the session.

This pattern — lazy-loading capabilities — is something you will want to replicate in any harness with a large tool surface. The system prompt is not free context.

Tier 3: MCP Tools (Dynamic)

Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers provide a fourth unbounded tier. Each connected MCP server can expose arbitrarily many tools. Claude Code loads MCP tool schemas at startup (or lazily via MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true), making them available alongside the built-in tools.

The practical effect: a Claude Code session connecting to three MCP servers — say copilot-mem, sec-sr-mem, and a custom database server — might have 80 tools available to the model. The tool surface scales with your infrastructure, not with what Anthropic ships.

graph LR
    subgraph "Always Loaded (6)"
        Bash
        Read
        Edit
        Write
        Agent
        AskUserQuestion
    end
    subgraph "Deferred via ToolSearch (20+)"
        CronCreate
        WebFetch
        TaskCreate
        LSP
        Workflow
        etc["..."]
    end
    subgraph "MCP Tools (unbounded)"
        mcp1["copilot-mem tools"]
        mcp2["custom-db tools"]
        mcp3["sec-sr-mem tools"]
    end
    Claude -->|"sees always"| Bash
    Claude -->|"loads on demand"| CronCreate
    Claude -->|"from MCP servers"| mcp1

1.5 Harness vs SDK vs Framework

The taxonomy matters when you are deciding what to build or adopt. These three terms are often used interchangeably and shouldn't be.

The Anthropic SDK

The @anthropic-ai/sdk npm package is a thin typed wrapper around the Messages API. It handles HTTP, streaming, retries, and type safety. It does not provide a control loop, tool execution, permission checking, or context management. If you call anthropic.messages.create(...), you get back a response and you are done — there is no loop, no state, no tools unless you implement them yourself. The SDK is a primitive, not an agent.

A Framework

Frameworks like LangChain, LlamaIndex, or CrewAI provide higher-level abstractions: agent classes, chain composition, memory stores, retriever integrations. They reduce boilerplate but introduce their own abstractions, often leaky, that can obscure what is actually happening between your code and the API. They are built on top of SDKs and implement harness concepts in reusable (but opinionated) ways. Good for prototyping; worth understanding deeply if you build on them.

A Harness

A harness is the complete, production-grade orchestration layer. It owns everything between the user and the model: the control loop, tool execution, permission enforcement, context management, session persistence, error recovery. Claude Code is a harness. It uses the Anthropic SDK internally, but the SDK is not the interesting part — the harness architecture is.

ConcernSDKFrameworkHarness
HTTP / streamingYesWraps SDKUses SDK
Control loopNoYes (abstract)Yes (concrete)
Tool executionNoPartialYes
Permission layerNoNoYes
Context managementNoPartialYes
Session persistenceNoOptionalYes
Production-hardenedn/aVariesYes (Claude Code)

When you are building your own harness (Part VI of this book), you will use the SDK as a dependency. You will likely steal architectural ideas from frameworks. But you are responsible for all of the concerns in the "Harness" column.

Claude Code sits in the harness row, and it is open to inspection. Every chapter in this book peels back a layer of it.

1.6 Runtime Lifecycle

Understanding the startup sequence is essential if you are building a harness or debugging startup behavior. The sequence is deterministic and hooks fire in a specific order.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant H as Harness
    participant FS as Filesystem
    participant MCP as MCP Servers
    participant Git as Git
    participant API as Claude API

    U->>H: launch (claude or claude -p "...")
    H->>H: parse CLI flags + load global settings
    H->>H: fire SessionStart hooks
    H->>FS: discover CLAUDE.md (project root → git root → ~/)
    FS-->>H: CLAUDE.md content (project instructions)
    H->>MCP: connect configured MCP servers
    MCP-->>H: tool schemas registered
    H->>Git: inject git status + branch + recent commits
    Git-->>H: git context (or empty if not a repo)
    H->>H: assemble initial system prompt
    H-->>U: ready (interactive: show prompt / print: run)
    U->>H: first user message
    H->>API: messages.create(system + tools + history)
    API-->>H: response (tool_use or text)

SessionStart hooks fire before anything else. This is where harness authors inject environment setup — loading state files, printing context messages to the conversation, warming caches. If your hook exits non-zero, the session can be aborted before it starts. Chapter 16 covers the full hook system.

CLAUDE.md discovery walks the directory tree looking for CLAUDE.md files. It checks the current working directory, parent directories up to the git root, and ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for global instructions. Found files are concatenated into the system prompt as project instructions. This is how the user in this session has a CLAUDE.md that specifies multi-domain workspace rules, Python coding standards, and shell scripting conventions — the harness injects all of it before the first API call.

MCP server connection happens after CLAUDE.md discovery. Each configured server is started (for stdio transport, the harness forks a subprocess) or connected to (for HTTP/SSE transport). Tool schemas are fetched and registered. If MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true, this step is deferred and the harness proceeds without waiting — tools become available as connections complete.

Git context injection reads the current branch, recent commits, and git status output. This context is injected into the system prompt so Claude immediately knows it is in a git repo, what the current state is, and what changed recently. In a large codebase, this context materially improves the model's first-turn code and refactoring decisions.

After all of this, the harness is ready. In interactive mode, it shows the prompt. In print mode (-p), it immediately begins executing the provided prompt.

1.7 Lab: Trace a "Fix This Bug" Prompt Through the Full Harness Lifecycle

This lab is conceptual but precise. Walk through every stage a real bug-fix request traverses from user input to committed patch.

The Prompt

fix the authentication timeout in src/auth/session.py — 
sessions are expiring after 5 minutes instead of 30

Stage 1: Startup (T=0ms)

The harness fires SessionStart hooks. If you have a hook at .claude/hooks/session_start.sh, it runs now. A real hook might:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Recover state from prior session
if [[ -f ~/.claude/projects/myapp/state.json ]]; then
    cat ~/.claude/projects/myapp/state.json | jq -r '.context_message'
fi

The hook's stdout is prepended to the conversation as context. This ensures the model knows, for instance, that a prior session was mid-refactor on the auth module.

Stage 2: System Prompt Assembly (T=10ms)

The harness assembles the system prompt. For this session in a Python project, it might inject:

[Project Instructions from CLAUDE.md]
Multi-domain workspace: AI security research, book writing...
Python: type hints, f-strings, pathlib, PEP 8. Use ruff.

[Git Context]
On branch: fix/auth-timeout
Recent commits:
  a1b2c3d chore: update dependencies
  e4f5g6h feat: add session refresh endpoint

[Git Status]
M src/auth/session.py
M tests/auth/test_session.py

[Tool Descriptions]
Bash: Execute shell commands...
Read: Read files from the local filesystem...
[...6 core tools + any MCP tools...]

The model sees all of this before it processes the user's "fix the authentication timeout" message. The git status already tells it that session.py is modified — the model might infer that another change is already in progress.

Stage 3: First API Call (T=50ms)

The harness sends the assembled system prompt plus the user message to the Claude API. The model responds with a tool_use block:

{
  "type": "tool_use",
  "name": "Read",
  "input": {
    "file_path": "/Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/src/auth/session.py"
  }
}

The model's first move is almost always to gather context before acting. It knows from the git status that session.py is relevant. It reads it.

Stage 4: Permission Check + Tool Execution (T=55ms)

The harness evaluates the Read call against the permission layer:

  • Is Read in the deny list? No.
  • Does the file path match any blocked patterns (.env, credentials, SSH keys)? No.
  • Is defaultMode set to something that requires confirmation? No, this session uses auto.

Permission granted. The harness reads session.py and returns it as a tool_result:

{
  "type": "tool_result",
  "tool_use_id": "toolu_abc123",
  "content": "     1\tSESSION_TIMEOUT_MINUTES = 5\n     2\t...\n"
}

Stage 5: Second API Call — The Model Investigates (T=100ms)

Back in the loop. Claude processes the file content and issues another tool_use:

{
  "type": "tool_use",
  "name": "Bash",
  "input": {
    "command": "grep -rn 'SESSION_TIMEOUT\\|session_timeout\\|timeout.*minutes' src/auth/ tests/auth/",
    "description": "Find all timeout references in auth module"
  }
}

The description field is not cosmetic. The harness uses it for the permission UI (users see what the command is doing) and the audit trail. Well-written descriptions make it possible to reconstruct what happened from logs.

Permission check: is this Bash call on the allow list? The command uses grep, which is benign. Allowed.

Stage 6: Root Cause Found (T=150ms)

The grep returns multiple hits showing the timeout constant is defined in three places — the session module, a config parser, and a legacy constants file that the config parser never reads. The model now has enough information to form a fix.

It issues an Edit call:

{
  "type": "tool_use",
  "name": "Edit",
  "input": {
    "file_path": "src/auth/session.py",
    "old_string": "SESSION_TIMEOUT_MINUTES = 5",
    "new_string": "SESSION_TIMEOUT_MINUTES = 30"
  }
}

Followed by another Edit for the config file, and a Bash call to run the tests:

{
  "type": "tool_use",
  "name": "Bash",
  "input": {
    "command": "cd /Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026 && python -m pytest tests/auth/test_session.py -v",
    "description": "Run auth session tests after timeout fix"
  }
}

Stage 7: Test Output + Final Loop (T=400ms)

Tests pass. The model receives the green output as a tool_result and produces its final text-only response — no more tool_use blocks:

Fixed the authentication timeout issue. The problem was SESSION_TIMEOUT_MINUTES 
being set to 5 in src/auth/session.py while the value in config/legacy_constants.py 
(also 5) was being read by the config parser instead. I've updated both:

- src/auth/session.py:1 → SESSION_TIMEOUT_MINUTES = 30
- config/legacy_constants.py:47 → AUTH_SESSION_TIMEOUT_MINUTES = 30

All 12 session tests pass. The config parser now reads the correct constant.

Stage 8: The Loop Terminates (T=401ms)

Text-only response means no more tool_use blocks. The control loop detects this and exits. The harness returns the final message to the user interface.

Total loop iterations: 5 (Read → Bash/grep → Edit × 2 → Bash/pytest → final text) Total API calls: 5 Total wall clock: ~400ms (assuming model latency ~80ms/call)

What This Trace Reveals

  • The model never has direct filesystem access. Every file it reads goes through the harness's Read tool executor.
  • Each API call is independent — the model reconstructs its understanding from the full conversation history every time. There is no "model memory" between API calls in the same session; the harness maintains the conversation state.
  • The permission layer evaluated every tool call, even trivial Read calls. In production harnesses, this evaluation needs to be fast — sub-millisecond.
  • The description field on Bash calls is load-bearing for auditability. In enterprise deployments, these descriptions feed audit logs.
  • The loop terminated at 5 iterations for a relatively simple bug. Complex refactors or multi-file architectural changes can run 50–200 iterations.

Summary

An agentic harness is the orchestration layer between an LLM and the world. It owns the control loop, assembles context, executes tools, enforces permissions, and manages the conversation state across turns. The model is reactive; the harness is what makes it autonomous.

Claude Code v2.1.220 is the reference implementation. It ships as a native binary for ten platforms, organizes its 52+ tools into three tiers (always-loaded, deferred via ToolSearch, and unlimited MCP), and follows a deterministic startup sequence: SessionStart hooks → CLAUDE.md discovery → MCP connection → git context → ready.

The distinction between SDK, framework, and harness matters when you are building. The SDK is a primitive. Frameworks are opinionated abstractions. A harness is the complete, production-hardened orchestration layer — and building one is what this book is about.

In Chapter 2, we go inside the configuration architecture: the five-layer settings cascade, the permission rule DSL, and the CLAUDE.md system that lets projects inject their own behavioral instructions into every session.

Chapter 2: Configuration Architecture

Every tool you use to control Claude Code — every permission rule, every model override, every key binding — lives in a configuration layer. Understanding where values come from and in what order they win is the difference between a harness that behaves predictably and one that surprises you in production. This chapter maps the full configuration architecture from first principles, using verified examples drawn from a real working setup.

2.1 The Settings Cascade

Claude Code resolves configuration through five overlapping layers, each capable of overriding the last. Resolution happens at startup; the merged result drives runtime behavior for the entire session.

~/.claude/settings.json          (1) Global — machine-wide defaults
.claude/settings.json            (2) Project — team-shared, checked into git
.claude/settings.local.json      (3) Local — personal overrides, gitignored
managed settings (MDM/policy)    (4) Enterprise-managed, read-only from user perspective
CLI flags                        (5) Session-only overrides, highest priority

The cascade is last-write-wins for scalar values and union for arrays (notably permission lists). That means if global sets effortLevel: "high" and local sets effortLevel: "xhigh", the session runs at xhigh. If global sets a deny rule and local adds additional allow rules, both are active.

Why five layers?

Each layer serves a distinct stakeholder:

LayerOwnerPurposeChecked into git?
Global (~/.claude/settings.json)Individual engineerPersonal defaults, machine-specific toolingNo
Project (.claude/settings.json)TeamShared permissions, hooks, project rulesYes
Local (.claude/settings.local.json)Individual engineerOverrides for the current project onlyNo (gitignore it)
ManagedIT/securityNon-negotiable enterprise policyN/A
CLI flagsSessionOne-off experiments, CI overridesN/A

The split between global and local is the key design point: your personal preferences (model choice, thinking mode, plugin list) belong at global scope; your project-specific personal additions (MCP server enablement, per-project defaultMode) belong in the local file. The project file is the only one other humans read, so it should contain only what the whole team agrees on.

The local file in practice

.claude/settings.local.json accumulates fast. It is the file Claude Code writes to when you confirm a new one-time permission at the prompt. After a few months on a large codebase, it will contain hundreds of granular Bash(...) allow entries — each one granted by you interactively during a prior session. This is intentional: the runtime never silently broadens its own permissions, and the paper trail lives here.

Add .claude/settings.local.json to .gitignore. If you commit it by accident, other engineers will inherit your personal permission grants.

2.2 The Settings JSON Schema

Every settings file should carry a $schema header:

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json"
}

This is not decoration. Your editor (VS Code, Neovim with LSP, IntelliJ) will load the schema and give you:

  • Autocomplete on every key name
  • Type validation (catches "effortLevel": "very-high" before runtime does)
  • Documentation on hover — useful when you can't remember whether the field is effortLevel or effort_level

The schema is published at SchemaStore, which most editors poll automatically. If your editor does not, add the URL manually to your JSON schema associations.

Schema validation at runtime

Claude Code validates settings at startup. A malformed settings file causes a startup warning, not a silent ignore. If you see unexpected behavior after editing a settings file, run claude doctor — it will surface schema violations.

2.3 Permission Rules

The permissions block is the most consequential part of your configuration. It controls what Claude can do without asking you.

The allow/deny structure

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(*)", "Read(*)", "Edit(*)", "Write(*)"],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Read(./**/*.pem)",
      "Read(~/.ssh/*)"
    ]
  }
}

Rules are evaluated in order: deny rules take precedence over allow rules. If Read(*) is in the allow list and Read(./.env) is in the deny list, .env is blocked regardless of position.

Glob syntax

The argument inside the parentheses is a glob pattern matched against the tool's primary argument. Each tool type interprets the pattern differently:

RuleMatches
Bash(*)Any shell command
Bash(git *)Any git subcommand
Bash(git commit*)git commit and git commit -m "..."
Edit(/src/**)Any file under /src/ recursively
Read(/path/to/file.txt)That exact file
Read(./**/*.pem)Any .pem file anywhere under the current directory
Read(~/.ssh/*)Any file directly inside ~/.ssh/

The ** glob crosses directory boundaries. The * glob does not. Bash(git *) would not match git commit -am "fix" because the space and -am are part of the argument — Bash(git*) matches the string starting with git, while Bash(git *) matches the literal prefix git followed by anything.

Real deny list: protecting secrets

Here is the deny list from the project settings for this workspace:

"deny": [
  "Read(./.env)",
  "Read(./.env.*)",
  "Read(./token.json)",
  "Read(./temp_cert.pem)",
  "Read(./temp_key.pem)",
  "Read(./*credentials*)",
  "Read(./*secret*)",
  "Read(./**/*.pem)",
  "Read(./**/*_key)",
  "Read(./**/*_secret*)",
  "Read(~/.config/gcloud/*credentials*)",
  "Read(~/.config/gcloud/*token*)",
  "Read(~/.azure/*)",
  "Read(~/.aws/credentials)",
  "Read(~/.aws/config)",
  "Read(~/.ssh/*)",
  "Read(~/.gnupg/*)"
]

This pattern catches the common credential locations across cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure), SSH, PGP, and the ubiquitous .env family. Copy this as a baseline for any project that handles real credentials.

defaultMode

The permissions.defaultMode field controls how unrecognized tool calls are handled:

ModeBehavior
defaultAsk for permission on each new tool/argument pattern
acceptEditsAuto-accept file edits, ask for everything else
autoAuto-approve anything not explicitly denied
bypassPermissionsSkip all permission checks (dangerous)
planNever execute — only plan and describe
dontAskExecute without prompting but respect deny list

In production harnesses, auto paired with a tight deny list gives you autonomy with guardrails. The default mode is appropriate for exploratory sessions where you want to approve each new capability as it is needed — and each approval accumulates in settings.local.json.

allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly

Enterprise environments can set this flag to true to prevent any locally-configured permission rules from taking effect. Only rules delivered via the managed settings layer (MDM, policy server) apply. Use this when you need to guarantee that engineers cannot accidentally or deliberately widen the permission surface.

2.4 Environment Variables

Claude Code exposes a significant amount of tunable behavior through environment variables. These live in the env block of any settings file, which means you can apply them per-scope — different token limits for CI vs. interactive sessions.

Token budget variables

VariablePurposeTypical value
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENSTotal context window budget1000000 (1M for claude-opus-4 class models)
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENSMax tokens per response128000
MAX_THINKING_TOKENSBudget for extended thinking100000

These three variables form the token economy of your session. The context limit caps how much conversation history, file content, and tool output can accumulate before the runtime triggers auto-compaction. The output limit caps how long any single response can be. The thinking limit caps how much chain-of-thought the model can generate when alwaysThinkingEnabled is true.

A concrete example: the global settings for this workspace set all three:

"env": {
  "CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS": "128000",
  "CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS": "1000000",
  "MAX_THINKING_TOKENS": "100000"
}

Tool concurrency and retry variables

VariablePurposeTypical value
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_TOOL_USE_CONCURRENCYParallel tool calls per turn8
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIESAPI retry count on transient errors5
CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_THRESHOLD_MINUTESMinutes of idle before session warning180
CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_TOKEN_THRESHOLDToken count at which idle check matters500000

CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_TOOL_USE_CONCURRENCY is particularly important for workflow-heavy harnesses. The runtime will dispatch up to N tool calls in parallel when the model requests them in the same turn. Setting this too low throttles multi-agent workflows unnecessarily; setting it too high can cause resource contention on machines with limited CPU or network bandwidth.

Tool search and MCP variables

VariablePurposeValues
ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCHWhether deferred tools are loaded on demand"true", "false", "auto"
ENABLE_MCP_LARGE_OUTPUT_FILESWrite large MCP outputs to temp files"1"
MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKINGSkip MCP connection wait in -p mode"true"

ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH with the value "auto" means the runtime decides at startup based on available context budget. When set to "true", the ToolSearch tool is always available and the full 52+ tool surface can be discovered on demand without loading all tool schemas into the system prompt upfront.

Infrastructure and debugging variables

VariablePurpose
DISABLE_TELEMETRYOpt out of usage telemetry
CLAUDE_ENABLE_STREAM_WATCHDOGRestart stalled streaming connections
CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMSNumber of agent team slots (integer)
CLAUDE_CODE_TEAMMATE_COMMANDShell command to dispatch teammates

CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS enables the agent team feature. Setting it to 3 provisions three teammate slots that can be dispatched from the chat interface. CLAUDE_CODE_TEAMMATE_COMMAND is the script that handles teammate launch — in a tmux-based setup, this is the entry point that creates a new pane and starts the teammate process.

2.5 Model Configuration

Model behavior is controlled through three complementary settings: which model to use, how hard it should think, and whether it should optimize for speed.

Model selection

The model field accepts a short alias or a full model identifier:

{ "model": "sonnet" }

Short aliases resolve to the latest version of that tier: opus, sonnet, haiku. Full identifiers pin exact versions: claude-opus-4-8, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5. For production harnesses, pin full identifiers in your project settings so that model updates do not silently change behavior. Use short aliases in global settings for interactive development where you always want the latest.

Effort levels

The effortLevel field controls the model's reasoning depth, which maps roughly to how much computation (and cost) the model spends per response:

LevelUse case
lowTriage, routing, classification — fast and cheap
mediumStandard development tasks
highComplex implementation, debugging
xhighArchitectural decisions, security review
maxMaximum available — research, critical analysis

high is the right default for an engineering harness. max is appropriate for agents doing security audit or architectural review where missing a detail is expensive. low is appropriate for agents doing repetitive mechanical work (file categorization, format conversion).

The --effort CLI flag overrides effortLevel for a single session without touching the settings file.

Fast mode

{ "fastMode": true }

Fast mode uses the same model at reduced latency — the model generates output more quickly at some cost to deliberateness. For interactive development where you are iterating rapidly, fast mode reduces friction significantly. For autonomous agents running overnight, turn it off and let the model take its time.

The /fast slash command toggles fast mode within a running session.

Extended thinking

{ "alwaysThinkingEnabled": true }

When enabled, the model generates a chain-of-thought before each response. The thinking is bounded by MAX_THINKING_TOKENS. Extended thinking increases cost and latency but materially improves correctness on multi-step reasoning tasks — exactly the problems harnesses tend to solve.

You can observe thinking summaries if showThinkingSummaries is also enabled. This is useful during development to understand why the model made a particular decision.

The compound effect

The combination used in this workspace — effortLevel: "high", fastMode: true, alwaysThinkingEnabled: true — is a deliberate tradeoff: maximum reasoning depth, with fast output streaming, bounded thinking budget. The result is an agent that thinks hard but does not take forever to start writing.

2.6 CLAUDE.md: Project Instructions

CLAUDE.md is the most powerful configuration artifact in the system. It is a markdown file loaded into the system prompt of every session that starts in that directory. Unlike settings files which control runtime behavior, CLAUDE.md controls the model's judgment — what it believes, how it approaches problems, what constraints it operates within.

Discovery and inheritance

Claude Code discovers CLAUDE.md through a hierarchical search:

  1. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — personal global instructions, always loaded
  2. CLAUDE.md in the current project root — loaded for this project
  3. CLAUDE.md in any parent directory up to the home directory — loaded in order

All discovered files are concatenated and injected into the system prompt. This means your personal preferences (from global) compound with project-specific rules (from project root).

What belongs in CLAUDE.md

CLAUDE.md is a set of standing instructions to the model. Think of it as the briefing you would give a new engineer joining the team:

  • Domain context: "This is a medical device firmware project. All code changes require FDA traceability."
  • Coding conventions: "Use type hints on all function signatures. Use f-strings over .format()."
  • Workflow rules: "Write a failing test before fixing any bug. Run ruff check --fix before committing."
  • Routing table: "When you see a bug report, hypothesize → investigate → root-cause → fix → test."

The CLAUDE.md for this workspace is long — it encodes routing logic that maps intent to workflow, coding standards for Python/TypeScript/shell, Git workflow rules, integration references, and domain-specific rules for security review, book writing, and trading automation.

The override mechanism

The project prompt says "these instructions OVERRIDE any default behavior." This is literal: CLAUDE.md content arrives late in the system prompt, after tool definitions but before the conversation history, which gives it strong positional influence over the model's decisions.

The format matters. Bullet lists, imperative mood, uppercase for emphasis (IMPORTANT: Never commit secrets), and routing tables (condition → action) are all high-signal formats. Prose paragraphs get less attention than structured directives.

claudeMdExcludes

Large codebases contain many subdirectories, and some of those directories contain their own CLAUDE.md files (documentation roots, vendored code, generated output). The claudeMdExcludes field prevents the runtime from loading instructions from irrelevant locations:

{
  "claudeMdExcludes": [
    "**/node_modules/**",
    "**/.venv/**",
    "**/dist/**",
    "**/build/**",
    "**/__pycache__/**",
    "**/.git/**"
  ]
}

Without this, the runtime will crawl into node_modules and load any CLAUDE.md files it finds there — potentially injecting package maintainer instructions into your session context. The exclude list above covers the standard generated/dependency directories for Node.js, Python, and most build systems.

Performance implication

Every character in CLAUDE.md is a token in the system prompt. The system prompt is cached by the API (5-minute TTL), so a stable CLAUDE.md amortizes its cost across turns. But a frequently-changing CLAUDE.md defeats the cache. Keep dynamic content (dates, run-specific state) out of CLAUDE.md and put it in hooks or first-user-message injection instead.

2.7 The Rules System

The rules system extends CLAUDE.md with file-scoped and domain-specific instructions organized into separate markdown files. Rather than one large CLAUDE.md that grows unbounded, you partition instructions into focused modules.

File structure

.claude/
└── rules/
    ├── python.md
    ├── security.md
    ├── testing.md
    ├── shell.md
    └── book-writing.md

Files in .claude/rules/ are imported into the session via @.claude/rules/filename.md directives in CLAUDE.md. Each file is a focused ruleset for one domain.

File-scoped activation with paths: frontmatter

Rules files support YAML frontmatter with a paths: key that restricts when the rule is injected:

---
paths:
  - "src/**/*.py"
  - "tests/**/*.py"
---

# Python Rules

Use type hints on all function signatures...

With this frontmatter, the Python rules are only injected into the system prompt when the session involves files matching those glob patterns. This is the mechanism that prevents Python style rules from polluting sessions focused on TypeScript or shell scripts.

A rules file without paths: frontmatter is always loaded — it is unconditional.

What makes a good rules file

The rules files in this workspace are terse and prescriptive. Compare the testing rules:

# Testing Rules

## Approach
- Write tests for new features and bug fixes
- For bug fixes: write a failing test FIRST, then fix the bug
- Prefer running single tests over full suite for speed during development
- Run full suite before committing

## Python Testing
- Framework: `pytest` with `pytest-asyncio` for async code
- Use fixtures for setup/teardown, not setUp/tearDown methods
- Use `tmp_path` fixture for filesystem tests
- Integration tests hit real services — never mock databases unless explicitly asked
- Name tests: `test_<what>_<condition>_<expected>`

Every line is an instruction, not an explanation. The model does not need to understand why — it needs to know what. Keep explanations minimal; save them for when a rule is counterintuitive and the model is likely to second-guess it.

Rules vs. CLAUDE.md

CLAUDE.md is the orchestration layer — routing logic, meta-instructions, project context. Rules files are the domain-specific codebooks. The split keeps CLAUDE.md readable and rules files focused. A senior engineer reading the project should be able to understand the overall workflow from CLAUDE.md in two minutes and then look up specific domain rules when needed.

2.8 Keybindings

.claude/keybindings.json maps keyboard shortcuts to named actions within the Claude Code TUI. The file is organized by context — each context is a named UI state that has its own binding namespace.

File structure

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-keybindings.json",
  "$docs": "https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/keybindings",
  "bindings": [
    {
      "context": "Global",
      "bindings": { "ctrl+t": "app:toggleTodos" }
    }
  ]
}

Contexts and their actions

The full context catalog, with all available bindings from the live configuration:

Global — always active, regardless of which panel has focus:

KeyActionEffect
ctrl+tapp:toggleTodosOpen/close the task/todo panel
ctrl+oapp:toggleTranscriptShow conversation transcript
ctrl+shift+oapp:toggleTeammatePreviewShow/hide agent team panel
ctrl+shift+fapp:globalSearchSearch across conversation
ctrl+shift+papp:quickOpenQuick command palette
ctrl+shift+bapp:toggleBriefToggle brief mode
ctrl+lapp:redrawForce TUI repaint (useful when terminal artifacts appear)

Chat — active when the chat input has focus:

KeyActionEffect
meta+pchat:modelPickerOpen model/effort selector
meta+ochat:fastModeToggle fast mode
meta+tchat:thinkingToggleToggle extended thinking
shift+tabchat:cycleModeCycle through permission modes
ctrl+x ctrl+kchat:killAgentsKill all running background agents
ctrl+gchat:externalEditorOpen current input in $EDITOR
ctrl+schat:stashStash the current input buffer
shift+upchat:messageActionsEnter message selector for history actions
ctrl+shift+-chat:undoUndo last message

KeyActionEffect

MessageSelector — active after shift+up to navigate history:

meta+up / meta+downmessageSelector:top / bottomJump to top/bottom

DiffDialog — active when reviewing a file change:

Design guidance for keybindings

Bind high-frequency operations. ctrl+x ctrl+k (kill agents) earns its chord because when you need to kill agents, you need to do it fast. ctrl+g (external editor) is valuable if you frequently write long prompts — it opens your $EDITOR, gives you full editing power, and sends on save.

Avoid overriding bindings that your terminal emulator uses. ctrl+c, ctrl+z, ctrl+d are reserved. The meta+ prefix (Option on macOS, Alt on Linux) is safer for application-level bindings that should not conflict with shell readline.

2.9 Lab: Design a Complete Settings Stack for a Multi-Team Enterprise Project

This lab walks through designing a production-grade configuration stack for a hypothetical company: three teams (backend, frontend, security), a shared platform repo, and an IT security team that enforces policy.

The scenario

  • Platform monorepo: Python backend, TypeScript frontend, infrastructure-as-code
  • Three teams each have different tool access needs
  • Security team must be able to audit all AI-assisted changes
  • IT mandates that Claude cannot read cloud credentials or private keys
  • All teams want Claude running autonomously during CI/CD pipelines

Layer design

Layer 1 — Global (~/.claude/settings.json): Each engineer sets their personal preferences. No permissions here — permissions belong to the project layer and below.

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "model": "sonnet",
  "effortLevel": "high",
  "fastMode": true,
  "alwaysThinkingEnabled": true,
  "autoMemoryEnabled": true,
  "cleanupPeriodDays": 90,
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS": "64000",
    "CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS": "500000",
    "MAX_THINKING_TOKENS": "50000",
    "ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH": "auto"
  }
}

Engineers on Opus-tier billing can set "model": "opus" and "effortLevel": "max" here without affecting teammates.

Layer 2 — Project (.claude/settings.json): Committed to git, reviewed in PRs. Establishes the baseline permission surface and shared tooling.

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git *)",
      "Bash(make *)",
      "Bash(npm run *)",
      "Bash(pytest *)",
      "Bash(ruff *)",
      "Read(*)",
      "Edit(/src/**)",
      "Edit(/tests/**)",
      "Write(/src/**)",
      "Write(/tests/**)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Read(./**/*.pem)",
      "Read(./**/*_key)",
      "Read(~/.aws/*)",
      "Read(~/.azure/*)",
      "Read(~/.ssh/*)",
      "Bash(git push *)",
      "Bash(rm -rf *)"
    ]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "./.claude/hooks/audit-log.sh",
            "timeout": 2000
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "SessionStart": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "./.claude/hooks/session-setup.sh",
            "timeout": 5000
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  "claudeMdExcludes": [
    "**/node_modules/**",
    "**/.venv/**",
    "**/dist/**",
    "**/build/**",
    "**/__pycache__/**"
  ],
  "worktree": {
    "symlinkDirectories": ["node_modules", ".venv"]
  },
  "attribution": {
    "commit": "Co-Authored-By: Claude AI <noreply@anthropic.com>",
    "pr": "Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/claude-code)"
  }
}

Key decisions in this layer:

  • Bash(git push *) is denied — Claude can stage and commit but humans push. This is a deliberate gate.
  • Edit() is scoped to /src/** and /tests/** — Claude cannot edit infrastructure or deployment configs without explicit expansion.
  • The PostToolUse hook fires an audit logger after every edit — the security team reads this log.

Layer 3 — Local (.claude/settings.local.json): Each engineer's personal expansion. The security team member might add:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Read(./.secret-scanning/**)",
      "Bash(trivy *)",
      "Bash(semgrep *)"
    ],
    "defaultMode": "auto"
  },
  "enabledMcpjsonServers": ["sec-sr-mem"]
}

The backend engineer adds:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(psql *)",
      "Bash(alembic *)"
    ],
    "defaultMode": "auto"
  }
}

The frontend engineer adds:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(vite *)",
      "Bash(vitest *)"
    ],
    "defaultMode": "auto"
  }
}

Each engineer has exactly the tools they need and no more. The shared deny list from the project layer still applies to everyone.

Layer 4 — Managed: IT delivers policy via MDM. This layer sets allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly: false (team can add to it) but adds non-negotiable additional deny rules for compliance:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Read(~/.config/gcloud/**)",
      "Bash(curl * | bash *)",
      "Bash(wget * | bash *)"
    ]
  }
}

The pipe-to-bash patterns are a common attack vector in supply chain scenarios. The managed layer ensures no one can accidentally allow them.

Layer 5 — CI flags: The CI pipeline runs Claude in print mode with explicit overrides:

claude -p \
  --output-format stream-json \
  --model claude-sonnet-4-6 \
  --permission-mode auto \
  "Review these changes for correctness and security issues"

The --permission-mode auto flag makes CI non-interactive while still respecting the project deny list.

CLAUDE.md structure for the multi-team repo

The project CLAUDE.md encodes routing logic that applies to everyone:

# Platform Monorepo

## Routing
- Bug fix → Debug workflow: hypothesize → investigate → write failing test → fix → verify
- Feature → Implement: plan if >3 files, code directly otherwise
- PR review → Security audit: OWASP/CWE scan, risk table
- Docs → Read existing style, match it exactly

## Conventions
@.claude/rules/python.md   (Python backend)
@.claude/rules/typescript.md (Frontend)
@.claude/rules/security.md  (All code)
@.claude/rules/testing.md   (All code)

## Critical constraints
IMPORTANT: Never push to main directly. All changes through PRs.
IMPORTANT: Never read or log environment variables containing SECRET, KEY, TOKEN, or PASSWORD.
IMPORTANT: All SQL changes require a migration file in /migrations/.

Rules file organization

Each rules file is self-contained and scoped:

.claude/rules/
├── python.md        (paths: src/**/*.py, tests/**/*.py)
├── typescript.md    (paths: frontend/**/*.ts, frontend/**/*.tsx)
├── security.md      (unconditional — applies everywhere)
├── testing.md       (unconditional — applies everywhere)
└── infra.md         (paths: infrastructure/**/*.tf, **/*.yaml)

The infrastructure rules file activates only when Terraform or YAML files are in context, keeping it from polluting backend coding sessions.

Verification

After designing this stack, verify it with three checks:

  1. Permission audit: Run claude -p "list the tools available to you" and confirm the tool surface matches intent.
  2. Deny list test: Run claude -p "read the contents of .env" and confirm it is blocked.
  3. Attribution check: Make a test commit and confirm the Co-Authored-By trailer appears.

If any check fails, debug with ctrl+d on the next permission prompt to see which rule is matching (or not matching) the request.

Summary

The configuration architecture of Claude Code is a layered system designed around a simple principle: each stakeholder owns exactly one layer, and the layers compose predictably. Global for personal preferences. Project for shared team baseline. Local for personal expansions on this project. Managed for non-negotiable policy. CLI flags for session-specific overrides.

The permissions system is the highest-stakes part of this architecture. A well-designed deny list is the difference between an autonomous agent that is genuinely safe to run overnight and one that is theoretically safe but silently dangerous. Design the deny list first, then open up the allow list.

CLAUDE.md and the rules system give you control over judgment that no settings field can encode. If your harness is doing the wrong thing in a way that is not a permission issue, the answer is almost always in CLAUDE.md: a missing instruction, an ambiguous directive, or a routing rule that does not cover the case you care about.

In the next chapter, we move from configuration to the tool system itself — the 52+ tools that form the action surface of every agent you build.

Next: Chapter 3 — Tool System Architecture

Chapter 3: Tool System Architecture

"A tool is not a function. It is a contract between the harness and the model — a declaration of capability, with explicit I/O semantics baked into the schema."

3.1 Tool Registration: JSON Schema to TypeScript Interfaces

Every tool Claude Code exposes to the model starts as a JSON Schema definition. That schema is the contract. It tells the model what parameters are required, what types they must be, and what constraints apply. The TypeScript interfaces in sdk-tools.d.ts are generated from those schemas, not written by hand — the file header says so explicitly:

/* This file was automatically generated by json-schema-to-typescript.
 * DO NOT MODIFY IT BY HAND. Instead, modify the source JSONSchema file,
 * and run json-schema-to-typescript to regenerate this file.
 */

This distinction matters architecturally. The JSON Schema is the runtime artifact. TypeScript is the development-time artifact. When the harness sends a tool schema to the Claude API, it sends the JSON Schema, not TypeScript. When you or I read sdk-tools.d.ts, we are reading the TypeScript projection of that JSON Schema — a more readable form of the same information.

The implication: if you are building a harness, your source of truth for tool definitions is JSON Schema, and TypeScript is a build artifact. Never write tool types by hand in TypeScript and expect them to drive the JSON Schema. The arrow goes the other way.

The Master Union Type

The root of sdk-tools.d.ts is a discriminated union of every input type the harness supports:

export type ToolInputSchemas =
  | AgentInput
  | BashInput
  | TaskOutputInput
  | ExitPlanModeInput
  | FileEditInput
  | FileReadInput
  | FileWriteInput
  | GlobInput
  | GrepInput
  | TaskStopInput
  | ListMcpResourcesInput
  | RefreshMcpToolsInput
  | McpInput
  | NotebookEditInput
  | ReadMcpResourceDirInput
  | ReadMcpResourceInput
  | ReportFindingsInput
  | TodoWriteInput
  | WebFetchInput
  | WebSearchInput
  | AskUserQuestionInput
  | SendFeedbackInput
  | ClaudeDesignInput
  | ProjectsInput
  | EnterPlanModeInput
  | TaskCreateInput
  | TaskGetInput
  | TaskUpdateInput
  | TaskListInput
  | REPLInput
  | WorkflowInput
  | CronCreateInput
  | CronDeleteInput
  | CronListInput
  | ScheduleWakeupInput
  | RemoteTriggerInput
  | ShowOnboardingRolePickerInput
  | MonitorInput
  | ProposeSkillsInput
  | ArtifactInput
  | PushNotificationInput
  | EnterWorktreeInput
  | ExitWorktreeInput
  | ToolOutputSchemas;

Count them: 42 distinct input types, plus the output union. Claude Code's tool surface has expanded to this from a much smaller initial set. The union is important for one reason beyond documentation: a harness using this SDK can exhaustively type-check tool dispatching with never branches to verify every tool is handled.

How the Schema Reaches Claude

The flow from JSON Schema to a model-callable tool:

flowchart LR
    A[JSON Schema\nsource files] -->|json-schema-to-typescript| B[sdk-tools.d.ts\nTypeScript types]
    A -->|harness reads at startup| C[Tool Registry\nin memory]
    C -->|system prompt assembly| D[Tool descriptions\nin system prompt]
    C -->|API call construction| E[tools[] array\nin Messages request]
    E -->|model calls tool| F[tool_use block\nwith input JSON]
    F -->|harness validates| G{InputValidationError?}
    G -->|valid| H[Tool executor]
    G -->|invalid| I[Error returned\nto model]

The harness validates every tool_use input against the JSON Schema before execution. If validation fails — missing required field, wrong type, value out of range — the model receives an InputValidationError in the tool_result rather than an execution attempt. This is the safety net that makes deferred tools safe: calling a deferred tool before its schema is loaded produces an InputValidationError with a clear message, not undefined behavior.

3.2 Input/Output Type Contracts

The convention is strict and enforced throughout the codebase: every tool has a corresponding *Input interface and a corresponding *Output type. No tool breaks this pattern.

The asymmetry between inputs and outputs is intentional:

  • Inputs are always interface — a single, well-known shape the model must produce.
  • Outputs are often type with union variants — the harness can return different shapes depending on what happened.

This reflects the different roles. The model is the caller; it must produce a predictable input. The harness is the callee; it returns richer, context-dependent results.

A Simple Pair: Bash

// Input: the model sends this
export interface BashInput {
  command: string;           // required
  timeout?: number;          // max 600000ms
  description?: string;      // human-readable label for permission UI
  run_in_background?: boolean;
  dangerouslyDisableSandbox?: boolean;
}

// Output: the harness returns this
export interface BashOutput {
  stdout: string;
  stderr: string;
  interrupted: boolean;
  backgroundTaskId?: string;    // set when run_in_background: true
  backgroundedByUser?: boolean; // user pressed Ctrl+B
  timedOutAfterMs?: number;     // set when command hit timeout and was auto-backgrounded
  dangerouslyDisableSandbox?: boolean;
  gitOperation?: {              // structured classification — not surfaced to model
    commit?: { sha: string; kind: "committed" | "amended" | "cherry-picked" };
    push?: { branch: string };
    pr?: { number: number; url?: string; action: string };
  };
  rawOutputPath?: string;       // large MCP tool outputs
  persistedOutputPath?: string; // output too large for inline
  persistedOutputSize?: number;
  staleReadFileStateHint?: string;
  ghRateLimitHint?: string;
}

Notice the gitOperation field: it is marked @internal in the source and is "not surfaced to the model." The harness includes it in the output type for client-side rendering — a TUI can show a git activity indicator without re-parsing stdout. The model never sees this field. This is a clean example of output fields serving multiple consumers: the model gets stdout/stderr/interrupted; the UI gets gitOperation.

A Complex Pair: FileEdit

The Edit tool output is richer than its input because the harness knows things the model does not — what the original file looked like, whether the user modified the diff before accepting, whether git saw the change:

export interface FileEditInput {
  file_path: string;  // absolute path required
  old_string: string; // exact text to replace — must be unique in file
  new_string: string; // replacement text
  replace_all?: boolean;
}

export interface FileEditOutput {
  filePath: string;
  oldString: string;
  newString: string;
  originalFile: string | null;   // full file contents before edit
  structuredPatch: {
    oldStart: number;
    oldLines: number;
    newStart: number;
    newLines: number;
    lines: string[];
  }[];
  userModified: boolean;         // user edited the proposed change
  replaceAll: boolean;
  gitDiff?: {
    filename: string;
    status: "modified" | "added";
    additions: number;
    deletions: number;
    changes: number;
    patch: string;
    repository?: string | null;  // GitHub owner/repo when available
  };
}

The structuredPatch field is the harness's unified diff in structured form — hunks with line numbers and content. The TUI uses this to render a diff view. The model can also read it if it needs to verify what was actually changed.

Empty Input Interfaces

Some tools take no input:

export interface EnterPlanModeInput {}
export interface TaskListInput {}
export interface CronListInput {}

These are not zero-parameter function calls encoded as empty objects by convention. They exist as explicit interface declarations because the JSON Schema generation pipeline requires a named schema entry for every tool, even if that schema has no properties. An empty interface is a valid JSON Schema with type: "object" and no required fields. When you implement your own harness, use the same pattern — never omit the input schema, even for parameter-less tools.

3.3 Core Tools: Always Loaded

Six tools are loaded unconditionally at startup. Their JSON Schema descriptions are baked into the system prompt before the first user turn. Any reduction in this set would break Claude Code's basic utility; any addition would increase baseline system prompt token cost.

graph TD
    subgraph "Core Tools — Always in System Prompt"
        Bash["Bash\nShell execution"]
        Read["Read (FileRead)\nText / image / PDF / notebook"]
        Edit["Edit (FileEdit)\nExact-match string replacement"]
        Write["FileWrite\nCreate or overwrite files"]
        Agent["Agent\nSpawn subagents"]
        AskUser["AskUserQuestion\nStructured user input"]
    end

Why These Six?

The selection reflects a minimal spanning set for agentic work:

  • Bash — the escape hatch. Anything not covered by a specific tool can be done via shell.
  • Read — you cannot act on what you cannot see. File reading is prerequisite to every other action.
  • Edit — targeted modification. The alternative to Edit is Write-the-whole-file, which is expensive in tokens and error-prone.
  • Write — file creation and full-file overwrites. Handles what Edit cannot.
  • Agent — parallelism and delegation. Without Agent, Claude Code is single-threaded. With it, work fans out.
  • AskUserQuestion — structured user interaction. The model needs a way to pause and collect decisions when it cannot proceed unilaterally.

Notably absent from core tools: WebFetch, WebSearch, Workflow, all scheduling tools. These are powerful but not universal. A task that never touches the web should not pay for web tool descriptions in its system prompt.

The AskUserQuestion Contract in Detail

AskUserQuestion has by far the most verbose input schema in the file. The questions parameter is typed as a discriminated tuple union of 1–4 question objects, each with a options array of 2–4 option objects — and each tuple variant is written out explicitly because JSON Schema tuple semantics do not support a compact "1 to N items" form when the items have specific structure. The generated TypeScript faithfully mirrors this verbosity.

The practical interface, collapsed to its semantics:

// Simplified mental model of AskUserQuestionInput
interface AskUserQuestionInput {
  questions: Array<{         // 1-4 questions
    question: string;        // full question text, ends with "?"
    header: string;          // max 12 chars — shown as chip/tag
    options: Array<{         // 2-4 options
      label: string;         // 1-5 words
      description: string;   // trade-off explanation
      preview?: string;      // rendered when option is focused
    }>;
    multiSelect: boolean;
  }>;
}

// Output
interface AskUserQuestionOutput {
  questions: /* same structure */[];
  answers: { [questionText: string]: string }; // comma-separated for multiSelect
  response?: string;  // freeform text if user typed instead of selecting
  annotations?: {     // per-question notes
    [questionText: string]: {
      preview?: string;
      notes?: string;
    };
  };
  afkTimeoutMs?: number; // set when dialog auto-resolved (user was away)
}

The afkTimeoutMs field reveals an important behavioral detail: in headless or background agent contexts, an unanswered question auto-resolves after a configurable idle timeout. The model can detect this and decide whether to proceed with the auto-selected answer or retry.

3.4 Deferred Tools: ToolSearch on Demand

The deferred tool system is the most consequential context-budget optimization in Claude Code's architecture. Every tool description in the system prompt consumes tokens on every API call, regardless of whether that turn uses the tool. For a session that does filesystem work and nothing else, carrying scheduling tool descriptions is pure waste.

How Deferral Works

When ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH="auto" is set (the default), tools outside the core six are not loaded into the system prompt at startup. Instead, the system prompt contains a notice:

"The following deferred tools are now available via ToolSearch. Their schemas are NOT loaded — calling them directly will fail with InputValidationError."

The model learns that deferred tools exist by name, but does not receive their schemas. When it decides it needs one — based on the task and the names in the deferred registry — it calls ToolSearch with a natural language query. The harness returns the full schema for matching tools. They are now active for the rest of the session.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Model
    participant Harness
    participant ToolRegistry

    Note over Model,ToolRegistry: Session start
    Harness->>Model: System prompt with 6 core schemas + deferred tool names

    Note over Model,ToolRegistry: Model realizes it needs scheduling
    Model->>Harness: ToolSearch("schedule recurring task")
    Harness->>ToolRegistry: Query for matching deferred tools
    ToolRegistry-->>Harness: CronCreate, CronDelete, CronList, ScheduleWakeup schemas
    Harness-->>Model: Full schemas for 4 scheduling tools
    Note over Model: Schemas now loaded — direct calls valid

    Model->>Harness: CronCreate({ cron: "*/5 * * * *", prompt: "check queue" })
    Harness->>ToolRegistry: Execute CronCreate
    ToolRegistry-->>Harness: CronCreateOutput { id, humanSchedule, recurring }
    Harness-->>Model: tool_result

What Happens When You Call a Deferred Tool Directly

The failure mode is explicit and instructive:

InputValidationError: Tool "CronCreate" schema is not loaded.
Call ToolSearch to load it before use.

This is intentional. The harness does not silently load the schema on demand when the tool is called directly — that would defeat the purpose. The model must explicitly request schemas through ToolSearch. This forces a deliberate act of tool discovery, which has the side effect of making the model's intent legible to observers watching the tool call log.

Deferred Tool Inventory

The full list of tools that defer under ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH="auto":

OrchestrationWorkflow
SchedulingCronCreate, CronDelete, CronList, ScheduleWakeup

LSPLSP

This list is not fixed in the version's config and can vary by permission mode and feature flags, but represents the operational set in Claude Code v2.1.220.

3.5 MCP Tools: Dynamic Registration

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting LLMs to external data sources and tools. Claude Code is a first-class MCP client: it connects to MCP servers at startup, discovers their tools, and registers those tools in the same harness registry that manages built-in tools. From the model's perspective, an MCP tool and a built-in tool are indistinguishable.

The Registration Flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant Claude as Claude Code (harness)
    participant Server as MCP Server

    Claude->>Server: Initialize (stdio or HTTP/SSE)
    Server-->>Claude: capabilities, serverInfo
    Claude->>Server: tools/list
    Server-->>Claude: Array<{ name, description, inputSchema }>
    Note over Claude: Register each tool as McpInput wrapper
    Note over Claude: Apply 2KB description cap
    Note over Claude: Add to system prompt if below budget

Every MCP tool is exposed to the model through a single wrapper input type:

export interface McpInput {
  [k: string]: unknown;
}

The McpInput interface is structurally open — any keys, any values. This is correct. MCP tools have arbitrary schemas defined by their server; the harness cannot predict them at compile time. Validation happens at the server boundary, not in the harness type system.

The output is similarly permissive:

export type McpOutput =
  | string
  | { type: string; [k: string]: unknown }[]
  | { [k: string]: unknown };

An MCP tool can return a plain string, a structured object, or an array of typed content blocks. The harness passes whatever the server returns directly to the model.

RefreshMcpTools: Hot-Reload

One built-in tool — RefreshMcpTools — is specifically for managing the MCP tool list at runtime:

export interface RefreshMcpToolsInput {
  server?: string; // omit to refresh all servers
}

export type RefreshMcpToolsOutput = {
  server: string;
  status: "refreshed" | "error" | "not_connected";
  toolCount?: number;
  added?: string[];   // tools the refresh added
  removed?: string[]; // tools the refresh removed
  error?: string;
}[];

If an MCP server adds or removes tools while Claude Code is running — during a deployment, for example — the model can call RefreshMcpTools to sync. The added and removed arrays tell it exactly what changed.

The 2KB Description Cap

MCP servers generated from OpenAPI specifications tend to produce tool descriptions containing the full API documentation: parameter descriptions, response examples, error codes, authentication notes. An OpenAPI-generated tool description can easily run 5KB–20KB per tool. Loading even ten such tools into the system prompt is prohibitive.

Claude Code caps MCP tool descriptions at 2KB. Descriptions that exceed this limit are truncated. The cap is applied per-tool, not globally, so a server with 20 tools can contribute at most 40KB of description text to the system prompt — still significant, but bounded.

The design implication for MCP server authors: write tool descriptions for the model, not for documentation. The model needs to know what the tool does and what its parameters mean. It does not need examples, caveats, or API version history. 2KB is generous for a clear tool description.

MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING

By default, Claude Code waits for all configured MCP servers to connect before proceeding with the session. If a server is slow to start or unavailable, this blocks startup.

Setting MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true skips this wait in non-interactive (-p print) mode. The session starts immediately; MCP tools become available as servers connect. Tools from a not-yet-connected server are simply absent until the server connects and RefreshMcpTools is called (or the harness handles reconnection automatically).

This is the right default for production pipelines where MCP reliability cannot be guaranteed. For interactive sessions where a user is watching, the blocking behavior is preferable — you do not want tool calls to fail mid-session because a server connected late.

Filesystem Tools: The Five Shapes of File I/O

The five filesystem tools are not interchangeable. Each has a distinct semantic contract:

Read (FileReadInput) handles polymorphic reading. The same interface reads text files, binary images, PDFs, and Jupyter notebooks. The output type is a discriminated union on the type field:

export type FileReadOutput =
  | { type: "text";       file: { filePath, content, numLines, startLine, totalLines, truncatedByTokenCap? } }
  | { type: "image";      file: { base64, type: MimeType, originalSize, dimensions? } }
  | { type: "notebook";   file: { filePath, cells } }
  | { type: "pdf";        file: { filePath, base64, originalSize } }
  | { type: "parts";      file: { filePath, originalSize, count, outputDir } }
  | { type: "file_unchanged"; file: { filePath }; source?: "seeded" }

The file_unchanged variant is the deduplication signal. When the harness detects that the content of a file has not changed since the last Read — or since it was seeded into the system prompt at startup — it returns this lean response instead of the full content. The source: "seeded" annotation distinguishes a dedup match against a prior Read tool call from a match against startup-seeded content (CLAUDE.md files, memory).

Edit (FileEditInput) does exact-match replacement. The old_string must exist in the file exactly once (unless replace_all: true). Uniqueness is enforced — if old_string matches multiple locations, the call fails with an error directing the model to include more surrounding context. This design prevents silent multi-site edits that the model did not intend.

Write (FileWriteInput) is unconditional. It creates the file if it does not exist, overwrites it if it does. The output tells you which case occurred via type: "create" | "update". The originalFile field contains the pre-write content when updating, which enables write idempotency checks without a separate Read.

Glob (GlobInput) does pattern-based file discovery. Output includes totalMatches (how many files matched before truncation) and countIsComplete (whether that count is exact or a lower bound). The truncated flag signals when results were cut at 100 files — a model doing a broad sweep needs to know whether it saw everything.

Grep (GrepInput) is ripgrep under the hood. The three output modes — content, files_with_matches, count — serve different patterns: reading matched lines with context, finding which files need attention, and quickly quantifying scope without reading content.

3.7 Token-Aware Design

Token cost is a first-class design concern in the tool system. Every architectural choice that seems odd on first read — deferred loading, description caps, empty input schemas, the file_unchanged response — exists to manage the context budget.

Tool Descriptions as Context Budget

A tool description is not free documentation. It appears in the system prompt, which is included in every API call. For a model processing 100 turns in a session, a 500-token tool description costs 50,000 tokens over the session lifetime. With prompt caching, the stable system prompt tokens are cached after the first call, reducing this to a one-time cost — but that cache has a 5-minute TTL, and long-running sessions will encounter cache misses.

The concrete tradeoff for a custom tool:

Short description (50 tokens):
  - System prompt cost: minimal
  - Risk: model misuses tool due to ambiguity

Detailed description (500 tokens):
  - System prompt cost: 10x higher
  - Benefit: fewer misuse errors, better parameter selection

The right answer depends on the tool. A tool used every turn (Bash, Read) can justify detailed descriptions because the description is cache-warmed and the model benefits from precision. A tool used once per session (EnterPlanMode) should be deferred so it only costs tokens in sessions that actually use it.

The Schema Size Cap: 2KB for MCP

The 2KB cap on MCP tool descriptions is enforced before the description enters the system prompt. If a tool description exceeds 2KB, it is truncated. The model receives a shortened description and must infer the rest from parameter names and types.

For custom MCP servers you control, the right approach is to write descriptions at or under 2KB from the start. The cap is not a guardrail for good descriptions — it is a safeguard against descriptions that are actually OpenAPI reference documentation copy-pasted into a tool schema.

For third-party MCP servers you do not control, the cap means you should test what the model actually receives and verify it is sufficient for correct tool use.

MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING and Startup Cost

Blocking MCP server connections at startup adds latency before the first response. For interactive use, users feel this as a pause. The MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true flag moves this cost out of the startup critical path:

Without flag:
  startup → connect all MCP servers → first response
  [user waits for slowest server]

With flag (non-interactive mode):
  startup → first response → [MCP connects in background]
  [model discovers tools as servers connect]

For automated pipelines where latency matters and MCP server availability is guaranteed, omitting MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING is correct — you want tool availability confirmed before processing the task. For long-running background agents where MCP connectivity is opportunistic, the non-blocking mode prevents a slow MCP server from stalling the entire agent.

The file_unchanged Optimization in Detail

The Read tool's deduplication mechanism deserves specific attention because it affects how you design agents that make multiple passes over a codebase.

When the model calls Read on a file it has already read in the same session (and the file has not been modified), the harness returns:

{ type: "file_unchanged", file: { filePath: "/path/to/file.ts" } }

This saves the entire file content from being re-serialized, transmitted to the API, and counted against the context window. For a 500-line file, this is the difference between ~2,000 tokens and 10 tokens.

The source: "seeded" annotation appears when the match is against content seeded at startup — CLAUDE.md files, memory files injected into the system prompt — rather than a prior Read tool call:

{ type: "file_unchanged", file: { filePath: "/project/CLAUDE.md" }, source: "seeded" }

This tells the model the file has not changed since session start. A model that needs to re-read CLAUDE.md can safely skip the Read call and rely on its system prompt copy.

3.8 Lab: Design a Custom Tool with Proper I/O Schema and Permission Integration

This lab walks through the full lifecycle of adding a custom tool to a harness: defining the JSON Schema, deriving TypeScript interfaces, implementing the executor, and integrating with the permission layer.

The Tool: DatabaseQuery

Purpose: Execute read-only SQL queries against a configured database and return structured results.

Requirements:

  • Model provides a SQL SELECT statement and optional timeout
  • Harness validates it is a read-only query (no INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, TRUNCATE)
  • Results return as structured rows, not raw text
  • Permission integration: queryable databases are configured via settings allow-list

Step 1: Define the JSON Schema

Start from the schema, not TypeScript. The schema is what the harness and the Claude API will use:

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "name": "DatabaseQuery",
  "description": "Execute a read-only SQL SELECT query against a configured database. Returns structured rows. Only SELECT statements are permitted — any mutation attempt returns an error without execution.",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "database": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Named database from the allowed list in harness settings (e.g. 'analytics', 'users-readonly')"
    },
    "query": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "A SQL SELECT statement. Must begin with SELECT. CTEs (WITH clauses) are permitted. EXPLAIN is permitted."
    },
    "timeout_ms": {
      "type": "number",
      "description": "Query timeout in milliseconds. Default 5000, max 30000.",
      "default": 5000,
      "maximum": 30000
    },
    "row_limit": {
      "type": "number",
      "description": "Maximum rows to return. Default 100, max 1000. Use lower values for large result sets.",
      "default": 100,
      "maximum": 1000
    }
  },
  "required": ["database", "query"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Design decisions encoded in the schema:

  • additionalProperties: false — the model cannot pass unknown parameters. This prevents prompt injection attempts that try to sneak extra parameters past validation.
  • database is a named string, not a connection string. The harness looks up actual connection details from its configuration. The model never sees credentials.
  • query has no length limit in the schema because SQL queries legitimately vary from one line to hundreds. Validation happens in the executor.
  • timeout_ms and row_limit have explicit maximum constraints that are enforced by the JSON Schema validator before the executor runs.

Step 2: Derive TypeScript Interfaces

From the schema above, the generated TypeScript:

export interface DatabaseQueryInput {
  database: string;
  query: string;
  timeout_ms?: number;  // default 5000, max 30000
  row_limit?: number;   // default 100, max 1000
}

export interface DatabaseQueryOutput {
  database: string;
  query: string;
  rows: Record<string, unknown>[];
  rowCount: number;
  columnNames: string[];
  truncated: boolean;         // true if row_limit was hit
  totalRows?: number;         // only set when truncated=true and db reports count
  durationMs: number;
  error?: string;             // set on query failure — rows will be empty
}
