The five filesystem tools form a hierarchy of abstraction. Glob discovers files by name. Grep filters by content. Read loads content for processing. Edit makes targeted modifications. Write creates or fully replaces files.

Understanding the contracts that TypeScript interfaces alone cannot express is what separates a harness that works from one that works reliably:

  • Read's file_unchanged dedup saves tokens but must be surfaced to the model or it causes confusion.
  • Edit's uniqueness constraint is a correctness guarantee, not a limitation — it prevents ambiguous replacements.
  • Write's read-before-write requirement is a safety check that prevents silent data loss.
  • Glob's 100-file truncation is a context budget safeguard, not a search limitation.
  • Grep defaults to head_limit: 250, which is usually right but must be adjusted for large codebases or unlimited needs.

The gitDiff integration on Edit and Write gives your harness a first-class audit trail without any additional infrastructure. Every change is self-describing.

The lab in Section 5.7 demonstrates how these five tools compose into a single coherent capability: a semantic code search that uses Glob for scoping, Grep for filtering and context extraction, and Read for deep inspection of the most relevant files. This composition pattern — narrow with Glob, filter with Grep, read selectively — is the foundation of almost every effective code navigation agent.

Chapter 6: Shell Execution — The Bash Tool

"The Bash tool is not a shell. It is a supervised subprocess with a memory for directories and amnesia for everything else."

6.1 Architecture: Persistent CWD, Non-Persistent Shell State

Before writing a single Bash call, you need to understand the one architectural fact that causes more harness bugs than any other: the Bash tool has a persistent working directory but a non-persistent shell state.

Each invocation spawns a fresh shell process. That process inherits the user's environment (via bash or zsh profile initialization), executes the command string, and exits. Variables, aliases, functions, sourced files — all of it dies with the process. The only thing that carries over between invocations is the current working directory.

Invocation 1:           Invocation 2:
  export FOO=bar          echo $FOO
  cd /tmp/workdir         pwd

Result 1: ok            Result 2:
                           (empty)       ← FOO is gone
                           /tmp/workdir  ← CWD persists

This is not a bug. It is a deliberate design constraint that makes shell execution safe and predictable across the control loop. Consider the alternative: if shell state persisted, a prior command could have set IFS, modified PATH, overwritten a critical alias, or left a trap handler installed — all of which would affect every subsequent command in ways the model cannot reason about. Starting fresh eliminates that class of problem.

What Persists

The persistent CWD is managed by the harness itself, not by the shell process. When your command ends with a cd and returns successfully, the harness records the new working directory and uses it as the starting directory for the next invocation. This means:

# Invocation 1 — navigate into a project
cd /Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/my-service && pwd

# Output: /Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/my-service

# Invocation 2 — still there
ls -la

# Output: lists files in my-service, not the original CWD

This CWD persistence is what lets a multi-turn investigation work naturally: the model navigates to a directory once, then runs a sequence of commands there without repeating the cd every time.

What Does Not Persist

StatePersists?
Working directoryYes
Shell variables (export FOO=bar)No
AliasesNo
FunctionsNo
Sourced filesNo
Background jobs (&)No — use run_in_background
set options (set -x, set -e)No
Trap handlersNo

Implications for Harness Design

If your commands depend on prior state, put the state-setup and the command in the same invocation using && chaining:

# Wrong — relies on state from previous invocation
# Invocation 1: cd /my-project && source .venv/bin/activate
# Invocation 2: python tests/run.py  ← .venv NOT active

# Correct — self-contained invocation
cd /my-project && source .venv/bin/activate && python tests/run.py

The same rule applies to environment variables your script exports. If you need DATABASE_URL available, inline it:

DATABASE_URL="postgresql://localhost/testdb" python -m pytest tests/

Shell initialization from the user's profile does run at the start of each invocation. This means tools installed via the user's shell profile (like nvm, pyenv, rvm) are available, but their state is re-initialized to the profile defaults every time. If a user's .zshrc activates a Python virtualenv, that activation happens fresh on every invocation — any modifications the prior command made to it are gone.

6.2 Parameters: command, description, timeout, run_in_background

The Bash tool's input interface is compact:

export interface BashInput {
  command: string;
  timeout?: number;           // milliseconds, max 600000 (10 min), default 120000 (2 min)
  description?: string;       // semantic label for permission UI and audit trail
  run_in_background?: boolean; // returns task_id, notification on completion
  dangerouslyDisableSandbox?: boolean; // covered in 6.4
}

command

The raw shell command string. The harness passes it directly to a shell subprocess. A few constraints worth knowing:

No interactive input. The shell subprocess has no stdin connected to the user's terminal. Commands that try to read from stdin will either hang until timeout or immediately fail with EOF, depending on the program.

Single string, not argv array. Unlike execve(), the command is shell-parsed. This means shell features work — pipes, redirects, subshell $(), brace expansion, glob patterns:

# All of these are valid
grep -rn "TODO" src/ | head -20
echo "build: $(date)" >> build.log
for f in *.py; do ruff check "$f"; done

It also means shell injection is a real concern if you are interpolating untrusted input into the command string. The harness does not sanitize command content. If your harness constructs commands from external data, you are responsible for escaping. Covered in section 6.4 and the lab.

Compound commands. Use && for conditional chaining (stop on failure), || for fallback, ; for unconditional sequencing:

# Run tests only if build succeeds
npm run build && npm test

# Fallback: try pip3, then pip
pip3 install -r requirements.txt || pip install -r requirements.txt

# Always run cleanup regardless of test result
make test ; make clean

As of v2.1.89, the hooks if condition filter correctly matches compound commands (ls && git push) and env-var prefixes (FOO=bar git push). Prior versions had a bug where these patterns evaded hook matching.

timeout

Timeout is specified in milliseconds. The defaults matter:

ValueScenario
120000 (2 min)Default — suitable for most build/test/lint commands
600000 (10 min)Maximum — long-running builds, Docker image pulls, large file operations
CustomSet explicitly for predictable operations

When a command exceeds its timeout, the process is killed and the tool returns an error. The harness does not wait for cleanup — the subprocess tree is terminated. If your command spawns child processes, they may not receive SIGTERM; they will be killed with SIGKILL.

Practical timeout guidance:

# Fast commands — no need to set timeout, default is fine
git status
ls -la
cat package.json

# Medium operations — default is fine but be aware
npm run build        # 30-120s is typical
pytest tests/unit/   # depends on suite size

# Long operations — set explicit timeout
# docker build . → can take 5-8 min
# Set to 540000ms (9 min) to give headroom under the 10-min max

If you are designing a harness that wraps Bash calls, expose the timeout as a parameter. Hardcoding 120s will break legitimately long operations. The ceiling of 600000ms is a hard limit in the implementation — no value above it is accepted.

description

The description field is covered in depth in section 6.7. For now: always provide it. It is the semantic label that explains what the command does in human terms:

// Minimal — permission UI shows a raw command string
{ command: "find /etc -name '*.conf' | xargs grep -l 'password'" }

// Better — permission UI shows intent before the raw command
{
  command: "find /etc -name '*.conf' | xargs grep -l 'password'",
  description: "Search system config files for password references"
}

run_in_background

Setting run_in_background: true changes the tool's behavior entirely. Instead of waiting for the command to finish and returning its output, the harness launches the command as a background task and immediately returns a task_id. The command continues running independently of the control loop.

This is how you run long-running processes, watch daemons, or kick off parallel work:

// Foreground (default): blocks until complete
{
  command: "npm test",
  timeout: 120000
}
// Returns after tests finish, with full output

// Background: returns immediately
{
  command: "python -m http.server 8080",
  run_in_background: true,
  description: "Start local HTTP server on port 8080"
}
// Returns: { task_id: "task_abc123" }

Background execution is detailed in section 6.3. One thing to know upfront: never use & in the command string to background a process. The & sends the process to the background within the subprocess shell, but that shell exits when the command string finishes, which terminates the backgrounded process along with it. Use run_in_background: true instead.

6.3 Background Execution: task_id, TaskOutput, TaskStop

Background execution is the pattern for any command that should not block the control loop. The use cases are broad: starting a development server, running a long test suite in parallel with other work, launching a file watcher, or initiating a database migration that takes several minutes.

The Background Lifecycle

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Model
    participant H as Harness
    participant P as Background Process

    M->>H: Bash({ command: "...", run_in_background: true })
    H->>P: spawn subprocess
    H-->>M: { task_id: "task_abc123" }
    Note over M,H: Control loop continues
    M->>H: Other tool calls execute here
    P-->>H: Process exits (success or failure)
    H-->>M: Notification: task_abc123 completed
    M->>H: TaskOutput({ task_id: "task_abc123" })
    H-->>M: { stdout: "...", stderr: "...", exit_code: 0 }

After the initial Bash call, the model receives a task ID and continues the control loop. When the background process finishes, the harness sends a notification to the model (as a tool result or system message). The model can then call TaskOutput to retrieve what the process produced.

Polling vs Notification

In a harness you build yourself, you decide how background completion is surfaced. Claude Code uses a notification-on-completion model: the harness injects the notification at the next available point in the conversation. This works well in interactive sessions where the model is doing other work while waiting.

In headless or pipeline contexts, you may want explicit polling:

// Start a background process
const startResult = await bash({
  command: "python scripts/heavy_migration.py",
  run_in_background: true,
  description: "Run database migration"
});
const taskId = startResult.task_id;

// Poll for completion (15-30s intervals — avoid long sleeps)
let done = false;
while (!done) {
  await sleep(20000); // 20 seconds
  const output = await taskOutput({ task_id: taskId });
  if (output.exit_code !== null) {
    done = true;
    // Process output.stdout / output.stderr
  }
}

TaskOutput and TaskStop

Two deferred tools manage background task lifecycle:

TaskOutput retrieves the accumulated output of a background task. It returns stdout, stderr, and exit code when available. Calling it before the process finishes returns whatever has been buffered so far — useful for streaming progress from long-running operations.

TaskStop cancels a running background task. It sends SIGTERM to the process, then SIGKILL after a grace period. Use this to:

  • Stop a dev server you started for testing
  • Abort a long-running migration that has hit an error condition
  • Clean up persistent watchers at end of session
// Stop the server we started earlier
await taskStop({ task_id: "task_abc123" });

Background tasks that are not explicitly stopped are terminated when the harness session ends. Do not rely on background processes surviving session termination — they will not.

Practical Patterns

Pattern 1: Start server, run tests against it, stop server

# Step 1: Start server in background
Bash({
  command: "cd /my-app && node server.js",
  run_in_background: true,
  description: "Start app server for integration tests"
})
// task_id: "task_server"

# Step 2: Wait for server to be ready
Bash({
  command: "timeout 30 bash -c 'until curl -s http://localhost:3000/health; do sleep 1; done'",
  description: "Wait for server health check"
})

# Step 3: Run tests
Bash({
  command: "cd /my-app && npm run test:integration",
  timeout: 300000,
  description: "Run integration test suite against live server"
})

# Step 4: Stop server
TaskStop({ task_id: "task_server" })

Pattern 2: Parallel long-running operations

# Start three independent long operations concurrently
Bash({ command: "make build-service-a", run_in_background: true, description: "Build service A" })
// task_id: "task_a"

Bash({ command: "make build-service-b", run_in_background: true, description: "Build service B" })
// task_id: "task_b"

Bash({ command: "make build-service-c", run_in_background: true, description: "Build service C" })
// task_id: "task_c"

# Collect all results
TaskOutput({ task_id: "task_a" })
TaskOutput({ task_id: "task_b" })
TaskOutput({ task_id: "task_c" })

Wall-clock time for three 2-minute builds: 2 minutes, not 6.

6.4 Sandbox Integration: What Gets Blocked

The Bash tool executes inside a sandbox. The sandbox's depth depends on your platform and configuration.

Sandbox Layers

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Bash Tool Input                        │
│              command: "curl http://evil.com"             │
└────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                         │
┌────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Permission Layer                         │
│  excludedCommands: ["curl", "wget", "nc", ...]           │
│  Rule match: Bash(curl *) → deny                         │
└────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                         │ allowed
┌────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Sandbox (Linux only)                    │
│  seccomp: blocks dangerous syscalls                      │
│  apply-seccomp helper: applies per-process filter        │
│  Network: domain allowlists, proxy port enforcement      │
│  Unix socket: blocked by default                         │
└────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                         │ passes sandbox
┌────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Shell Subprocess                         │
│              command executes here                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

On Linux, the harness uses seccomp syscall filtering via an apply-seccomp helper. This provides kernel-level enforcement: system calls not on the allowlist fail with EPERM regardless of what the command tries to do. Network traffic is routed through domain allowlists; attempts to reach unlisted domains are blocked at the proxy level. Unix socket connections are blocked by default.

On macOS/Windows, the sandbox is primarily the permission layer. Seccomp is Linux-specific. This means the macOS sandbox relies more heavily on the excludedCommands list and permission rules for protection.

Network Sandbox

Network access from Bash commands is controlled by:

  • allowedDomains: list of domains the subprocess may reach (e.g., ["api.github.com", "registry.npmjs.org"])
  • httpProxyPort / socksProxyPort: route network through a proxy that enforces the domain list
  • allowLocalBinding: whether the subprocess can bind to local ports (important for starting servers)

If your workflow requires network access from Bash commands — package installation, API calls, git operations — those domains must be in the allowlist. Blocking registry.npmjs.org will break npm install.

excludedCommands

The excludedCommands array in settings lists shell command names that bypass the sandbox. This is the escape hatch for tools that the sandbox would otherwise block (some security tools, packet capture utilities). Use it sparingly: each entry is a command that runs without sandbox protection.

{
  "excludedCommands": ["wireshark", "tcpdump"]
}

Note that excludedCommands names commands the sandbox exempts — it does not block them. The naming is counterintuitive: these commands are "excluded from sandbox restrictions," not "excluded from execution."

dangerouslyDisableSandbox

Setting dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true on a Bash input removes all sandbox protections for that invocation. Every syscall, every network connection, every socket — unrestricted.

{
  command: "strace -p $(pgrep my-service)",
  dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true,
  description: "Attach strace to running service for debugging"
}

The name is a deliberate red flag. Use it only when:

  1. The command is known and trusted
  2. The sandbox would block a legitimate low-level operation (strace, packet capture, raw socket operations)
  3. The command is not constructed from user-supplied input

Never use dangerouslyDisableSandbox in a harness that processes commands built from external or untrusted data.

autoAllowBashIfSandboxed

When the sandbox is enabled, autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in settings causes all Bash calls to be auto-approved without permission prompts. The assumption is that if the sandbox is active, system-level enforcement compensates for the lack of per-call approval. This is a convenience setting for automated environments where interactive permission prompts would block execution — but it means the permission layer no longer provides a check on Bash. Understand the trade-off before enabling it.

allowUnsandboxedCommands

Setting allowUnsandboxedCommands: false blocks any command that would run outside the sandbox. Use this in high-security environments where you want to guarantee that no command runs without sandboxing. If a command requires dangerouslyDisableSandbox and this flag is false, it will be blocked.

The v2.1.84 PowerShell Fix

Prior to v2.1.84, PowerShell commands with a trailing & could bypass background job handling and escape certain restrictions. This was fixed. If you are running a harness on Windows with the opt-in PowerShell tool (available since v2.1.84), ensure you are on a version at or above this fix.

6.5 Output Structure: BashOutput

Bash output is straightforward:

export interface BashOutput {
  // stdout and stderr combined in a single stream
}

The implementation combines stdout and stderr into a single interleaved stream, preserving the order in which output appeared. This matches what you see when running a command in a terminal. There is no way to separate stdout from stderr after the fact — if your workflow needs to distinguish them, pipe stderr to stdout explicitly (cmd 2>&1) or redirect stderr to a file:

# Capture stderr separately
my-command > /tmp/stdout.txt 2> /tmp/stderr.txt
cat /tmp/stdout.txt
# stderr is in /tmp/stderr.txt for separate inspection

Output Truncation

Long output is not automatically truncated by the Bash tool at the harness level, but it does consume context window. A command that dumps 100,000 lines of log will push that content into the conversation, consuming tokens that could be used for other context. Defensive patterns:

# Limit output explicitly
grep -rn "error" /var/log/ | head -50

# Summarize in the command
wc -l src/**/*.py

# Write to file, read selectively
make build > /tmp/build.log 2>&1
tail -20 /tmp/build.log

Exit Codes

The Bash tool does not expose the exit code as a separate field — it is embedded in the output when the command fails. A non-zero exit is indicated in the tool result as an error state. The harness does not automatically retry failed commands; Claude receives the failure output and decides whether to retry, adjust the command, or escalate.

6.6 Interactive Command Limitations

The Bash tool has no interactive TTY. This is a hard architectural constraint with specific consequences.

What Does Not Work

Interactive rebase:

git rebase -i HEAD~3  # BLOCKED — requires editor/terminal interaction

Interactive add:

git add -i           # BLOCKED — requires interactive menu
git add -p           # BLOCKED — requires hunk-by-hunk input

Text editors:

vim src/main.py      # BLOCKED — opens in TTY that doesn't exist
nano config.txt      # BLOCKED
emacs file.py        # BLOCKED

Interactive programs:

python -i            # BLOCKED — interactive interpreter
irb                  # BLOCKED — interactive Ruby
psql -U postgres     # BLOCKED unless piping commands
ftp, sftp            # BLOCKED in interactive mode

Password prompts:

sudo apt install pkg  # BLOCKED if sudo requires password
ssh user@host        # BLOCKED if requires password (use SSH keys)

What to Do Instead

For git operations that would normally be interactive, the Bash tool supports their non-interactive equivalents:

Interactive (blocked)Non-interactive equivalent
git rebase -i HEAD~3git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~ HEAD or scripted rebase
git add -pgit add -A or git add <specific-files>
vim fileUse the Edit or Write tools
psql interactivepsql -c "SELECT ..." db_name
python -iUse the REPL tool (in-process JS) or write a script

For sudo operations, configure sudo to not require a password for specific commands, or handle privilege via other means (Docker, capability sets).

Never use -i flags with commands that expect terminal interaction. The git rebase -i and git add -i patterns will hang until the timeout fires, then fail. The model should recognize these blocked patterns and substitute non-interactive equivalents automatically — but harness engineers should not construct commands with interactive flags and expect them to work.

Background Processes and the & Operator

This deserves repetition because the failure mode is silent:

# This does NOT work as intended
node server.js &   # Starts node, shell forks it to background
                   # Shell exits immediately after `&`
                   # node process is orphaned and killed

# This WORKS
Bash({
  command: "node server.js",
  run_in_background: true,
  description: "Start Node server"
})
// Returns task_id for the running process

The & operator forks the process within the subprocess shell. When the shell exits (immediately, since the command string is done), the OS sends SIGHUP to the process group, which terminates the backgrounded process. The harness has no handle on a process backgrounded with &. Use run_in_background: true.

6.7 The description Field: Permission UX, Audit Trail, User Comprehension

The description field is optional in the type signature but mandatory in practice. It is the most under-leveraged parameter in the Bash tool, and the gap between engineers who use it well and those who skip it is visible in both security posture and operational quality.

Permission Dialog UX

When a Bash call requires user confirmation, the permission dialog shows the description prominently. The user sees the description before they see the command. A good description communicates intent so clearly that the user can approve or deny without reading the full command:

Permission requested:
  [Bash] Delete compiled artifacts older than 7 days
         find build/ -name "*.o" -mtime +7 -delete

   [Allow]  [Deny]  [View command]

Compare to the no-description case:

Permission requested:
  [Bash] find build/ -name "*.o" -mtime +7 -delete

   [Allow]  [Deny]

The second dialog requires the user to parse shell syntax to understand intent. For a security-conscious user, that is friction that pushes toward denial.

Auto-Approval Rates

The harness's auto-mode classifier uses the description — along with the command and permission rules — to decide whether to auto-approve, auto-deny, or prompt. Commands with clear, accurate descriptions that match known-safe patterns get higher auto-approval rates. The classifier treats a missing or vague description as a signal to prompt rather than auto-approve.

This has a practical implication: writing good descriptions reduces friction. A workflow that would require ten manual approvals without descriptions might run entirely hands-free with them.

Audit Trail

Every Bash call — description, command, result, timestamp — is recorded in the session transcript. In enterprise deployments, this transcript feeds audit logging. The description is what makes that log useful:

# Hard to audit
[2026-07-28T14:23:11Z] Bash: "find / -name id_rsa 2>/dev/null"
[2026-07-28T14:23:14Z] Bash: "cat /home/ubuntu/.ssh/id_rsa"

# With descriptions — clear intent, clear investigation
[2026-07-28T14:23:11Z] Bash(desc="Locate SSH private key files for security audit"): ...
[2026-07-28T14:23:14Z] Bash(desc="Read found SSH key — SECURITY AUDIT ONLY"): ...

The second version is defensible in an audit review. The first is not.

Description Writing Guidelines

State what changes, not what runs:

Bad:  "Run ruff"
Good: "Lint and auto-fix Python files in src/"

Name the target:

Bad:  "Delete files"
Good: "Delete .pyc compiled bytecode files from project root"

Include scope when destructive:

Bad:  "Remove old branches"
Good: "Delete merged git branches older than 30 days (non-main only)"

Use consistent verbs: List, Create, Delete, Update, Start, Stop, Run, Check, Search, Build, Deploy. Consistency makes audit logs scannable.

Do not describe the tool: "Execute bash command to..." is redundant — everything in the Bash tool is a bash command. Describe what the command accomplishes.

v2.1.89 Stale-Edit Warning

As of v2.1.89, the Bash tool emits a warning when a formatter or linter modifies a file that the model previously read in the same session. This prevents a class of bug where:

  1. Model reads src/auth/session.py
  2. Model generates an Edit for session.py based on its read
  3. A Bash call (e.g., ruff format src/) runs between the read and the edit
  4. The formatter changes the file
  5. The model's Edit uses the pre-format version of the file, causing a conflict or overwriting the formatter's changes

The warning surfaces in the Bash output as an advisory message listing the files that were modified. The model can then re-read those files before attempting edits. This is not automatic recovery — it is a prompt for the model to handle the state change. Harness engineers should be aware of this: if your workflow runs formatters, trigger them before the read phase, not between reads and edits.

6.8 Lab: Safe Command Executor with Allowlist, Audit Logging, and Timeout Management

This lab implements a hardened wrapper around the Bash tool concept — a SafeCommandExecutor class in TypeScript that you could drop into your own harness. It enforces an explicit command allowlist, logs every execution to an audit trail, and manages timeouts with configurable per-command overrides.

Design Goals

  1. Allowlist enforcement — no command executes unless its root verb is on the approved list
  2. Audit logging — every call is timestamped, attributed, and logged to a structured JSONL file
  3. Timeout management — per-command timeout overrides with a safe global ceiling
  4. Injection prevention — flag suspicious patterns before execution
  5. Clean result type — always returns { stdout, success, durationMs } regardless of how the subprocess exits

Types and Interfaces

// executor.ts
interface CommandPolicy {
  /** The command name (first token, e.g., "git", "npm", "pytest") */
  command: string;
  /** Allowed argument patterns (glob-style, optional) */
  argsPattern?: RegExp;
  /** Per-command timeout override in milliseconds */
  timeout?: number;
  /** Human-readable description of why this command is allowed */
  rationale: string;
}

interface ExecutionRequest {
  command: string;
  description: string;
  /** Caller-requested timeout — will be clamped to policy ceiling */
  timeoutMs?: number;
  /** True to run without blocking */
  background?: boolean;
}

interface ExecutionResult {
  success: boolean;
  output: string;
  durationMs: number;
  taskId?: string; // set when background: true
}

interface AuditRecord {
  timestamp: string;          // ISO 8601
  command: string;
  description: string;
  policyMatch: string | null; // which allowlist entry matched, or null if denied
  outcome: "allowed" | "denied" | "error";
  durationMs: number;
  exitCode?: number;
}

The Allowlist

// allowlist.ts
import type { CommandPolicy } from "./executor.js";

export const DEFAULT_ALLOWLIST: CommandPolicy[] = [
  {
    command: "git",
    argsPattern: /^(status|log|diff|branch|fetch|pull|push|add|commit|checkout|stash|tag|show|blame|grep|clone|remote|rebase|merge|cherry-pick|reset|revert|describe|shortlog)\b/,
    timeout: 60000,
    rationale: "Standard git workflow operations"
  },
  {
    command: "npm",
    argsPattern: /^(install|ci|run|test|build|lint|audit|outdated|list)\b/,
    timeout: 300000,  // 5 min for installs
    rationale: "Node.js package management and script execution"
  },
  {
    command: "python",
    argsPattern: /^(-m\s+(pytest|ruff|mypy|black|isort|coverage)|tests\/|scripts\/)/,
    timeout: 300000,
    rationale: "Python test and tooling invocations"
  },
  {
    command: "pytest",
    timeout: 300000,
    rationale: "Direct pytest invocation"
  },
  {
    command: "ruff",
    argsPattern: /^(check|format)\b/,
    timeout: 60000,
    rationale: "Python linter and formatter"
  },
  {
    command: "grep",
    timeout: 30000,
    rationale: "Text search in files"
  },
  {
    command: "find",
    argsPattern: /^[./]/,  // must start with a path, not /etc or /usr
    timeout: 30000,
    rationale: "File discovery within project directories"
  },
  {
    command: "cat",
    timeout: 10000,
    rationale: "File content display"
  },
  {
    command: "ls",
    timeout: 5000,
    rationale: "Directory listing"
  },
  {
    command: "wc",
    timeout: 10000,
    rationale: "Word/line count"
  },
  {
    command: "tail",
    timeout: 10000,
    rationale: "Log tail operations"
  },
  {
    command: "head",
    timeout: 10000,
    rationale: "File head operations"
  }
];

The Executor

// executor.ts
import { appendFileSync } from "fs";
import { join } from "path";
import type { CommandPolicy, ExecutionRequest, ExecutionResult, AuditRecord } from "./types.js";

const MAX_TIMEOUT_MS = 600000; // 10 minutes — hard ceiling from BashInput spec
const AUDIT_LOG_PATH = join(process.env.HOME ?? "/tmp", ".claude", "bash-audit.jsonl");

// Patterns that indicate potential injection attempts
const INJECTION_PATTERNS: RegExp[] = [
  /;\s*(rm|dd|mkfs|chmod\s+777|curl.*\|.*sh|wget.*\|.*sh)/,
  /\$\(.*rm\s+-rf/,
  />\s*\/etc\//,
  />\s*\/usr\//,
  /`[^`]*rm[^`]*`/,
];

export class SafeCommandExecutor {
  private allowlist: CommandPolicy[];
  private auditPath: string;

  constructor(allowlist: CommandPolicy[], auditPath: string = AUDIT_LOG_PATH) {
    this.allowlist = allowlist;
    this.auditPath = auditPath;
  }

  private extractRootVerb(command: string): string {
    // Handle env-var prefixes: FOO=bar git status → git
    const withoutEnvVars = command.replace(/^(\w+=\S+\s+)+/, "").trim();
    // Handle cd && cmd: cd /tmp && git status → git
    const afterCd = withoutEnvVars.replace(/^cd\s+\S+\s*&&\s*/, "").trim();
    return afterCd.split(/\s+/)[0] ?? "";
  }

  private extractArgs(command: string): string {
    const verb = this.extractRootVerb(command);
    const idx = command.indexOf(verb);
    return command.slice(idx + verb.length).trim();
  }

  private findPolicy(command: string): CommandPolicy | null {
    const verb = this.extractRootVerb(command);
    const args = this.extractArgs(command);

    for (const policy of this.allowlist) {
      if (policy.command !== verb) continue;
      if (policy.argsPattern && !policy.argsPattern.test(args)) continue;
      return policy;
    }
    return null;
  }

  private checkInjection(command: string): string | null {
    for (const pattern of INJECTION_PATTERNS) {
      if (pattern.test(command)) {
        return `Injection pattern detected: ${pattern.source}`;
      }
    }
    return null;
  }

  private resolveTimeout(request: ExecutionRequest, policy: CommandPolicy): number {
    const requested = request.timeoutMs ?? policy.timeout ?? 120000;
    // Clamp to [1000, MAX_TIMEOUT_MS]
    return Math.min(Math.max(requested, 1000), MAX_TIMEOUT_MS);
  }

  private writeAudit(record: AuditRecord): void {
    try {
      appendFileSync(this.auditPath, JSON.stringify(record) + "\n", "utf-8");
    } catch {
      // Audit write failure must not block execution
      process.stderr.write(`[audit-warn] Failed to write audit record: ${record.command}\n`);
    }
  }

  async execute(request: ExecutionRequest): Promise<ExecutionResult> {
    const startMs = Date.now();
    const { command, description } = request;

    // 1. Injection check
    const injectionReason = this.checkInjection(command);
    if (injectionReason !== null) {
      const durationMs = Date.now() - startMs;
      this.writeAudit({
        timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
        command,
        description,
        policyMatch: null,
        outcome: "denied",
        durationMs,
      });
      return {
        success: false,
        output: `[SafeCommandExecutor] Denied: ${injectionReason}`,
        durationMs,
      };
    }

    // 2. Allowlist check
    const policy = this.findPolicy(command);
    if (policy === null) {
      const verb = this.extractRootVerb(command);
      const durationMs = Date.now() - startMs;
      this.writeAudit({
        timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
        command,
        description,
        policyMatch: null,
        outcome: "denied",
        durationMs,
      });
      return {
        success: false,
        output: `[SafeCommandExecutor] Denied: "${verb}" is not on the allowed command list`,
        durationMs,
      };
    }

    // 3. Resolve timeout
    const timeoutMs = this.resolveTimeout(request, policy);

    // 4. Build the BashInput — this is what you pass to the Bash tool in your harness
    const bashInput = {
      command,
      description,
      timeout: timeoutMs,
      run_in_background: request.background ?? false,
    };

    // 5. Log intent before execution
    const intentRecord: AuditRecord = {
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      command,
      description,
      policyMatch: policy.rationale,
      outcome: "allowed",
      durationMs: 0, // will update after
    };

    // 6. Execute via your harness Bash tool (abstracted here as callBashTool)
    let result: ExecutionResult;
    try {
      const rawOutput = await callBashTool(bashInput);
      const durationMs = Date.now() - startMs;
      result = {
        success: true,
        output: rawOutput,
        durationMs,
        taskId: request.background ? extractTaskId(rawOutput) : undefined,
      };
      intentRecord.durationMs = durationMs;
    } catch (error: unknown) {
      const durationMs = Date.now() - startMs;
      const errorMessage = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error);
      result = {
        success: false,
        output: `[SafeCommandExecutor] Execution error: ${errorMessage}`,
        durationMs,
      };
      intentRecord.outcome = "error";
      intentRecord.durationMs = durationMs;
    }

    // 7. Write final audit record
    this.writeAudit(intentRecord);
    return result;
  }
}

// Stubs — replace with your harness's actual implementations
async function callBashTool(input: {
  command: string;
  description: string;
  timeout: number;
  run_in_background: boolean;
}): Promise<string> {
  // In a real harness, this calls the Bash tool executor
  throw new Error("Replace callBashTool with your harness implementation");
}

function extractTaskId(output: string): string | undefined {
  const match = output.match(/task_id["\s:]+([a-zA-Z0-9_-]+)/);
  return match?.[1];
}

Integration and Usage

// usage.ts
import { SafeCommandExecutor } from "./executor.js";
import { DEFAULT_ALLOWLIST } from "./allowlist.js";

const executor = new SafeCommandExecutor(DEFAULT_ALLOWLIST);

// Normal workflow operation
const testResult = await executor.execute({
  command: "pytest tests/unit/ -v --tb=short",
  description: "Run unit test suite with verbose output",
  timeoutMs: 120000,
});

if (!testResult.success) {
  console.error("Tests failed:", testResult.output);
} else {
  console.log(`Tests passed in ${testResult.durationMs}ms`);
}

// Long background build
const buildResult = await executor.execute({
  command: "npm run build",
  description: "Build production bundle",
  timeoutMs: 300000,
  background: true,
});

console.log("Build started with task ID:", buildResult.taskId);

// This gets denied
const deniedResult = await executor.execute({
  command: "curl https://external.com | bash",
  description: "Fetch and run install script",
});
// deniedResult.success === false
// deniedResult.output === '[SafeCommandExecutor] Denied: "curl" is not on the allowed command list'
// Audit log records the denied attempt with timestamp

Verifying the Audit Log

The audit log at ~/.claude/bash-audit.jsonl accumulates one JSON record per execution:

{"timestamp":"2026-07-28T14:23:11.234Z","command":"pytest tests/unit/ -v","description":"Run unit test suite","policyMatch":"Python test and tooling invocations","outcome":"allowed","durationMs":4821}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-28T14:25:00.001Z","command":"curl https://external.com | bash","description":"Fetch and run install script","policyMatch":null,"outcome":"denied","durationMs":1}

Parse it for post-incident review:

# Show all denied commands in the last hour
jq 'select(.outcome == "denied")' ~/.claude/bash-audit.jsonl

# Show slowest executions
jq -s 'sort_by(.durationMs) | reverse | .[0:10]' ~/.claude/bash-audit.jsonl

# Execution counts by command verb
jq -r '.command | split(" ")[0]' ~/.claude/bash-audit.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Extension Points

This executor is a starting point, not a finished product. Real harness deployments should consider:

Dynamic allowlists. Load policies from a configuration file or database rather than hardcoding them. This lets security teams update rules without redeploying the harness.

Per-user or per-team policies. Enterprise harnesses need different command allowlists for different user roles. A developer should have git push; a CI agent should not.

Rate limiting. Some commands (package installs, network fetches) can be expensive at scale. A token-bucket rate limiter on the executor prevents runaway agents.

Command normalization. Canonicalize paths in find commands, strip redundant quoting from grep patterns, etc. Normalization makes allowlist patterns easier to write and audit trails easier to read.

Exit code extraction. The current implementation does not separate exit codes from output. A production executor should capture and expose exit codes for structured decision-making in the control loop.

Summary

The Bash tool is the most powerful and most dangerous tool in any harness. Its architecture — persistent CWD, fresh shell state per invocation — is intentional: it makes the execution surface predictable across turns while preserving stateless safety guarantees.

The parameter surface is small: command, description, timeout, run_in_background, and dangerouslyDisableSandbox. The description field is the one engineers underestimate most. Used correctly, it reduces permission friction, feeds audit logs, and makes workflows defensible in review. Used poorly, it is noise in the log and friction in the UI.

Background execution via run_in_background: true — never & — unlocks parallel long-running operations. TaskOutput and TaskStop manage their lifecycle. The sandbox provides defense in depth on Linux; on other platforms the permission layer carries more weight.

Interactive commands (git rebase -i, editors, password prompts) do not work and cannot be made to work — the TTY is not there. Substitute non-interactive equivalents. Never construct commands from untrusted input without validation; the harness does not sanitize command strings.

The lab implements a production-grade executor that enforces all of these principles with allowlist checking, injection detection, per-command timeout management, and structured audit logging. Drop it into any harness as the foundation for safe, auditable shell execution.

Chapter 7: Web Tools — WebFetch and WebSearch

"The model cannot browse the web. Your harness can. There is a meaningful difference."

7.1 WebFetch: The Fetch-Parse-Extract Pipeline

When Claude needs to read a URL, it does not receive raw HTML. The harness runs a three-stage pipeline before a single byte reaches the model:

URL input
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Stage 1: Fetch                     │
│  HTTP GET → follow redirects        │
│  auto-upgrade HTTP → HTTPS          │
│  15-minute cache check              │
└────────────────────┬────────────────┘
                     │ raw HTML / bytes
                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Stage 2: Convert                   │
│  HTML → Markdown                    │
│  strip nav, ads, boilerplate        │
│  preserve code blocks, tables       │
└────────────────────┬────────────────┘
                     │ markdown text
                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Stage 3: Extract                   │
│  small fast model runs your prompt  │
│  against the markdown content       │
│  returns extracted result string    │
└────────────────────┬────────────────┘
                     │ result
                     ▼
            WebFetchOutput.result

The key insight: you provide the extraction instructions. The prompt field is not decoration — it is what the internal model uses to decide what to return from the page. A vague prompt produces a vague result. A precise prompt produces a precise result.

The Interface

export interface WebFetchInput {
  url: string;     // fully-formed valid URL, HTTP auto-upgraded to HTTPS
  prompt: string;  // what to extract from the page content
}

export interface WebFetchOutput {
  bytes: number;        // size of fetched content
  code: number;         // HTTP response code
  codeText: string;     // HTTP response text
  result: string;       // processed result from applying prompt to content
  durationMs: number;
  url: string;          // the URL that was fetched
  artifactRead?: { slug: string; ver?: string };
}

The result field is what you act on. The rest — bytes, code, codeText, durationMs — are diagnostic metadata. The artifactRead field appears when the URL points to a hosted Claude artifact; the harness can read its own published artifacts as first-class resources.

Writing Effective Prompts

The extraction prompt is the leverage point. Compare these two calls to the same URL:

// Weak: vague extraction, produces a summary of the whole page
{
  url: "https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html",
  prompt: "tell me about pathlib"
}

// Strong: targeted extraction, produces a usable reference
{
  url: "https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html",
  prompt: "extract all method signatures from the Path class with their parameters and return types, formatted as a markdown table"
}

The strong prompt gives the internal extraction model a concrete, verifiable task. The result will be a table you can directly use.

Practical prompt patterns that work well:

Use CasePrompt Pattern
API documentation"List all endpoints with HTTP method, path, and required parameters"
Release notes"Extract all breaking changes and new features from this changelog page"
Comparison"Extract the feature comparison table between products A and B"
Error troubleshooting"Find the solution or workaround for this error: [paste error]"
Code examples"Extract all code examples related to authentication, preserving the code blocks"

What Comes Back

The result is a string — it can be a paragraph, a list, a table, or even a code block, depending on what you asked for and what the page contained. If the page content is very large, the extraction model may summarize. This is by design: the goal is to return what is relevant to your prompt, not a faithful copy of the page.

The bytes field tells you the size of the fetched content before conversion. A value of 500KB for a documentation page is normal. If bytes is unexpectedly small (under 1KB), the page likely blocked the request or returned a minimal error page — check code and codeText.

7.2 WebSearch: Query to Ranked Results

WebSearch takes a natural-language query and returns a list of search results with titles and URLs. It does not fetch the pages. The workflow for research is: search first, fetch selectively.

The Interface

export interface WebSearchInput {
  query: string;                    // min 2 chars
  allowed_domains?: string[];       // only include results from these
  blocked_domains?: string[];       // never include results from these
}

export interface WebSearchOutput {
  query: string;
  results: (
    | { tool_use_id: string; content: { title: string; url: string }[] }
    | string
  )[];
  durationSeconds: number;
  searchCount?: number;
}

The results field is a union type. In normal operation you get the object variant: a tool_use_id (the internal identifier for this search call) and content — an array of { title, url } pairs. The string variant appears when the search engine returns an unstructured result or when the search fails partway; you should check for and handle this defensively.

The searchCount field, when present, tells you how many underlying search requests were made. For most queries this is 1. Complex queries or domain-filtered searches may trigger multiple.

durationSeconds reflects total search time. Values above 3-4 seconds may indicate the search backend is under load.

Citation Requirement

Using WebSearch results carries a citation obligation. When your agent presents findings derived from search results, it must include a Sources: section with the URLs used. This is not a style preference — it is a tool usage requirement enforced at the harness level. Harnesses that surface search results to users without sourcing are violating the contract.

## Findings

The latest version of Pydantic (v2.10) introduces...

## Sources
- https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/changelog/
- https://pypi.org/project/pydantic/

Geographic Limitation

WebSearch is only available when running in the United States. Harnesses deployed in other regions will encounter failures. If you are building a globally-deployed harness, plan for this: either route search requests through a US endpoint, substitute a different search MCP server, or degrade gracefully to WebFetch-only operation when WebSearch fails.

Usage Tracking

As of v2.1.92, web_search_requests and web_fetch_requests appear as distinct counters in the usage stats returned with each response. When running cost analysis with /cost, you will see cache-hit breakdowns that include web tool calls. Harnesses that run many search-and-fetch cycles can accumulate meaningful usage; the counters give you visibility into this.

7.3 Domain Filtering

Both tools support domain filtering, but the semantics differ and understanding the difference matters.

WebSearch: allowed_domains and blocked_domains

For WebSearch, these arrays filter which results are included in the returned list:

// Only return results from official Python docs
{
  query: "asyncio event loop best practices",
  allowed_domains: ["docs.python.org", "peps.python.org"]
}

// Exclude forums and Q&A sites
{
  query: "asyncio event loop best practices",
  blocked_domains: ["stackoverflow.com", "reddit.com", "quora.com"]
}

The allowed_domains and blocked_domains options are mutually exclusive in practice — combining them produces unpredictable behavior depending on which constraint takes precedence. Pick one approach per query.

When to use allowed_domains: You need authoritative information from specific sources — official documentation, trusted security databases (nvd.nist.gov, cve.mitre.org), or specific vendors. The search engine may return many low-quality results for technical queries; filtering to known-good domains improves signal-to-noise ratio significantly.

When to use blocked_domains: You want broad coverage but want to exclude aggregator sites, cached copies, or low-quality sources. Blocking mirrors and content farms keeps results fresh and authoritative.

flowchart LR
    Q[Query] --> SE[Search Engine]
    SE --> R1["result: docs.python.org"]
    SE --> R2["result: stackoverflow.com"]
    SE --> R3["result: blog.example.com"]
    SE --> R4["result: realpython.com"]

    subgraph "allowed_domains: [docs.python.org, peps.python.org]"
        R1 --> PASS1[included]
        R2 --> FAIL1[excluded]
        R3 --> FAIL2[excluded]
        R4 --> FAIL3[excluded]
    end

Network-Level Filtering in Settings

Separate from the per-call options, Claude Code's settings layer has allowedDomains (global network sandbox). This is different in scope: it controls which domains the entire harness can reach over the network, not which results WebSearch returns. An allowedDomains restriction at the settings level will cause WebFetch to fail for any URL outside the list, regardless of what the model requests.

Harness authors building restricted environments should use both layers:

  • Settings allowedDomains: network-level allowlist (which hosts can be reached at all)
  • WebSearch.allowed_domains: search-result filter (which results are returned)

7.4 The 15-Minute Cache

Both WebFetch and WebSearch cache their results automatically for 15 minutes. The cache is:

  • Automatic: no opt-in or configuration required
  • Self-cleaning: entries expire after 15 minutes without intervention
  • Shared across tool calls: a URL fetched by one tool call in a session is served from cache by the next call to the same URL within the window
  • Keyed by URL + prompt for WebFetch (the same URL with a different prompt is a cache miss)

Practical Implications

Cache hits are fast and free. A WebFetch that costs 800ms and several hundred tokens on a cold fetch returns almost instantly from cache. For research workflows that touch the same documentation page multiple times — reading it once to understand structure, then again with a more targeted prompt — the second call is effectively zero cost.

15 minutes is long enough for a research session. In practice, most research agents fetch a URL, process it, and move on. Revisiting the same URL within a session is uncommon for fresh research. The 15-minute window covers it comfortably.

Design for cache misses. If your workflow runs longer than 15 minutes and needs to re-verify a URL, treat each access as a potential cache miss. Do not assume the cached version is still valid for latency-sensitive decisions.

Cache hit visibility. As of v2.1.92, cache-hit breakdowns appear in /cost output. You can observe how many tool calls were served from cache versus requiring fresh network requests.

/cost output (example)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Tokens:  42,300 input (12,100 cache read), 2,100 output
Tools:   web_fetch_requests: 8 (3 cache hits), web_search_requests: 4
Cost:    ~$0.09

Cache Key Precision

For WebSearch, the cache key includes the full query string, allowed_domains, and blocked_domains. Changing any of these triggers a fresh search. If you are running a multi-agent workflow where several agents search for related but slightly different queries, each gets its own cache entry — there is no semantic deduplication. Design queries to be reusable within a session if cache efficiency matters.

7.5 Redirect Handling

HTTP redirects are common: documentation sites redirect to versioned paths, CDN nodes redirect based on geography, URLs get canonicalized. WebFetch handles same-host redirects transparently. Cross-host redirects are different.

Cross-Host Redirect Behavior

When a URL redirects to a different hostname, WebFetch does not silently follow it. Instead, it reports the redirect and provides the destination URL. The tool output will include the redirect URL in its result, and the url field in WebFetchOutput will reflect where the request ended up.

The practical flow for your agent:

Step 1: Request URL A
   WebFetch("http://example.com/old-path", "extract content")
   
Step 2: Response indicates cross-host redirect to URL B
   result: "Redirected to https://new-example.com/current-path"
   url: "https://new-example.com/current-path"
   
Step 3: Make a new request to URL B
   WebFetch("https://new-example.com/current-path", "extract content")

Why not auto-follow? Cross-host redirects change the origin of the content. Security-conscious harnesses need to know if a documentation URL is silently redirecting to a third-party domain — that is a supply chain risk, not a transparent optimization. The explicit report-and-follow pattern keeps your agent aware of what domains it is actually consuming.

HTTP to HTTPS Upgrade

HTTP URLs are upgraded to HTTPS automatically before the request is made. If you pass http://example.com, the harness fetches https://example.com. The url field in the response will reflect the HTTPS version. This is unconditional — you cannot opt out of the upgrade. For any URL that only exists on HTTP (rare in 2026, but relevant if you are working with local test servers or legacy infrastructure), WebFetch will fail.

7.6 Authenticated Content: The Hard Boundary

This is the most important limitation in the web tools. WebFetch cannot access authenticated or private content. This is not a configuration issue — it is a fundamental architectural constraint. The harness fetches URLs as an unauthenticated HTTP client. If the server requires authentication — a session cookie, an OAuth token, a corporate SSO challenge — the request fails.

What Fails

ServiceWhy It Fails
Google Docs / Google SheetsRequires Google login, returns login redirect
ConfluenceRequires Atlassian SSO or basic auth
JiraRequires Atlassian authentication
Private GitHub reposRequires auth token or session
Azure DevOps (authenticated pages)Requires AAD authentication
Internal corporate wikisBehind SSO
Notion pages (private)Requires Notion auth
Slack archivesRequires Slack auth

The failure mode is usually a 401 or 302 redirect to a login page. WebFetchOutput.code will be 401 or 200 (with a login page HTML as content), result will contain something useless like "Please sign in to continue."

Fallback Patterns

Pattern 1: MCP tool for the service. If you need to read Confluence, Jira, or GitHub, use an MCP server that handles authentication. The MCP server runs with credentials and makes authenticated API calls on your behalf; the harness receives the result without ever touching the auth flow.

GitHub URL (private repo)  →  Use gh CLI via Bash
Jira ticket               →  Use Jira MCP server
Confluence page           →  Use Confluence MCP server
ADO work item             →  Use ADO REST API via Bash + PAT

Pattern 2: gh CLI for GitHub. For GitHub specifically, avoid WebFetch entirely. The gh CLI handles authentication natively and provides structured output:

# Instead of WebFetch("https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/42")
gh issue view 42 --repo owner/repo --json title,body,comments

# Instead of WebFetch("https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123")
gh pr view 123 --repo owner/repo --json title,body,files,reviews

The structured JSON output from gh is far more useful than the markdown extraction WebFetch would produce even if authentication were not an issue.

Pattern 3: Export then fetch. For Confluence pages or internal documentation, an intermediate export step makes the content accessible:

1. Bash: curl -u "$CONFLUENCE_USER:$CONFLUENCE_TOKEN" \
          "https://confluence.internal/rest/api/content/12345?expand=body.storage" \
          -o /tmp/page.json
2. Read: /tmp/page.json  (or extract body.storage field)
3. Process: the content is now local, no WebFetch needed

Pattern 4: Artifact export for Notion/Google Docs. Export to PDF or HTML first, download to a local path, then use Read to process it. This is slower but gives you full content fidelity.

flowchart TD
    A[Need content from authenticated URL] --> B{Can use CLI tool?}
    B -->|GitHub| C["gh CLI via Bash"]
    B -->|ADO| D["ADO REST API via Bash + PAT"]
    B -->|Other| E{MCP server available?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Use MCP tool]
    E -->|No| G[Export → Download → Read]
    C & D & F & G --> H[Content available to agent]

What Succeeds

Public content works reliably:

  • Public GitHub repos, issues, PRs (but gh CLI is still better)
  • Public npm package pages (npmjs.com)
  • PyPI package pages (pypi.org)
  • Public documentation sites
  • Public CVE databases (nvd.nist.gov, cve.mitre.org)
  • Wikipedia
  • API documentation sites (stripe.com/docs, openai.com/docs, etc.)
  • Stack Overflow public questions

7.7 Lab: Build a Multi-Source Research Agent

This lab builds a research agent that gathers information on a technical topic from multiple independent sources, cross-validates findings, and produces a sourced report. It demonstrates all the web tool mechanics: domain-filtered search, selective fetch with targeted prompts, cache efficiency, and fallback handling.

Goal

Given a topic — for example, "Python asyncio event loop performance in 3.12 vs 3.11" — the agent should:

  1. Search for relevant sources using domain filtering
  2. Fetch the top 3-5 most authoritative sources with targeted extraction prompts
  3. Identify any claims that appear in multiple independent sources (triangulation)
  4. Produce a sourced report with a confidence level per claim

Architecture

flowchart TD
    INPUT[Topic string] --> SEARCH1
    INPUT --> SEARCH2

    SEARCH1["WebSearch\nallowed_domains: [docs.python.org, peps.python.org]\nquery: topic + 'official docs'"]
    SEARCH2["WebSearch\nblocked_domains: [reddit.com, quora.com]\nquery: topic + 'benchmark analysis'"]

    SEARCH1 --> URLS1[Official doc URLs]
    SEARCH2 --> URLS2[Technical blog URLs]

    URLS1 --> RANK[Rank by domain authority\n+ title relevance]
    URLS2 --> RANK

    RANK --> TOP5[Top 5 URLs]

    TOP5 --> FETCH1["WebFetch URL1\nprompt: extract claims"]
    TOP5 --> FETCH2["WebFetch URL2\nprompt: extract claims"]
    TOP5 --> FETCH3["WebFetch URL3\nprompt: extract claims"]

    FETCH1 & FETCH2 & FETCH3 --> TRIANGULATE[Cross-validate claims\nacross sources]

    TRIANGULATE --> REPORT[Sourced report\nwith confidence levels]

Implementation

The following workflow script implements this pattern. The meta literal is pure — no computed values.

export const meta = {
  name: "multi-source-research",
  description: "Research a technical topic across multiple independent sources",
  phases: ["search", "fetch", "triangulate", "report"],
};

export default async function research({ args, agent, parallel, phase, log, budget }) {
  const topic = args as string;

  // Phase 1: Parallel searches across different source types
  await phase("search");
  log(`Searching for: ${topic}`);

  const [officialResults, technicalResults] = await parallel([
    () => agent(`
      Use WebSearch with allowed_domains ["docs.python.org", "peps.python.org", "devguide.python.org"]
      to search for: ${topic}
      Return a JSON array of {title, url} objects, maximum 5 results.
    `, { schema: { type: "array", items: { type: "object", properties: { title: { type: "string" }, url: { type: "string" } } } } }),

    () => agent(`
      Use WebSearch with blocked_domains ["reddit.com", "quora.com", "stackexchange.com"]
      to search for: ${topic} performance benchmark
      Return a JSON array of {title, url} objects, maximum 5 results.
    `, { schema: { type: "array", items: { type: "object", properties: { title: { type: "string" }, url: { type: "string" } } } } }),
  ]);

  log(`Found ${officialResults.length} official + ${technicalResults.length} technical sources`);

  // Combine and deduplicate by URL
  const allUrls = [...officialResults, ...technicalResults]
    .filter(Boolean)
    .slice(0, 5);

  // Phase 2: Fetch each source with targeted extraction
  await phase("fetch");

  const extractions = await parallel(
    allUrls.map(({ title, url }) => async () => {
      log(`Fetching: ${title}`);
      return agent(`
        Use WebFetch on this URL: ${url}
        
        Use this extraction prompt:
        "Extract all specific claims about performance, benchmarks, or behavioral changes.
         For each claim, note: (1) what was claimed, (2) any numbers or metrics cited,
         (3) whether it is presented as measured data or opinion.
         Format as a JSON array of claim objects."
        
        Return the extracted claims as a JSON array, or an empty array if the page
        was unavailable or contained no relevant claims.
        Include the source URL in each claim object.
      `, {
        schema: {
          type: "array",
          items: {
            type: "object",
            properties: {
              claim: { type: "string" },
              metric: { type: "string" },
              type: { enum: ["measured", "opinion", "unclear"] },
              source_url: { type: "string" },
            },
          },
        },
      });
    })
  );

  const allClaims = extractions.flat().filter(Boolean);
  log(`Extracted ${allClaims.length} claims across ${allUrls.length} sources`);

  // Phase 3: Triangulate — find claims that appear in multiple sources
  await phase("triangulate");

  const triangulation = await agent(`
    Given these claims extracted from multiple sources about "${topic}":
    
    ${JSON.stringify(allClaims, null, 2)}
    
    Identify:
    1. Claims that appear in 2+ independent sources (high confidence)
    2. Claims that appear in only 1 source (needs verification)  
    3. Claims that directly contradict each other (conflicted)
    
    Return a JSON object with three arrays: high_confidence, needs_verification, conflicted.
    Each item should include the claim text, source URLs supporting it, and a confidence score 0-1.
  `, {
    schema: {
      type: "object",
      properties: {
        high_confidence: { type: "array" },
        needs_verification: { type: "array" },
        conflicted: { type: "array" },
      },
    },
  });

  // Phase 4: Generate sourced report
  await phase("report");

  const report = await agent(`
    Write a technical research report on: "${topic}"
    
    Use these triangulated findings:
    ${JSON.stringify(triangulation, null, 2)}
    
    Format:
    ## Summary
    [2-3 sentence executive summary]
    
    ## High-Confidence Findings
    [Bullet list of claims with 2+ source support — include confidence level]
    
    ## Claims Requiring Verification
    [Bullet list of single-source claims — note the source]
    
    ## Conflicting Evidence
    [Any claims that conflict across sources — explain the discrepancy]
    
    ## Sources
    [Full URL list of all sources consulted]
    
    The Sources section is required. Do not omit it.
  `);

  return report;
}

Running the Agent

claude -p 'Run the multi-source-research workflow for the topic: "Python asyncio event loop performance changes in 3.12"' \
  --output-format text

What to Observe

Cache behavior: If you run the same topic twice within 15 minutes, the second run fetches URLs from cache. The durationMs values in the WebFetch outputs will drop from 500-1500ms to near-zero. You will see this reflected in /cost as cache-hit counts.

Domain filtering effectiveness: Compare runs with and without allowed_domains. The filtered run returns fewer but higher-quality results; the unfiltered run may return SEO farms or outdated blog posts. For technical research, filtering is almost always worth it.

Prompt specificity effects: Change the extraction prompt from the detailed version to a simple "summarize this page" and compare the quality of allClaims. The detailed prompt with structured JSON schema output produces claims that can actually be triangulated. The vague prompt produces prose that cannot be compared across sources.

Redirect handling: Some URLs returned by search will redirect. The agent's extraction step should handle this gracefully — the WebFetch call will return information about the redirect, and the model should either follow it or skip the source. Add a fallback in the extraction step:

// In the fetch step, check for redirect indication in result
if (result.includes("Redirected to")) {
  const redirectUrl = extractRedirectUrl(result);
  log(`Following redirect to ${redirectUrl}`);
  // Make a new WebFetch call with the redirect URL
}

Authenticated content failures: If any of the search results point to a Confluence wiki, internal documentation, or login-gated content, the extraction step will return an empty array or an error result. The agent should treat this as a zero-claim source and continue, not stop. The triangulation step is designed to handle sparse data — a source that returns nothing is simply not counted.

Extending the Lab

Add MCP fallback for GitHub: If a search result URL is a GitHub URL, route it through gh CLI instead of WebFetch:

// Before calling WebFetch, check if URL is GitHub
if (url.includes("github.com")) {
  // Use gh CLI for better auth + structured output
  const ghOutput = await agent(`
    Use Bash to run: gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path} or 
    gh issue view {number} --repo {owner}/{repo} --json body
    for URL: ${url}
  `);
  return parseGhOutput(ghOutput);
}

Add a completeness critic: After generating the report, spawn a separate agent to review it for gaps:

const critique = await agent(`
  Review this research report and identify:
  1. Questions about "${topic}" that the report does not answer
  2. Sources that should have been checked but were not
  3. Claims that seem too strong given the evidence cited
  
  Report: ${report}
`);

if (critique.includes("missing")) {
  log("Completeness critic found gaps — running supplemental search");
  // Run targeted searches for the identified gaps
}

Budget-aware depth: Use the budget object to scale how many sources are fetched:

const sourceCount = budget.remaining() > 100_000 ? 8 : 3;
const topUrls = allUrls.slice(0, sourceCount);

Patterns and Anti-Patterns

Pattern: Search-Then-Fetch Selectivity

Do not fetch every URL returned by WebSearch. Search results include titles and URLs — use them to filter before fetching. If you need information about a specific library version, a result titled "Python 2.7 asyncio backport" is not worth fetching. The cheapest fetch is one that never happens.

// Filter search results before fetching
const relevantUrls = searchResults
  .filter(r => r.title.toLowerCase().includes("3.12") || r.title.toLowerCase().includes("performance"))
  .slice(0, 3);

Pattern: Structured Extraction for Machine Processing

When another part of your agent will process the WebFetch result, write extraction prompts that produce structured data. Prose extraction produces text that is hard to compare across sources. JSON extraction produces data you can merge, deduplicate, and analyze.

// For machine processing: structured prompt
prompt: "Extract as JSON array: [{version, change_type, description, breaking: bool}]"

// For human display: prose is fine
prompt: "Summarize the key changes for a developer who is upgrading"

Pattern: Defensive Extraction

Pages change, CDNs rate-limit, and search results sometimes point to dead links. Write extraction handling that expects partial failure:

const result = await webFetch(url, prompt);

// code 200 with near-zero bytes may mean anti-bot page
if (result.bytes < 500) {
  log(`Skipping ${url}: suspiciously small response (${result.bytes} bytes)`);
  return null;
}

// Non-200 means the resource is unavailable
if (result.code !== 200) {
  log(`Skipping ${url}: HTTP ${result.code}`);
  return null;
}

Anti-Pattern: Fetching Before Searching

A common mistake in research agents is starting with WebFetch on a URL the agent already knows — the library homepage, the documentation root — rather than searching for the specific page that answers the question. The search step is not overhead; it is navigation. Let the search engine find the right page instead of fetching the root and navigating manually.

Anti-Pattern: Assuming Fetch Equals Read

WebFetch produces a processed extraction, not a faithful copy of the page. The internal model decides what to include. For tasks that require complete fidelity — exhaustive API reference, full example code, complete change history — fetch the raw content via Bash with curl and Read it directly:

# For complete fidelity, bypass WebFetch entirely
curl -s "https://api.example.com/openapi.json" -o /tmp/openapi.json
# Then: Read /tmp/openapi.json

Anti-Pattern: Ignoring Redirect Signals

When WebFetch reports a cross-host redirect, ignoring it and treating the response as if it were from the original domain is a correctness error. The content came from a different host. Update your source attribution accordingly.

Summary

WebFetch and WebSearch are the harness's connection to public web content. They implement a fetch-convert-extract pipeline that transforms URLs into model-ready information rather than raw HTML. Understanding the pipeline — HTML to markdown to extraction model to result string — tells you where to invest precision: the extraction prompt.

The 15-minute cache keeps repeat accesses fast and efficient. Domain filtering lets you tune signal-to-noise ratio for searches. Cross-host redirect handling keeps your agent aware of where its content actually originates.

The hard boundary is authentication. WebFetch is an unauthenticated client. Anything behind a login — Confluence, Jira, private GitHub, corporate wikis — requires an MCP server or a CLI tool that handles auth separately. Design your research workflows with this constraint in mind from the start, not as an afterthought.

The research agent pattern — search with domain filtering, fetch with structured extraction, triangulate across sources, report with citations — is the foundation for any multi-source knowledge agent. Chapter 33 extends it into a full knowledge management system with memory persistence and fact decay.

In Chapter 8, we move inside the codebase: the LSP tool provides go-to-definition, find-references, and call hierarchy operations for navigating large codebases without reading every file manually.

Next: Chapter 8: Language Server Protocol — The LSP Tool

Chapter 8: Language Server Protocol — The LSP Tool

"grep knows nothing about types. LSP knows everything."

8.1 The Nine Operations

The LSP tool is the only member of the harness tool catalog that is purpose-built for semantic code navigation. Where Grep finds text and Read retrieves file contents, LSP understands the structure of your code — the type system, the call graph, the symbol hierarchy. It talks to a running Language Server to answer questions that would otherwise require parsing an entire codebase.

There are nine operations, each mapping directly to the Language Server Protocol specification:

OperationWhat it answers
goToDefinitionWhere is this symbol defined?
findReferencesWhere is this symbol used?
hoverWhat type is this? What does the documentation say?
documentSymbolWhat functions, classes, and variables are in this file?
workspaceSymbolFind all symbols matching a name across the entire project
goToImplementationWhich concrete classes implement this interface?
prepareCallHierarchyGet the call hierarchy item at this position
incomingCallsWhat functions call this function?
outgoingCallsWhat functions does this function call?

Understanding when to use each operation — and why it beats the text-search alternative — is the core skill this chapter develops.

goToDefinition

The most common operation. Given a symbol at a file position, returns the exact location where that symbol is declared.

The grep-based equivalent would be something like grep -rn "def process_event\|function processEvent\|processEvent =" across the codebase. That approach returns false positives (comments, string literals, other identifiers that share a substring), misses renamed symbols, and cannot distinguish between two processEvent functions in different modules. LSP returns the exact definition: file, line, character.

When the model is working on a large codebase and encounters an unfamiliar function call, goToDefinition is the correct tool. It does not guess. It asks the language server, which has already parsed and indexed the code.

findReferences

The inverse of goToDefinition. Given a definition site, returns every call site, import statement, type annotation, or other reference across the workspace. This operation is load-bearing for refactoring — before you rename a function or change a signature, you need to know every location that calls it.

Grep approximates this by searching for the identifier string. It will miss references in files where the identifier was imported under an alias (import { processEvent as pe } from './handler') and will include false positives in string literals and comments. LSP finds references at the semantic level: only actual code references, including aliased imports.

hover

Returns the documentation and type information for a symbol — equivalent to hovering your cursor over an identifier in VS Code and seeing the tooltip. For TypeScript, this means the full type signature. For Python with type hints, it means the resolved type annotation. For Rust, it means the expanded trait bounds and lifetime annotations.

This operation is underused. When a model is reading unfamiliar code and encounters a type or function it needs to understand, a single hover call returns what a human editor user would see in the tooltip: the signature, the docstring, the type parameters. It eliminates the need to chase goToDefinition just to read a function's signature.

documentSymbol

Returns an outline of a file: all named symbols (functions, classes, methods, variables, interfaces, enums) with their positions. This is the programmatic equivalent of the "Outline" panel in VS Code.

The practical use case: when the model needs to understand the structure of a 3000-line file before deciding which section to edit, documentSymbol returns a structured map of the file in a single call. No need to read the entire file first. The model can get the outline, identify the relevant section, and then read only that part.

workspaceSymbol

Like documentSymbol but across the entire project. Accepts a search string and returns all matching symbols from all indexed files. This is the tool you reach for when you know the name of what you are looking for but not where it lives.

Example: you are debugging a PaymentProcessor class that is failing. You know it exists somewhere in a large TypeScript monorepo. workspaceSymbol with query "PaymentProcessor" returns every class, interface, function, and variable matching that name across all workspace files, with their locations.

goToImplementation

Navigates from an interface or abstract method declaration to its concrete implementations. In a codebase with a Serializable interface and twelve classes that implement it, goToImplementation at the interface declaration returns all twelve concrete classes.

This is particularly valuable when working with dependency-injected architectures where code operates on interface types and the concrete implementations are registered elsewhere.

prepareCallHierarchy

Returns the call hierarchy item at a given position — a prerequisite step before calling incomingCalls or outgoingCalls. It establishes the identity of the function at the cursor position in a form the language server can use for hierarchy traversal.

In practice, agents typically call prepareCallHierarchy followed immediately by one of the call direction operations. You rarely use it in isolation.

incomingCalls and outgoingCalls

These two operations map the call graph. incomingCalls answers "what calls this function?" and outgoingCalls answers "what does this function call?"

The combination lets a model trace execution paths without reading every file in the call chain. For debugging, this is essential: given a failing function, incomingCalls shows every entry point that can trigger it. For impact analysis, outgoingCalls shows the complete dependency surface of a function before you modify it.

8.2 Parameters

Every LSP operation shares the same four parameters:

interface LSPInput {
  operation: 
    | "goToDefinition"
    | "findReferences"
    | "hover"
    | "documentSymbol"
    | "workspaceSymbol"
    | "goToImplementation"
    | "prepareCallHierarchy"
    | "incomingCalls"
    | "outgoingCalls";
  filePath: string;       // absolute or relative path to the file
  line: number;           // 1-based, must be > 0
  character: number;      // 1-based, must be > 0
}

There are three things worth internalizing about this interface.

All four parameters are required for all operations. Even workspaceSymbol, which logically operates on a project-wide scope, requires filePath, line, and character. The language server uses the file path to determine which workspace the request belongs to when multiple projects are open. Use the search term as the value you are navigating from — position the cursor on any identifier of that type in the codebase.

Line and character are 1-based, matching editor conventions. If you read a file with the Read tool and see line number 47 in the cat -n output, you pass line: 47 to LSP. No offset arithmetic. The harness documentation is explicit that values must be greater than 0 — passing line: 0 is an error.

Character counts columns, not bytes. In files with multi-byte characters (Unicode identifiers, Asian language comments), character position counts Unicode code points from column 1. In ASCII files, character position equals the column number. To target a specific identifier, identify which column it starts on. For an identifier processEvent beginning at column 12, pass character: 12.

Practical example — TypeScript

Given this TypeScript file at src/handlers/payment.ts:

1  import { PaymentGateway } from '../services/gateway';
2  import { processTransaction } from '../utils/transaction';
3
4  export class PaymentHandler {
5    private gateway: PaymentGateway;
6
7    async handlePayment(amount: number): Promise<void> {
8      const result = await processTransaction(amount, this.gateway);
9      if (!result.success) {
10       throw new Error(result.message);
11     }
12   }
13 }

To jump to the definition of processTransaction (which begins at column 29 on line 8):

operation: "goToDefinition"
filePath: "src/handlers/payment.ts"
line: 8
character: 29

To get the type information for result on line 8, column 13:

operation: "hover"
filePath: "src/handlers/payment.ts"
line: 8
character: 13

The hover response might return:

const result: TransactionResult
