interface TransactionResult {
  success: boolean;
  message: string;
  transactionId?: string;
}

That single call replaces reading the processTransaction function definition, finding its return type annotation, and tracing that type to its interface declaration — three separate file reads collapsed into one LSP call.

8.3 Server Lifecycle

The LSP tool is backed by language servers — long-lived processes that index your codebase and answer navigation queries. The harness manages these servers transparently, but understanding the lifecycle matters when you are debugging failures or building agents that use LSP heavily.

Auto-Start

Language servers start automatically on the first LSP request for a given file type. There is no explicit server start command. The first call to LSP on a .ts file starts the TypeScript language server. The first call on a .py file starts the configured Python language server (pylsp, pyright, or similar). Subsequent calls to files of the same type reuse the running server.

This means the first LSP call for a new file type carries startup latency — anywhere from 200ms for a small project to several seconds for a large monorepo while the server indexes. Subsequent calls are fast. Agents that use LSP heavily should expect a warm-up period at the start of a session on a new codebase.

The language server must be configured for the file type — if no server is available for a file extension, LSP returns an error. Built-in support covers the most common languages; plugin-provided servers extend coverage to Rust and Swift (see Section 8.4).

Crash Recovery

Language servers occasionally crash. The v2.1.89 changelog entry is worth quoting directly:

Fixed LSP server zombie state after crash — server now restarts on next request instead of failing until session restart.

Before v2.1.89, a crashed language server left a zombie process that continued to hold its port. Subsequent LSP calls to that server failed silently — the harness could not distinguish "server is slow" from "server is dead," and the session had to be restarted to recover LSP functionality.

After v2.1.89, crash recovery is automatic. When the harness detects that a language server has exited unexpectedly, it clears the process handle. The next LSP request triggers a fresh server start as if the file type were being seen for the first time. Recovery is transparent to the model — the next call succeeds after the restart latency.

For practical purposes: if you observe a series of LSP failures in a long-running agent session, the first failure may be a crash; the second request should succeed after auto-restart. Build agents to retry LSP calls exactly once on failure before escalating to grep-based fallback.

Server Scope

Each language server handles one language. You can have a TypeScript server, a Python server, and a Go server running simultaneously in the same Claude Code session. They do not share state. The harness routes each LSP call to the appropriate server based on the file extension of filePath.

8.4 Plugin-Provided LSP Servers

The built-in LSP support covers common languages. Two languages with dedicated plugin-provided LSP integration are available from the official marketplace:

rust-analyzer-lsp — provides LSP support for Rust files (.rs) backed by rust-analyzer, the official Rust language server. rust-analyzer delivers full Rust semantic analysis: type inference across trait bounds, macro expansion, lifetime analysis, and the complete Rust call graph including calls through trait objects.

swift-lsp — provides LSP support for Swift files (.swift) via sourcekit-lsp, Apple's official Swift language server.

Both plugins are available through the claude-plugins-official marketplace. Installation follows the standard plugin workflow:

# List available official plugins
claude plugins search --marketplace claude-plugins-official

# Install Rust LSP support
claude plugins install rust-analyzer-lsp

# Install Swift LSP support  
claude plugins install swift-lsp

After installation, LSP calls on .rs and .swift files work identically to built-in language support. The plugin handles server binary management, startup configuration, and workspace root detection.

Why Plugin Distribution

Shipping rust-analyzer and sourcekit-lsp as plugin-provided rather than built-in is an intentional design decision. Both language servers are large binaries with platform-specific builds. rust-analyzer ships separate binaries for each platform/architecture combination (darwin-arm64, darwin-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, windows-x64). Including these in the base Claude Code distribution would significantly increase download size for users who do not write Rust or Swift.

The plugin distribution model lets Rust and Swift developers opt in while keeping the base install lean. It also allows plugin-provided language servers to be updated independently of the Claude Code release cycle — a critical property when rust-analyzer ships frequent updates tracking the Rust edition.

8.5 LSP vs Grep: A Precision Comparison

Before the lab, it is worth being concrete about when LSP's type-awareness matters versus when grep is sufficient. The decision affects both correctness and performance — LSP calls carry server startup cost and require a running language server; grep is always available.

Reach for LSP when:

  • You need exact definition locations without false positives from similarly-named identifiers
  • You are about to rename or change the signature of a function and need to find all callers
  • You need to understand what type a variable is without reading its full initialization chain
  • You are navigating a codebase with multiple classes that implement the same interface
  • You need the call graph (incomingCalls / outgoingCalls) for impact analysis

Grep is sufficient when:

  • You are searching for a string literal or error message
  • You need to find files that import a specific module
  • You are doing an initial survey of an unfamiliar codebase before the language server has finished indexing
  • The identifier is unique enough that text matching has no false-positive risk
  • No language server is configured for the file type

The sharpest illustration: imagine a TypeScript codebase with a function named get that appears in dozens of files — array destructuring, object getters, HTTP client calls, ORM methods. A grep for get( returns hundreds of matches across every category. A findReferences call on the specific get method of your ORM client returns exactly the lines that call that specific method, filtered by type. The difference is not a quality-of-life improvement; for large codebases it is the difference between useful output and noise.

8.6 Lab: Build a Code Navigation Agent

This lab builds an agent that uses LSP to trace the full execution path from an entry point function to its deepest dependencies, then generates a structured call graph report. The agent demonstrates all nine operations working together.

Goal

Given an entry point function name and file, the agent:

  1. Locates the function using workspaceSymbol and confirms with hover
  2. Traverses its outgoing call graph using outgoingCalls recursively (depth-limited)
  3. Finds all callers of each discovered function using incomingCalls
  4. Gets the type signatures of all functions in the graph using hover
  5. Gets all symbols in each discovered file using documentSymbol
  6. Generates a structured report: function → signature → callers → callees

Setup

The lab uses a TypeScript project with the following structure:

src/
├── api/
│   └── handler.ts          # Entry point: handleRequest()
├── services/
│   ├── auth.ts             # validateToken(), checkPermissions()
│   ├── database.ts         # queryUser(), updateRecord()
│   └── cache.ts            # getCached(), setCached()
└── utils/
    ├── logger.ts           # log(), logError()
    └── validator.ts        # validateInput(), sanitize()

Step 1: Locate the Entry Point

operation: "workspaceSymbol"
filePath: "src/api/handler.ts"
line: 1
character: 1

The workspaceSymbol call with query "handleRequest" returns the exact location. Confirm it with hover to get the function signature:

operation: "hover"
filePath: "src/api/handler.ts"
line: 12
character: 17

Example hover response:

async function handleRequest(
  req: IncomingRequest,
  ctx: RequestContext
): Promise<Response>

Step 2: Prepare the Call Hierarchy

operation: "prepareCallHierarchy"
filePath: "src/api/handler.ts"
line: 12
character: 17

This registers handleRequest as the root of the hierarchy traversal.

Step 3: Traverse Outgoing Calls

operation: "outgoingCalls"
filePath: "src/api/handler.ts"
line: 12
character: 17

The response lists each function that handleRequest directly calls, with the call sites and the target location. Each entry includes the callee name and its definition file and position. For each discovered callee, repeat prepareCallHierarchy → outgoingCalls to traverse one level deeper. Limit depth to avoid infinite recursion in circular call graphs.

A complete traversal at depth 2 for this codebase might discover:

handleRequest
├── validateToken       (src/services/auth.ts:8:14)
├── checkPermissions    (src/services/auth.ts:24:14)
├── validateInput       (src/utils/validator.ts:5:14)
├── queryUser           (src/services/database.ts:12:14)
│   ├── getCached       (src/services/cache.ts:8:14)
│   └── log             (src/utils/logger.ts:4:14)
└── log                 (src/utils/logger.ts:4:14)

Step 4: Get Type Signatures

For each function in the discovered graph, call hover at its definition position. This populates the report with actual type signatures rather than just names:

operation: "hover"
filePath: "src/services/auth.ts"
line: 8
character: 14

Response:

function validateToken(
  token: string,
  options?: TokenOptions
): Promise<AuthResult>

Repeat for each node in the call graph. After this step, every node has a verified signature.

Step 5: Find All References for Impact Analysis

For the entry point and any function you intend to modify, call findReferences:

operation: "findReferences"
filePath: "src/api/handler.ts"
line: 12
character: 17

This reveals all the code paths that can trigger handleRequest — middleware registrations, test files, integration harnesses. Before modifying a function's signature, this list is the complete impact surface.

Step 6: Get File Structure

For each file in the call graph, call documentSymbol to understand its complete structure. This shows whether the file has other functions, how they relate, and whether the function under analysis is a method of a class or a standalone export:

operation: "documentSymbol"
filePath: "src/services/auth.ts"
line: 1
character: 1

Response (abbreviated):

AuthService (class) [line 4]
  validateToken (method) [line 8]
  checkPermissions (method) [line 24]
  refreshToken (method) [line 41]
tokenCache (variable) [line 2]

This reveals that validateToken is a method on AuthService, not a standalone function — a detail that matters for call semantics and that grep-based search would not surface without reading the file.

Step 7: Generate the Report

After completing the traversal, the agent has enough data to produce a structured call graph report:

## Call Graph: handleRequest

**Entry point:** `src/api/handler.ts:12` — `handleRequest(req: IncomingRequest, ctx: RequestContext): Promise<Response>`

**Direct callers:** 3 locations (route registrations in `src/api/router.ts:45`, `src/api/router.ts:89`, test file `tests/api/handler.test.ts:23`)

### Call Graph (depth 2)

| Function | File | Signature | Called By |
|---|---|---|---|
| `handleRequest` | `api/handler.ts:12` | `(req, ctx) => Promise<Response>` | router.ts (×2), test (×1) |
| `validateToken` | `services/auth.ts:8` | `(token, opts?) => Promise<AuthResult>` | handleRequest |
| `checkPermissions` | `services/auth.ts:24` | `(userId, resource) => Promise<boolean>` | handleRequest |
| `validateInput` | `utils/validator.ts:5` | `(data: unknown) => ValidationResult` | handleRequest |
| `queryUser` | `services/database.ts:12` | `(id: string) => Promise<User \| null>` | handleRequest |
| `getCached` | `services/cache.ts:8` | `(key: string) => T \| undefined` | queryUser |
| `log` | `utils/logger.ts:4` | `(msg: string, level?: LogLevel) => void` | queryUser, handleRequest |

### Modification Impact

To change the signature of `handleRequest`:
- Update 2 route registrations in `src/api/router.ts`
- Update 1 test case in `tests/api/handler.test.ts`
- No downstream callee signatures need changing

To change the signature of `validateToken`:
- Update 1 call site in `src/api/handler.ts:18`
- `AuthService.validateToken` — update the class method definition
- Check for other `AuthService` consumers via `findReferences` on the class

What the Lab Demonstrates

This lab uses all nine operations in a coherent workflow:

  • workspaceSymbol to locate symbols by name
  • hover to get verified type signatures
  • prepareCallHierarchy → outgoingCalls → incomingCalls for call graph traversal
  • goToDefinition to confirm symbol locations
  • findReferences to determine modification impact
  • documentSymbol to understand file structure in context

None of this is achievable with grep at the same level of precision. The type signatures, interface implementations, method ownership, and aliased references are only visible at the semantic layer that LSP provides.

The agent pattern — traverse, enrich, report — generalizes to other scenarios: security audits that trace data from user input to persistence, performance analysis that identifies the call chains responsible for latency, and dependency analysis that maps what would break if a module is replaced.

Summary

The LSP tool provides nine operations that give the model semantic, type-aware code navigation. Unlike text search, LSP understands the structure of your code: where symbols are defined, where they are used, what types they carry, and how functions call each other.

The parameter contract is uniform across all nine operations: filePath, line, and character (both 1-based, matching editor conventions), plus the operation name. Language servers start automatically on first use for a given file type. Since v2.1.89, crashes recover automatically — the server restarts on the next request rather than failing until session restart. Rust and Swift support is available via the rust-analyzer-lsp and swift-lsp plugins from the official marketplace.

The decision framework is straightforward: use LSP when you need precision — finding all references to a specific method, not all occurrences of a string; jumping to the exact definition of a type, not grepping for its name. Use grep when the language server is unavailable, when indexing is in progress, or when you are genuinely searching for text rather than navigating a symbol.

In Chapter 9, we move from code navigation to planning: the EnterPlanMode and ExitPlanMode tools that give the model a structured design phase before it begins modifying code.

Next: Chapter 9: Planning Tools — EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, AskUserQuestion

Chapter 9: Planning Tools — EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, AskUserQuestion

"The fastest way to waste an afternoon is to let an agent start implementing something it doesn't fully understand."

9.1 Plan Mode Lifecycle

Every agentic harness faces the same tension: the model is capable enough to start immediately, but complex tasks benefit from a pause — a moment where the agent surveys the terrain, assembles a coherent plan, and gets human sign-off before touching production state. Plan mode is the harness's answer to that tension.

Plan mode is a first-class execution state in Claude Code. It is not a convention or a prompt trick. It is a distinct mode with enforced behavioral constraints: while in plan mode, the agent can explore freely but cannot write or modify files. It is strictly read and reason, never act.

The lifecycle has five stages:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant H as Harness
    participant A as Agent
    participant FS as Filesystem

    U->>A: "Migrate the auth module to OAuth 2.0"
    A->>H: EnterPlanMode
    H-->>A: {message: "Plan mode active"}
    Note over A: Can Read, Grep, Glob, Bash (read-only)<br/>Cannot Edit or Write
    A->>FS: Read auth module files
    A->>FS: Grep for all session references
    A->>FS: Read existing tests
    A->>FS: Write plan to ~/.claude/plans/jolly-knitting-ullman.md
    A->>H: ExitPlanMode
    H-->>U: Display plan for review
    U->>H: Approve
    H-->>A: {plan: "...", isAgent: false}
    Note over A: Now can Edit and Write
    A->>FS: Implement changes

Stage 1: EnterPlanMode. The agent calls EnterPlanMode with no parameters. The harness immediately restricts the agent's tool surface — Edit and Write calls will fail until plan mode is exited. The agent receives a confirmation message and begins its exploration phase.

Stage 2: Exploration. This is the most important part of plan mode and the one engineers most often underestimate. A thorough exploration phase produces a plan that is actually executable. The agent reads files, greps for patterns, follows import chains, checks test coverage, reads existing documentation. It is not writing yet — it is building the complete picture. Skipping or rushing this phase produces a plan with wrong assumptions, missed edge cases, and a dependency order that will fail partway through.

Stage 3: Write the plan file. After exploration, the agent writes a plan file into ~/.claude/plans/. This file is the artifact. It should contain what will be done, in what order, and why — enough detail that a senior engineer reading it would know exactly what the implementation will produce before a single line of code changes.

Stage 4: ExitPlanMode. The agent calls ExitPlanMode. The harness reads the plan file, surfaces it to the user, and waits. This is the approval gate.

Stage 5: Implementation. The user approves. The harness returns the plan content to the agent with isAgent: false (or true if running as a subagent awaiting leader approval). The edit and write constraints are lifted. The agent implements what the plan described.

When to Use Plan Mode

Plan mode is for non-trivial implementation tasks. The decision threshold matters — using plan mode for every change creates friction without value; skipping it for complex changes is how multi-file refactors go wrong.

TaskPlan mode?
Fix a typo in a string literalNo
Rename a variable across 3 filesNo
Add a single API endpoint with a testJudgment call
Migrate authentication systemYes
Refactor a module to a new interface used in 15 placesYes
Implement a new feature spanning 5+ filesYes
Anything where the implementation order mattersYes

The clearest signal: if the agent could start implementing and then realize partway through that an earlier decision was wrong — requiring a rollback — plan mode was warranted.

What the Constraints Actually Enforce

In plan mode, the harness does not disable Edit and Write at the tool description level. It enforces the constraint at execution time: if the agent tries to call Edit or Write while plan mode is active, the tool returns a tool_result explaining that modifications are not permitted in plan mode. The agent sees this as an error and adjusts.

This enforcement matters because it is honest. The model cannot accidentally write files while it thinks it is still planning. The constraint is runtime, not advisory.

Bash commands are permitted in plan mode, because they are essential for exploration. The agent needs to run grep, find, cat, git log, and similar read-only commands. The harness trusts the agent to stay read-only during exploration — it cannot statically verify that a Bash command is read-only the way it can verify that Edit is a write operation. This means plan mode's write-protection is not a full sandbox; it is a behavioral constraint paired with architectural enforcement for the deterministically-write tools.

9.2 The Plan File

The plan file is not ephemeral. It is a persistent artifact written to ~/.claude/plans/ with a randomly-generated human-readable name — a kebab-case string in the pattern of adjective-noun-surname: jolly-knitting-ullman.md, brave-sorting-mergesort.md. The naming scheme is deliberate whimsy that makes plans easy to identify in a directory listing without requiring a content hash or timestamp.

File Content

The harness does not enforce a schema on the plan file. The agent writes free-form markdown. A well-structured plan looks like this:

# Plan: Migrate Auth Module to OAuth 2.0

## Objective
Replace the current session-token auth in `src/auth/` with OAuth 2.0 using
the `python-oauth2lib` library. All existing tests must continue to pass.
No external-facing API changes.

## Current State
- `src/auth/session.py` manages tokens using a homegrown HMAC scheme
- `src/auth/middleware.py` validates tokens on every request
- `src/auth/models.py` defines the User and Session models
- `tests/auth/` has 23 tests covering happy path and expiry cases
- No refresh token support exists today

## What Changes
1. Add `OAuthProvider` class in `src/auth/oauth.py`
2. Update `Session` model to store OAuth tokens (add `refresh_token` field)
3. Migrate `middleware.py` to use OAuth token validation
4. Update `session.py` to delegate to `OAuthProvider`
5. Add migration `0012_add_refresh_token.py` for the DB schema change
6. Update `tests/auth/test_session.py` — 4 tests need new fixtures

## Risks
- Migration 0012 is irreversible once applied to production
- The OAuth library's token validation is synchronous; the middleware is async
  → Need to wrap with `asyncio.to_thread` or find the async variant

## Implementation Order
Must follow this order to avoid circular imports:
1. models.py (data layer first)
2. oauth.py (new provider, no dependencies on existing auth)
3. session.py (update to use oauth.py)
4. middleware.py (update last — depends on session.py)
5. migration file
6. tests

## Files Modified
- src/auth/models.py
- src/auth/session.py
- src/auth/middleware.py
- tests/auth/test_session.py

## Files Created
- src/auth/oauth.py
- migrations/0012_add_refresh_token.py

This is not a template the harness enforces — it is what a good agent produces when it has explored thoroughly. The quality of the plan file directly predicts the quality of the implementation.

planWasEdited

When the user reviews the plan in the Claude Code web UI or presses Ctrl+G in the terminal UI, they can edit the plan directly in the interface. The harness tracks whether the file was modified between the time the agent wrote it and the time the user approved.

When ExitPlanMode returns, the planWasEdited field carries this signal:

export interface ExitPlanModeOutput {
  plan: string | null;
  isAgent: boolean;
  filePath?: string;
  hasTaskTool?: boolean;
  planWasEdited?: boolean;
  awaitingLeaderApproval?: boolean;
  requestId?: string;
}

When planWasEdited is true, the agent should re-read the plan from the returned content (or filePath) before implementing. The user may have adjusted scope, reordered steps, or added constraints. An agent that ignores planWasEdited and implements from its in-memory version of the plan will diverge from what the user approved.

A well-written harness agent handles this explicitly:

const result = await exitPlanMode();

if (result.planWasEdited) {
  // User changed the plan — use their version, not ours
  const approvedPlan = result.plan ?? fs.readFileSync(result.filePath!, 'utf8');
  // Re-parse and proceed with the edited plan
  await implementFromPlan(approvedPlan);
} else {
  // Plan was approved as-written
  await implementFromPlan(inMemoryPlan);
}

awaitingLeaderApproval and requestId

In multi-agent workflows, a subagent running as a teammate does not surface plans directly to the user. Instead, it sets awaitingLeaderApproval: true and returns a requestId. The leader agent is responsible for receiving this approval request, reviewing the plan, and either approving or rejecting it.

This is the harness's mechanism for human-in-the-loop approval in agent hierarchies. An autonomous agent team does not bypass plan review just because there is no interactive terminal. The approval request routes up the hierarchy until it reaches either a human or a designated leader agent with approval authority.

The requestId is an opaque string — a UUID — that the leader uses when responding to the approval request. It allows the harness to correlate approvals with the correct pending plan even when multiple subagents are waiting simultaneously.

9.3 AskUserQuestion

AskUserQuestion is the structured interaction tool. Where the rest of the tool surface is about doing things — reading files, running commands, writing code — AskUserQuestion is about resolving ambiguity before doing the wrong thing.

The interface is richer than it first appears:

export interface AskUserQuestionInput {
  questions: [{
    question: string;      // clear, ends with ?
    header: string;        // max 12 chars, shown as chip/tag
    options: [{
      label: string;       // 1-5 words
      description: string;
      preview?: string;    // markdown in monospace box (single-select only)
    }];
    multiSelect: boolean;
  }];
  answers?: { [question: string]: string };
  annotations?: { [question: string]: { preview?: string; notes?: string } };
  metadata?: { source?: string };
}

The constraints are deliberate UX choices:

  • 1–4 questions per call. More than four and the user will feel interrogated. Fewer than one and you should just proceed.
  • 2–4 options per question. Forces the agent to think about the actual decision space before presenting it. If you cannot fit the real choices into four options, the question is probably too broad.
  • Header max 12 chars. This renders as a chip or tag in the UI — it needs to be a label, not a sentence. "Database", "Strategy", "Timeline" are headers. "Which option for the database migration approach?" is not.

The Preview Field

When any option in a single-select question includes a preview field, the UI switches from a simple list to a side-by-side layout: the option list on the left, the preview rendered in a monospace box on the right. As the user highlights different options, the preview updates to show what they would get.

This is the agent's mechanism for showing rather than telling. Instead of describing what a generated output would look like, the agent can generate a concrete sample and attach it to the option:

await askUserQuestion({
  questions: [{
    question: "Which error message format should the API use?",
    header: "Error Format",
    multiSelect: false,
    options: [
      {
        label: "RFC 7807 Problem Details",
        description: "Standard format with type, title, status, detail fields",
        preview: `{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/not-found",
  "title": "Resource Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "User with ID 'abc123' does not exist",
  "instance": "/users/abc123"
}`
      },
      {
        label: "Simple JSON",
        description: "Minimal error object with code and message",
        preview: `{
  "code": "NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "User with ID 'abc123' does not exist"
}`
      },
      {
        label: "GraphQL-style",
        description: "Errors array for consistency with GraphQL clients",
        preview: `{
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "User with ID 'abc123' does not exist",
      "extensions": { "code": "NOT_FOUND" }
    }
  ]
}`
      }
    ]
  }]
});

The user sees all three formats side by side. They do not need to remember option descriptions — they can see the actual output. For decisions where visual comparison matters (code style, output format, schema design), this is significantly better than a text description.

Note that preview only works meaningfully for single-select questions. If multiSelect is true, the side-by-side layout does not apply — the preview field is ignored.

multiSelect

When multiSelect: true, the user can select multiple options. The answer returned is the selected labels joined with commas:

"RFC 7807 Problem Details,GraphQL-style"

The agent parses this by splitting on , (comma-space). An agent that forgets to handle multiselect answers as a list rather than a single string will misinterpret the user's choices for any selection after the first.

The "Other" Option

Users always have an implicit "Other" option available. They can type a free-form response instead of selecting from the provided options. When this happens, the response field of AskUserQuestionOutput is populated with the user's text:

export interface AskUserQuestionOutput {
  questions: [...];
  answers: { [k: string]: string };
  response?: string;
  annotations?: { [k: string]: { preview?: string; notes?: string } };
  afkTimeoutMs?: number;
}

An agent reading the output should always check response first. If it is set, the user bypassed the structured options and gave their own answer. Ignoring response and only reading answers will silently discard the user's actual intent:

const output = await askUserQuestion({ questions: [...] });

for (const q of output.questions) {
  const answer = output.answers[q.question];
  const freeform = output.response;

  if (freeform) {
    // User gave a custom answer — parse it and adapt
    handleFreeformAnswer(freeform);
  } else if (answer) {
    handleStructuredAnswer(q.question, answer);
  }
}

Annotations

Annotations let the harness attach additional context to questions — a preview at the question level (not the option level) and notes that appear below a question. This is useful when the agent wants to explain the current state before asking the user to choose:

await askUserQuestion({
  questions: [{
    question: "How should we handle the deprecated endpoints?",
    header: "Endpoints",
    multiSelect: false,
    options: [
      { label: "Remove now", description: "Delete deprecated routes and their handlers" },
      { label: "Sunset header", description: "Keep routes but add Sunset and Deprecation headers" },
      { label: "Proxy forward", description: "Redirect deprecated paths to new equivalents" }
    ]
  }],
  annotations: {
    "How should we handle the deprecated endpoints?": {
      notes: "3 endpoints were deprecated in v2.1: /api/v1/users, /api/v1/sessions, /api/v1/tokens. Analytics shows 8 active callers in the last 30 days (3 internal, 5 unknown).",
      preview: "GET /api/v1/users → currently 1,240 req/day\nGET /api/v1/sessions → currently 890 req/day\nPOST /api/v1/tokens → currently 2,100 req/day"
    }
  }
});

The user sees the actual traffic data before making the deprecation decision. The annotation is not a description of the options — it is context about the situation that the agent discovered during exploration.

9.4 The afkTimeoutMs Auto-Resolution

In headless and automated environments, there is no human waiting at the terminal to answer AskUserQuestion dialogs. This creates a problem: if the agent asks a question and no one answers, the workflow stalls indefinitely.

The harness solves this with afkTimeoutMs. When the user does not respond to an AskUserQuestion within a configurable idle period, the harness auto-resolves the dialog. The first available option is selected as the default. The AskUserQuestionOutput returns with afkTimeoutMs set to the duration that elapsed before auto-resolution:

const output = await askUserQuestion({ questions: [...] });

if (output.afkTimeoutMs !== undefined) {
  // Auto-resolved — user was not present
  // afkTimeoutMs is the milliseconds that elapsed before timeout
  console.log(`Auto-resolved after ${output.afkTimeoutMs}ms idle`);
  // Treat answers with lower confidence — consider logging or notifying
}

What This Means for Harness Design

afkTimeoutMs being set is not an error — it is a signal. It tells the agent:

  1. The user was not present at the time of the question.
  2. The answer was auto-selected, not chosen.
  3. Decisions based on this answer carry reduced confidence.

Well-designed agents handle this differently from user-selected answers. In an architecture decision workflow, an auto-resolved answer might trigger a conservative default (preserve backward compatibility, do not delete, choose the reversible option) rather than proceeding with full confidence. In a teammate scenario, the auto-resolution might trigger a notification to the leader agent that approval was given by timeout, not by explicit review.

Headless Agents and Question Design

Because headless agents will frequently encounter afkTimeoutMs, the option ordering in AskUserQuestion matters more than it might seem. The first option is the auto-resolved default. Structure your questions so the first option is the safe, conservative, or most reversible choice:

// Good ordering — first option is safe default
options: [
  { label: "Preview mode", description: "Generate plan only, no changes" },
  { label: "Apply changes", description: "Implement immediately" },
  { label: "Apply and commit", description: "Implement and commit to git" }
]

// Bad ordering — destructive action is the default
options: [
  { label: "Drop and recreate", description: "Delete existing tables" },
  { label: "Migrate in place", description: "Use ALTER TABLE" },
  { label: "Skip migration", description: "Leave schema unchanged" }
]

In the bad example, a headless agent that times out will silently drop tables. The good example times out into a preview that produces no side effects.

9.5 Structured Answers

The output of AskUserQuestion carries two answer channels: the answers map for structured selections and response for freeform text.

The answers Map

answers is a flat map from question text to the user's selection. For single-select questions, the value is the label of the selected option. For multi-select, the value is a comma-separated string of selected labels:

// Single-select result
answers: {
  "Which database migration strategy should we use?": "Migrate in place"
}

// Multi-select result
answers: {
  "Which components need to be updated?": "Auth module,Session model,Middleware"
}

The key is the exact question text — including punctuation. This is worth noting: if you construct question text dynamically (interpolating filenames, counts, or context), you need to use the same dynamic value as the key when reading back from answers. A subtle mismatch — a trailing space, a different variable — produces an undefined lookup that silently discards the user's answer.

The robust pattern is to capture the question text when constructing the input and reuse it when reading the output:

const questionText = `Which of these ${files.length} files should be refactored?`;

const output = await askUserQuestion({
  questions: [{
    question: questionText,
    header: "Files",
    multiSelect: true,
    options: files.map(f => ({ label: f.name, description: f.path }))
  }]
});

const selected = output.answers[questionText]?.split(", ") ?? [];

The response Field

response captures what the user typed when they chose "Other" instead of selecting from the provided options. It is a plain string — no structure, no parsing guarantees. The agent needs to interpret it.

The presence of response means the agent's options did not fully model the decision space. This is useful feedback. A well-instrumented harness logs these freeform responses — they reveal gaps in the agent's understanding of what the user actually needs.

When response is set and answers is empty for a question, the user gave a fully freeform answer. When both response and entries in answers are set, the user selected options and also added text. Both are meaningful.

Pre-filling Answers

The answers input field on AskUserQuestionInput lets the harness pre-fill answers before presenting the dialog to the user. This is useful in two scenarios:

Resuming a workflow. If the agent was interrupted and needs to re-ask a question, it can pre-fill with the previously-recorded answer so the user does not have to re-enter it.

Suggesting a default. The agent can pre-fill the most likely answer based on its analysis, letting the user confirm or override rather than selecting from scratch:

await askUserQuestion({
  questions: [{
    question: "Which authentication approach should we migrate to?",
    header: "Auth Strategy",
    multiSelect: false,
    options: [
      { label: "OAuth 2.0 + PKCE", description: "Recommended for SPAs" },
      { label: "OAuth 2.0 + client credentials", description: "For service-to-service" },
      { label: "API keys", description: "Simple, no refresh flow" }
    ]
  }],
  answers: {
    "Which authentication approach should we migrate to?": "OAuth 2.0 + PKCE"
  }
});

The dialog opens with "OAuth 2.0 + PKCE" pre-selected. The user can accept it or choose differently.

9.6 Lab: Build an Architecture Decision Workflow

This lab builds a realistic workflow that uses plan mode and structured questions together: an agent that helps engineers make and document architecture decisions, producing an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) as output.

Workflow Design

The workflow has three phases:

  1. Discovery. Enter plan mode, explore the codebase to understand the relevant context.
  2. Decision. Use AskUserQuestion to capture the decision and its rationale.
  3. Documentation. Exit plan mode, write the ADR file.
flowchart TD
    A([User: "Create ADR for caching strategy"]) --> B[EnterPlanMode]
    B --> C[Read current architecture]
    C --> D[Grep for existing cache usage]
    D --> E[Read dependencies]
    E --> F[Write plan: ADR outline]
    F --> G[ExitPlanMode — user reviews outline]
    G --> H{User approved?}
    H -->|Yes| I[AskUserQuestion: context questions]
    I --> J[AskUserQuestion: decision questions]
    J --> K[Assemble ADR content]
    K --> L[Write ADR to docs/adr/]
    H -->|No, edited| G2[Re-read edited plan]
    G2 --> I

Implementation

async function runAdrWorkflow(topic: string): Promise<void> {
  // Phase 1: Enter plan mode and explore
  await enterPlanMode();

  // Explore the codebase for relevant context
  const packageJson = await read({ file_path: "./package.json" });
  const cacheUsage = await bash({
    command: "grep -rn 'cache\\|redis\\|memcached\\|lru' src/ --include='*.ts' -l",
    description: "Find existing cache usage"
  });
  const existingAdrs = await bash({
    command: "ls docs/adr/ 2>/dev/null || echo 'No ADRs yet'",
    description: "List existing ADRs"
  });

  // Write the plan — what the ADR will cover
  const planContent = `# Plan: ADR for ${topic}

## Exploration Findings
- Packages: ${extractRelevantDeps(packageJson)}
- Files with cache usage: ${cacheUsage.output}
- Existing ADRs: ${existingAdrs.output}

## ADR Outline
1. Context: Why this decision is needed
2. Decision drivers: Performance targets, team constraints
3. Considered options: 3 alternatives with tradeoffs
4. Decision: Which option and why
5. Consequences: What changes, what risks remain

## Files to Create
- docs/adr/ADR-${nextAdrNumber()}-${slugify(topic)}.md
`;

  await write({
    file_path: `${process.env.HOME}/.claude/plans/adr-workflow.md`,
    content: planContent
  });

  // Exit plan mode — user sees and approves the outline
  const approval = await exitPlanMode();

  if (!approval.plan) {
    throw new Error("Plan was rejected or not found");
  }

  // Use the approved plan (may have been edited)
  const workingPlan = approval.planWasEdited
    ? approval.plan
    : planContent;

  // Phase 2: Gather decision details with structured questions
  const contextAnswers = await askUserQuestion({
    questions: [
      {
        question: "What is the primary driver for this architectural decision?",
        header: "Driver",
        multiSelect: false,
        options: [
          {
            label: "Performance",
            description: "Latency or throughput requirements are the forcing function",
            preview: "Example context:\n\"API p99 latency exceeds 500ms under load.\nDB queries are the bottleneck (avg 200ms).\"\n\nThis ADR will focus on cache hit rates\nand eviction strategies."
          },
          {
            label: "Cost",
            description: "Infrastructure or operational cost needs to decrease",
            preview: "Example context:\n\"Database RCU costs $4,200/month.\nCache layer could reduce this by 60-80%.\"\n\nThis ADR will focus on cost modeling\nand ROI projections."
          },
          {
            label: "Scalability",
            description: "The current approach does not scale to projected load",
            preview: "Example context:\n\"Current architecture handles 500 req/s.\nProjected growth: 5,000 req/s in 6 months.\"\n\nThis ADR will focus on horizontal\nscaling characteristics."
          },
          {
            label: "Consistency",
            description: "Cache invalidation or data consistency is a current problem",
            preview: "Example context:\n\"Stale data causes user-visible inconsistencies.\n3 incidents in Q3 traced to cache.\"\n\nThis ADR will focus on invalidation\nstrategies and consistency guarantees."
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        question: "Which team constraints apply?",
        header: "Constraints",
        multiSelect: true,
        options: [
          { label: "No new infra", description: "Cannot add new infrastructure dependencies" },
          { label: "On-call limit", description: "Team on-call capacity is already at limit" },
          { label: "Budget cap", description: "Monthly infrastructure budget is fixed" },
          { label: "SLA requirement", description: "Decision must maintain existing SLA commitments" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  });

  const decisionAnswers = await askUserQuestion({
    questions: [
      {
        question: "Which caching approach should be adopted?",
        header: "Decision",
        multiSelect: false,
        options: [
          {
            label: "Redis cluster",
            description: "Distributed cache, supports pub/sub for invalidation",
            preview: `// Cache read pattern\nconst cached = await redis.get(key);\nif (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);\n\nconst result = await db.query(...);\nawait redis.setex(key, TTL, JSON.stringify(result));\nreturn result;`
          },
          {
            label: "In-process LRU",
            description: "No network hop, zero infra, per-instance cache",
            preview: `// Cache read pattern\nconst lru = new LRUCache({ max: 1000, ttl: 60_000 });\n\nconst cached = lru.get(key);\nif (cached) return cached;\n\nconst result = await db.query(...);\nlru.set(key, result);\nreturn result;`
          },
          {
            label: "CDN edge cache",
            description: "Cache at the CDN layer for public read-heavy endpoints",
            preview: `// Response headers pattern\nres.set('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=300');\nres.set('Surrogate-Key', \`user-\${userId}\`);\n\n// Invalidation\nawait cdn.purgeByTag(\`user-\${userId}\`);`
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        question: "What is the status of this ADR?",
        header: "Status",
        multiSelect: false,
        options: [
          { label: "Proposed", description: "Under discussion, not yet decided" },
          { label: "Accepted", description: "Decision made, implementation pending" },
          { label: "Superseded", description: "Replaces an earlier ADR" }
        ]
      }
    ],
    annotations: {
      "Which caching approach should be adopted?": {
        notes: `Based on codebase exploration:\n${cacheUsage.output || "No existing cache usage found"}`
      }
    }
  });

  // Phase 3: Write the ADR
  const driver = contextAnswers.answers["What is the primary driver for this architectural decision?"];
  const constraints = contextAnswers.answers["Which team constraints apply?"]?.split(", ") ?? [];
  const decision = decisionAnswers.answers["Which caching approach should be adopted?"];
  const status = decisionAnswers.answers["What is the status of this ADR?"];
  const freeform = decisionAnswers.response;

  const adrContent = assembleAdr({
    topic,
    driver,
    constraints,
    decision: freeform ?? decision,
    status,
    workingPlan
  });

  const adrNumber = nextAdrNumber();
  const adrPath = `docs/adr/ADR-${String(adrNumber).padStart(4, '0')}-${slugify(topic)}.md`;

  await write({ file_path: adrPath, content: adrContent });

  console.log(`ADR written to ${adrPath}`);
}

The assembleAdr Function

function assembleAdr(params: {
  topic: string;
  driver: string;
  constraints: string[];
  decision: string;
  status: string;
  workingPlan: string;
}): string {
  const { topic, driver, constraints, decision, status } = params;
  const date = new Date().toISOString().split('T')[0];

  return `# ADR-${nextAdrNumber()}: ${topic}

## Status: ${status}
## Date: ${date}

## Context

${driver} is the primary driver for this decision.${
    constraints.length > 0
      ? `\n\nConstraints: ${constraints.join(", ")}.`
      : ""
  }

## Decision

${decision}

## Consequences

### Positive
- Addresses the ${driver.toLowerCase()} requirement
- Decision is documented and reviewable

### Negative
- Requires implementation and migration effort
- Team needs to understand the new approach

### Risks
- See constraints: ${constraints.join(", ") || "none identified"}
`;
}

Running the Lab

To exercise this workflow locally:

  1. Create a test project directory with a src/ folder and some TypeScript files that reference caching.
  2. Create a docs/adr/ directory (or let the workflow handle its absence).
  3. Invoke runAdrWorkflow("read-through cache strategy").
  4. In the plan mode approval step, edit the plan outline — add a constraint or change a section heading. Observe that planWasEdited is true in the ExitPlanMode output.
  5. In the question steps, try typing a custom answer in the "Other" field instead of selecting an option. Observe that response is set.
  6. Kill the process during the second AskUserQuestion and restart it. Add afkTimeoutMs handling — log a warning and default to the safe option.

What to Observe

The lab surfaces three behaviors that are easy to miss in documentation:

Plan editing is load-bearing. When you edit the plan and watch the agent re-read it from the file rather than its in-memory copy, you see why planWasEdited exists. The agent implementing from an outdated in-memory plan after the user changed it is a real failure mode.

Preview layout changes UX. In the decision question, all three options have preview content. If you compare this dialog to the same question without previews, the difference in decision confidence is immediate — seeing the actual code pattern changes how quickly and confidently the user picks.

afkTimeoutMs changes behavior semantics. When the timeout fires and auto-selects "Proposed" as the ADR status, the resulting document is correct but incomplete. A production workflow should detect this and either flag the ADR for review or send a notification that the status was auto-filled.

Summary

Plan mode and AskUserQuestion are the harness's tools for deliberate collaboration. Plan mode enforces a separation between thinking and acting — the agent explores and designs before it writes a single file, and the user approves before implementation begins. AskUserQuestion gives the agent a structured way to resolve genuine ambiguity while staying productive.

The key implementation details to carry forward:

  • EnterPlanMode takes no parameters and restricts Edit and Write at execution time.
  • The plan file lives in ~/.claude/plans/ and is the artifact that survives the approval gate.
  • planWasEdited in ExitPlanModeOutput is not informational — the agent must re-read the plan from the returned content if it is set.
  • awaitingLeaderApproval and requestId enable plan approval routing in multi-agent hierarchies.
  • AskUserQuestion supports 1–4 questions with 2–4 options each; the preview field activates a side-by-side layout for single-select questions.
  • Option ordering matters: the first option is the afkTimeoutMs auto-resolution default — make it the safe choice.
  • Always check response before answers — freeform answers override the structured option surface.

In Chapter 10, we go into the Task system: TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskUpdate, TaskOutput, and TaskStop — the harness's mechanism for long-running background work that outlives the current control loop iteration.

Next: Chapter 10: The Task System

Chapter 10: Task Management — TaskCreate/Get/Update/List

"A task that exists only in the model's context window is not a task. It is a hope."

10.1 Task Lifecycle: pending → in_progress → completed (or deleted)

The task system is Claude Code's answer to a fundamental problem in long-running agentic work: the model's working memory is a context window. Every time the control loop makes another API call, the model reconstructs its understanding of what it was doing from the conversation history. For short tasks — five tool calls, done in thirty seconds — this is fine. For multi-hour workflows spanning hundreds of tool calls, it is not. The conversation gets compressed, context gets lost, and the model drifts.

Tasks are persistent, structured state that lives outside the context window. They survive compaction. A subagent can pick up a task that another agent created an hour ago. An autonomous daemon can check what work remains after a session restart. Tasks are the harness's equivalent of a ticket system — lightweight, structured, and authoritative even when the model's own memory is not.

The lifecycle is a state machine with four states:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> pending : TaskCreate
    pending --> in_progress : TaskUpdate(status=in_progress)
    in_progress --> pending : TaskUpdate(status=pending)
    in_progress --> completed : TaskUpdate(status=completed)
    completed --> [*]
    pending --> deleted : TaskUpdate(status=deleted)
    in_progress --> deleted : TaskUpdate(status=deleted)

pending is the initial state. A pending task exists and is known, but no agent has claimed it. In a multi-agent system, pending tasks are the pool of available work. The rule is simple: work on tasks in ID order — lowest UUID first — to avoid two agents claiming the same task.

in_progress means an agent has claimed the task and is actively working on it. The protocol is explicit: mark the task in_progress before you start work, not after you think about it. This is how multi-agent systems avoid duplicate effort. The moment you call TaskUpdate({taskId, status: "in_progress"}), you have claimed the task.

completed is terminal. A task is completed only when the work is fully done — implementation complete, tests passing, documentation updated, whatever the definition of done is for that task. Do not mark completed speculatively. The harness does not verify completion; the model is on its honor.

deleted is permanent removal. Use it for tasks that are no longer relevant — requirements changed, the work was superseded, the task was created by mistake. Deleted tasks do not appear in TaskList.

Tasks persist to ~/.claude/tasks/ as UUID-named files. The UUID is the task ID:

~/.claude/tasks/
├── 0ae4483c-d05d-4401-b142-6e178f173fd5.json
├── 1b7f2234-a891-4c12-b339-9d4e2f8a1c67.json
└── 3cc89105-e123-4567-8abc-def012345678.json

This means tasks survive session restarts, --resume, and context compaction. They are the closest thing to persistent project state in the standard harness.

When a task is created in Claude Code v2.1.84+, the TaskCreated hook fires. This is an extension point: a hook at .claude/hooks/ listening for TaskCreated events can write to an external ticket system, update a dashboard, or send a notification. The hook receives the task ID and subject in its JSON payload.

10.2 TaskCreate: subject, description, activeForm, metadata

TaskCreate takes four fields. Understanding what each one is for — and what the harness does with it — prevents the common mistake of treating them as cosmetic.

export interface TaskCreateInput {
  subject: string;       // brief title, imperative form
  description: string;   // what needs to be done
  activeForm?: string;   // present continuous shown in spinner ("Running tests")
  metadata?: { [k: string]: any };
}

export interface TaskCreateOutput {
  task: { id: string; subject: string };
}

subject is the task title. Write it in imperative form — "Implement auth timeout fix", "Run regression tests", "Review PR #1234". It appears in TaskList output and in the spinner UI. Keep it under sixty characters; it gets truncated in narrow terminals.

description is where the actual work specification lives. This is the field a subagent reads when it picks up a task. It should be self-contained: what needs to be done, what constraints apply, what done looks like. Do not assume the agent reading the description has any of the context from when the task was created. Write it as if handing off to a colleague who is starting cold.

A good description:

Refactor the session timeout constant in src/auth/session.py.

The constant SESSION_TIMEOUT_MINUTES is currently defined in three places:
- src/auth/session.py:1
- config/legacy_constants.py:47
- config/app_settings.py:83

The config parser reads only config/legacy_constants.py. The other two are dead.

Steps:
1. Consolidate to a single source of truth in config/app_settings.py
2. Update the config parser to read from app_settings.py
3. Remove the dead constants from session.py and legacy_constants.py
4. Run pytest tests/auth/ — all tests must pass before marking complete

A bad description: "Fix the timeout thing we talked about earlier."

activeForm is the present-continuous string shown in the spinner while an agent is working on this task: "Refactoring session timeout", "Running auth tests", "Reviewing PR diff". It is cosmetic in function but important in practice — it is what a human watching the spinner reads to understand what is happening right now. If not provided, the harness falls back to something generic.

metadata is an arbitrary key-value store attached to the task. It supports any JSON-serializable values. Common uses:

// Link to external ticket
metadata: { jiraId: "AUTH-1234", priority: "high" }

// Record origin context
metadata: { createdBy: "sec-pr-agent", orgId: "NMDAbbott", prId: "35989" }

// Track implementation details
metadata: { targetFile: "src/auth/session.py", testCommand: "pytest tests/auth/" }

Metadata uses merge semantics on TaskUpdate: keys you provide are merged into the existing metadata, and keys you set to null are deleted. You do not need to re-send the entire metadata object to add one key.

A minimal TaskCreate call:

// Minimal — description carries the weight
const result = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Implement rate limiting middleware",
  description: `
Add rate limiting to all public API endpoints.

Requirements:
- 100 requests/minute per IP for unauthenticated requests
- 1000 requests/minute per API key for authenticated requests
- Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header when exceeded
- Use Redis for the token bucket (connection at REDIS_URL env var)
- Tests in tests/middleware/test_rate_limit.py

Definition of done: all existing tests pass + new tests cover the happy path,
rate-exceeded path, and authenticated vs unauthenticated distinction.
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Implementing rate limiting",
  metadata: { milestone: "v2.1", estimatedHours: 3 }
});

// result.task.id is the UUID you use for all subsequent calls
const taskId = result.task.id;

10.3 TaskUpdate: status transitions, addBlocks/addBlockedBy, owner assignment

TaskUpdate is the most powerful task operation. It handles status transitions, dependency graph mutations, and ownership changes in a single call.

export interface TaskUpdateInput {
  taskId: string;
  status?: "pending" | "in_progress" | "completed" | "deleted";
  subject?: string;
  description?: string;
  activeForm?: string;
  owner?: string;
  metadata?: { [k: string]: any };  // merge keys, null to delete
  addBlocks?: string[];      // task IDs this task blocks
  addBlockedBy?: string[];   // task IDs that block this task
}

export interface TaskUpdateOutput {
  success: boolean;
  taskId: string;
  updatedFields: string[];
  error?: string;
  statusChange?: { from: string; to: string };
}

Status Transitions

The status workflow enforces intent. The rule is: mark in_progress before starting, mark completed only when fully done.

// Claim the task before starting work
await TaskUpdate({ taskId, status: "in_progress" });

// ... do the work ...

// Verify: run tests, check output, confirm done
// Only then:
await TaskUpdate({ taskId, status: "completed" });

The statusChange field in the output tells you what the previous status was. This matters in multi-agent systems where another agent may have already claimed the task between your TaskList and your TaskUpdate. If statusChange.from is "in_progress" but you expected "pending", someone else has the task.

To handle a blocked situation without abandoning work, keep the task in_progress and create a new task for the blocker:

// Discovered mid-work that Redis is not configured
await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Configure Redis for rate limiting tests",
  description: "REDIS_URL is not set in .env.test. Add local Redis config.",
  activeForm: "Configuring Redis"
});

// Keep the original task in_progress — you will return to it
// Do NOT flip it back to pending unless you are truly releasing it

The Dependency Graph: addBlocks and addBlockedBy

This is the feature that separates the task system from a flat todo list. addBlocks and addBlockedBy create directed edges in the dependency graph. A task that has blockers in blockedBy cannot be started — in a well-disciplined multi-agent system, agents skip tasks whose dependencies are unresolved.

The graph is built incrementally. You can establish dependencies at creation time or add them later as you discover them:

// Task A: write the database schema
const schemaTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Write database schema for user sessions",
  description: "...",
});

// Task B: write the session service — depends on A
const serviceTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Implement SessionService class",
  description: "...",
});

// Establish the dependency
await TaskUpdate({
  taskId: serviceTask.task.id,
  addBlockedBy: [schemaTask.task.id]
});
// Now serviceTask.blockedBy = [schemaTask.task.id]
// schemaTask.blocks = [serviceTask.task.id]

The edges are bidirectional in the data model but semantically one-directional: blockedBy means "I cannot start until these are done", blocks means "these tasks are waiting for me." When you call addBlockedBy on task B with task A's ID, the harness automatically adds task B's ID to task A's blocks array. You do not need to call addBlocks separately.

Visualizing a dependency graph for a realistic feature implementation:

graph TD
    A["Schema migration\n(pending)"]
    B["SessionService class\n(pending)"]
    C["Rate limit middleware\n(pending)"]
    D["Integration tests\n(pending)"]
    E["Update API docs\n(pending)"]
    F["Deploy to staging\n(pending)"]

    A -->|blocks| B
    A -->|blocks| C
    B -->|blocks| D
    C -->|blocks| D
    D -->|blocks| E
    D -->|blocks| F

    style A fill:#f0f0f0
    style B fill:#ffe0b2
    style C fill:#ffe0b2
    style D fill:#fff9c4
    style E fill:#fff9c4
    style F fill:#fff9c4

In this graph, A is the only task immediately available (no blockers). B and C become available when A completes. D is blocked by both B and C — it cannot start until both are done. E and F are blocked by D.

A multi-agent orchestrator scanning this list with TaskList would:

  1. See A is pending with no blockers → assign it
  2. Poll or watch; when A completes, B and C are unblocked → assign both in parallel
  3. When both B and C complete, D is unblocked → assign it
  4. When D completes, E and F are unblocked → assign both in parallel

Owner Assignment

The owner field is a free-form string identifying which agent holds a task. The harness does not enforce ownership semantics — it is a coordination mechanism, not a lock. By convention:

// Claim with your agent ID before marking in_progress
await TaskUpdate({
  taskId,
  owner: "agent-sec-pr-nmda",
  status: "in_progress"
});

In a team-based agent system, agents scan TaskList and skip tasks whose owner is set to a different agent name. This is a cooperative protocol — it relies on agents following the convention, not on the harness enforcing it.

10.4 TaskGet: full details including description, blocks, blockedBy

TaskList gives you a summary. TaskGet gives you everything.

export interface TaskGetInput {
  taskId: string;
}

export interface TaskGetOutput {
  task: {
    id: string;
    subject: string;
    description: string;
    status: "pending" | "in_progress" | "completed";
    blocks: string[];     // tasks waiting on this one
    blockedBy: string[];  // tasks that must complete first
  } | null;
}

The task field is null if the task does not exist or has been deleted. Always check for null before accessing fields.

The primary use of TaskGet is reading the full description before starting work:

const result = await TaskGet({ taskId: "0ae4483c-d05d-4401-b142-6e178f173fd5" });

if (!result.task) {
  // Task was deleted or never existed — skip
  return;
}

if (result.task.status === "in_progress" && result.task.owner !== myAgentId) {
  // Another agent owns this task — skip
  return;
}

// Read the full description to understand what needs to be done
const { description, blockedBy, blocks } = result.task;

// Check if all blockers are resolved before claiming
// (In practice, TaskList already filters this — TaskGet is for the full spec)

TaskGet is also how you inspect the dependency graph from a specific task's perspective. When you complete a task and want to know what you have unblocked:

// After marking a task completed
await TaskUpdate({ taskId: schemaTaskId, status: "completed" });

// Check what was unblocked
const completed = await TaskGet({ taskId: schemaTaskId });
if (completed.task) {
  const nowUnblocked = completed.task.blocks; // task IDs waiting on this one
  // You could trigger agents for these, or just let the next TaskList pick them up
}

10.5 TaskList: summary view (id, subject, status, owner, blockedBy)

TaskList takes no parameters and returns a summary of all non-deleted tasks:

export interface TaskListInput {}  // no parameters

export interface TaskListOutput {
  tasks: {
    id: string;
    subject: string;
    status: "pending" | "in_progress" | "completed";
    owner?: string;
    blockedBy: string[];
  }[];
}

This is the harness's global work queue. Every autonomous agent in a multi-agent system calls TaskList after completing a task to find what to do next. The absence of parameters is intentional — the list is global, not scoped per agent.

Reading the list intelligently requires filtering. A well-behaved agent applies these rules in order:

  1. Skip completed tasks — already done
  2. Skip in_progress tasks owned by another agent — claimed
  3. Skip tasks with unresolved blockedBy — not yet available
  4. From the remaining pending tasks with no blockers, take the lowest ID first

In practice:

const { tasks } = await TaskList({});

// Build a set of completed task IDs for fast lookup
const completedIds = new Set(
  tasks.filter(t => t.status === "completed").map(t => t.id)
);

// Find the next available task
const available = tasks
  .filter(t => t.status === "pending")
  .filter(t => !t.owner || t.owner === myAgentId)
  .filter(t => t.blockedBy.every(depId => completedIds.has(depId)))
  .sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id));  // lowest UUID first

if (available.length === 0) {
  // Check if there is still in_progress work (wait) or all done (terminate)
  const inProgress = tasks.filter(t => t.status === "in_progress");
  if (inProgress.length > 0) {
    // Work is ongoing — wait and retry
  } else {
    // Nothing left — all done or graph is stuck (cycle or orphaned tasks)
  }
}

const next = available[0];

Call TaskList after completing each task, not just at startup. The task graph is dynamic — tasks can be added by other agents mid-flight. Polling the list is how an agent discovers newly unblocked work.

10.6 The TodoWrite Tool: alternative lightweight todo list

TodoWrite is a simpler, flat alternative to the full task system. No UUIDs, no dependency graph, no ownership, no persistence to disk — just an in-memory list of items with statuses.

export interface TodoWriteInput {
  todos: {
    content: string;
    status: "pending" | "in_progress" | "completed";
    activeForm: string;
  }[];
}

export interface TodoWriteOutput {
  oldTodos: { content: string; status: string; activeForm: string }[];
  newTodos: { content: string; status: string; activeForm: string }[];
}

TodoWrite replaces the entire list on every call. The output gives you oldTodos (what was there before) and newTodos (what is there now). To update a single item's status, you re-send the entire list with that item's status changed.

When to use TodoWrite instead of TaskCreate:

ConcernTaskCreate/UpdateTodoWrite
Persistence across sessionsYes — ~/.claude/tasks/No — in-memory only
Multi-agent coordinationYes — owner + blockedByNo
Dependency graphYes — blocks/blockedByNo
External hooks (TaskCreated)YesNo
SimplicityHigher overheadMinimal
When it fitsLong-running, multi-agent workSingle-session, single-agent checklists

A typical TodoWrite pattern for a single-agent sequential workflow:

// Establish the work plan at the start
await TodoWrite({
  todos: [
    { content: "Read and understand current session.py", status: "pending", activeForm: "Reading session module" },
    { content: "Find all timeout constant references", status: "pending", activeForm: "Searching codebase" },
    { content: "Consolidate to single source of truth", status: "pending", activeForm: "Refactoring constants" },
    { content: "Run pytest tests/auth/", status: "pending", activeForm: "Running tests" },
    { content: "Commit with descriptive message", status: "pending", activeForm: "Committing changes" },
  ]
});

// After completing step 1, update the list
await TodoWrite({
  todos: [
    { content: "Read and understand current session.py", status: "completed", activeForm: "Reading session module" },
    { content: "Find all timeout constant references", status: "in_progress", activeForm: "Searching codebase" },
    // ... rest unchanged
  ]
});

The oldTodos in the response lets you verify what was there before the write — useful for detecting concurrent modification if you are somehow sharing a TodoWrite list (unusual, and not recommended; use TaskCreate for multi-agent scenarios).

TodoWrite is the right tool when you are a single agent working through a linear checklist within one session and you want the spinner to show meaningful progress text. Use TaskCreate when work spans sessions, involves multiple agents, or requires dependency tracking.

10.7 Lab: Implement a Project Manager Agent Using Task Dependencies and Ownership

This lab builds a project manager agent — an agent whose job is to decompose a feature request into tasks, establish the dependency graph, assign agents to execute the work, and monitor completion.

The Scenario

Build a rate limiting feature for an API service. The work spans multiple concerns: database migration, service implementation, middleware, tests, documentation, and deployment. The project manager agent coordinates four worker agents running in parallel where possible, serialized where dependencies require it.

Step 1: The Project Manager Agent

Create the agent definition at .claude/agents/project-manager.md:

---
name: project-manager
description: Decomposes feature requests into tasks, manages dependencies, assigns work to worker agents
tools: TaskCreate, TaskUpdate, TaskList, TaskGet, Agent
model: claude-sonnet-4-6
effort: medium
---

You are a project manager agent. Your job is to:
1. Decompose the given feature request into discrete, well-specified tasks
2. Establish dependency relationships between tasks
3. Assign tasks to worker agents in dependency order
4. Monitor completion and unblock downstream tasks
5. Report completion when all tasks are done

Always write task descriptions that are self-contained — a worker agent reading the description
must not need any other context to complete the work.

Mark yourself as owner of tasks you are managing. Use "pm-agent" as your owner ID.
Work on tasks in ID order (lowest first) when multiple are available.

Step 2: Decompose the Feature into Tasks

The project manager receives a feature request and creates the full task graph before assigning any work:

// Project manager creates all tasks first, then wires dependencies

// Leaf tasks (no blockers)
const migrationTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Write Redis session schema and migration",
  description: `
Create the Redis key schema for session storage.

Schema:
- Key pattern: session:{uuid}
- Value: JSON with { userId, createdAt, expiresAt, ipAddress }
- TTL: set to expiresAt - now in seconds

Files to create:
- src/db/migrations/0042_add_session_redis.py
- src/db/session_schema.py (document the key pattern and field spec)

Done when: migration runs cleanly against test Redis instance,
schema doc is accurate, pytest tests/db/test_session_schema.py passes.
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Writing session schema",
  metadata: { component: "database", estimatedHours: 1 }
});

const redisConfigTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Configure Redis test environment",
  description: `
Add Redis configuration to test environment.

Requirements:
- Add REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/1 to .env.test
- Add redis (>=4.6.0) to requirements-test.txt
- Verify connection in conftest.py with a pytest fixture that flushes test DB between runs

Done when: pytest fixtures connect to Redis and cleanup between tests.
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Configuring test Redis",
  metadata: { component: "infrastructure", estimatedHours: 0.5 }
});

// Tasks blocked by migration
const serviceTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Implement SessionService class",
  description: `
Build the SessionService using the schema from task ${migrationTask.task.id}.

Requirements:
- src/services/session_service.py
- Methods: create(userId, ipAddress) → sessionId, get(sessionId) → Session | None,
  invalidate(sessionId) → bool, extend(sessionId, minutes) → bool
- Use the key pattern from src/db/session_schema.py
- Handle Redis connection errors with SessionStorageError
- All methods typed, docstrings, no magic values

Done when: pytest tests/services/test_session_service.py passes (write the tests).
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Implementing SessionService",
  metadata: { component: "service", estimatedHours: 2 }
});

const middlewareTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Implement session auth middleware",
  description: `
Build FastAPI middleware that validates session tokens using SessionService.

Middleware behavior:
- Extract Bearer token from Authorization header
- Call SessionService.get(token) — if None, return 401 Unauthorized
- Attach session object to request.state.session
- Log failed auth attempts (not the token itself)
- Skip auth for paths in UNAUTHENTICATED_PATHS (config value)

Files:
- src/middleware/session_auth.py
- Update src/app.py to register the middleware

Done when: pytest tests/middleware/test_session_auth.py passes.
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Implementing auth middleware",
  metadata: { component: "middleware", estimatedHours: 1.5 }
});

// Integration tests blocked by service + middleware
const integrationTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Write end-to-end session auth integration tests",
  description: `
Integration tests for the full session auth flow.

Test scenarios:
1. Create session → make authenticated request → succeeds
2. Make request with expired session → 401 returned
3. Make request with invalid token → 401 returned
4. Invalidate session → subsequent request returns 401
5. Concurrent requests on same session → all succeed

Tests in tests/integration/test_session_auth_e2e.py
Use real Redis (from .env.test fixture), real FastAPI test client.
No mocks.

Done when: all 5 scenarios pass.
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Writing integration tests",
  metadata: { component: "testing", estimatedHours: 2 }
});

// Docs and deploy blocked by integration tests
const docsTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Document session auth API in OpenAPI spec",
  description: `
Update the OpenAPI documentation to reflect session auth requirements.

Changes:
- Add Bearer token security scheme
- Mark all protected endpoints with the security scheme
- Document 401 response for all protected endpoints
- Add /auth/session (POST) and /auth/session/{id} (DELETE) endpoints to spec
- Update README.md authentication section

Done when: openapi.yaml validates with spectral and docs accurately reflect the implementation.
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Writing API docs",
  metadata: { component: "documentation", estimatedHours: 1 }
});

const deployTask = await TaskCreate({
  subject: "Deploy session auth to staging",
  description: `
Deploy the session auth feature to staging environment.

Checklist:
1. Confirm REDIS_URL is set in staging environment secrets
2. Run migration in staging: python -m alembic upgrade head
3. Deploy updated service image
4. Smoke test: create session via /auth/session, make authenticated request, verify 200
5. Monitor error rate for 5 minutes post-deploy

Done when: smoke test passes and error rate is nominal.
  `.trim(),
  activeForm: "Deploying to staging",
  metadata: { component: "deployment", estimatedHours: 1 }
});

Step 3: Wire the Dependency Graph

// Service and middleware both depend on the schema migration
await TaskUpdate({
  taskId: serviceTask.task.id,
  addBlockedBy: [migrationTask.task.id]
});
await TaskUpdate({
  taskId: middlewareTask.task.id,
  addBlockedBy: [migrationTask.task.id]
});

// Integration tests depend on both service and middleware
await TaskUpdate({
  taskId: integrationTask.task.id,
  addBlockedBy: [serviceTask.task.id, middlewareTask.task.id, redisConfigTask.task.id]
});

// Docs and deploy depend on integration tests passing
await TaskUpdate({
  taskId: docsTask.task.id,
  addBlockedBy: [integrationTask.task.id]
});
await TaskUpdate({
  taskId: deployTask.task.id,
  addBlockedBy: [integrationTask.task.id]
});

The dependency graph now looks like this:

graph TD
    A["Schema migration\n(pending)"]
    B["Redis config\n(pending)"]
    C["SessionService\n(pending)"]
    D["Auth middleware\n(pending)"]
    E["Integration tests\n(pending)"]
    F["API docs\n(pending)"]
    G["Deploy to staging\n(pending)"]

    A -->|unblocks| C
    A -->|unblocks| D
    B -->|unblocks| E
    C -->|unblocks| E
    D -->|unblocks| E
    E -->|unblocks| F
    E -->|unblocks| G

    style A fill:#c8e6c9
    style B fill:#c8e6c9
    style C fill:#ffe0b2
    style D fill:#ffe0b2
    style E fill:#fff9c4
    style F fill:#ffcdd2
    style G fill:#ffcdd2

A and B are immediately available (green). C and D become available when A completes (orange). E becomes available when B, C, and D all complete (yellow). F and G are last (red).

Step 4: The Execution Loop

async function executeProjectPlan(workerAgentCount: number = 4) {
  const completedIds = new Set<string>();

  while (true) {
    const { tasks } = await TaskList({});

    // Update our completed set
    tasks
      .filter(t => t.status === "completed")
      .forEach(t => completedIds.add(t.id));

    // Find available work
    const available = tasks
      .filter(t => t.status === "pending")
      .filter(t => !t.owner)
      .filter(t => t.blockedBy.every(dep => completedIds.has(dep)))
      .sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id));

    // Check for completion
    const unfinished = tasks.filter(t => t.status !== "completed");
    if (unfinished.length === 0) {
      break; // All done
    }

    // Assign available tasks to worker agents (up to workerAgentCount at once)
    const toAssign = available.slice(0, workerAgentCount);

    await Promise.all(toAssign.map(async (task) => {
      // Claim the task before spawning the worker
      await TaskUpdate({
        taskId: task.id,
        owner: "worker-agent",
        status: "in_progress"
      });

      // Read the full spec
      const { task: fullTask } = await TaskGet({ taskId: task.id });
      if (!fullTask) return;

      // Spawn a worker agent with the task spec
      await Agent({
        prompt: `
You are a worker agent. Complete the following task and mark it completed when done.

Task ID: ${task.id}
Subject: ${fullTask.subject}

Description:
${fullTask.description}

When you are fully done (implementation complete, tests passing):
Call TaskUpdate({ taskId: "${task.id}", status: "completed" })

Do not mark completed until the work is fully verified.
        `.trim(),
        description: `Execute: ${task.subject}`,
        run_in_background: true
      });
    }));

    // Wait before next poll — give workers time to make progress
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 15000));
  }
}

Step 5: Verify the Outcome

After the loop terminates:

const { tasks } = await TaskList({});
const summary = {
  total: tasks.length,
  completed: tasks.filter(t => t.status === "completed").length,
  inProgress: tasks.filter(t => t.status === "in_progress").length,
  pending: tasks.filter(t => t.status === "pending").length,
};

// All tasks should be completed
console.log(summary);
// { total: 7, completed: 7, inProgress: 0, pending: 0 }

Key Lessons from the Lab

The dependency graph is set up before any work begins. The project manager creates all tasks and wires all dependencies in a single upfront pass. This prevents a worker from starting integration tests before the service is ready, regardless of race conditions.

TaskGet provides the full specification. TaskList gives you enough to know which tasks are available. TaskGet gives you the description you need to actually do the work. Workers call TaskGet to read the spec, not TaskList.

Claim before spawn. The TaskUpdate setting owner and status: "in_progress" happens before the Agent call, not inside the worker. If the worker fails to start, the task remains in_progress with an owner — a human or orchestrator can detect stuck tasks and reset them.

Polling over events. The 15-second poll loop is simpler and more reliable than event-driven approaches in the standard harness. The TaskCreated hook can supplement this for external notification, but the execution loop itself should poll.

TodoWrite would be wrong here. This workflow spans multiple agents, requires dependency tracking, persists across possible session restarts, and involves hours of work. TodoWrite's in-memory, flat, single-agent model would fail on all of those requirements. Use TaskCreate whenever work crosses agent boundaries or session boundaries.

Summary

The task system provides persistent, structured work state that survives context compaction and session restarts. A task lifecycle moves from pending through in_progress to completed, with deleted as a permanent removal path. The golden rules: mark in_progress before starting, mark completed only when fully done, use TaskList after each completion to find what is next.

TaskCreate demands self-contained descriptions — write them as if handing off to a cold-start colleague.
