The addBlocks and addBlockedBy dependency graph is what enables parallel, coordinated multi-agent execution: workers scan the list, take only tasks whose blockers are resolved, and the execution order emerges from the graph without a central coordinator having to micromanage sequencing.

TaskGet is for reading full task specs before execution. TaskList is for finding available work. TaskUpdate is the coordination mechanism: status transitions claim and release work, owner prevents double-assignment, and metadata carries implementation-specific context that does not belong in the description.

TodoWrite is the lightweight alternative — no persistence, no dependencies, no ownership, just a flat checklist for single-agent sequential work within one session. The choice is straightforward: if work crosses agent or session boundaries, use TaskCreate. If it does not, TodoWrite is simpler.

In Chapter 11, we go deeper into the Agent tool — the primitive that makes multi-agent orchestration possible: subagent types, isolation modes, structured output, and the async output pattern that lets you fire many agents without blocking the orchestrator.

Next: Chapter 11: The Agent Tool — Spawning Subagents

Part III: Orchestration — Multi-Agent Systems

Chapter 11: The Agent Tool — Spawning Subagents

"A single model reasoning in a loop is a worker. A harness that spawns workers is a factory."

11.1 Core Parameters

The Agent tool is the most structurally significant tool in Claude Code's core six. Every other core tool interacts with the environment — files, shells, the user. Agent interacts with more instances of itself, turning a single agentic loop into a directed graph of them.

The interface is defined at the TypeScript level as AgentInput:

export interface AgentInput {
  description: string;       // 3-5 word task description
  prompt: string;            // the full task for the agent
  subagent_type?: string;    // built-in or custom agent type
  model?: "sonnet" | "opus" | "haiku" | "fable";
  run_in_background?: boolean;  // default true in newer versions
  name?: string;             // makes agent addressable via SendMessage
  isolation?: "worktree" | "remote";
}

Each parameter has a distinct role and failure mode when misused.

description — The 3-5 Word Contract

The description is not a comment. It is a structural identifier. The harness displays it in the terminal UI while the agent runs, writes it to audit logs, uses it as the label in task tracking, and returns it in the async output payload so callers can correlate results to intent.

The constraint — 3 to 5 words — is intentional. If you cannot describe what an agent is doing in 3 to 5 words, the agent is probably doing too many things. Well-formed descriptions:

"Analyze auth module security"
"Review API endpoint coverage"
"Refactor database connection pool"

Poorly-formed descriptions that appear in practice:

"Do the thing we discussed"
"Fix bugs and stuff"
"Review everything in the whole project and also check for security issues and performance problems"

The last example is not just bad UX — it signals a design problem. An agent with an unfocusable description is probably an agent that will produce unfocusable output.

prompt — Self-Contained Task Package

The prompt is the most consequential parameter. It is the only thing the subagent receives from the parent. There is no implicit context transfer. The subagent starts fresh.

This is the most common mistake engineers make when first using Agent: they write a short prompt assuming the subagent shares the parent's context:

// WRONG: subagent has no idea what "the auth module" refers to
await Agent({
  description: "Review auth security",
  prompt: "Review the auth module for security issues and report your findings.",
});

The subagent will either make a broad guess about what "auth module" means, read the entire codebase looking for auth-related files, or ask a clarifying question it has no way to get answered. The fix is to make the prompt self-contained:

// CORRECT: prompt contains everything the subagent needs
await Agent({
  description: "Review auth security",
  prompt: `You are reviewing the authentication module of a Python web application.
  
The repository is at /Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/myapp.
The auth module lives at src/auth/ and contains:
- session.py: session management, timeout logic
- middleware.py: request authentication decorators
- tokens.py: JWT creation and validation

Review these files for:
1. Hardcoded secrets or credentials
2. Insecure token validation (algorithm confusion, expired-but-accepted)
3. Missing authorization checks on session operations
4. Input validation gaps on user-supplied data

Return your findings as a structured list with: file path, line number, severity (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW), and a one-line description. End with a summary count per severity level.`,
});

The rule: write every Agent prompt as if the subagent has never seen your codebase, never read your conversation, and knows nothing except what you tell it in the prompt.

model — Matching Cost to Task

The four model options map to deliberate cost/capability tradeoffs:

ModelBest for
haikuFast, token-cheap tasks: file scanning, regex search, format conversion, structured extraction from known schemas
sonnetMost multi-step tasks: code review, debugging, refactoring, writing documentation
opusTasks requiring deep reasoning: architecture decisions, complex security analysis, synthesizing contradictory information
fableSpecialized creative and long-form writing tasks

The default when model is omitted is sonnet. That is the right default for most tasks. Reach for haiku when you are spawning many parallel agents for tasks that are essentially structured transformation. Reach for opus when you need the subagent to reason through ambiguous, high-stakes decisions and the latency cost is worth it.

A common pattern is to use haiku for the fan-out stage of a map/reduce workflow and sonnet for the reduce stage that synthesizes findings:

// Fan out with haiku — fast and cheap
const scanJobs = files.map(f => Agent({
  description: "Scan file for secrets",
  prompt: buildSecretScanPrompt(f),
  model: "haiku",
}));

// Reduce with sonnet — needs reasoning to synthesize
const synthesis = await Agent({
  description: "Synthesize security findings",
  prompt: buildSynthesisPrompt(await Promise.all(scanJobs)),
  model: "sonnet",
});

11.2 Execution Modes

The run_in_background parameter controls whether the parent's control loop blocks while the subagent runs or continues immediately.

Background (Default)

In newer versions of Claude Code, run_in_background defaults to true. Calling Agent without specifying this parameter launches the subagent in the background and returns an async result:

// Returns immediately with status: "async_launched"
const result = await Agent({
  description: "Long security audit",
  prompt: auditPrompt,
  // run_in_background: true is the default
});

// result.status === "async_launched"
// result.outputFile contains the path where output will appear

The async return object contains the path where the subagent will write its completed output. You can poll this file to check progress, or register a ScheduleWakeup to be notified when it completes.

Background mode is the right choice for:

  • Tasks that take more than a few seconds
  • Independent work that can proceed in parallel with the parent
  • Fan-out patterns where you launch N agents simultaneously
  • Any task where you want the parent to remain responsive

Foreground (Synchronous)

Setting run_in_background: false blocks the parent's control loop until the subagent completes. The return value is the full AgentOutput struct:

const result = await Agent({
  description: "Validate schema format",
  prompt: validationPrompt,
  run_in_background: false,
});

// result.status === "completed"
// result.content contains the subagent's final text
// result.totalDurationMs tells you how long it took

Foreground mode is appropriate when:

  • The parent needs the subagent's output before it can proceed
  • The task is short enough that blocking is acceptable
  • You are building a pipeline where each stage feeds the next
  • You need the full AgentOutput metadata (token counts, tool stats) immediately

The mental model: background is async/await with a deferred await; foreground is async/await with an immediate await. Both are asynchronous in the sense that the subagent runs in its own context — foreground simply holds the parent at the join point.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Parent Agent
    participant A1 as Subagent 1 (bg)
    participant A2 as Subagent 2 (fg)

    P->>A1: Agent(..., run_in_background: true)
    Note over P: returns immediately with outputFile
    P->>A2: Agent(..., run_in_background: false)
    Note over P: BLOCKS here
    A2-->>P: AgentOutput (completed)
    Note over P: continues
    Note over A1: still running independently
    A1-->>P: writes to outputFile (async)

11.3 Built-in Agent Types

The subagent_type parameter selects from a set of built-in agent configurations. Each type pre-configures the subagent with a specific system prompt, tool set, and behavioral constraints optimized for a class of tasks.

Using a built-in type lets you skip writing the full system prompt for common tasks:

await Agent({
  description: "Review PR diff quality",
  prompt: "Review the diff at /tmp/pr-diff.patch for code quality issues.",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
});

The built-in types and their configurations:

Explore

Read-only codebase navigation. Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, Bash — no Edit or Write. The behavioral constraint against mutation is enforced at the tool level, not by prompting. This means an Explore subagent genuinely cannot modify files regardless of what the prompt instructs.

Use Explore when you need to gather information without any risk of side effects. It is the appropriate type for the fan-out stage of a read/analyze/synthesize pattern.

code-reviewer

Evaluates code for quality, correctness, performance, and adherence to best practices. The system prompt primes it to prioritize actionable findings over commentary, cite specific file paths and line numbers, and tier issues by severity. Well-suited for pre-commit or pre-merge checks.

security-reviewer

Targets security-specific analysis: authentication and authorization logic, input validation gaps, hardcoded secrets, injection vectors, cryptographic misuse, and dangerous API usage. It references OWASP and CWE categories in its output. The system prompt does not overlap significantly with code-reviewer — you can usefully run both on the same codebase and get complementary findings.

debugger

Investigates errors, stack traces, and unexpected behavior. The system prompt emphasizes hypothesis formation before evidence gathering, systematic elimination of causes, and distinguishing root cause from symptoms. Useful for hard-to-reproduce bugs where you want a disciplined investigative process rather than a quick grep.

researcher

Deep research, tool comparison, and documentation synthesis. The researcher type is configured to use WebSearch and WebFetch aggressively and to structure its output with sources, tradeoffs, and a concrete recommendation. Use it when you need a decision brief, not a summary.

doc-writer

Creates and updates documentation: READMEs, ADRs, runbooks, API docs. The system prompt establishes a practitioner voice and instructs the agent to read existing documentation before writing, match established style, and verify all code references before including them.

Plan

Software architect for implementation planning. Returns a structured implementation plan: affected files, proposed changes, risks, and sequencing. Does not write code. The output is designed to be reviewed by a human or fed into another agent as the prompt for implementation. Use it before a large refactor when you want an explicit plan step.

general-purpose

No specialized configuration. A clean slate with the full tool surface available. Use it when the task does not fit any specific type, or when you are iterating on a custom prompt and do not want any built-in system prompt interfering.

claude-code-guide

Answers questions about Claude Code itself — its tools, configuration, behaviors, and internals. Useful when your harness needs to self-document or when you are building tooling that generates Claude Code configuration.

The built-in types are a starting point, not a ceiling. As shown in section 11.4, you can define custom agents that supersede or extend any of these patterns.

11.4 Custom Agents

When the built-in types are not precise enough, you define custom agents as Markdown files in .claude/agents/. The harness discovers these at startup and makes them available as values for subagent_type.

The file format uses YAML frontmatter followed by the agent's system prompt:

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality, bugs, performance, and best practices.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: sonnet
effort: high
memory: project
---

You are a senior software engineer performing a code review. You have been asked to review a specific piece of code and provide actionable feedback.

## Your Process

1. Read the files you have been asked to review
2. Identify issues across these dimensions:
   - **Correctness**: Logic errors, off-by-one, null handling, race conditions
   - **Security**: Input validation, SQL injection, credential exposure, insecure defaults
   - **Performance**: Unnecessary allocations, N+1 queries, missing indexes, synchronous I/O in hot paths
   - **Maintainability**: Missing types, unclear naming, copy-paste duplication, untested behavior

## Output Format

Structure your output as:
- A severity-ranked list of findings (CRITICAL > HIGH > MEDIUM > LOW > INFO)
- Each finding: `file_path:line_number — [SEVERITY] description`
- A brief summary section with total counts per severity

Be direct. Skip findings that are purely stylistic unless they indicate a maintainability risk.

Frontmatter Fields

FieldRequiredDescription
nameYesIdentifier used in subagent_type. Must match the filename stem.
descriptionYesOne-line description shown in tool selection and UI
toolsNoComma-separated list of tools this agent can use. Omit to allow all tools.
modelNoDefault model for this agent type. Caller can override via AgentInput.model.
effortNolow, medium, or high. Maps to thinking/effort budgets in the API.
memoryNoproject loads the project's CLAUDE.md. none gives a clean context.

The tools field is a security and focus boundary. A custom Explore-style agent with tools: Read, Grep, Glob genuinely cannot call Bash or Edit — the harness enforces this at the tool registry level. When building multi-agent pipelines, use the tools field to give each agent the minimum surface it needs. An agent that only needs to read files should not have Bash access.

Organizing Custom Agents

A mature project might have several agents:

.claude/agents/
├── code-reviewer.md        # quality + correctness
├── security-reviewer.md    # OWASP-focused security analysis
├── migration-planner.md    # database schema migration plans
├── changelog-writer.md     # git log → user-facing changelog
└── test-gap-finder.md      # identifies untested code paths

Each is purpose-built for a specific workflow. The migration planner has tools: Read, Bash (it needs to query the database schema) but not Edit (planning only). The changelog writer has tools: Bash only (it runs git log and formats output) with no file access needed.

11.5 Named Agents and Continued Conversations

The name parameter makes a subagent addressable. Once launched with a name, the parent can send follow-up messages to that specific agent instance and it will respond with full context of the prior exchange intact:

// Launch a named agent
await Agent({
  description: "Persistent review session",
  prompt: initialPrompt,
  name: "reviewer",
  run_in_background: false,
});

// Send a follow-up — the agent remembers the prior exchange
await SendMessage({
  to: "reviewer",
  message: "Now focus specifically on the token validation logic in tokens.py and check for algorithm confusion vulnerabilities.",
});

Named agents are a different execution model from spawning a new Agent call. Key differences:

New Agent CallNamed Agent via SendMessage
ContextFresh startFull prior conversation preserved
CostNew session overheadContinuation, no re-initialization
Use caseIndependent parallel tasksMulti-turn investigation
StateNone from priorComplete

Named agents are appropriate when:

  • You are conducting an investigation that requires back-and-forth with the same agent
  • The agent has accumulated valuable context (read files, formed hypotheses) that would be expensive to re-establish
  • You want the semantics of a conversation, not a function call

An unnamed Agent call is the right choice when:

  • The task is fully self-contained
  • You want guaranteed isolation (fresh context means no contamination from prior work)
  • You are running many parallel agents and do not need to address them individually

A critical point: a new Agent call — even with the same subagent_type and prompt — always starts fresh. There is no implicit memory between Agent invocations. If you launch an agent, receive its output, and then launch another agent expecting it to remember the first agent's work, you will get an entirely clean slate. Put the first agent's findings into the second agent's prompt explicitly.

11.6 Isolation Modes

The isolation parameter controls what environment the subagent operates in. Two modes exist: "worktree" and "remote".

Worktree Isolation

await Agent({
  description: "Refactor payment module",
  prompt: refactorPrompt,
  isolation: "worktree",
});

Worktree isolation creates a new git worktree for the subagent — a separate checkout of the repository at a new directory path, on a new branch. The subagent operates inside this worktree: its Read, Edit, Write, and Bash calls all land in the isolated directory. Changes it makes are committed to the worktree branch, not the parent's branch.

The setup overhead is 200–500ms. This is not negligible. For short-lived agents, the isolation cost may exceed the agent's actual work time.

When to use worktree isolation:

You need it when two or more parallel agents will mutate the same repository and their edits might conflict. Without isolation, Agent 1 and Agent 2 both editing src/api/routes.py simultaneously will interleave their changes non-deterministically — one will overwrite the other's edits, or produce a merged file that is syntactically broken.

With worktree isolation, each agent works in its own branch. The parent then merges or cherry-picks the results.

When not to use worktree isolation:

For the majority of Agent use cases. If agents are read-only (all Explore subagents), isolation adds cost with zero benefit. If agents mutate different, non-overlapping parts of the repository, they will not conflict without isolation. Reserve worktree for the specific case where parallel mutation of overlapping files is unavoidable.

graph TD
    P[Parent Agent<br/>main branch] -->|Agent isolation: worktree| A1[Subagent 1<br/>worktree/branch-1<br/>edits src/auth/]
    P -->|Agent isolation: worktree| A2[Subagent 2<br/>worktree/branch-2<br/>edits src/auth/]
    P -->|Agent no isolation| A3[Subagent 3<br/>main branch<br/>reads src/api/]
    A1 -->|merge| M[Parent merges results]
    A2 -->|merge| M
    A3 -->|output only| P

Remote Isolation

await Agent({
  description: "Run integration tests",
  prompt: testPrompt,
  isolation: "remote",
});

Remote isolation runs the subagent in a cloud environment — an ephemeral, separate machine. It always runs in the background (no foreground option for remote). The return includes a sessionUrl for monitoring and an outputFile path for collecting results:

// remote_launched return type
{
  status: "remote_launched",
  taskId: "task_abc123",
  sessionUrl: "https://claude.ai/agents/task_abc123",
  description: "Run integration tests",
  prompt: testPrompt,
  outputFile: "/tmp/claude-agents/task_abc123.output.json",
}

Use remote isolation when:

  • The task requires a clean environment (fresh dependencies, clean state)
  • You want to avoid side effects on the local machine
  • The task is long-running and you want it to survive the parent session ending
  • The task requires more resources than the local machine can provide

Remote isolation is significantly more expensive in both latency and cost than local execution. The cold start for a remote environment is measured in seconds, not milliseconds.

11.7 Output Structure

When a synchronous subagent completes (or when you read the outputFile of an async agent), you receive an AgentOutput. Understanding its structure matters for building robust multi-agent pipelines.

type AgentOutput = {
  status: "completed";
  agentId: string;
  agentType?: string;
  content: { type: "text"; text: string; citations?: unknown[] | null }[];
  resolvedModel?: string;
  modelsUsed?: string[];
  totalToolUseCount: number;
  totalDurationMs: number;
  totalTokens: number;
  usage: {
    input_tokens: number;
    output_tokens: number;
    cache_creation_input_tokens: number | null;
    cache_read_input_tokens: number | null;
    server_tool_use: { web_search_requests: number; web_fetch_requests: number } | null;
    service_tier: string | null;
    cache_creation: {
      ephemeral_1h_input_tokens: number;
      ephemeral_5m_input_tokens: number;
    } | null;
  };
  toolStats?: {
    readCount: number;
    searchCount: number;
    bashCount: number;
    editFileCount: number;
    linesAdded: number;
    linesRemoved: number;
    otherToolCount: number;
  };
  prompt: string;
  worktreePath?: string;
  worktreeBranch?: string;
}

Fields Worth Examining

content is an array, not a string. In practice, most subagents return a single text block, but the array structure means you must access result.content[0].text to get the string. Forgetting this and treating content as a string is a common bug that produces [object Object] in downstream prompts.

resolvedModel vs modelsUsed — resolvedModel is the model the agent was instantiated with. modelsUsed is the list of models actually invoked during the run, which may differ if the agent internally spawned its own subagents that used different models.

toolStats is the most actionable diagnostic field. If a security review agent reports readCount: 3 on a 200-file codebase, something went wrong — it did not look at enough code. If a refactor agent shows linesAdded: 1200, linesRemoved: 8, that is a suspicious ratio worth investigating. Build monitoring on toolStats when running agents in production pipelines.

totalDurationMs is wall-clock time from the moment the agent received its prompt to when it returned. This includes all API call latency and tool execution time. It is useful for SLA monitoring and for deciding whether to upgrade or downgrade the model for a given task.

usage.cache_read_input_tokens tells you how much context was served from cache. In a fan-out pattern where many agents receive similar system prompts, high cache hit rates meaningfully reduce cost. The harness handles cache warming automatically — understanding the field lets you verify it is working.

The Null Case

Agent returns null if the user skips or cancels the agent mid-run. Production code must handle this:

const result = await Agent({
  description: "Analyze test coverage",
  prompt: coveragePrompt,
  run_in_background: false,
});

if (result === null) {
  // User skipped the agent — handle gracefully
  return { skipped: true, findings: [] };
}

const text = result.content[0]?.text ?? "";

Omitting the null check and immediately accessing result.content will throw in interactive sessions where the user presses Escape while an agent is running.

11.8 Async Output and Progress Checking

Background agents (the default) return the async_launched variant of AgentOutput:

{
  status: "async_launched";
  agentId: string;
  description: string;
  resolvedModel?: string;
  modelsUsed?: string[];
  prompt: string;
  outputFile: string;
  canReadOutputFile?: boolean;
}

The outputFile path is where the agent will write its completed AgentOutput struct as JSON when it finishes. Polling this file is how you check progress:

async function waitForAgent(outputFile: string, pollIntervalMs = 5000): Promise<AgentOutput> {
  while (true) {
    try {
      const raw = await fs.readFile(outputFile, "utf-8");
      const result = JSON.parse(raw) as AgentOutput;
      if (result.status === "completed") {
        return result;
      }
    } catch {
      // File not yet written — agent still running
    }
    await sleep(pollIntervalMs);
  }
}

The canReadOutputFile boolean tells you whether the current process has filesystem access to the output path. For remote agents, this will be false — the output file lives in the cloud environment, not locally. In that case, you collect results through the sessionUrl or a configured webhook, not by polling a local file.

ScheduleWakeup Integration

The harness provides ScheduleWakeup as a more efficient alternative to polling. Rather than checking every N seconds, you register a wakeup that fires when an agent completes:

// Launch background agent
const launched = await Agent({
  description: "Full codebase audit",
  prompt: auditPrompt,
  name: "auditor",
});

// Register wakeup rather than polling
await ScheduleWakeup({
  message: "Auditor agent complete — read results and synthesize report",
  triggerOnAgentComplete: launched.agentId,
});

// Parent session can end here; wakeup will restart it

This is the production pattern for long-running agents. Polling every 5 seconds for an agent that will run for 3 minutes wastes context and keeps the parent session alive unnecessarily.

11.9 Lab: 3-Agent Review System

This lab builds a review pipeline that launches three independent specialized agents in parallel, collects their findings, and synthesizes a unified report. The architecture demonstrates several patterns from the preceding sections: parallel fan-out, self-contained prompts, output structure handling, and reduce-phase synthesis.

The Architecture

flowchart TD
    P[Orchestrator Agent] -->|parallel launch| A1[Code Reviewer<br/>haiku]
    P -->|parallel launch| A2[Security Reviewer<br/>sonnet]
    P -->|parallel launch| A3[Test Gap Finder<br/>haiku]
    A1 -->|AgentOutput| C[Synthesizer<br/>sonnet]
    A2 -->|AgentOutput| C
    A3 -->|AgentOutput| C
    C --> R[Unified Report]

The orchestrator launches three agents simultaneously, waits for all three to complete, then passes all three outputs to a synthesis agent. The synthesis agent does not do any additional analysis — its job is to de-duplicate findings, resolve conflicts between reviewers, and produce a single prioritized report.

The Orchestrator

async function runTripleReview(targetPath: string): Promise<string> {
  const repoContext = `
Repository: ${targetPath}
Run: find "${targetPath}/src" -name "*.py" -o -name "*.ts" | head -50
Review all files found.`;

  // Launch all three in parallel — foreground so we block until all complete
  const [codeResult, secResult, testResult] = await Promise.all([
    Agent({
      description: "Review code quality",
      prompt: buildCodeReviewPrompt(targetPath, repoContext),
      subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
      model: "haiku",
      run_in_background: false,
    }),
    Agent({
      description: "Review security posture",
      prompt: buildSecurityReviewPrompt(targetPath, repoContext),
      subagent_type: "security-reviewer",
      model: "sonnet",
      run_in_background: false,
    }),
    Agent({
      description: "Find test coverage gaps",
      prompt: buildTestGapPrompt(targetPath, repoContext),
      model: "haiku",
      run_in_background: false,
    }),
  ]);

  // Handle null (user cancelled one or more agents)
  if (!codeResult || !secResult || !testResult) {
    throw new Error("One or more review agents were cancelled");
  }

  // Extract text from content arrays
  const codeFindings = codeResult.content[0]?.text ?? "(no output)";
  const secFindings = secResult.content[0]?.text ?? "(no output)";
  const testFindings = testResult.content[0]?.text ?? "(no output)";

  // Log tool usage for monitoring
  console.error(`Code reviewer: ${codeResult.toolStats?.readCount ?? 0} files read, ${codeResult.totalDurationMs}ms`);
  console.error(`Security reviewer: ${secResult.toolStats?.readCount ?? 0} files read, ${secResult.totalDurationMs}ms`);
  console.error(`Test gap finder: ${testResult.toolStats?.readCount ?? 0} files read, ${testResult.totalDurationMs}ms`);

  // Synthesize
  const synthesis = await Agent({
    description: "Synthesize review findings",
    prompt: buildSynthesisPrompt(codeFindings, secFindings, testFindings),
    model: "sonnet",
    run_in_background: false,
  });

  if (!synthesis) {
    throw new Error("Synthesis agent was cancelled");
  }

  return synthesis.content[0]?.text ?? "(synthesis produced no output)";
}

The Prompt Builders

Each prompt is fully self-contained. The reviewers receive the repository path, a description of what they are looking for, and explicit output format instructions.

function buildCodeReviewPrompt(targetPath: string, repoContext: string): string {
  return `You are a senior engineer performing a code quality review.

${repoContext}

Read the source files at ${targetPath}/src/ and review them for:
- Type safety issues (missing types, unsafe casts, implicit any)
- Error handling gaps (uncaught exceptions, swallowed errors, missing null checks)
- Performance anti-patterns (synchronous I/O in async contexts, unnecessary loops, memory leaks)
- Maintainability issues (deeply nested logic, functions over 50 lines, unexplained magic numbers)

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Return a JSON array. Each element:
{
  "file": "relative/path/to/file.py",
  "line": 42,
  "severity": "CRITICAL" | "HIGH" | "MEDIUM" | "LOW",
  "category": "type-safety" | "error-handling" | "performance" | "maintainability",
  "description": "One sentence describing the issue."
}

End with a plain-text summary: total findings by severity.`;
}

function buildSecurityReviewPrompt(targetPath: string, repoContext: string): string {
  return `You are a security engineer performing a vulnerability assessment.

${repoContext}

Read the source files at ${targetPath}/src/ and identify:
- Hardcoded credentials, API keys, or secrets
- SQL injection or command injection vectors
- Authentication logic flaws (missing checks, bypassable conditions, algorithm confusion)
- Input validation gaps on user-supplied data
- Insecure cryptographic usage (weak algorithms, static IVs, predictable randomness)
- Exposed internal error details in API responses

Reference OWASP Top 10 and CWE categories where applicable.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Return a JSON array. Each element:
{
  "file": "relative/path/to/file.py",
  "line": 42,
  "severity": "CRITICAL" | "HIGH" | "MEDIUM" | "LOW",
  "cwe": "CWE-89",
  "owasp": "A03:2021",
  "description": "One sentence describing the vulnerability."
}

End with a plain-text summary: total findings by severity and whether immediate remediation is required.`;
}

function buildTestGapPrompt(targetPath: string, repoContext: string): string {
  return `You are a QA engineer identifying test coverage gaps.

${repoContext}

Read the source files at ${targetPath}/src/ and ${targetPath}/tests/ (if it exists).

For each source module, identify:
- Functions or methods with no corresponding test
- Error paths that are only tested in the happy path
- Edge cases absent from tests (empty input, None, boundary values, concurrent access)

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Return a JSON array. Each element:
{
  "source_file": "relative/path/to/source.py",
  "function": "function_name",
  "gap_type": "no-test" | "missing-error-path" | "missing-edge-case",
  "description": "One sentence describing what is untested."
}

End with a count of untested functions vs total functions found.`;
}

The Synthesis Prompt

The synthesizer receives the raw output of all three reviewers. Its job is editorial, not analytical.

function buildSynthesisPrompt(
  codeFindings: string,
  secFindings: string,
  testFindings: string
): string {
  return `You are synthesizing findings from three independent code reviewers into a unified engineering report.

## Code Quality Findings
${codeFindings}

## Security Findings
${secFindings}

## Test Coverage Gaps
${testFindings}

Produce a unified report with the following structure:

### Executive Summary
Two to three sentences. Total issue count, highest severity found, and one headline risk.

### Critical and High Priority Issues
List only CRITICAL and HIGH severity findings, de-duplicated. If the code reviewer and security reviewer both flagged the same line for related reasons, merge them into one finding and note both perspectives. Format: \`file:line — [SEVERITY] description\`

### Medium Priority Issues
Same format. Group by category (security / code quality / test coverage).

### Low Priority Issues
Aggregate by category only — no individual line citations needed at this severity.

### Recommended Action Order
Three to five specific, ordered remediation steps. Focus on what to fix first given dependencies and blast radius.

Be direct. No boilerplate. Every sentence in the report should inform a decision.`;
}

Running the Lab

# From the project root
claude -p "Run the triple review system on the src/ directory and save the report to /tmp/review-report.md" \
  --allowedTools "Agent,Read,Bash,Write"

Or integrate it into an existing harness session by calling runTripleReview("/path/to/project") from an Agent prompt.

What the Lab Demonstrates

Context isolation in practice. Each reviewer receives a self-contained prompt. You can verify this works correctly by checking the toolStats.readCount on each result — each agent should have independently read the source files rather than receiving pre-loaded content from the parent.

Model selection by task. The code reviewer and test gap finder use haiku — their tasks are essentially structured extraction from source files, which does not require deep reasoning. The security reviewer uses sonnet because recognizing subtle authentication flaws and algorithm confusion vulnerabilities benefits from stronger reasoning. The synthesizer uses sonnet because de-duplication and editorial prioritization require judgment calls.

Defensive output handling. The orchestrator checks for null from each agent (user cancellation), accesses content[0]?.text with a fallback, and logs toolStats for monitoring. These are not optional niceties — they are the difference between a pipeline that degrades gracefully and one that throws in production.

Synthesis as a first-class step. The synthesizer does not receive the raw source code. It receives only the reviewers' output. This is intentional: the synthesis task is fundamentally different from the analysis tasks, it should not be contaminated with thousands of lines of source code that it does not need, and the smaller context makes the synthesis step faster and cheaper.

Summary

The Agent tool transforms a single agentic loop into a directed workflow. The key behaviors to internalize:

  • Subagents start with no context from the parent. Every prompt must be self-contained.
  • Named agents preserve conversation state; new Agent calls always start fresh.
  • Background execution is the default; foreground blocks until completion.
  • Worktree isolation is expensive (200–500ms) and necessary only when parallel agents mutate overlapping files.
  • The AgentOutput.content field is an array — access content[0].text, never treat it as a string.
  • Agent returns null on user cancellation; production code must handle this.
  • Match model to task: haiku for structured extraction, sonnet for reasoning, opus for deep ambiguous analysis.
  • toolStats is the primary diagnostic signal for whether an agent actually did the work you expected.

The three-agent review system in the lab is a minimal but complete pattern for parallel multi-agent coordination. The same architecture — fan out with specialized agents, collect structured output, synthesize with a reduce-phase agent — applies to code migration, documentation generation, security auditing, and any other task that benefits from independent perspectives on the same codebase.

In Chapter 12, we go into the SendMessage tool — the mechanism for addressing named agents, passing structured payloads between running agents, and building coordination protocols that go beyond simple fan-out.

Next: Chapter 12: SendMessage and Inter-Agent Communication

Chapter 12: Workflow Engine — Deterministic Orchestration

"A workflow is not a prompt. A workflow is a program that deploys agents the way a compiler deploys instructions — structured, sequenced, and verifiable."

The Workflow tool is the point at which Claude Code stops being a reactive assistant and becomes a programmable orchestration engine. Where the Agent tool spawns a single subagent and waits, Workflow executes a full JavaScript program — phases, pipelines, parallel fans, token budgets — in a sandboxed runtime that coordinates dozens of subagents while you watch progress roll in.

This chapter is the most technically dense in the book. The interface is deceptively simple; the constraints are precise and unforgiving. Every concept here requires understanding not just what a function does but why it is designed the way it is and what breaks when you use it wrong.

12.1 Script Anatomy

A workflow script has two mandatory parts: a meta block at the top, and a body that runs in an implicit async context.

export const meta = {
  name: 'audit-codebase',
  description: 'Find and verify all security issues in the codebase'
}

const files = args.files ?? ['src/']

phase('Scan')
log(`Starting audit of ${files.length} target(s)`)

const findings = await pipeline(
  files,
  f => agent(`List all security-relevant files in ${f}`, {
    label: `scan:${f}`,
    schema: { type: 'object', properties: { paths: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } } }, required: ['paths'] }
  }),
  (result, file) => agent(`Audit these files for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities: ${result.paths.join(', ')}`, {
    label: `audit:${file}`,
    schema: FINDING_SCHEMA
  })
)

phase('Synthesize')
const report = await agent('Synthesize these audit findings into a prioritized report', {
  label: 'synthesize',
  schema: REPORT_SCHEMA
})

log(`Audit complete — ${report.critical} critical, ${report.high} high`)

The body is a plain async JavaScript module. There is no explicit async function main() wrapper; the engine wraps the body for you. await works at the top level.

The exec model

When you invoke the Workflow tool, the harness does not block waiting for results. It:

  1. Parses the script (syntax check; the error field in the output reflects this)
  2. Persists the script to the session directory (the returned scriptPath tells you where)
  3. Launches the workflow in a background runtime
  4. Returns immediately with status: "async_launched" and a taskId

The taskId lets you monitor progress via the task system. The transcriptDir in the output tells you where subagent transcripts are written — useful for post-mortem debugging. The workflow runs whether or not the session stays open.

The two-part contract

The meta block and the body have a strict separation of concerns:

  • meta is structural metadata: name, description. It is parsed statically before execution. This is why it must be a pure literal — the parser cannot evaluate expressions, and it never tries.
  • Body is executable logic: any JavaScript you want, using the script API globals. It runs at runtime, after meta is safely extracted.

You can think of meta as a package manifest and the body as application code. They serve different audiences. The harness reads meta to index the workflow, display it in the task list, and validate it without running it. The runtime reads the body and executes it.

12.2 The Meta Constraint: Pure Literal Only

This constraint eliminates an entire class of bugs before they become production incidents.

// CORRECT — pure literal
export const meta = {
  name: 'find-todos',
  description: 'Find all TODO comments across the codebase'
}

// WRONG — variable reference
const WORKFLOW_NAME = 'find-todos'
export const meta = { name: WORKFLOW_NAME }  // syntax check fails

// WRONG — template literal
export const meta = {
  name: `audit-${Date.now()}`,              // fails: Date.now() disallowed; template fails meta parse
  description: `Run audit`
}

// WRONG — spread
const base = { description: 'Audit' }
export const meta = { ...base, name: 'audit' }  // spread fails meta parse

// WRONG — function call
export const meta = {
  name: getName(),                           // fails
  description: buildDescription('audit')
}

The parser that reads meta is not a full JavaScript evaluator. It extracts the object literal using static analysis — it looks for the token sequence export const meta = { and reads the literal that follows. Anything that requires runtime evaluation is invisible to it.

Why this constraint exists

Workflow scripts are indexed and resumed across sessions. The harness needs to read meta.name and meta.description without executing the script body — both for the task list UI and for the resume system that needs to match script identity to cached run state. If meta could contain runtime expressions, the harness would need to run the script just to read its name, creating a circular dependency.

The constraint also prevents a subtle class of non-determinism. A meta that included Date.now() would produce a different name on every run, breaking resume matching entirely.

Accepted values

The only accepted values in meta are string literals and numeric literals. Two fields are read:

FieldRequiredPurpose
nameYesUnique identifier for the workflow, used in resume matching
descriptionNoHuman-readable description for the task list

description in the tool input (WorkflowInput.description, WorkflowInput.title) is silently ignored — the runtime always reads from meta.description. This is a common source of confusion for engineers who try to set the displayed name through the tool call parameters.

12.3 agent(prompt, opts): Spawn a Subagent

agent() is the primitive unit of work in every workflow. It spawns a subagent, waits for completion, and returns the result.

// Without schema — returns the final text as a string
const summary = await agent('Summarize the architecture of src/core/')

// With schema — returns a validated JavaScript object
const issues = await agent('List all TODOs in the codebase', {
  label: 'find-todos',
  schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      todos: {
        type: 'array',
        items: {
          type: 'object',
          properties: {
            file: { type: 'string' },
            line: { type: 'number' },
            text: { type: 'string' }
          },
          required: ['file', 'line', 'text']
        }
      },
      total: { type: 'number' }
    },
    required: ['todos', 'total']
  }
})
// issues.todos[0].file — type-safe access guaranteed by schema enforcement

Return value semantics

The return value depends entirely on whether schema is provided:

  • Without schema: returns the agent's final text output as a plain string. Use this when you want a narrative response that you will pass to another agent or display directly.
  • With schema: the runtime parses the agent's output as JSON and validates it against the schema. If validation passes, you get a typed JavaScript object. If validation fails, the runtime retries the agent with an error message appended — you never see the parse failure in your code, only the validated result.
  • User skips: if the user cancels an agent mid-run, agent() returns null. Your code must handle this. Passing null to a subsequent agent as part of a pipeline causes the pipeline to drop that item. Calling .property on null throws — guard it.
const result = await agent('Analyze this file', { schema: SCHEMA })
if (result === null) {
  log('User skipped analysis — continuing without this result')
} else {
  log(`Found ${result.issues.length} issues`)
}

Agent options

OptionTypeDefaultEffect
labelstringauto-generatedDisplay name in progress UI and transcript directory
phasestringcurrent phaseGroup this agent under a named phase (overrides phase() global)
schemaJSON Schema objectnoneEnforce structured output; enables object return value
model'opus' \'sonnet' \'haiku'inheritsOverride the model for this specific agent
isolation'worktree'noneRun agent in an isolated git worktree
agentType'Explore' \'Edit'defaultAgent persona: Explore for analysis, Edit for code changes

isolation: 'worktree'

When isolation is enabled, the agent runs inside a fresh git worktree — a separate working directory with the same commit state but no shared filesystem state with other agents. This is essential when multiple agents are making concurrent edits to the same codebase. Without isolation, concurrent Edit calls from separate agents cause conflicts and corrupted files.

// Concurrent editors MUST use worktree isolation
const patches = await parallel([
  () => agent('Refactor the auth module', { isolation: 'worktree', agentType: 'Edit' }),
  () => agent('Refactor the billing module', { isolation: 'worktree', agentType: 'Edit' }),
  () => agent('Refactor the notification module', { isolation: 'worktree', agentType: 'Edit' })
])
// Each agent works in its own worktree. Merge patches afterward.

The symlinkDirectories field in your .claude/settings.json worktree configuration (Chapter 2) controls which directories are symlinked rather than copied in each worktree — critical for node_modules and .venv which are large and read-only from the agent's perspective.

agentType

Explore agents are given a read-only persona — they are instructed to investigate and analyze without making changes. Use this for all discovery and verification phases. Edit agents are given full modification permissions. The distinction matters for both safety and prompt quality: an Explore agent that "accidentally" tries to write a file is working against its instructions.

12.4 pipeline(items, ...stages): Process Items Without a Barrier

pipeline() processes a list of items through a sequence of stages. The critical behavioral property: there is no barrier between stages. As soon as item A finishes stage 1, it immediately enters stage 2, while items B and C may still be in stage 1.

const results = await pipeline(
  sourceFiles,
  // Stage 1: analyze each file
  (file) => agent(`Analyze ${file} for security issues`, {
    label: `analyze:${file}`,
    schema: ANALYSIS_SCHEMA
  }),
  // Stage 2: verify each analysis (receives previous result, original item, index)
  (analysis, file, idx) => agent(`Verify this finding from ${file}: ${analysis.summary}`, {
    label: `verify:${file}`
  }),
  // Stage 3: generate a fix for each verified finding
  (verification, file) => agent(`Generate a minimal fix for the verified issue in ${file}`, {
    label: `fix:${file}`,
    schema: FIX_SCHEMA
  })
)

Stage callback signature

Each stage function receives three arguments:

(previousResult, originalItem, index) => Promise<any>
  • previousResult: the output of the previous stage for this item. For the first stage, this is the original item itself.
  • originalItem: the original item from the input array, unchanged across all stages.
  • index: the zero-based position of this item in the original array.

The originalItem parameter is essential when you need to reference the original data in a later stage where the previous result has transformed it into something else (a schema object, a parsed structure, etc.).

No barrier: the timing model

The absence of a barrier is what gives pipeline() its wall-clock efficiency:

gantt
    title pipeline() — 3 files, 3 stages (no barrier)
    dateFormat  ss
    axisFormat  %Ss

    section File A
    Stage 1 :a1, 0, 3s
    Stage 2 :a2, after a1, 4s
    Stage 3 :a3, after a2, 2s

    section File B
    Stage 1 :b1, 1s, 3s
    Stage 2 :b2, after b1, 4s
    Stage 3 :b3, after b2, 2s

    section File C
    Stage 1 :c1, 2s, 3s
    Stage 2 :c2, after c1, 4s
    Stage 3 :c3, after c2, 2s

File A starts stage 2 at T=3s. File B starts stage 2 at T=4s. File C starts stage 2 at T=5s. None of them wait for the others to finish a stage before progressing. The wall-clock time equals the duration of the slowest single chain (A, B, or C end-to-end), not the sum of all stages across all items.

Contrast this with a naive sequential loop:

// Naive — sequential. Wall clock = sum of all work.
const results = []
for (const file of sourceFiles) {
  const analysis = await agent(`Analyze ${file}`)
  const verification = await agent(`Verify: ${analysis}`)
  results.push(verification)
}

For 10 files with 3 stages of 4 seconds each, the sequential version takes 120 seconds. The pipeline version takes ~14 seconds (longest chain, plus scheduling overhead).

Error handling in pipeline

If a stage function throws, the item is silently dropped — it resolves to null in the output array and no subsequent stages run for that item. This is the correct behavior for workflows where one bad file should not abort the entire run.

const results = await pipeline(
  files,
  async (file) => {
    // Throw to skip this item
    if (!file.endsWith('.py')) throw new Error('Not a Python file')
    return agent(`Analyze ${file}`, { schema: SCHEMA })
  },
  (analysis, file) => agent(`Fix issues in ${file}`, { schema: FIX_SCHEMA })
)

// Filter nulls from results
const valid = results.filter(Boolean)
log(`Processed ${valid.length} of ${files.length} files`)

The filter(Boolean) pattern is standard pipeline hygiene — always filter the output array before using it.

12.5 parallel(thunks): Concurrent Execution With a Barrier

parallel() takes an array of zero-argument functions (thunks), executes them all concurrently, and waits for every one to finish before returning. This is a barrier.

const [security, performance, correctness] = await parallel([
  () => agent('Audit the codebase for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities', {
    label: 'security-audit',
    phase: 'Analysis'
  }),
  () => agent('Profile the critical path and identify bottlenecks', {
    label: 'perf-audit',
    phase: 'Analysis'
  }),
  () => agent('Verify all public API contracts match their documentation', {
    label: 'correctness-audit',
    phase: 'Analysis'
  })
])

// All three are guaranteed complete here
log(`Security: ${security}, Performance: ${performance}`)

The barrier guarantee

Every thunk resolves before parallel() returns — including thunks that throw. A throwing thunk resolves to null in the output array. parallel() itself never rejects. This is a critical difference from Promise.all(), which rejects on the first failure and may leave other promises in flight.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Workflow
    participant A as Agent 1
    participant B as Agent 2
    participant C as Agent 3

    W->>A: spawn (thunk 0)
    W->>B: spawn (thunk 1)
    W->>C: spawn (thunk 2)
    Note over W: BARRIER — waiting
    A-->>W: result[0]
    B-->>W: result[1] (null — threw)
    C-->>W: result[2]
    Note over W: ALL done — returns [r0, null, r2]

pipeline vs parallel: the decision rule

This is the most important design decision in workflow authoring:

Use caseChoose
Processing a list of items through multiple transformationspipeline
Running independent analyses that do not share dataparallel
Want wall-clock = slowest single item chainpipeline
Want wall-clock = slowest single thunk (barrier)parallel
Items feed into next stage as soon as readypipeline
Must have all results before proceedingparallel

A common composition: use parallel to launch multiple independent domain audits (security, performance, documentation), then pass all results to a single synthesis agent. Use pipeline to process a file list through scan → verify → fix.

// Outer parallel: three independent domain analyses
const [secFindings, perfFindings, docFindings] = await parallel([
  () => pipeline(files, f => agent(`Security scan: ${f}`, { schema: SEC_SCHEMA })),
  () => pipeline(files, f => agent(`Perf scan: ${f}`, { schema: PERF_SCHEMA })),
  () => pipeline(files, f => agent(`Doc coverage: ${f}`, { schema: DOC_SCHEMA }))
])

// Single synthesis after all domains complete
const report = await agent(
  `Synthesize these findings into a unified report`,
  { schema: REPORT_SCHEMA }
)

12.6 phase(title): Group Agents Under Named Phases

phase() is a display primitive. It sets the current phase label — all subsequent agent() calls are associated with this phase in the progress UI until phase() is called again with a new title.

phase('Discovery')
const structure = await agent('Map the module structure', { label: 'map-structure' })

phase('Analysis')
const issues = await pipeline(
  structure.modules,
  m => agent(`Analyze ${m}`, { label: `analyze:${m}`, schema: ISSUE_SCHEMA })
)

phase('Synthesis')
const report = await agent('Synthesize findings', { label: 'synthesize' })

The user sees the phase titles as the workflow progresses:

[Discovery] map-structure ....
[Analysis] analyze:auth (3/12) ....
[Analysis] analyze:billing (4/12) ....
[Synthesis] synthesize ....

Phases map directly to the phases array in the meta block if you want to pre-declare them:

export const meta = {
  name: 'code-audit',
  description: 'Comprehensive code audit in three phases',
  phases: ['Discovery', 'Analysis', 'Synthesis']
}

Pre-declaring phases in meta lets the UI show a progress bar with known phase count. Without pre-declaration, phases are shown as they appear but no total-count progress is available.

Overriding phase per agent

The phase option in agent() opts a specific agent into a named phase regardless of the global phase() call:

phase('Analysis')

// This agent shows under 'Analysis'
const mainAnalysis = await agent('Analyze the core module', { label: 'core' })

// This one shows under 'Background' regardless of the current global phase
const background = await agent('Check dependency licenses', {
  label: 'licenses',
  phase: 'Background'
})

This is useful when you spawn fire-and-forget agents that logically belong to a different context than your main workflow phase.

12.7 log(message): Emit Narrator Progress Lines

log() emits a progress line visible to the user during workflow execution. Use it sparingly and purposefully — it is not a debug logger, it is a narrator.

log('Starting audit of 47 Python files')

const results = await pipeline(files, analyzeFile)
const valid = results.filter(Boolean)

log(`Analysis complete — ${valid.length} files processed, ${files.length - valid.length} skipped`)

if (valid.some(r => r.severity === 'critical')) {
  log('Critical issues found — escalating to full verification')
}

Good log() calls:

  • Mark phase transitions with context: log('Switching to verification — 12 findings to check')
  • Report counts at milestones: log(${results.length} agents spawned)
  • Surface decision points: log('Budget below 50k — skipping deep verification')

Bad log() calls:

  • Debug noise: log('entering loop')
  • Redundant narration: log('calling agent') immediately before an agent() call

The user can already see agent labels and phase titles in the progress UI. log() is for information that would otherwise be invisible — counts, decisions, budget state, conditional branch taken.

12.8 args: Input Value from the Workflow Tool Call

args is the verbatim JavaScript object from the args field of the Workflow tool call. It is not a string; it is actual JSON deserialized into a JavaScript object.

// Tool call args field:
// { "files": ["src/auth/", "src/billing/"], "severity": "high" }

// In the script:
const files = args.files         // ["src/auth/", "src/billing/"]
const minSeverity = args.severity  // "high"

The stringified-JSON trap

The single most common args mistake is passing a JSON string instead of a JSON object:

// WRONG — args.files will be undefined because args is a string, not an object
// Tool call: { "args": "{\"files\": [\"src/\"]}" }

// CORRECT — args is actual JSON
// Tool call: { "args": { "files": ["src/"] } }

If you find yourself calling JSON.parse(args) or JSON.parse(args.config) in a script body, something is wrong at the call site. The Workflow tool's args field is typed as { [k: string]: unknown } — it must be a JSON object, never a string.

Defensive defaults

args may be null or an empty object if the workflow is called without arguments. Always provide defaults:

const files = args?.files ?? ['.']
const depth = args?.depth ?? 'full'
const model = args?.model ?? 'sonnet'
const exclude = Array.isArray(args?.exclude) ? args.exclude : []

The ?. optional chaining handles the null case. The ?? nullish coalescing handles the missing-key case. Both are necessary.

12.9 budget: Token Budget Tracking

budget exposes the token budget from the user's +500k directive. Use it to scale workflow depth to available resources.

// budget.total:       number | null (null if no target set)
// budget.spent():     number — output tokens used across all workflows this session
// budget.remaining(): number — max(0, total - spent()), or Infinity if no target

log(`Budget: ${budget.total ?? 'unlimited'}, spent: ${budget.spent()}, remaining: ${budget.remaining()}`)

The +500k directive

When a user prepends +500k to a prompt (or any token-count prefix), they are signaling a desired token budget for the operation. The Workflow runtime reads this and populates budget.total. Without a directive, budget.total is null and budget.remaining() returns Infinity.

Budget-adaptive patterns

Budget tracking enables workflows that self-regulate depth based on available tokens:

// Scale verification depth based on remaining budget
const FULL_VERIFY_COST_ESTIMATE = 8000    // tokens per file for deep verify
const LIGHT_VERIFY_COST_ESTIMATE = 2000   // tokens per file for surface verify

const useDeepVerify = budget.remaining() > files.length * FULL_VERIFY_COST_ESTIMATE

const verifiedFindings = await pipeline(
  findings,
  finding => agent(
    useDeepVerify
      ? `Deep verify: trace this finding through all call sites: ${finding.summary}`
      : `Surface verify: confirm this is a real issue: ${finding.summary}`,
    { label: `verify:${finding.id}` }
  )
)

Budget-limited loops

For workflows that run iterative improvement cycles, check budget before each iteration:

let iteration = 0
const improvements = []

while (budget.remaining() > 50_000 && iteration < 10) {
  log(`Iteration ${++iteration} — ${budget.remaining()} tokens remaining`)
  
  const improvement = await agent(`Iteration ${iteration}: Find the next highest-value improvement`)
  if (!improvement) break
  
  improvements.push(improvement)
  
  // Apply and verify
  await agent(`Apply this improvement: ${improvement}`, { isolation: 'worktree', agentType: 'Edit' })
}

log(`Completed ${iteration} improvement iterations`)

No budget directive

When budget.total is null, the workflow has no resource constraint from the user. Do not treat this as zero — treat it as unlimited. The guard if (budget.total && budget.remaining() > threshold) short-circuits cleanly when budget.total is null.

12.10 Agent Options: The Full Reference

All options for agent() in one place:

const result = await agent('prompt text', {
  // Display label in progress UI and transcript directory.
  // Use colon-separated hierarchy: 'verify:auth:tokens'
  label: 'verify:auth',
  
  // Override the current phase() for this specific agent.
  phase: 'Verification',
  
  // JSON Schema for structured output. Enables object return value.
  // Must be valid draft-07 JSON Schema.
  schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      issues: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
      severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'] },
      confident: { type: 'boolean' }
    },
    required: ['issues', 'severity', 'confident']
  },
  
  // Model tier for this agent. 'opus' for complex reasoning,
  // 'haiku' for high-volume mechanical tasks.
  model: 'sonnet',
  
  // 'worktree' gives this agent an isolated git worktree.
  // Required for concurrent agents that make file edits.
  isolation: 'worktree',
  
  // 'Explore' = read-only persona. 'Edit' = full modification access.
  agentType: 'Explore'
})

Model selection strategy

Matching model tier to task complexity is the primary cost-control lever in a workflow:

Task typeRecommended modelReasoning
Discovery, file listing, categorizationhaikuMechanical, high-volume, low reasoning demand
Code analysis, issue detectionsonnetGood balance of reasoning and throughput
Architectural synthesis, security auditopusMaximum reasoning for high-stakes conclusions
Structured data extractionhaiku with schemaSchema enforcement compensates for reasoning limits

In a large pipeline with 100 files, using haiku for the scan stage and sonnet only for verification of actual findings can reduce cost by 5-10x while maintaining result quality.

Label naming conventions

Labels appear in the transcript directory as folder names and in the progress UI. Use a colon-delimited hierarchy:

phase:subphase:item-identifier

Examples:

  • scan:auth — the scan phase, auth module
  • verify:finding:CWE-89 — verifying a specific finding
  • fix:billing:invoice-generator — generating a fix for a specific file

Avoid labels with slashes (these become path separators in the transcript directory). Avoid labels longer than 40 characters — they get truncated in the progress UI.

12.11 Concurrency: Limits and the Lifetime Cap

Two hard limits govern all workflow execution:

Simultaneous agent cap

min(16, CPU_CORES - 2)

On a machine with 12 CPU cores, the cap is 10 simultaneous agents. On a machine with 4 cores, the cap is 2. This is computed once at harness startup. You cannot configure it.

The practical implication: parallel([...100 thunks]) does not spawn 100 agents simultaneously. The runtime queues them and issues agents in batches up to the concurrency cap. The 100 agents will complete correctly — just in batches of (say) 10.

This is invisible to your script logic, but it matters for timing estimates. Do not assume all parallel() thunks start at T=0. On a 4-core machine, parallel([...20 thunks]) starts 2 agents at T=0, starts the next 2 when one completes, and so on.

Lifetime agent cap: 1000

A single workflow can spawn at most 1000 agents total. This includes all agents from nested pipeline() and parallel() calls and inline agent() calls. If the 1001st agent call is made, it returns null — same as a user-skipped agent.

For workflows processing large codebases, count your agents before running:

const files = args.files  // could be thousands
const AGENTS_PER_FILE = 3  // scan + verify + fix

if (files.length * AGENTS_PER_FILE > 900) {
  // Leave 100 agents for synthesis
  log(`WARNING: ${files.length} files × ${AGENTS_PER_FILE} = ${files.length * AGENTS_PER_FILE} agents — truncating to 300 files`)
  files.splice(300)
}

Workflow lifetime, not harness lifetime

The 1000-agent cap is per-workflow-run, not per harness session. Different workflows launched in the same session each get their own 1000-agent budget. A resumed workflow (via resumeFromRunId) picks up its count from the prior run — cached agent results do not consume new budget.

12.12 Resume Semantics and Script Iteration

Every workflow run is persisted. This is one of the most underused features in the engine.

The persistence model

When the Workflow tool returns, scriptPath in the output tells you where the script was saved:

~/.claude/projects/-Users-DOANTX26-Documents-2026/workflows/wf_a3b9kx/script.js

And runId identifies the execution:

wf_a3b9kx

To resume a failed or partial run:

// Re-invoke Workflow tool with:
{
  scriptPath: '...the returned scriptPath...',
  resumeFromRunId: 'wf_a3b9kx',
  args: { files: ['src/'] }
}

Cache semantics

The resume system uses a longest unchanged prefix strategy:

  • Agents that ran identically (same prompt, same args, same position in the execution graph) return cached results instantly
  • Agents after the first change re-run
  • A script edit that changes stage 3 logic still caches stages 1 and 2

For expensive workflows — say, a 200-file audit where each file spawns 3 agents — this means a bug in your synthesis stage can be fixed and re-run without re-paying for all 600 analysis agents. Only the synthesis stage re-runs.

100% cache hit: same script + same args + same resumeFromRunId. Use this deliberately when you want to re-run reporting or synthesis without re-running analysis.

The iteration workflow

The correct development cycle for complex workflows:

  1. Run the workflow — get runId and scriptPath back
  2. Observe the progress and partial results
  3. Edit the script with the Write or Edit tool using the returned scriptPath
  4. Re-invoke with scriptPath + resumeFromRunId
  5. Cached stages return immediately; changed stages re-run
  6. Repeat until the workflow produces the result you want

This is dramatically faster than restarting from scratch. A 30-minute full run becomes a 2-minute incremental re-run if you only change the synthesis prompt.

12.13 Lab: Build a Comprehensive Code Audit Workflow

This lab assembles every concept in the chapter into a production-quality audit workflow. It processes a codebase through three phases — find, verify, synthesize — with budget awareness, proper error handling, and resume support.

The specification

Given a list of directories, the workflow should:

  1. Discover all source files in each directory
  2. Audit each file for security and correctness issues
  3. Verify all high-severity findings with a second agent
  4. Synthesize a final report with prioritized remediation recommendations

Step 1: Define schemas

Schemas are the most important architectural decision in a workflow — they are the contracts between agents.

export const meta = {
  name: 'code-audit',
  description: 'Comprehensive three-phase code audit: find, verify, synthesize',
  phases: ['Discovery', 'Audit', 'Verification', 'Synthesis']
}

const FILE_LIST_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    files: {
      type: 'array',
      items: { type: 'string' },
      description: 'Absolute paths to source files found'
    },
    count: { type: 'number' }
  },
  required: ['files', 'count']
}

const FINDING_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          file: { type: 'string' },
          line: { type: 'number' },
          severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'] },
          cwe: { type: 'string' },
          summary: { type: 'string' },
          recommendation: { type: 'string' }
        },
        required: ['file', 'line', 'severity', 'summary', 'recommendation']
      }
    },
    clean: { type: 'boolean' }
  },
  required: ['findings', 'clean']
}

const VERIFICATION_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    confirmed: { type: 'boolean' },
    false_positive_reason: { type: 'string' },
    additional_context: { type: 'string' }
  },
  required: ['confirmed']
}

const REPORT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    executive_summary: { type: 'string' },
    critical_count: { type: 'number' },
    high_count: { type: 'number' },
    medium_count: { type: 'number' },
    low_count: { type: 'number' },
    confirmed_findings: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'object' } },
    remediation_order: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    estimated_effort_hours: { type: 'number' }
  },
  required: ['executive_summary', 'critical_count', 'high_count', 'confirmed_findings']
}

Step 2: Discovery phase

// Input: list of directories, or default to current directory
const targetDirs = args?.dirs ?? ['.']
const excludePatterns = args?.exclude ?? ['node_modules', '.venv', 'dist', 'build']
const minSeverity = args?.min_severity ?? 'medium'

log(`Starting audit of ${targetDirs.length} director${targetDirs.length === 1 ? 'y' : 'ies'}`)
log(`Minimum severity: ${minSeverity} | Budget: ${budget.total ? budget.remaining() + ' tokens remaining' : 'unlimited'}`)

phase('Discovery')

// Discover files in all target directories concurrently
const discoveries = await parallel(
  targetDirs.map(dir => () => agent(
    `List all source code files in ${dir}. Exclude: ${excludePatterns.join(', ')}. ` +
    `Include: .py, .js, .ts, .go, .rs, .java, .rb, .php, .c, .cpp files only. ` +
    `Return absolute paths.`,
    {
      label: `discover:${dir}`,
      schema: FILE_LIST_SCHEMA,
      model: 'haiku'   // mechanical listing task
    }
  ))
)

// Flatten all file lists, remove nulls from failed discoveries
const allFiles = discoveries
  .filter(Boolean)
  .flatMap(d => d.files)

log(`Discovered ${allFiles.length} source files across ${targetDirs.length} director${targetDirs.length === 1 ? 'y' : 'ies'}`)

if (allFiles.length === 0) {
  log('No source files found — check your target directories')
  // workflow ends — no return statement needed, body just completes
}

Step 3: Audit phase with budget guard

// Guard against 1000-agent cap: each file uses 2 agents (audit + possibly verify)
const MAX_FILES = 450  // leaves 100 agents for synthesis and overhead
const filesToAudit = allFiles.length > MAX_FILES
  ? (log(`Truncating to ${MAX_FILES} files to stay within agent budget`), allFiles.slice(0, MAX_FILES))
  : allFiles

phase('Audit')
log(`Auditing ${filesToAudit.length} files...`)

// pipeline: files flow through audit continuously — no barrier between files
const auditResults = await pipeline(
  filesToAudit,
  (file) => agent(
    `Audit this file for security vulnerabilities and correctness issues: ${file}\n\n` +
    `Focus on: injection flaws (CWE-89, CWE-78), authentication issues (CWE-287), ` +
    `cryptographic weaknesses (CWE-326, CWE-327), path traversal (CWE-22), ` +
    `hardcoded credentials (CWE-798), and logic errors that could cause data loss.\n\n` +
    `Use your Read tool to examine the file contents. Report only real issues — ` +
    `if the file is clean, set clean: true and findings: [].`,
    {
      label: `audit:${file.split('/').pop()}`,
      schema: FINDING_SCHEMA,
      model: 'sonnet',
      agentType: 'Explore'
    }
  )
)

// Collect all findings, filtering nulls
const allFindings = auditResults
  .filter(Boolean)
  .flatMap(r => r.findings)

const highSeverityFindings = allFindings.filter(
  f => f.severity === 'critical' || f.severity === 'high'
)
const otherFindings = allFindings.filter(
  f => f.severity === 'medium' || f.severity === 'low'
)

log(`Audit complete — ${allFindings.length} total findings: ` +
    `${highSeverityFindings.length} high/critical, ${otherFindings.length} medium/low`)

Step 4: Verification phase with budget awareness

phase('Verification')

// Only verify high/critical findings — and only if budget allows
const shouldVerify = (
  highSeverityFindings.length > 0 &&
  (budget.total === null || budget.remaining() > highSeverityFindings.length * 3000)
)

let confirmedHighSeverity = highSeverityFindings

if (shouldVerify) {
  log(`Verifying ${highSeverityFindings.length} high/critical findings...`)
  
  const verifications = await pipeline(
    highSeverityFindings,
    (finding, _, idx) => agent(
      `Verify this security finding is a real issue and not a false positive.\n\n` +
      `Finding: ${finding.summary}\n` +
      `File: ${finding.file} line ${finding.line}\n` +
      `CWE: ${finding.cwe ?? 'not specified'}\n\n` +
      `Use your Read tool to examine the file at the specified location. ` +
      `Check: is this actually exploitable? Is there sanitization or mitigation ` +
      `elsewhere that resolves this? Set confirmed: true only if this is a genuine issue.`,
      {
        label: `verify:${idx}:${finding.file.split('/').pop()}`,
        schema: VERIFICATION_SCHEMA,
        model: 'sonnet',
        agentType: 'Explore'
      }
    )
  )

  // Pair verification results with findings, keep only confirmed
  confirmedHighSeverity = highSeverityFindings.filter((finding, idx) => {
    const v = verifications[idx]
    return v && v.confirmed
  })

  const falsePositives = highSeverityFindings.length - confirmedHighSeverity.length
  log(`Verification complete — ${confirmedHighSeverity.length} confirmed, ${falsePositives} false positives eliminated`)
} else if (highSeverityFindings.length === 0) {
  log('No high/critical findings to verify')
} else {
  log(`Skipping verification — insufficient budget (${budget.remaining()} tokens remaining)`)
}

Step 5: Synthesis phase

phase('Synthesis')

const allConfirmedFindings = [
  ...confirmedHighSeverity,
  ...otherFindings  // medium/low are accepted without verification
]

log(`Synthesizing report for ${allConfirmedFindings.length} confirmed findings...`)

const findingsSummary = allConfirmedFindings
  .map(f => `- [${f.severity.toUpperCase()}] ${f.file}:${f.line} — ${f.summary}`)
  .join('\n')

const report = await agent(
  `Generate a comprehensive security audit report for an engineering team.\n\n` +
  `Confirmed findings (${allConfirmedFindings.length} total):\n${findingsSummary}\n\n` +
  `The report should include:\n` +
  `1. Executive summary (2-3 sentences suitable for a VP of Engineering)\n` +
  `2. Counts by severity\n` +
  `3. The confirmed findings list with their recommendations\n` +
  `4. A remediation order — prioritize by severity and blast radius\n` +
  `5. Estimated total effort hours for remediation\n\n` +
  `Be direct and actionable. This is an internal engineering document, not a sales document.`,
  {
    label: 'synthesize-report',
    schema: REPORT_SCHEMA,
    model: 'opus'  // architectural synthesis — use opus
  }
)

if (!report) {
  log('Synthesis failed — producing minimal report from raw findings')
  // Fallback: emit raw findings
  log(`Raw findings: ${JSON.stringify(allConfirmedFindings, null, 2)}`)
} else {
  log(`Report complete`)
  log(`Executive summary: ${report.executive_summary}`)
  log(`Severity breakdown: ${report.critical_count} critical, ${report.high_count} high, ${report.medium_count ?? 0} medium, ${report.low_count ?? 0} low`)
  log(`Estimated remediation effort: ${report.estimated_effort_hours ?? 'unknown'} hours`)
  log(`Remediation order: ${report.remediation_order?.join(' → ') ?? 'see findings'}`)
}

Running the workflow

Invoke from the Workflow tool:

// In a Claude Code session, use the Workflow tool:
{
  script: '...the full script above...',
  args: {
    dirs: ['src/', 'lib/'],
    exclude: ['node_modules', '__pycache__', '.venv'],
    min_severity: 'medium'
  }
}

Or for a large repo with a token budget:

+500k audit src/ with code-audit workflow, exclude tests/

The +500k directive populates budget.total so the verification phase self-regulates.

Iterating on the workflow

After the first run:

  1. Check the transcript directory from transcriptDir in the tool output
  2. Find agents that produced poor results (read their transcript)
  3. Edit the prompt for that stage in the script at scriptPath
  4. Re-invoke with resumeFromRunId — preceding stages return from cache, the edited stage re-runs

If the synthesis prompt is wrong but the 200-file audit was correct, re-running with the fix costs only one synthesis agent call — not 400 audit calls.

Summary

The Workflow engine is the most expressive tool in the Claude Code harness. It transforms one-shot agent calls into structured programs with phases, pipelines, parallel fans, and token budgets.

The key constraints to carry into production:

meta must be a pure literal. Static parsing, not runtime evaluation. Variables, template literals, spreads, and function calls all fail.

pipeline() has no barrier. Items flow through stages as soon as the previous stage completes. Wall-clock time equals the slowest single item chain. Use this for per-item transformations.

parallel() has a barrier. All thunks must complete before it returns. Throws resolve to null, never reject. Use this for independent analyses that need to be combined.

args is actual JSON, not a string. The args field is { [k: string]: unknown }. Passing a stringified JSON string is the most common invocation mistake.

Agent cap is min(16, cores-2) simultaneous and 1000 lifetime. Design against these limits explicitly when processing large file sets.

Resume semantics save expensive re-runs. Every workflow persists its script and run ID. Edit the script, re-invoke with resumeFromRunId, and only changed stages re-execute.

The code audit workflow in section 12.12 is production-ready. Copy it, adjust the schemas for your domain, and use it as the foundation for any multi-agent analysis task.

In Chapter 13, we move to the task system — how long-running background work is tracked, resumed, and composed across sessions.

Next: Chapter 13: Task System — Background Work and Session Continuity

Chapter 13: Advanced Workflow Patterns

"The pipeline is not a stage graph. It is a promise: every item either finishes or fails cleanly, and no item waits for another."

13.1 pipeline() vs parallel(): When Barriers Help vs Hurt

The single most consequential decision in multi-agent workflow design is choosing between pipeline() and parallel(). Both run work concurrently. The difference is whether you insert a synchronization barrier — a point where all upstream work must complete before any downstream work begins. Get this wrong and you trade throughput for false structure, or correctness for speed.

pipeline() is the default. It processes a collection of items through a sequence of per-item transforms, running each item independently through all stages. Items that complete early do not wait for slower items. A throw in any stage drops that item to null for the rest of the pipeline. The result is an array of the same length as the input, with null in positions that failed or were skipped.

parallel() is a barrier. It launches a collection of tasks simultaneously and waits for all of them to settle before returning. Every caller downstream of parallel() is blocked until the slowest task finishes.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "pipeline() — per-item flow, no barrier"
        direction TB
        I1[item A] --> S1A[stage 1] --> S2A[stage 2] --> S3A[stage 3]
        I2[item B] --> S1B[stage 1] --> S2B[stage 2] --> S3B[stage 3]
        I3[item C] --> S1C[stage 1] --> S2C[stage 2] --> S3C[stage 3]
    end

    subgraph "parallel() — barrier, all-or-wait"
        direction TB
        T1[task 1] --> BAR{wait for all}
        T2[task 2] --> BAR
        T3[task 3] --> BAR
        BAR --> DOWN[downstream code]
    end

When barriers genuinely help

A barrier is justified when downstream logic has a cross-item dependency — when it needs to look across all results together. Three concrete cases:

Deduplication. You are running N finders to collect bugs across a large codebase. Two finders may return the same issue. You cannot deduplicate per-item; you need all findings in hand before you can run seen.has(key(b)). A parallel() barrier followed by a dedup pass is the correct structure here, not a pipeline.

Early-exit / circuit breaking. You are running N verifiers on a candidate solution. If any verifier returns critical: true, you want to abort all remaining work and surface the critical finding immediately.
