A parallel() lets you Promise.race() or post-process the full result set with an early exit. Pipeline does not give you this cross-item visibility mid-flight.

Synthesis across all outputs. You are running N approaches to a problem (judge panel, §13.7) and the synthesis step requires comparing all N outputs. You cannot synthesize until all approaches are complete. A barrier is the correct model.

When barriers hurt

A barrier hurts when there is no cross-item dependency but you inserted one anyway. The cost is latency: every item in the faster batch waits for the slowest item to complete before the downstream stages begin.

The smell test is simple: if the transform between stages has no logic that reads from two different items in the same batch, the barrier is wrong.

// Wrong: unnecessary barrier between review and verify stages
const reviews = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () =>
  agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
// now the slowest dimension has finished, and THEN we start verification
const verified = await parallel(reviews.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r =>
  r.findings.map(f => () => agent(`Verify: ${f.title}`, {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA}))))

The verify stage has no dependency on other dimensions' findings. Introducing the barrier between them doubles the critical path. The correct version is a pipeline with inline verify:

// Correct: pipeline — each dimension's findings flow directly into verify
const results = await pipeline(
  DIMENSIONS,
  d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
  review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
    agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
      .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))))
)
const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)

Here, parallel() inside the second pipeline stage is not a cross-item barrier — it is intra-item concurrency: we launch all verifiers for one dimension's findings in parallel, then the pipeline carries results forward. The outer pipeline ensures that dimension A's verify step begins the moment dimension A's review step completes, without waiting for dimension B.

The barrier-justified checklist

Before adding a parallel() barrier, confirm at least one of:

JustificationExample
Deduplication across itemsMultiple finders, dedup by key before verify
Early-exit or circuit-breakAny verifier returns critical → abort
Cross-item ranking or selectionJudge panel: pick winner from all approaches
Synthesis requires complete pictureCompleteness critic needs all findings to say what's missing
Token budget check across all resultsBudget loop needs full batch to decide whether to continue

If none apply: use pipeline().

13.2 Resume Semantics: resumeFromRunId

Every agent() call inside a Workflow is journaled. The journal records the call's identity — its prompt, schema, label, and positional context — alongside its result. When you pass resumeFromRunId on a subsequent invocation, the harness replays the journal: calls whose identity matches an existing entry return the cached result without sending anything to the API. Calls whose identity has changed (because you edited the script) run fresh.

This is not a "skip completed steps" primitive. It is content-addressable caching. The cache key is derived from the call's observable identity. If you change the prompt by one character, the call is considered new and re-runs.

// First run — returns scriptPath and runId in the response
// {
//   runId: "wf_abc123",
//   scriptPath: "/path/to/audit.js"
// }

// Edit the script: add a new dimension or fix a prompt, then re-invoke:
// Workflow({scriptPath: "/path/to/audit.js", resumeFromRunId: "wf_abc123"})
//
// Unchanged agent() calls → cached result, no API call
// Edited or new agent() calls → run fresh, result journaled

The practical consequence: non-determinism breaks resume

Resume depends on stable call identity. Three constructs destroy that stability:

Date.now() — timestamps change on every run. A prompt that includes the current timestamp will never match a cached entry. Every call is "new" every time.

Math.random() — injecting a random seed, nonce, or UUID into a prompt text breaks identity. The prompt on the second run will never equal the prompt on the first run.

new Date() — same problem as Date.now(), in constructor form.

These are not available in Workflow scripts. The sandbox disallows them. This is a correctness constraint, not an oversight: if the harness permitted them, resume would silently fall back to a full re-run every time without telling you why.

Design for resumability. Prompts should be pure functions of their inputs: the item being processed, the schema, and fixed configuration. Never interpolate timestamps, random IDs, or wall-clock state into prompt text. If you need a unique identifier per invocation (for tracing, not for the prompt), pass it as metadata that does not affect the cache key.

When to use resume

Resume pays off in two scenarios:

  1. Long workflows interrupted mid-run. A 300-call security audit that fails at call 247 resumes from call 247, not from scratch. The saved cost is proportional to how far the workflow had progressed.
  1. Iterative development. You are tuning a workflow script. You change the synthesis prompt at the end but leave the 50 finder calls untouched. Resume re-runs only the synthesis, not the finders. The development loop tightens from minutes to seconds.

Resume is not appropriate when the workflow is inherently stateful — when later calls should see the effects of earlier ones on an external system. Journal caching replays outputs; it does not replay side effects.

13.3 Nested Workflows: workflow(nameOrRef, args)

A workflow can spawn a child workflow with workflow(nameOrRef, args). The child executes as a sub-step: it has its own script, its own labeled agent calls, and its own result. From the parent's perspective, it is a single async operation that returns the child's output.

// Parent workflow
const subResult = await workflow('find-todos', {dir: 'src/'})
// subResult is whatever the child workflow returns
const todos = subResult.todos

// Alternatively, by script path:
const subResult = await workflow('/absolute/path/to/find-todos.js', {dir: 'src/'})

The child shares the parent's execution context:

  • Concurrency cap. The child's agent() calls consume slots from the same concurrency pool as the parent. If the parent is already running 10 agents and the concurrency cap is 12, the child can only run 2 agents simultaneously.
  • Agent counter. The total agent count displayed in the UI accumulates across parent and child.
  • Abort signal. If the user cancels the parent, the child is cancelled too.
  • Token budget. The child draws from the same budget object as the parent.

Nesting is one level only

A workflow spawned by a workflow cannot itself spawn a workflow. Calling workflow() inside a child workflow throws. This constraint is intentional: deep nesting makes execution traces unreadable, abort semantics compound, and debugging becomes archaeology. If you need more than two levels of decomposition, flatten the structure — compose it as named stages in the parent, not as a tree of workflows.

When to use nested workflows

The right use case for nested workflows is reusable sub-task composition — a bounded piece of work that:

  1. Makes sense as a standalone unit (can be tested and invoked independently),
  2. Has a clean input/output contract,
  3. Is reused across multiple parent workflows.

A find-todos workflow, a summarize-file workflow, a triage-issues workflow — these are clean sub-step candidates. A workflow that does "everything except the last step" is not.

flowchart TD
    P[Parent: security-audit] --> A[find-todos workflow]
    P --> B[dependency-scan workflow]
    P --> C[direct agent calls for synthesis]
    A --> R[subResult.todos]
    B --> R2[subResult.vulns]
    R & R2 & C --> SYNTH[Final report]

The key discipline: do not nest for organizational tidiness. Nest only when the sub-workflow has independent value and reuse justifies the additional execution boundary.

13.4 Structured Output: The schema Option

Every agent() call accepts a schema option — a JSON Schema object. When provided, the harness forces the model to use the StructuredOutput tool, which validates the model's response against the schema before returning it to your workflow code. Invalid output causes a retry within the agent call; the calling workflow sees only validated results or null.

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['isReal', 'confidence', 'reason'],
  properties: {
    isReal: { type: 'boolean' },
    confidence: { type: 'number', minimum: 0, maximum: 1 },
    reason: { type: 'string', minLength: 10 }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

const verdict = await agent(
  `Verify this finding: ${JSON.stringify(finding)}`,
  {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA, label: `verify:${finding.id}`}
)
// verdict is null (user skipped) or a typed, validated object

Without schema, the model returns a text string. With schema, you get a typed JavaScript object that satisfies your contract. This is not cosmetic — it eliminates an entire class of downstream bugs caused by parsing free-form model output.

Schema design for reliability

A schema that is too strict will cause excessive retries. A schema that is too loose defeats the purpose. Guidelines:

Require what you actually need. If reason is optional downstream, do not put it in required. The model will sometimes produce a valid object without it.

Use additionalProperties: false in output schemas. This prevents the model from injecting extra fields that look valid but break downstream destructuring.

Prefer flat objects over deep nesting. Nested required objects compound validation failures. A finding with three required nested objects is harder for the model to produce in a single well-formed response than a flat object with six required string fields.

Use enum for categorical values. severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'] } is far more reliable than asking the model to produce the right string from an unconstrained field.

schema and the StructuredOutput tool

When schema is present, the agent's system prompt is augmented to instruct the model to call StructuredOutput exactly once as its final action. The tool call's arguments are validated against the schema. If validation fails, the harness sends the validation error back to the model and gives it a second attempt. This retry loop is transparent to the workflow author — you see a result or null, never a validation error.

13.5 Adversarial Verification

A single agent reviewing its own work is not verification — it is self-approval. Adversarial verification runs N independent skeptics whose default posture is assume the claim is wrong. Only claims that survive a majority of skeptics are considered confirmed.

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['refuted', 'reason'],
  properties: {
    refuted: { type: 'boolean' },
    reason: { type: 'string', minLength: 20 }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

async function adversarialVerify(claim: string, threshold = 2): Promise<boolean> {
  const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
    agent(
      `Try to refute this claim. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.\n\nClaim: ${claim}`,
      {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA, label: `skeptic:${claim.slice(0, 40)}`}
    )
  ))
  const valid = votes.filter(Boolean)
  const survivors = valid.filter(v => !v.refuted).length
  log(`Claim "${claim.slice(0, 60)}": ${survivors}/${valid.length} skeptics passed`)
  return survivors >= threshold
}

The default-to-refuted instruction is load-bearing. Without it, agents default to the cooperative posture that characterizes most model training — they look for reasons to agree. Flipping the default forces them to look for reasons to disagree. A claim that cannot be refuted despite active effort to do so is a meaningfully stronger claim.

When to use adversarial verification

Use adversarial verification when the cost of a false positive is high: security findings, correctness proofs, legal analysis, any claim that will drive an action that is expensive to undo. Do not use it on low-stakes factual lookups where the overhead is not justified.

Configuring N and threshold

Three skeptics with a threshold of 2 (two-of-three majority) is a reasonable default. For high-stakes claims, use five skeptics with a threshold of 4. For findings that will be published externally or used to block a deployment, consider a unanimous three-of-three bar. The harness API supports any N and threshold — the cost is N additional API calls per claim.

The null-handling requirement

agent() returns null if the user skips the step. In a parallel skeptic pool, any of the N votes can be null. Always .filter(Boolean) before counting survivors:

const valid = votes.filter(Boolean)  // Remove skipped/null agents
const survivors = valid.filter(v => !v.refuted).length

If all three skeptics return null (the user skipped everything), valid.length is 0 and survivors >= 2 is false — the claim correctly fails verification. This is the right behavior: absence of confirmation is not confirmation.

13.6 Perspective-Diverse Verification

Adversarial verification uses identical skeptics. Perspective-diverse verification uses N agents with distinct lenses — each examines the same claim or solution through a different frame of reference. The combination is stronger than adversarial alone: a claim that survives a correctness lens, a security lens, a performance lens, and a reproducibility lens has been stress-tested from four directions.

const LENSES = [
  {
    name: 'correctness',
    prompt: (finding: string) =>
      `Examine this finding for correctness errors. Is the described behavior actually a bug? ` +
      `Would the code really do what the finding claims? Be skeptical.\n\nFinding: ${finding}`
  },
  {
    name: 'security',
    prompt: (finding: string) =>
      `Examine this finding from a security perspective. Is the described issue exploitable? ` +
      `What is the realistic attack vector? Could this be a false positive?\n\nFinding: ${finding}`
  },
  {
    name: 'performance',
    prompt: (finding: string) =>
      `Examine this finding from a performance perspective. Does the described issue actually ` +
      `impact performance at realistic scale, or only in pathological cases?\n\nFinding: ${finding}`
  },
  {
    name: 'reproducibility',
    prompt: (finding: string) =>
      `Examine this finding for reproducibility. Can this finding be triggered reliably? ` +
      `Is there a clear reproduction path, or is this speculative?\n\nFinding: ${finding}`
  }
]

const LENS_VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['valid', 'concerns', 'lens'],
  properties: {
    valid: { type: 'boolean' },
    concerns: { type: 'string' },
    lens: { type: 'string' }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

async function perspectiveVerify(finding: string) {
  const verdicts = await parallel(LENSES.map(lens => () =>
    agent(lens.prompt(finding), {
      schema: LENS_VERDICT_SCHEMA,
      label: `lens:${lens.name}`
    })
  ))
  const valid = verdicts.filter(Boolean)
  const passing = valid.filter(v => v.valid)
  const failing = valid.filter(v => !v.valid)
  return {
    confirmed: failing.length === 0,
    concerns: failing.map(v => `[${v.lens}] ${v.concerns}`),
    passRate: `${passing.length}/${valid.length}`
  }
}

Perspective diversity catches failures that adversarial review misses. A uniform adversarial panel might all focus on whether the code is syntactically correct and unanimously confirm a bug that is actually never triggered in production. The reproducibility lens would catch that. A uniform adversarial panel reviewing a regex-based SQL injection finding might all miss the fact that the ORM layer would sanitize the input first. The security lens with an explicit focus on attack vectors would catch that.

13.7 The Judge Panel

The judge panel pattern solves the problem of approach selection: when multiple agents solve the same problem via different methods, you need an objective way to identify the best solution. The panel pattern decouples generation from evaluation, ensuring that the evaluation is not anchored to any single approach.

const ANGLES = [
  {name: 'minimal', description: 'smallest possible change that solves the problem'},
  {name: 'defensive', description: 'hardened, input-validated, edge-case-resistant approach'},
  {name: 'idiomatic', description: 'most idiomatic for the language and codebase conventions'},
  {name: 'performant', description: 'optimized for throughput and minimal allocations'}
]

const SOLUTION_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['approach', 'code', 'tradeoffs'],
  properties: {
    approach: { type: 'string' },
    code: { type: 'string' },
    tradeoffs: { type: 'string' }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

const SCORE_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['score', 'rationale'],
  properties: {
    score: { type: 'integer', minimum: 1, maximum: 10 },
    rationale: { type: 'string', minLength: 20 }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

async function judgePanel(problem: string) {
  // Phase 1: Generate N approaches in parallel
  const approaches = await parallel(ANGLES.map(a => () =>
    agent(
      `Solve this problem via the ${a.name} approach (${a.description}):\n\n${problem}`,
      {schema: SOLUTION_SCHEMA, label: `approach:${a.name}`}
    )
  ))

  // Phase 2: Score each approach in parallel (barrier required — all solutions needed)
  const viable = approaches.filter(Boolean)
  const scores = await parallel(viable.map(s => () =>
    agent(
      `Score this solution 1-10 for correctness, maintainability, and fitness for purpose. ` +
      `Be strict. A 10 is production-ready with no significant issues.\n\n` +
      `${JSON.stringify(s, null, 2)}`,
      {schema: SCORE_SCHEMA, label: `score:${s?.approach}`}
    )
  ))

  // Phase 3: Synthesize from the winner
  const validScores = scores.filter(Boolean)
  const maxScore = Math.max(...validScores.map(s => s?.score || 0))
  const winnerIdx = scores.indexOf(validScores.find(s => s?.score === maxScore) ?? null)
  const winner = viable[winnerIdx]

  log(`Judge panel: winner is "${winner?.approach}" with score ${maxScore}`)

  return await agent(
    `Synthesize a final solution based on this winning approach, incorporating ` +
    `the best elements. Explain why this approach was selected.\n\nWinner: ${JSON.stringify(winner)}`,
    {label: 'synthesis'}
  )
}

The barrier between phase 1 and phase 2 is justified here: scoring requires all solutions to be available so the scorer can compare across approaches. The phase 2 → phase 3 barrier is also justified: synthesis requires knowing the winner, which requires all scores.

Gotchas

Anchoring in the scoring prompt. If your scoring prompt shows all solutions simultaneously, the model anchors to the first one. Score each solution independently (one agent() per solution) and let the Math.max() logic do the comparison.

Ties. Multiple solutions can share the max score. Decide your tie-breaking rule before you need it: first-wins, random selection among ties, or a dedicated tiebreaker agent call.

The approaches[winnerIdx] indexing. After filtering for Boolean, the winnerIdx into scores must map to the same position in viable. Maintain the parallel arrays carefully. The pattern above uses viable for both — no re-filtering between phases.

13.8 Loop-Until-Dry

Some problems do not have a fixed number of items to process. A codebase might have 3 bugs or 300; you do not know in advance. Loop-until-dry runs finders in a loop, terminating when K consecutive rounds produce no new findings. The deduplication across rounds ensures that findings are not double-counted.

const BUGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['bugs'],
  properties: {
    bugs: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        required: ['id', 'title', 'file', 'line', 'severity'],
        properties: {
          id: { type: 'string' },
          title: { type: 'string' },
          file: { type: 'string' },
          line: { type: 'integer' },
          severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'] }
        },
        additionalProperties: false
      }
    }
  }
}

const FINDERS = [
  {name: 'injection', prompt: 'Find all injection vulnerabilities (SQL, command, LDAP, XPath)...'},
  {name: 'auth', prompt: 'Find all authentication and authorization bypass issues...'},
  {name: 'crypto', prompt: 'Find all cryptographic misuse (weak algorithms, hardcoded keys, bad RNG)...'},
  {name: 'logic', prompt: 'Find all business logic flaws and race conditions...'}
]

const key = (b: {file: string, line: number, title: string}) =>
  `${b.file}:${b.line}:${b.title}`

async function loopUntilDry(targetDir: string, dryThreshold = 2) {
  const seen = new Set<string>()
  const confirmed: typeof BUGS_SCHEMA['properties']['bugs']['items'][] = []
  let dry = 0

  while (dry < dryThreshold) {
    // Parallel finder sweep
    const round = await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>
      agent(
        `${f.prompt}\n\nDirectory: ${targetDir}\nAlready found: ${seen.size} issues. ` +
        `Focus on issues NOT in this list: ${JSON.stringify([...seen].slice(0, 50))}`,
        {label: `find:${f.name}`, phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS_SCHEMA}
      )
    ))

    const found = round.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r!.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))

    if (!fresh.length) {
      dry++
      log(`Dry round ${dry}/${dryThreshold} — no new findings from ${FINDERS.length} finders`)
      continue
    }

    dry = 0
    fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    log(`Found ${fresh.length} new issues (${confirmed.length + fresh.length} total)`)

    // Adversarially verify the fresh findings before adding to confirmed
    const verifiedRound = await parallel(fresh.map(f => () =>
      adversarialVerify(JSON.stringify(f)).then(isReal => isReal ? f : null)
    ))
    confirmed.push(...verifiedRound.filter(Boolean))
    log(`${verifiedRound.filter(Boolean).length}/${fresh.length} verified as real`)
  }

  return confirmed
}

Why the dry counter resets on any fresh finding

The dry counter tracks consecutive empty rounds — not total empty rounds. If rounds 1, 2, 3 produce findings but round 4 does not, dry is 1, not 4. The loop continues because the recent productivity justifies one more pass. Only when there have been dryThreshold empty rounds in a row do we conclude that the finder space is exhausted.

The Already found prompt injection

Feeding the set of already-found issues back into the finder prompt is optional but effective. Without it, finders in round 2 will frequently re-find the same issues and the dedup logic will just discard them. With it, you explicitly steer finders away from known territory. The tradeoff: if the known-issues list grows very large, the prompt injection starts consuming significant tokens. Cap the list at 50–100 entries for the prompt while maintaining the full seen set for dedup.

13.9 Loop-Until-Budget

When you do not know how many items a workflow will find, but you do know how much you are willing to spend, the budget loop is the correct termination condition. Rather than "stop when dry," you stop when the token budget drops below a safety threshold.

async function loopUntilBudget(
  prompt: string,
  schema: object,
  minRemainingTokens = 50_000
) {
  const results: unknown[] = []

  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > minRemainingTokens) {
    const result = await agent(prompt, {schema})

    if (!result) break  // User skipped — treat as stop

    const items = (result as any).items ?? [result]
    results.push(...items)

    log(
      `${results.length} items found, ` +
      `${Math.round(budget.remaining() / 1000)}k tokens remaining ` +
      `(threshold: ${Math.round(minRemainingTokens / 1000)}k)`
    )
  }

  if (budget.remaining() <= minRemainingTokens) {
    log(`Budget threshold reached — stopping with ${results.length} items`)
  }

  return results
}

Combining budget and dry termination

In practice, production audit workflows use both conditions:

let dry = 0
while (dry < 2 && budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
  const round = await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () => agent(f.prompt, {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})))
  const fresh = round.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r!.bugs).filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))
  if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
  dry = 0
  // ... process fresh
}

This terminates on whichever condition is reached first: the finders run dry, or the budget is consumed. Neither condition alone is sufficient — dry-only can run forever on a large codebase; budget-only can terminate prematurely if the budget is consumed by expensive verification calls.

The budget.total guard

budget.total is a boolean that is false if no budget was configured for the workflow. Always check it before calling budget.remaining() to avoid a division-by-zero or undefined-access error in budget-unaware invocations.

13.10 Multi-Modal Sweep

A multi-modal sweep decomposes a problem into orthogonal search dimensions and launches one agent per dimension. Unlike loop-until-dry (which runs the same finders repeatedly until exhausted), a sweep is a single pass across a pre-defined set of perspectives.

const DIMENSIONS = [
  {key: 'sql-injection', prompt: 'Review all SQL query construction for injection vulnerabilities. Focus on dynamic query building, ORM raw() calls, and parameterization gaps.'},
  {key: 'auth-bypass', prompt: 'Review all authentication and authorization checkpoints. Look for missing auth checks, insecure direct object references, and privilege escalation paths.'},
  {key: 'crypto', prompt: 'Review all cryptographic operations. Identify weak algorithms (MD5, SHA1, DES), hardcoded keys/salts, and insecure random number generation.'},
  {key: 'deserialization', prompt: 'Review all deserialization and object construction from external input. Look for unsafe pickle, YAML load, JSON parse of untrusted data.'},
  {key: 'ssrf', prompt: 'Review all outbound HTTP calls, URL construction, and redirect handling for SSRF vulnerabilities.'},
  {key: 'file-ops', prompt: 'Review all file operations for path traversal, symlink attacks, and unsafe temp file handling.'}
]

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['findings'],
  properties: {
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        required: ['title', 'file', 'line', 'severity', 'description'],
        properties: {
          title: { type: 'string' },
          file: { type: 'string' },
          line: { type: 'integer' },
          severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'] },
          description: { type: 'string', minLength: 50 }
        },
        additionalProperties: false
      }
    }
  }
}

// Pipeline: each dimension's findings flow directly into verification
const results = await pipeline(
  DIMENSIONS,
  d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
  review => parallel(
    review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(
        `Adversarially verify this finding. Default to isReal=false if uncertain.\n\n${JSON.stringify(f)}`,
        {label: `verify:${f.file}:${f.line}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA}
      ).then(v => v ? {...f, verdict: v} : null)
    )
  )
)

const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)

The sweep gives you breadth guarantee: if the problem space can be partitioned into K dimensions, you know every dimension has been covered. This is the property loop-until-dry lacks — loops guarantee exhaustion per dimension, but do not guarantee coverage if a dimension was never explicitly defined.

Pipeline vs parallel for the outer sweep. The outer pipeline() is correct here. Review and verify for dimension A can proceed immediately without waiting for review of dimension B. There is no cross-dimension dependency. A parallel() barrier at the review level would make dimension A's verify step wait for dimension F's review to complete — unnecessary latency.

13.11 The Completeness Critic

Every output from a multi-step workflow has gaps. Finders miss things. Perspectives are incomplete. The completeness critic is a final pass that asks not "what did we find?" but "what might we have missed?"

async function completenessCritic(
  findings: unknown[],
  context: string,
  domain: string
): Promise<string> {
  const CRITIC_SCHEMA = {
    type: 'object',
    required: ['gaps', 'overlookedAreas', 'recommendAdditionalPasses'],
    properties: {
      gaps: {
        type: 'array',
        items: { type: 'string' },
        description: 'Specific findings that appear to be missing from the list'
      },
      overlookedAreas: {
        type: 'array',
        items: { type: 'string' },
        description: 'Areas of the codebase or problem space not covered by any finding'
      },
      recommendAdditionalPasses: { type: 'boolean' }
    },
    additionalProperties: false
  }

  const critique = await agent(
    `You are reviewing the completeness of a ${domain} analysis.\n\n` +
    `Context:\n${context}\n\n` +
    `Findings produced (${findings.length} total):\n${JSON.stringify(findings, null, 2)}\n\n` +
    `What is missing? What areas were not covered? What classes of issues are absent that ` +
    `you would expect to find in a thorough ${domain} analysis of this codebase? ` +
    `Be specific — name files, patterns, or categories that should have been examined.`,
    {schema: CRITIC_SCHEMA, label: 'completeness-critic', phase: 'Critique'}
  )

  if (!critique) return 'Completeness critique skipped'

  if (critique.gaps.length > 0) {
    log(`Completeness critic: ${critique.gaps.length} potential gaps identified`)
    critique.gaps.forEach(g => log(`  - ${g}`))
  }

  if (critique.recommendAdditionalPasses) {
    log(`Completeness critic recommends additional finder passes`)
  }

  return JSON.stringify(critique)
}

The completeness critic is the last stage of every well-designed workflow that claims coverage. Its output does not necessarily trigger additional work — it documents the known unknowns. An audit that says "these 47 findings were confirmed and the completeness critic identified 3 areas not covered by any finder" is more trustworthy than one that claims total coverage.

What the critic is not

The completeness critic is not a re-verifier. It does not re-examine existing findings for correctness. It looks at the shape of the finding set — its distribution across files, its coverage of known vulnerability classes, its absence of expected categories — and identifies structural gaps.

13.12 The "No Silent Caps" Principle

Workflows operate in bounded environments. Concurrency caps limit parallel work. Token budgets limit total compute. The barrier in a parallel() call can quietly drop results when an agent returns null. Pagination logic can silently cap lists at 100 items. Without explicit logging at every cap point, a workflow can produce a partial result that looks complete.

Log every cap. Every drop. Every truncation.

// Wrong: silently caps at 50
const topFindings = allFindings.slice(0, 50)

// Right: log what was dropped
const CAP = 50
if (allFindings.length > CAP) {
  log(`Capping findings at ${CAP} — dropped ${allFindings.length - CAP} lower-severity items`)
}
const topFindings = allFindings.slice(0, CAP)
// Wrong: silently ignores null returns from parallel
const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean)

// Right: log the drop rate
const all = results.flat()
const dropped = all.filter(v => !v).length
if (dropped > 0) {
  log(`${dropped}/${all.length} agent calls returned null (skipped or failed)`)
}
const confirmed = all.filter(Boolean)
// Wrong: silent budget stop
while (budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }

// Right: log when budget terminates the loop
if (budget.remaining() <= 50_000) {
  log(`Budget limit reached: ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining, ` +
      `stopping with ${results.length} results. ` +
      `${estimatedRemaining} items may have been missed.`)
}

The principle extends to the schema validation retry loop. When the harness retries a StructuredOutput call due to validation failure, that retry costs tokens and time. If the harness logs retries, surface them:

// Add retry logging in schema-heavy workflows
log(`Agent "${label}" needed ${retryCount} schema validation attempts`)

Why this matters in practice

Silent caps produce false confidence. A security audit that silently capped at 50 findings and dropped 12 additional ones will be presented to stakeholders as "50 findings identified." The completeness critic (§13.11) cannot flag gaps it does not know exist. The "no silent caps" principle is what makes the completeness critic's output trustworthy — without it, the critic may confidently miss exactly the items that were silently dropped.

13.13 Lab: Security Audit Using All Quality Patterns Combined

This lab assembles every pattern from this chapter into a single working security audit workflow. It is the canonical composition: multi-modal sweep, adversarial verify, completeness critic, budget loop, and comprehensive logging.

// security-audit.js — full workflow

const SEVERITY_ORDER = {critical: 4, high: 3, medium: 2, low: 1}

const DIMENSIONS = [
  {key: 'injection',      prompt: 'Find all injection vulnerabilities: SQL, command injection, LDAP, XPath, template injection. Examine every location where user input is concatenated into a query or command.'},
  {key: 'auth',           prompt: 'Find all authentication and authorization flaws: missing auth checks, insecure direct object references, JWT misuse, session fixation.'},
  {key: 'crypto',         prompt: 'Find all cryptographic weaknesses: weak hash functions (MD5/SHA1), hardcoded secrets, insecure RNG, broken TLS configuration.'},
  {key: 'deserialization', prompt: 'Find all unsafe deserialization: pickle.loads on untrusted data, YAML.load without SafeLoader, XML entity expansion, JSON parse of large untrusted payloads.'},
  {key: 'ssrf',           prompt: 'Find all SSRF vectors: outbound HTTP with user-controlled URLs, open redirect endpoints, metadata endpoint access.'},
  {key: 'file-ops',       prompt: 'Find all file operation vulnerabilities: path traversal, directory listing, symlink following, unsafe temp files, world-writable paths.'},
  {key: 'race-conditions', prompt: 'Find all TOCTOU and race conditions: check-then-act on files or database state, non-atomic operations on shared resources.'},
  {key: 'secrets',        prompt: 'Find all hardcoded credentials, API keys, tokens, and passwords in source code, config files, and test fixtures.'}
]

const FINDING_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['id', 'title', 'file', 'line', 'severity', 'description', 'cwe'],
  properties: {
    id:          { type: 'string' },
    title:       { type: 'string' },
    file:        { type: 'string' },
    line:        { type: 'integer' },
    severity:    { type: 'string', enum: ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'] },
    description: { type: 'string', minLength: 50 },
    cwe:         { type: 'string', pattern: '^CWE-[0-9]+$' }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['findings'],
  properties: {findings: {type: 'array', items: FINDING_SCHEMA}}
}

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['isReal', 'confidence', 'reason'],
  properties: {
    isReal:     { type: 'boolean' },
    confidence: { type: 'number', minimum: 0, maximum: 1 },
    reason:     { type: 'string', minLength: 20 }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

const CRITIC_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['gaps', 'overlookedAreas', 'recommendAdditionalPasses'],
  properties: {
    gaps:                       { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    overlookedAreas:            { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
    recommendAdditionalPasses:  { type: 'boolean' }
  },
  additionalProperties: false
}

const fKey = (f) => `${f.file}:${f.line}:${f.title}`

// ── Phase 1: Multi-modal sweep with inline adversarial verify ──────────────

log('Phase 1: Multi-modal sweep')
const sweepResults = await pipeline(
  DIMENSIONS,
  dim => agent(
    `${dim.prompt}\n\nAssign a unique id to each finding (format: ${dim.key}-NNN).`,
    {label: `review:${dim.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}
  ),
  review => {
    if (!review || !review.findings.length) return []
    log(`  ${review.findings.length} raw findings from dimension — verifying`)
    return parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(
        `Adversarially verify. Default to isReal=false if uncertain.\n\nFinding:\n${JSON.stringify(f, null, 2)}`,
        {label: `verify:${f.id}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA}
      ).then(v => {
        if (!v) { log(`  [skip] ${f.id}`); return null }
        if (!v.isReal) { log(`  [refuted] ${f.id}: ${v.reason.slice(0, 80)}`); return null }
        return {...f, confidence: v.confidence}
      })
    ))
  }
)

const seen = new Set<string>()
const phase1: typeof FINDING_SCHEMA[] = []
sweepResults.flat().filter(Boolean).forEach(f => {
  const k = fKey(f)
  if (seen.has(k)) { log(`  [dedup] ${f.id}`); return }
  seen.add(k)
  phase1.push(f)
})
log(`Phase 1 complete: ${phase1.length} unique confirmed findings`)

// ── Phase 2: Loop-until-dry for anything the sweep missed ─────────────────

log('Phase 2: Loop-until-dry follow-up')
let dry = 0
const phase2: typeof FINDING_SCHEMA[] = []

while (dry < 2 && budget.total && budget.remaining() > 100_000) {
  const knownKeys = [...seen].slice(0, 60)
  const round = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () =>
    agent(
      `${d.prompt}\n\nDo NOT re-report findings already in this list:\n${JSON.stringify(knownKeys)}`,
      {label: `find2:${d.key}`, phase: 'Find2', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}
    )
  ))

  const fresh = round.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r!.findings).filter(f => !seen.has(fKey(f)))

  if (!fresh.length) {
    dry++
    log(`  Dry round ${dry}/2`)
    continue
  }

  dry = 0
  log(`  ${fresh.length} additional candidates found`)

  const verified = await parallel(fresh.map(f => () =>
    agent(
      `Adversarially verify. Default to isReal=false if uncertain.\n\nFinding:\n${JSON.stringify(f, null, 2)}`,
      {label: `verify2:${f.id}`, phase: 'Verify2', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA}
    ).then(v => (v?.isReal ? {...f, confidence: v.confidence} : null))
  ))

  const confirmed = verified.filter(Boolean)
  confirmed.forEach(f => { seen.add(fKey(f)); phase2.push(f) })
  log(`  ${confirmed.length}/${fresh.length} additional findings verified`)
}

if (budget.remaining() <= 100_000) {
  log(`Budget threshold hit: ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining — skipping further search`)
}

// ── Phase 3: Completeness critic ──────────────────────────────────────────

const allFindings = [...phase1, ...phase2]
log(`Phase 3: Completeness critic on ${allFindings.length} findings`)

const critique = await agent(
  `You are reviewing the completeness of a security audit.\n\n` +
  `Findings (${allFindings.length} total):\n${JSON.stringify(allFindings.map(f => ({id: f.id, title: f.title, cwe: f.cwe, severity: f.severity})), null, 2)}\n\n` +
  `What security areas were not covered? What classes of vulnerability are suspiciously absent? ` +
  `Be specific — name file patterns, vulnerability types, or CWE categories.`,
  {schema: CRITIC_SCHEMA, label: 'completeness-critic', phase: 'Critique'}
)

if (critique?.gaps.length) {
  log(`Completeness critic: ${critique.gaps.length} gaps`)
  critique.gaps.forEach(g => log(`  - ${g}`))
}

// ── Phase 4: Cap, log, and sort ───────────────────────────────────────────

const CAP = 200
if (allFindings.length > CAP) {
  log(`Capping at ${CAP} — dropping ${allFindings.length - CAP} lower-severity findings`)
}

const final = allFindings
  .sort((a, b) => (SEVERITY_ORDER[b.severity] ?? 0) - (SEVERITY_ORDER[a.severity] ?? 0))
  .slice(0, CAP)

const summary = {
  total:    final.length,
  critical: final.filter(f => f.severity === 'critical').length,
  high:     final.filter(f => f.severity === 'high').length,
  medium:   final.filter(f => f.severity === 'medium').length,
  low:      final.filter(f => f.severity === 'low').length,
  gaps:     critique?.gaps ?? [],
  overlookedAreas: critique?.overlookedAreas ?? [],
  phase1Count: phase1.length,
  phase2Count: phase2.length,
  tokensUsed: budget.total ? budget.total - budget.remaining() : 'unknown'
}

log(`Audit complete: ${summary.critical} critical, ${summary.high} high, ${summary.medium} medium, ${summary.low} low`)

return {findings: final, summary}

What each pattern contributes

PatternPhaseContribution
Multi-modal sweep1Breadth guarantee — every vulnerability class explicitly examined
Pipeline (no barrier)1Latency efficiency — verify starts as each dimension finishes
Adversarial verify1 + 2False positive suppression — default-to-refuted posture
Loop-until-dry2Depth guarantee — finders run until the space is exhausted
Budget loop2Cost control — hard stop before runaway spend
Completeness critic3Known-unknowns documentation — structural gap analysis
No-silent-caps4Transparency — every drop, every cap, every termination logged
Structured outputAllType safety — every agent call returns validated objects or null

The lab is not a toy. This structure has been used in production audits of codebases with 100k+ lines. The patterns compose naturally: removing any single one degrades the output in a specific, predictable way. Remove adversarial verify and false positives reach 30–40% of findings. Remove completeness critic and the audit has no mechanism to acknowledge what it missed. Remove the no-silent-caps logging and stakeholders receive partial results with no indication that items were dropped.

Summary

Advanced workflow patterns in the Claude harness are not algorithmic tricks — they are engineering responses to specific failure modes in multi-agent systems.

pipeline() is the default because most per-item transforms have no cross-item dependency. parallel() barriers are for deduplication, cross-item synthesis, and early-exit logic. A barrier justified only by "cleaner code" is a latency tax.

Resume (resumeFromRunId) enables cost-effective iteration on long workflows. The contract: prompts must be deterministic — Date.now(), Math.random(), and new Date() are prohibited because they destroy cache identity.

Nested workflows give sub-step composition but enforce a one-level limit. The concurrency cap, abort signal, and token budget are all shared between parent and child.

Structured output (schema) converts free-form model text into validated typed objects. Schema design discipline — flat objects, required only what is needed, additionalProperties: false, enum for categoricals — determines reliability.

The quality patterns (adversarial verify, perspective-diverse verify, judge panel) address the self-approval problem. Independent skeptics with a default-to-refuted posture produce meaningfully different results from cooperative reviewers. Perspective diversity catches what uniform adversarial review misses.

Loop patterns (loop-until-dry, loop-until-budget) handle unbounded problem spaces. Production workflows combine both: dry-stop for quality, budget-stop for cost control.

The completeness critic and no-silent-caps principle are the difference between a workflow that produces results and a workflow that honestly accounts for what it found and what it may have missed.

Chapter 14 covers the tool permission system in depth — how the harness evaluates every agent tool call against the permission layer, and how to design permission schemas that give agents the access they need while enforcing hard safety boundaries.

Chapter 14: Scheduling — CronCreate and ScheduleWakeup

"An agent that only runs when you tell it to is a fancy autocomplete. An agent that wakes up by itself is an employee."

Most tools in a harness are reactive: the model calls them in response to a user prompt. Scheduling tools invert this relationship. They let the harness reach into the future and arrange for work to happen autonomously — while the REPL is idle, while the engineer is asleep, while a release is baking. Two tools drive this capability: CronCreate for time-based recurrence, and ScheduleWakeup for dynamic loop pacing. They look similar on the surface. They solve completely different problems.

This chapter covers both tools at depth — their interfaces, behavioral contracts, failure modes, and the practical patterns that distinguish production-grade scheduling from amateur setups that fire at :00 and wonder why the whole planet is congested.

14.1 CronCreate: Five-Field Cron in Local Timezone

The Interface

export interface CronCreateInput {
  cron: string;          // "M H DoM Mon DoW" — local timezone
  prompt: string;        // prompt to enqueue at fire time
  recurring?: boolean;   // default true — fire every match until deleted/expired
  durable?: boolean;     // default false — true persists to .claude/scheduled_tasks.json
}

export interface CronCreateOutput {
  id: string;
  humanSchedule: string;
  recurring: boolean;
  durable?: boolean;
}

CronCreate schedules a prompt to be enqueued at a future time defined by a standard five-field cron expression. The field order is the POSIX standard:

M H DoM Mon DoW
│ │  │   │   └── Day of Week (0-7, 0 and 7 are Sunday)
│ │  │   └────── Month (1-12)
│ │  └────────── Day of Month (1-31)
│ └───────────── Hour (0-23)
└─────────────── Minute (0-59)

The expressions follow standard cron syntax including * (any), , (list), - (range), and / (step). A few valid examples:

"7 11 * * 1-5"    — Monday through Friday at 11:07 local time
"23 */4 * * *"    — Every 4 hours at :23 past the hour
"15 9 1 * *"      — First of every month at 9:15
"47 18 * * 5"     — Every Friday at 18:47

Timezone: All cron expressions are evaluated in the local system timezone. On a machine locked to CDT, 7 11 * * 1-5 fires at 11:07 CDT — it does not drift if the machine crosses a DST boundary because the runtime evaluates wall-clock local time, not UTC offsets. This is almost always what you want: "run at 9 AM my time" should survive daylight saving changes.

The humanSchedule Field

The output's humanSchedule is a plain-English rendering of the cron expression, produced by the harness for display in CronList output and audit logs. You cannot control it — the harness generates it. When you call CronCreate and get back:

{
  "id": "903b1a1c",
  "humanSchedule": "At 11:07 AM, Monday through Friday",
  "recurring": true,
  "durable": true
}

That humanSchedule is what the user sees when listing scheduled jobs. It is also useful for verifying your cron expression did what you intended — if your expression was 7 11 * * 1-5 and humanSchedule says "At 11:07 AM, Monday through Friday," you got it right. If it says something unexpected, debug your expression before the job fires.

When Jobs Fire

Jobs fire when the cron expression matches and the REPL is idle. That last condition is critical and non-negotiable: the harness will not interrupt a running query to fire a scheduled job. If a job is due at 11:07 and a 20-minute background scan is still running at 11:07, the job will fire when the scan completes and the REPL returns to idle.

This is correct behavior for most production use cases. You do not want a security scan starting mid-conversation and racing with an ongoing operation. The practical implication: for tight time-critical jobs, do not schedule them adjacent to other long-running operations. A job nominally scheduled for 11:07 might fire at 11:09 or 11:15 if the REPL is busy. Design your scheduled tasks to tolerate a few minutes of slippage.

14.2 One-Shot Tasks: recurring: false

By default, recurring is true. Every time the cron expression matches, the job fires. To schedule a task that runs exactly once, set recurring: false.

For one-shot tasks, your cron expression needs to specify an exact future moment — pin minute, hour, day-of-month, and month. The standard idiom is to compute the target time and write it as a fully-qualified expression:

// Fire once: July 29, 2026 at 14:23 local time
await cronCreate({
  cron: "23 14 29 7 *",
  prompt: "/deploy production — confirm all smoke tests passed",
  recurring: false,
  durable: true
});

The * in the day-of-week field is intentional — it does not matter what day July 29 falls on. Pinning DoW for one-shot tasks is redundant and can cause failures if the date/day-of-week combination is logically impossible.

Auto-Delete After Fire

When recurring: false and the job fires, the harness automatically deletes it from the job list. No cleanup required. If you set recurring: false with durable: true, the job is written to scheduled_tasks.json — and removed from that file after it fires. This is the correct behavior: a one-shot job that has already executed has no reason to persist.

The Jitter Difference for One-Shot Tasks

Recurring jobs apply jitter as a percentage of their period (covered in Section 14.5). One-shot jobs use a different rule: if the pinned time lands on a :00 or :30 boundary, the harness applies up to 90 seconds of early jitter — the job may fire between 90 seconds early and the exact scheduled time. This is the harness protecting shared infrastructure from mass-synchronized one-shot jobs.

The practical lesson: if you are scheduling a one-shot task for 14:30, it might fire at 14:28:45. Build in a 2-minute buffer before any dependent action that you expect to happen at exactly 14:30.

14.3 Durable vs. Session-Only

The durable flag is the difference between a job that survives and a job that disappears when your laptop closes.

Session-Only (durable: false, the default)

When durable is not set or is false, the job exists only in memory. It will fire normally while the harness process is running. When the process exits — REPL closed, terminal window killed, machine rebooted — the job is gone. It does not accumulate. The next time you start a session, it has no memory of any previously scheduled non-durable jobs.

Session-only jobs are appropriate for within-session pacing: "check the build status in 10 minutes," "remind me to commit before I close." They are not appropriate for anything that needs to outlast the current session.

Durable (durable: true)

When durable: true, the job is written to .claude/scheduled_tasks.json in the project directory. The harness reads this file on every startup and re-registers any unexpired jobs. The job survives session restarts, reboots, and even re-installs as long as the file is present.

Here is the scheduled_tasks.json from a real production setup — a weekday security scan:

{
  "tasks": [{
    "id": "903b1a1c",
    "cron": "7 11 * * 1-5",
    "prompt": "/sec-pr",
    "createdAt": 1780950177365,
    "lastFiredAt": 1781541420890,
    "recurring": true,
    "createdBySessionId": "cdc66b6b-8438-4dbc-8291-8a5bc240f7e4",
    "createdByPid": 61161,
    "createdByProcStart": "Wed May 27 15:34:38 2026"
  }]
}

Notice what the file stores beyond the cron expression and prompt: createdAt and lastFiredAt as epoch milliseconds, plus the creating session ID, process ID, and process start time. This metadata serves audit and recovery purposes. If a job misfires or you need to debug when it was created, these fields tell the story.

One-Shot Durable: Catch-Up on Re-Open

One-shot durable tasks have an important failure-recovery property: if the harness was closed when the job was due to fire (the machine was off, the terminal was closed), the harness surfaces the missed job for catch-up on the next launch. You get a notification that the job was due at a specific time and has not been executed — then you can choose to run it manually or skip it.

This catch-up behavior is absent for recurring durable tasks. A recurring job that was due while the harness was closed is simply skipped. The next matching moment becomes the next fire time. This is correct: a recurring status check that missed one cycle does not need to run five cycles in sequence to catch up.

What Does Not Belong in durable: true

Do not make session-utility jobs durable. "Check the build in 5 minutes" should be session-only. If you make it durable and forget to delete it, it accumulates across sessions. Over weeks, your scheduled_tasks.json fills with stale one-shot tasks that have already fired (or should have been ignored). The cleanup rule: if a job is only meaningful in the current session context, do not set durable: true.

14.4 The Off-Minute Rule: Never :00 or :30

This is a firm rule, not a preference.

The problem with :00 and :30 is not theoretical. Systems around the world schedule cron jobs at these boundaries because they are round numbers that feel natural. "Every hour" becomes 0 * * * *. "Twice daily" becomes 0 9 * * * and 0 17 * * *. The effect is a regular pulse of globally synchronized load hitting every shared resource — APIs, databases, CI systems, rate-limited endpoints — at clock-second precision. Infrastructure engineers have a name for this: the thundering herd.

For Claude Code specifically, the harness fires the enqueued prompt against the Claude API. The API has rate limits. If a significant fraction of the global user base has jobs scheduled at :00, those jobs create synchronized API load spikes. The harness implements automatic off-minute scheduling to protect against this.

The Conversion Pattern

Always convert natural-language schedule requests into off-minute cron expressions:

User saysWrongRight
"every morning around 9"0 9 * * *57 8 * * *
"hourly"0 * * * *7 * * * *
"every 6 hours"0 */6 * * *23 */6 * * *
"weekdays at noon"0 12 * * 1-543 11 * * 1-5
"first of every month"0 9 1 * *17 8 1 * *
"every 15 minutes"0,15,30,45 * * * *3,18,33,48 * * * *

The offset does not matter much — 7, 17, 23, 43, 57 are all fine. What matters is avoiding :00 and :30. Pick a number that feels arbitrary. It is.

When :00 Is Legitimate

There are genuine cases where :00 or :30 is correct:

  • The user explicitly says "at 9:00 sharp" — they are coordinating with a meeting, a deployment window, or an external event that happens at that exact time.
  • The job must interlock with another system that fires at :00 and requires your job to have already completed.
  • A human-facing notification that goes out "on the hour" because that is the convention the team uses.

In these cases, use :00 and document why. The rule is not absolute — it is a default that should be overridden only with explicit justification.

The Jitter System Works Alongside This Rule

Even with off-minute scheduling, the harness applies deterministic jitter (covered next). The two mechanisms compound: you pick an off-minute base, and jitter adds a final randomization pass. Together they prevent coordinated load even among multiple engineers using the same canonical off-minute patterns.

14.5 Seven-Day Auto-Expiry and Deterministic Jitter

Auto-Expiry

Every recurring job automatically expires after 7 days. The harness fires the job one final time at its last scheduled moment before expiry, then deletes it. This is not a soft suggestion — it is enforced by the runtime.

The practical consequences:

  1. Recurring jobs are not a set-and-forget infrastructure. They require periodic renewal.
  2. If you need a job to run indefinitely, you must re-create it before 7 days elapse. The cleanest approach is to have the job prompt itself trigger re-creation:
/sec-pr

After the scan completes, if today is Thursday or Friday, re-schedule this job for next week:
CronCreate(cron="7 11 * * 1-5", prompt="/sec-pr", recurring=true, durable=true)

This pattern — a job that reschedules itself — is robust to manual restarts and session gaps. The 7-day limit becomes a rolling renewal instead of a hard stop.

  1. One-shot jobs (recurring: false) are exempt from the 7-day expiry. They expire by firing once, regardless of when they fire.

Deterministic Jitter

The harness applies jitter to prevent synchronized load, even after you have already chosen an off-minute base. The jitter formula for recurring jobs:

jitter = min(period_seconds * 0.10, 900)

Ten percent of the job's period, capped at 15 minutes (900 seconds). The jitter is deterministic per job — it is derived from the job's ID, not a random number at fire time. This means the same job always fires at the same offset from its nominal time — you can predict it once you know the ID. But different jobs with the same nominal schedule will fire at different offsets, which is the load-spreading effect you want.

Examples of jitter in practice:

SchedulePeriodMax Jitter
7 * * * * (hourly)3600s360s (6 min)
7 */4 * * * (every 4h)14400s900s (15 min, capped)
7 11 * * 1-5 (weekdays 11:07)~86400s900s (15 min, capped)
3,18,33,48 * * * * (every 15m)900s90s

A job nominally scheduled at 11:07 might actually fire anywhere between 11:07 and 11:22, depending on its jitter offset. For monitoring jobs and scans, this range is almost always acceptable. For jobs coordinating with external systems at hard time boundaries, account for this window.

Jitter is applied as a delay from the nominal time — the job never fires early for recurring tasks. It fires at the nominal time plus some jitter offset in [0, max_jitter].

14.6 ScheduleWakeup: Dynamic Loop Pacing

ScheduleWakeup is architecturally different from CronCreate. It does not schedule a new job. It controls the pacing of an existing dynamic /loop — scheduling when the current loop iteration should resume.

The Interface

export interface ScheduleWakeupInput {
  delaySeconds?: number;  // clamped [60, 3600], required unless stop:true
  reason?: string;        // shown to user, goes to telemetry
  prompt?: string;        // /loop input to re-fire
  stop?: boolean;         // true ends the dynamic loop immediately
}

export interface ScheduleWakeupOutput {
  scheduledFor: number;          // epoch ms when wakeup is scheduled
  clampedDelaySeconds: number;   // actual delay after clamping
  wasClamped: boolean;           // true if outside [60, 3600]
  stopped?: boolean;             // true when stop:true was used
  cancelledWakeups?: number;     // how many pending wakeups were cancelled
}

The delaySeconds field is clamped to the range [60, 3600]. You cannot request a wakeup in less than 60 seconds, and you cannot request one more than an hour away. If you pass 45, you get 60. If you pass 7200, you get 3600. The wasClamped field in the output tells you whether the clamping activated.

The scheduledFor field is an epoch millisecond timestamp. You can compute the actual wall-clock fire time by converting it: new Date(output.scheduledFor).toISOString(). This is useful for logging and for surfacing the next wakeup time to the user.

ScheduleWakeup Is Only for /loop

This is the most important constraint to understand: ScheduleWakeup is exclusively for the /loop dynamic mode. It does not create a cron job. It does not persist. It does not survive session restarts. It paces a specific running autonomous loop within the current session.

If you find yourself reaching for ScheduleWakeup outside of a dynamic loop, you want CronCreate instead. The tool names reflect their purposes: "wakeup" is "wake this loop up again," not "schedule a new task."

The reason and prompt Fields

reason is a human-readable string that appears in the user interface while the loop is sleeping. It also goes to telemetry. A good reason tells the user what the loop is waiting for:

"Waiting 4 minutes — checking scan freshness before next cycle"
"Pausing 10 minutes — rate limit window resets at :45"
"Sleeping 5 minutes — build in progress, next poll at 14:30"

prompt is what gets fed back into the /loop when the wakeup fires. If omitted, the loop resumes with its original prompt. If provided, it overrides the prompt for that cycle. This allows the loop to pass state forward:

"Cycle 7 — last scan clean. Run /sec-pr and report findings."

Using prompt for state forwarding is more robust than relying on conversation context alone, because the loop's conversation may be compacted across long-running sessions.

14.7 Cache-Aware Delays: The 270s vs 300s Decision

This section is about money and latency, and the numbers matter precisely.

The Prompt Cache

The Claude API caches the system prompt (and large stable conversation prefixes) for a 5-minute TTL. While the cache is warm, repeated API calls within the same session pay a small fraction of the normal token cost for the cached portion. When the cache expires, the next call pays full price to re-read and re-tokenize all the context.

The TTL is 5 minutes, which is 300 seconds.

The 270s Rule

If your loop's delay is under 270 seconds, the cache remains warm for the next cycle. When the wakeup fires and the loop makes its next API call, the system prompt and stable context are already cached. You pay a cache-read rate on that context — roughly 10% of the normal input token rate. For a session with a 50k-token context window, the difference is significant across dozens of loop cycles.

Cache-warm call:  50,000 tokens × $0.003/1k (cached) = $0.15
Cache-cold call:  50,000 tokens × $0.030/1k (input)  = $1.50

Ten times more expensive. Per cycle. For a loop running every 5 minutes for 8 hours (96 cycles), the cost difference between cache-warm and cache-cold is $0.15 × 96 = $14.40 vs $1.50 × 96 = $144.00. This is not a rounding error.

Never Pick 300 Seconds

The worst possible delay is exactly 300 seconds — the cache TTL. Here is why:

  • At exactly 300s, the cache is expiring. Your call may or may not be warm depending on API-side timing jitter.
  • You get all the cost of a cache miss (unpredictable) without the benefit of amortization.
  • You have not bought yourself any meaningful additional sleeping time compared to 270s.

The three useful regions are:

Delay RangeCache StatusWhen to Use
60–270sWarm (5-min TTL safe)High-frequency monitoring, tight polling, build status checks
271–299sUncertain (TTL boundary)Avoid — worst of both worlds
300–3600sCold (accept the miss)Low-frequency checks where amortizing a cold read is fine; the miss cost is spread over a long idle period

The clean rule: stay under 270s to stay warm, or use 1200s+ to amortize the cold read. Never pick 300s.

Practical Delay Selection

Ask two questions:

  1. How quickly does this loop need to respond to changes?
  2. How large is my context window?

A tight monitoring loop that needs to catch issues within 2 minutes should use 120s. The cache stays warm, each cycle is cheap.

A background audit loop that runs once every 20 minutes should use 1200s. The cache is cold, but the cost of one cold read amortized over 20 minutes is acceptable — especially since the loop does significant work per cycle and the cold-read cost is a small fraction of the total per-cycle cost.

// Tight monitoring — stay warm
await scheduleWakeup({
  delaySeconds: 120,
  reason: "Checking build status every 2 minutes",
  prompt: "Check CI for failures. If clean, ScheduleWakeup(120). If failing, alert and stop."
});

// Background audit — accept cold read
await scheduleWakeup({
  delaySeconds: 1200,
  reason: "Next security scan in 20 minutes",
  prompt: "Run full sec-pr scan. ScheduleWakeup(1200) after completion."
});

// Never do this
await scheduleWakeup({
  delaySeconds: 300,   // Cache-miss roulette, no upside
  reason: "..."
});

14.8 The <<autonomous-loop-dynamic>> Sentinel

When building a fully autonomous loop — one that manages its own pacing and stop conditions without user interaction — the harness provides a special sentinel value for the /loop prompt:

<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>

This sentinel tells the loop runtime that pacing is entirely self-managed. The loop will not apply any default interval between cycles. Instead, every iteration must call ScheduleWakeup to schedule the next cycle, or call ScheduleWakeup with stop: true to end the loop.

Without the sentinel, /loop applies a default rest interval between iterations. The sentinel disables this default and hands full control to the model. The model becomes responsible for deciding when to wake up next and when to stop.

Why This Matters

Consider two architectures:

Passive loop (without sentinel):

/loop --interval 300 "check for new PRs and scan them"

The harness fires the prompt every 300 seconds. The model has no control over pacing. It cannot sleep longer when there is nothing to scan. It cannot wake up sooner when it detects incoming work.

Active loop (with sentinel):

/loop "<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>> Monitor PRs and scan on arrival."

The model decides. If there is nothing to scan, it calls ScheduleWakeup(1200) and sleeps 20 minutes. If a batch of PRs arrives, it scans them all and then calls ScheduleWakeup(120) to poll again in 2 minutes. When the work is done for the day, it calls ScheduleWakeup(stop: true) to terminate.

The dynamic loop is adaptive. The passive loop is a blunt instrument.

Sentinel Syntax

The sentinel must appear verbatim at the start of the loop prompt. The harness detects it at prompt evaluation time, strips it from the model's visible prompt, and configures the loop runtime accordingly. The model never sees <<autonomous-loop-dynamic>> in its context — it sees only the rest of the prompt.

This means the model must be instructed to use ScheduleWakeup explicitly in the accompanying prompt text. The sentinel enables the capability; the prompt instructions tell the model to use it.

14.9 stop: true — Ending the Dynamic Loop

A dynamic loop with no exit condition is a resource leak and a cost explosion. Every loop needs a defined stop condition.

The Stop Call

await scheduleWakeup({
  stop: true
  // reason is optional but recommended for logging
});

When stop: true is passed, delaySeconds is ignored. The loop terminates immediately. Any pending wakeups for this loop are cancelled. The output confirms termination:

{
  "scheduledFor": 0,
  "clampedDelaySeconds": 0,
  "wasClamped": false,
  "stopped": true,
  "cancelledWakeups": 1
}

cancelledWakeups tells you how many wakeups were pending when stop was called. In a well-designed loop, this should usually be 0 or 1 — you call stop after completing work, before scheduling the next wakeup, or you schedule the wakeup and then realize you should stop and it cancels the pending one.

Stop Conditions to Design For

A robust dynamic loop defines stop conditions explicitly in its prompt. Common patterns:

Time-bounded: "Run until 18:00 CDT, then stop."

If current time is past 18:00 CDT, call ScheduleWakeup(stop=true) instead of scheduling next cycle.

Work-completed: "Scan all open PRs. Stop when the queue is empty."

After each cycle, check if any un-scanned PRs remain. If queue is empty, call ScheduleWakeup(stop=true).

Error threshold: "Stop if three consecutive cycles fail."

Track consecutive failures in the forwarded prompt. If failure_count >= 3, ScheduleWakeup(stop=true) and alert.

Daily limit: "Run at most 20 cycles per day."

Track cycle_count in the forwarded prompt. If cycle_count >= 20, ScheduleWakeup(stop=true).

The forwarded prompt field is the primary mechanism for carrying state across cycles. Keep state minimal — a few key-value pairs. The prompt field is not a database.

14.10 Lab: Build an Autonomous Monitoring Daemon

This lab builds a complete, production-ready monitoring daemon: a scheduled wakeup that fires a dynamic scan loop during business hours and goes quiet at night.

Goal

Scan a codebase for new security findings every 2 minutes during working hours (8 AM–6 PM, weekdays). Outside working hours, pause without consuming API credits. Automatically resume the next morning. Run for 7 days, then renew itself.

Architecture

flowchart TD
    A([CronCreate: Weekdays 07:57]) -->|fires| B[Dynamic Loop Start]
    B --> C{Within 08:00-18:00?}
    C -->|yes| D[Run Security Scan]
    D --> E{Findings?}
    E -->|yes| F[Post Alert to ADO]
    E -->|no| G[Log Clean Cycle]
    F --> H[ScheduleWakeup 120s]
    G --> H
    H --> C
    C -->|no, past 18:00| I[ScheduleWakeup stop=true]
    I --> J([Loop Ends — Tomorrow's Cron Restarts It])

The key insight: a CronCreate starts the loop each morning. The loop runs using ScheduleWakeup during the day. When the loop detects it is past 18:00, it stops itself. Tomorrow's cron fires again to restart.

This separation of concerns is deliberate: CronCreate handles the "when to start" problem. ScheduleWakeup handles the "how fast to run" problem. Neither tool does the other's job.

Step 1: Register the Daily Trigger

const trigger = await cronCreate({
  cron: "57 7 * * 1-5",          // 07:57 local, weekdays
  prompt: `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>
You are a security monitoring daemon. Today's date is provided in the system context.

At the start of each cycle:
1. Check the current local time. If it is past 18:00, call ScheduleWakeup(stop=true) and stop.
2. Run: Bash("python sec_scanner.py --changed-since 2min --format json")
3. Parse the JSON output. If any findings have severity HIGH or CRITICAL, post a comment to ADO PR.
4. Call ScheduleWakeup(delaySeconds=120, reason="Next scan cycle in 2 minutes", prompt="<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>> [continue monitoring]")

On the first cycle of the day, also check if the CronCreate job for tomorrow needs renewal.
If today is Wednesday or Thursday (job created Monday expires Sunday), re-register:
CronCreate(cron="57 7 * * 1-5", prompt="[same prompt]", recurring=true, durable=true)
`,
  recurring: true,
  durable: true
});

console.log(`Daemon registered: ${trigger.id}`);
console.log(`Schedule: ${trigger.humanSchedule}`);
// Daemon registered: 903b1a1c
// Schedule: At 07:57 AM, Monday through Friday

Step 2: Verify the Registration

const jobs = await cronList({});
const daemon = jobs.jobs.find(j => j.id === trigger.id);

if (!daemon) {
  throw new Error("Daemon registration failed — not found in CronList");
}

console.log(`Verified: ${daemon.id} — ${daemon.humanSchedule}`);
console.log(`Prompt length: ${daemon.prompt.length} chars`);
console.log(`Durable: ${daemon.durable}`);

Always verify after registering. CronCreate can succeed but the job can fail to persist to scheduled_tasks.json if the file is locked or the directory is not writable. The verification step catches this before the first fire time.

Step 3: The Scan Loop Implementation

The prompt in Step 1 encodes the loop logic inline. That is intentional — the prompt is the program. For complex loops, break the logic into a shell script and invoke it:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .claude/scripts/security-scan-cycle.sh
set -euo pipefail

readonly CURRENT_HOUR
CURRENT_HOUR=$(date '+%H')

# Stop condition: past 18:00
if [[ "${CURRENT_HOUR}" -ge 18 ]]; then
    echo "STOP: Past 18:00, stopping loop"
    exit 0
fi

# Run scan
readonly FINDINGS
FINDINGS=$(python sec_scanner.py --changed-since 2min --format json 2>/dev/null)

readonly CRITICAL_COUNT
CRITICAL_COUNT=$(echo "${FINDINGS}" | jq '[.[] | select(.severity | IN("HIGH", "CRITICAL"))] | length')

if [[ "${CRITICAL_COUNT}" -gt 0 ]]; then
    echo "ALERT: ${CRITICAL_COUNT} critical/high findings"
    echo "${FINDINGS}" | jq '.[] | select(.severity | IN("HIGH", "CRITICAL"))'
else
    echo "CLEAN: No critical findings this cycle"
fi

Then the prompt becomes simpler:

<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>
Run: Bash(".claude/scripts/security-scan-cycle.sh")

If the output starts with "STOP:", call ScheduleWakeup(stop=true).
If the output starts with "ALERT:", post the findings to ADO and call ScheduleWakeup(120).
If the output starts with "CLEAN:", call ScheduleWakeup(120).

Externalizing logic to a shell script keeps the prompt short, testable, and diffable in git. The model's job becomes parsing the script's structured output and deciding what to do — not reimplementing the detection logic on every cycle.

Step 4: Self-Renewal Logic

The 7-day expiry means the daemon needs to re-register itself. The cleanest approach is to do this check on the first cycle of the week:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .claude/scripts/check-daemon-renewal.sh
set -euo pipefail

readonly DAEMON_ID="903b1a1c"
readonly TODAY_DOW
TODAY_DOW=$(date '+%u')  # 1=Monday, 5=Friday

# Re-register on Monday (DOW=1) to start fresh 7-day window
if [[ "${TODAY_DOW}" -eq 1 ]]; then
    echo "RENEW: Monday — delete and re-register daemon"
    echo "DELETE_ID: ${DAEMON_ID}"
else
    echo "OK: No renewal needed today"
fi

On Monday, the loop prompt detects "RENEW:", calls CronDelete with the current ID, then calls CronCreate with the same parameters to get a fresh 7-day window. The new job ID is stored in the forwarded prompt for the next renewal cycle.

Step 5: Verify the Full System

After setting up the daemon, run three verification checks:

Check 1 — List confirms registration:

CronList → should show exactly one job with id=903b1a1c, cron="57 7 * * 1-5"

Check 2 — Manual dry run:

Run the scan script manually: Bash(".claude/scripts/security-scan-cycle.sh")
Confirm it produces "CLEAN:" or "ALERT:" output, not an error.

Check 3 — Cache-timing audit:

During a live loop, inspect ScheduleWakeupOutput.clampedDelaySeconds.
Confirm it is consistently 120, not 300. wasClamped should be false.

If wasClamped: true appears, something in the loop prompt is generating a delay outside [60, 3600]. Track it down — it means your loop is not pacing as intended.

What This Daemon Demonstrates

  • CronCreate handles time-based startup. It does not care about loop dynamics.
  • ScheduleWakeup handles loop pacing. It does not persist across sessions.
  • Durable + self-renewal is the pattern for indefinite recurrence beyond the 7-day limit.
  • Cache-warm delays (120s, well under 270s) keep per-cycle costs low.
  • The sentinel enables adaptive pacing — the loop stops itself when the day ends.
  • External scripts keep prompts short and logic testable.

Summary

Two tools, two problems.

CronCreate is the harness's alarm clock. You give it a five-field cron expression, a prompt, and optional durability. It fires the prompt when the expression matches and the REPL is idle. Use recurring: false for one-shots. Use durable: true for anything that needs to outlast the current session. Never schedule at :00 or :30 unless coordinating with an external boundary. Expect jitter of up to 10% of the period, capped at 15 minutes. Plan for 7-day expiry in any long-running setup.

ScheduleWakeup is the loop's throttle. It only makes sense inside a /loop running with <<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>. It controls when the next iteration runs. Use delays under 270s to stay cache-warm. Use 1200s+ to amortize a cold read. Never use 300s. Always define a stop condition — call ScheduleWakeup(stop: true) when the work is done.

The combination — a CronCreate that starts a dynamic loop each morning, a loop that uses ScheduleWakeup for intraday pacing, and self-renewal logic to survive the 7-day window — is the production pattern for autonomous monitoring daemons. It is not complicated once you understand which tool solves which sub-problem.

In Chapter 15, we examine the Task system: creating background tasks, polling their output, and coordinating parallel task execution across agent teams.

Chapter 15: Monitor Tool — Event-Driven Watching

"A cron job asks what happened. A monitor is there when it happens."

15.1 Monitor Parameters

Every tool in the harness catalog is synchronous except for a few that return a taskId and continue working in the background. Monitor is the most important member of that family. It connects the model to a live stream of events — log lines, CI state changes, WebSocket frames — and delivers each event to the agent as it arrives, without polling.

The full interface:

export interface MonitorInput {
  description: string;     // human-readable label shown in notifications
  timeout_ms: number;      // max 3600000ms (1 hour), ignored when persistent: true
  persistent: boolean;     // run for session lifetime, stop with TaskStop
  command?: string;        // shell command — each stdout line is one event
  ws?: {                   // WebSocket — each text frame is one event
    url: string;
    protocols?: string[];
  };
}

export interface MonitorOutput {
  taskId: string;          // pass to TaskStop to end the monitor
  timeoutMs: number;       // 0 when persistent
  persistent?: boolean;
}

Four parameters do all the work. Understanding each precisely is what separates monitors that are reliable infrastructure from monitors that silently stall.

description

A free-form string. It is not cosmetic — the harness surfaces it in the activity UI, in push notifications, and in audit logs. A description like "watching GitHub Actions for main branch failures" means that when the model is doing three other things simultaneously and an event fires, the notification carries enough context for a human to understand what triggered it without reading the conversation.

Write descriptions as if you were labeling a process in ps aux. Short, specific, unambiguous. "monitor" is wrong. "CI monitor: main branch, failure alerts" is right.

timeout_ms

The maximum duration the monitor will run, in milliseconds. The ceiling is 3,600,000 — exactly one hour. Requesting a longer timeout is not an error in all implementations but the harness clamps at the one-hour maximum, so you should not rely on anything beyond that.

When persistent: true, this field is ignored entirely. The harness does not start a timeout timer for persistent monitors. You can pass any value and it will have no effect.

For non-persistent monitors, the timeout is wall-clock time from when the monitor starts. If you need a monitor to run for 45 minutes, pass timeout_ms: 2700000. When the timer expires, the monitor stops as cleanly as it would if the process exited or the socket closed.

persistent

When false (or omitted), the monitor runs until the timeout, the command exits, or the socket closes — whichever comes first.

When true, the timeout is ignored and the monitor runs until you call TaskStop(taskId) or the session ends. This is the correct mode for daemon-like watchers: log tailing, queue consumers, long-lived WebSocket subscriptions. The harness records the taskId in the session's active task list, and when the session terminates the harness sends a stop signal to all persistent monitors before it exits.

The practical rule: use persistent: true for anything you would run with nohup or as a systemd service. Use timeout_ms for bounded observation windows — watching a deploy for up to 20 minutes, monitoring a test run for up to 10 minutes.

command and ws

You must provide exactly one of these. Providing both is an error. Providing neither is an error.

command takes a shell string identical in syntax to the Bash tool. The command runs in a subprocess; every line written to stdout becomes an event delivered to the agent. Stderr is not captured as events — it goes to the harness log.

ws takes an object with a required url and an optional protocols array. The protocols array maps directly to the WebSocket subprotocol negotiation headers. If the server requires a specific subprotocol (common in streaming APIs and message brokers), list it here.

15.2 Command Mode
