When the harness assembles the skill list, it evaluates each skill's paths globs against the current working directory's file tree. A skill with no paths is always visible. A skill with paths is visible only when at least one file in the working directory matches at least one glob in the list.

---
name: tf-lint
description: Lint and validate Terraform configurations
paths:
  - "**/*.tf"
  - "**/*.tfvars"
  - ".terraform/**"
---

This skill appears when working in a Terraform infrastructure repository. It does not appear in a Python service, a React app, or a book repository. The user's skill menu reflects the active environment rather than the user's entire history of skill creation.

Practical Patterns

Language-specific skills. A skill for Python type-checking should restrict to **/*.py. A TypeScript refactoring skill should restrict to **/*.ts and **/*.tsx. Skills without path restrictions in a polyglot workspace clutter the menu with irrelevant options.

Project-tier skills. Skills that only make sense in a specific project can use highly specific globs:

paths:
  - "backend/scripts/secpr_*.py"

This skill only activates in the specific directory that contains the scripts it needs. It is invisible in every other project, even though the SKILL.md is a global skill.

Config-presence detection. A deployment skill that requires a particular CI configuration can gate on that file's existence:

paths:
  - ".github/workflows/**"
  - "azure-pipelines.yml"

When neither path matches, the skill does not appear — a useful signal that deployment via that skill is not applicable here.

Path Matching in --bare Mode

Skills resolve correctly in --bare mode via /skill-name even when path restrictions are in effect. --bare mode disables the active menu and autocomplete but not skill resolution itself. If a user types /tf-lint in a directory with no Terraform files, the skill still invokes. The paths field controls visibility in the menu, not the ability to invoke by name.

17.6 Real Skills: Production Examples

The 23 skills in the production workspace range from two-line procedural helpers to 2500-line autonomous systems. Understanding the design decisions in each reveals the full range of what the skill system can express.

sec-pr: Autonomous Security Review

The sec-pr skill is the most complex in the workspace. Its frontmatter sets the baseline:

---
name: sec-pr
description: Security PR review for Azure DevOps pull requests. Use when user
  says "sec-pr", "PR security review", "scan PR", "review PR security", "PR
  scan", "security scan PR", "check sec-pr", "sec-pr status", "approve PR".
  Without a PR number, auto-discovers all active PRs across all repos and
  scans them.
argument-hint: "[pr-number | org-name (optional)]"
model: claude-opus-4-6
effort: high
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Agent
---

The description seeds 10 distinct invocation phrases. Any of them routes to this skill. The user never needs to remember the exact command name — natural language works.

model: claude-opus-4-6 and effort: high are justified by the task: the skill reads 30-50 files per PR, reasons about authentication flows, generates complete patch code, posts structured content to ADO, and manages a state machine that persists across monitor ticks. This requires the best reasoning available. The model switch is invisible to the user; they just type /sec-pr.

The skill body encodes an 8-phase pipeline: Acquisition → Quick Scan → Agent Dispatch → Consolidation → Report Generation → Post to ADO → Vote → Monitor. Each phase is documented with exact bash commands, Python snippets, and decision tables. The body is 1500+ lines — not a specification for a human to implement, but a complete operational runbook for the model to execute.

This is the defining characteristic of a production skill: it should be complete enough that the model can execute it correctly in a fresh context with no prior memory of the workflow. The skill body is a self-contained instruction set.

dt: Autonomous Trading

The /dt skill illustrates the model override applied to maximize decision quality:

---
name: dt
description: Decode Trader — autonomous SPY 0DTE paper trading. Buy calls or
  puts only. Dispatches tmux team for parallel analysis + execution. Use when
  user says "dt", "decode trader", "trade", "trading", "position", "what's
  the play", "market update", or "close position".
argument-hint: [optional: close|status]
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Agent
model: claude-opus-4-6
effort: high
---

Two design decisions stand out. First, model: claude-opus-4-6 combined with effort: high commits to maximum reasoning for every invocation. Trading decisions carry real financial consequence even in a paper account — the cost of a wrong model choice is higher than the cost of a more expensive API call. Second, the allowed-tools list includes Agent, enabling the skill to spawn a 4-agent tmux team for parallel analysis.

The skill body encodes a complete trading system: signal chain, 4-pillar entry gate, agent deployment protocol, position management rules, context hygiene requirements, and session recovery procedures. The model executing /dt is not making ad hoc decisions; it is following a documented methodology that was refined over dozens of trading sessions.

research: Minimal but Complete

The research skill is the opposite end of the spectrum:

---
name: research
description: Deep research on technical topics using web search, documentation,
  and codebase exploration.
---

No model override. No allowed-tools restriction. No effort override. No paths restriction. The body is 30 lines: scope clarification, parallel source gathering, synthesis format.

The simplicity is appropriate. Research is a general workflow that applies everywhere, benefits from the full tool surface, and does not require a specific model. The skill exists to give the workflow a name and a consistent output format, not to encode a complex operational system.

deploy-check: Locked Down with disable-model-invocation

The deploy-check skill introduces a field not covered in the schema overview:

---
name: deploy-check
description: Pre-deployment readiness check.
disable-model-invocation: true
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
effort: high
---

disable-model-invocation: true runs the skill as a pure script executor — the commands in the body run directly without an API call. This is the correct pattern for purely mechanical skills: git status checks, secret scans, test runs, build validation. There is no reasoning to do. The output is deterministic. Running it through the model adds latency and cost with no benefit.

The allowed-tools restriction to Bash, Read, Grep, Glob — with Agent absent — ensures the skill cannot spawn subagents, further constraining it to the simple mechanical execution pattern it was designed for.

Skills Compared to Hooks and Plugins

The skill system sits alongside two other harness extension points: hooks and plugins. Understanding where each applies prevents the common mistake of building a skill when a hook is more appropriate, or reaching for a plugin when a skill is sufficient.

MechanismTriggerScopeStatefulness
SkillUser invocation (/name)ConversationEphemeral (single invocation)
HookHarness lifecycle event (file write, tool call, session end)BackgroundEphemeral (single event)
Plugin/MCPModel request during any conversationAny conversationPersistent (server lifetime)

A skill is the right choice when the user initiates the workflow explicitly. The user types /sec-pr because they want a security review right now. Skills are on-demand.

A hook is the right choice when you want something to happen automatically in response to a harness event — not when the user asks, but when the harness does something. PostToolUse hooks that log every file write. PreToolUse hooks that validate commands before execution. Stop hooks that save session state when the agent exits. Hooks are reactive.

A plugin (MCP server) is the right choice when you need persistent state, a long-running process, or capabilities that multiple conversations should share. The dt-mem trading memory server is an MCP plugin, not a skill, because it needs to store data that persists between sessions and be accessible to multiple agent invocations simultaneously.

The failure mode for conflating these: building a skill that should be a hook means you are manually invoking something that could be automatic. Building a hook that should be a skill means you are executing something automatically that should be explicitly requested.

17.7 Restricting the Skill System

Two settings give operators control over the skill system in environments where unrestricted slash commands are not appropriate.

disableSkillShellExecution

Set in settings.json:

{
  "disableSkillShellExecution": true
}

This blocks inline shell execution in skill bodies. Skills that contain bash code blocks will have those blocks interpreted as text rather than executed. The model can still reason about the commands and produce output, but the harness will not run them.

The practical use case is an environment where shell execution requires explicit approval for all commands, not just those in skills. If your PreToolUse hooks apply shell approval requirements, disableSkillShellExecution prevents skills from bypassing those requirements through their own execution path.

Skills that use the Bash tool explicitly (via allowed-tools: Bash) are not affected by disableSkillShellExecution. The setting only blocks the inline shell execution path within skill bodies. Removing Bash from allowed-tools in the skill frontmatter and setting disableSkillShellExecution together produces a fully execution-restricted skill system.

--disable-slash-commands

The CLI flag:

claude --disable-slash-commands

Disables all skill invocation. The /skills menu does not appear. Typing /skill-name is treated as literal text, not as a skill invocation. ProposeSkills proposals are suppressed. The skill discovery paths are still read (skills are still registered internally), but no user-facing skill functionality is active.

This is the correct setting for automated pipeline usage where interactive slash commands make no sense, and for restricted deployments where the operator wants to constrain Claude Code to a specific tool set without any user-extensible shortcuts.

Note that --disable-slash-commands does not disable built-in slash commands like /clear, /model, and /compact. It disables user-defined skills only.

Combining Restrictions

For maximum restriction — skills present in the manifest but not executable by users:

{
  "disableSkillShellExecution": true
}
claude --disable-slash-commands --bare

--bare mode suppresses the CLAUDE.md injection and the full interactive UI. Combined with --disable-slash-commands, it gives you a model interaction surface with no user-extensible behavior and no project-injected context — a clean baseline for controlled evaluation environments.

17.8 Lab: Build a Deployment Skill with Pre-Flight Validation and Post-Deploy Monitoring

This lab builds a complete deployment skill from scratch. The skill validates readiness before deploying, executes the deployment, and monitors post-deploy health. It demonstrates every frontmatter field and shows how a multi-phase skill body coordinates with the harness.

What We Are Building

A /deploy skill for a Python web service that:

  1. Validates the working tree is clean and tests pass (pre-flight)
  2. Checks the target environment is reachable and healthy (environment check)
  3. Executes deployment via the project's deploy script (execution)
  4. Monitors health endpoints for 60 seconds post-deploy (monitoring)
  5. Reports status with rollback instructions if health checks fail

Step 1: Create the Skill Directory

mkdir -p /Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/.claude/skills/deploy

Skills live in a directory, not a file. The directory name matches the skill name. The SKILL.md lives inside:

.claude/skills/deploy/
└── SKILL.md

Step 2: Write the Frontmatter

Create /Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md:

---
name: deploy
description: Deploy the current service to staging or production. Runs
  pre-flight checks, executes deployment, monitors health. Use when user
  says "deploy", "ship it", "push to staging", "release", or "go live".
argument-hint: "[staging|prod] [--skip-tests]"
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
effort: high
paths:
  - "deploy.sh"
  - "Makefile"
  - "pyproject.toml"
  - "Dockerfile"
---

Design rationale for each field:

description seeds five natural-language invocations. The user can say /deploy staging or /deploy prod — both parse correctly from $ARGUMENTS.

argument-hint shows the user the two valid environments and the optional test-skip flag. The hint is documentation; the skill body handles actual parsing.

allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob — no Agent needed. This is a sequential workflow: validate, deploy, monitor. No parallel subagents required.

effort: high — deployment requires careful reasoning about whether each check passed. High effort gives the model adequate thinking budget for the pre-flight decision logic.

paths restricts the skill to directories that contain deployment artifacts. A Python library without a deploy.sh will not show /deploy in its skills menu.

Step 3: Write the Skill Body

# /deploy — Service Deployment

You are executing a production deployment workflow. Execute every phase
completely. Do not skip a phase if the previous one fails — report the
failure clearly and provide rollback instructions.

**Environment:** $ARGUMENTS
Parse `$ARGUMENTS` as: first word is environment (`staging` or `prod`),
optional `--skip-tests` flag skips the test phase.

If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, default to `staging`.
If `$ARGUMENTS` contains `prod` or `production`, set ENV=prod and double-check
every pre-flight gate before proceeding.

---

## Phase 1 — Pre-Flight Validation

Run every check. Report each result as PASS or FAIL. Do not proceed to
Phase 2 if any check fails with FAIL severity.

### 1.1 Working Directory Clean

git status --porcelain git log origin/main..HEAD --oneline


Expected: empty output for both. Any uncommitted changes or unpushed
commits = FAIL.

### 1.2 Tests Pass (skip if --skip-tests)

python -m pytest tests/ --tb=short -q 2>&1


Expected: all tests pass. Any failure = FAIL. Record the failure output.
If `--skip-tests` is set, report as SKIPPED and note it in the final report.

### 1.3 No Secrets in Changed Files

git diff origin/main..HEAD -- '.py' '.yaml' '.env' '.json' | \ grep -E '^\+' | \ grep -iE '(password|secret|token|api[_-]?key)\s*[:=]\s*["\x27][^"\x27]{8,}'


Expected: no output. Any match = FAIL with the matching line quoted.

### 1.4 Dependencies Audited

pip audit --format=json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c " import json, sys data = json.load(sys.stdin) vulns = data.get('vulnerabilities', []) critical = [v for v in vulns if v.get('fix_versions')] print(f'Vulnerabilities: {len(vulns)} total, {len(critical)} with fixes') for v in critical[:5]: print(f' {v[\"name\"]} {v[\"version\"]}: {v[\"description\"][:80]}') "


Expected: zero vulnerabilities with available fixes. Unfixed vulns = WARN.
Vulns with available fixes = FAIL.

### Pre-Flight Gate

| Check | Result | Severity |
|-------|--------|----------|
| Git clean | — | FAIL stops deploy |
| Tests pass | — | FAIL stops deploy |
| No secrets | — | FAIL stops deploy |
| Dependencies | — | WARN allows deploy |

**If any FAIL:** Stop here. Do not proceed to Phase 2. Report:

DEPLOY BLOCKED Pre-flight failures: [list of failing checks] Fix the failures and re-run /deploy.


---

## Phase 2 — Environment Health Check

Verify the target environment is reachable and in a state that can
accept a deployment.

### 2.1 Resolve Target URL

Read deploy config

cat deploy.sh | grep -E 'STAGING_URL|PROD_URL|TARGET_URL' cat .env.deploy 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'URL|HOST|ENDPOINT'


Extract the health endpoint URL for the target environment from the
deploy configuration. If not found, report that the environment URL
is not configured and stop.

### 2.2 Current Health Baseline

curl -sf --max-time 10 "${HEALTH_URL}/health" | python3 -m json.tool 2>/dev/null echo "HTTP status: $(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 10 ${HEALTH_URL}/health)"


Expected: HTTP 200, JSON body with `status: "ok"` or equivalent.
Record the baseline response for comparison after deploy.

If the health endpoint is not reachable: **FAIL — target environment
is down. Cannot deploy to a dead environment. Page on-call.**

---

## Phase 3 — Execute Deployment

bash deploy.sh $ENV 2>&1 | tee /tmp/deploy_output_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).log DEPLOY_EXIT=$?


Capture full output. Record the log path.

If `DEPLOY_EXIT` is non-zero: **FAIL — deployment script exited with
error. Do not proceed to health monitoring. Initiate rollback (Phase 5).**

Expected output: deployment script reports success, new version deployed,
service restarting.

---

## Phase 4 — Post-Deploy Health Monitoring

Monitor the health endpoint for 60 seconds after deployment. Check
every 10 seconds. The service may take up to 30 seconds to restart.

for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do sleep 10 STATUS=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 10 "${HEALTH_URL}/health" 2>/dev/null) BODY=$(curl -sf --max-time 10 "${HEALTH_URL}/health" 2>/dev/null) echo "Check ${i}/6 ($(date +%H:%M:%S)): HTTP ${STATUS}" [[ "${STATUS}" == "200" ]] && echo " Body: $(echo $BODY | python3 -c 'import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d.get("version","?"),d.get("status","?"))' 2>/dev/null)" done


**Success criteria:** HTTP 200 on at least 4 of the last 4 checks
(checks 3-6). A 200 on check 1 or 2 that reverts later means the
service restarted but then crashed.

**If health checks fail after check 3:** The deployment is unstable.
Proceed to Phase 5 (Rollback).

---

## Phase 5 — Rollback (only if Phase 3 or 4 failed)

bash deploy.sh $ENV --rollback 2>&1 | tee /tmp/rollback_output_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).log


If the deploy script does not support `--rollback`, report the manual
rollback steps extracted from the deploy script's comments or a
`ROLLBACK.md` if it exists.

After rollback, re-run the Phase 4 health check to confirm the previous
version is healthy.

---

## Phase 6 — Report

Report the full deployment result in this format:

DEPLOYMENT REPORT — $ENV ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Time: [timestamp] Version: [deployed version or commit SHA] Status: DEPLOYED / FAILED / ROLLED BACK

Pre-flight: Git clean [PASS/FAIL] Tests [PASS/FAIL/SKIPPED] No secrets [PASS/FAIL] Dependencies [PASS/WARN]

Deployment: [PASS/FAIL] Log: /tmp/deploy_output_[timestamp].log

Health: Check 1/6 [HTTP status] Check 2/6 [HTTP status] Check 3/6 [HTTP status] Check 4/6 [HTTP status] Check 5/6 [HTTP status] Check 6/6 [HTTP status] Final: [STABLE/UNSTABLE]

[If FAILED or ROLLED BACK:] ROLLBACK INSTRUCTIONS: bash deploy.sh $ENV --rollback [manual steps if script does not support --rollback]

Step 4: Verify the Skill Appears

In a directory that contains a deploy.sh or Makefile:

/skills

The /deploy skill should appear. If it does not, verify:

  1. The directory is named deploy (matching the name: field)
  2. The SKILL.md frontmatter is valid YAML (no tabs, correct quoting)
  3. The paths globs match something in the working directory

To test in a directory without those files, invoke directly by name:

/deploy staging

The skill activates regardless of path matching when invoked by explicit name.

Step 5: Test with --skip-tests

/deploy staging --skip-tests

The skill parses --skip-tests from $ARGUMENTS and skips Phase 1.2. The final report marks tests as SKIPPED and notes the flag was set.

Step 6: Extend with ProposeSkills

After running /deploy a few times, the model may observe that you always deploy to staging first and then verify before deploying to prod. It might propose a deploy-promote skill that encodes the two-stage workflow as a single command. That proposal is the skills system working as designed: turning repeated behavior into an explicit, nameable command.

Summary

The skills system is the harness's mechanism for turning repeated workflows into named, invocable commands. The SKILL.md frontmatter controls the execution environment — model, tool surface, effort level, context restrictions. The skill body controls the model's behavior — the instructions it follows when /name is typed.

Skills are appropriate when the user initiates the workflow explicitly. Hooks are appropriate when the workflow should trigger automatically. MCP plugins are appropriate when the workflow needs persistent state across sessions. The three mechanisms are complementary, not competitive.

The production skill library in this workspace spans the full range from 30-line research assistants to 2500-line autonomous security review systems. What they share: each skill body is complete enough to execute correctly in a fresh context, each frontmatter is specific enough that the skill appears exactly when it is relevant, and each allowed-tools list is exactly as broad as the skill's actual needs.

Build skills the way you would write a runbook: for a competent reader who has never seen the workflow before and needs to execute it correctly on the first attempt.

Chapter 18: Plugin Architecture — Shareable Extensions

"A plugin is not a feature. It is a contract — between author, marketplace, and enterprise operator."

18.1 Plugin Structure: The Six Directories and Two Files

A Claude Code plugin is a directory with a specific shape. That shape is not arbitrary — every directory maps to a capability class, and the harness knows exactly what to look for in each one. Understanding the structure before anything else is the right starting point because it makes everything that follows predictable.

The canonical plugin layout:

my-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json          # plugin manifest (required)
├── commands/                # /command-name markdown files
│   └── do-thing.md
├── agents/                  # named agent definitions
│   └── reviewer.md
├── skills/                  # reusable prompt fragments
│   └── analyze-deps.md
├── hooks/                   # event-driven behavior
│   └── PreToolUse.ts
├── bin/                     # executables invocable from Bash tool
│   └── my-scanner
└── .mcp.json                # MCP server declarations

The .claude-plugin/ directory is the sentinel. When the harness scans for plugins — on install, on session start, when enumerating capabilities — it looks for this directory. A directory without .claude-plugin/plugin.json is not a plugin; it is just a directory.

Each of the other directories is optional. A plugin can ship nothing but a command and still be valid. A plugin can ship nothing but hooks. The structure is additive — you include the directories that correspond to the capabilities you need.

The .claude-plugin/ Directory

The .claude-plugin/ directory exists to separate plugin metadata from plugin content. Everything in it is read by the harness itself, not by the model. The only required file is plugin.json. In practice you may also find CHANGELOG.md and LICENSE in this directory, though those are conventions rather than harness-enforced requirements.

commands/

Each markdown file in commands/ defines a slash command. The filename becomes the command name: do-thing.md registers as /do-thing (or /plugin-name:do-thing if namespacing is active). The file content is the command prompt — the instruction set the model receives when a user invokes the command.

Commands are the most visible capability in a plugin. They are what users interact with directly.

agents/

Agent files define named subagent types that can be spawned with subagent_type: "agent-name" in the Agent tool. An agent definition is a markdown file containing the system prompt for that agent — its role, its tool constraints, its output format, its escalation criteria.

The code-review plugin ships five agent files: security-reviewer.md, performance-reviewer.md, test-coverage-reviewer.md, code-style-reviewer.md, and architecture-reviewer.md. Each is specialized. Each gets spawned in parallel when the /code-review command runs.

skills/

Skills are reusable prompt fragments. They are not commands — a user cannot invoke a skill directly. Skills are included by commands, agents, and hooks through the !include directive. A skill named analyze-deps.md might contain a structured procedure for dependency analysis that three different commands all reference.

The plugin-dev plugin ships seven skills that cover every aspect of plugin creation. Skills are how that plugin avoids repeating identical procedure text across seven different commands.

hooks/

Hook files define event-driven behavior that fires automatically based on harness events. A hook named PreToolUse.ts registers for the PreToolUse event. A hook named SessionStart.ts runs at the beginning of every session that has this plugin enabled.

The hookify plugin's core directory is hooks/ — it is a plugin whose primary product is hook generation and management.

bin/

Executables in bin/ become available to the Bash tool when the plugin is installed. This is how a plugin ships a scanner, a linter, a formatter, or any other CLI tool that Claude can invoke during a task. The harness adds the plugin's bin/ directory to the PATH when executing Bash tool calls, making the executables available without absolute paths.

This is a powerful surface. A plugin that ships a bin/secret-scanner binary gives Claude a high-performance secret detection tool it can run on any file or directory. The binary does not have to be written in any particular language — it just needs to be executable.

.mcp.json

This file declares MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers that the plugin provides. When installed, these servers are registered with the harness and become available as additional tool sources. The copilot-mem plugin is almost entirely .mcp.json — its plugin manifest declares an MCP memory server, and that server provides the memory tools.

18.2 Plugin Manifest: The plugin.json Contract

The plugin.json file is the contract between a plugin and the harness. It is small, but every field matters.

{
  "name": "code-review",
  "description": "Automated code review for pull requests using multiple specialized agents with confidence-based scoring",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": {
    "name": "Boris Cherny",
    "email": "boris@anthropic.com"
  }
}

This is the actual manifest from the official code-review plugin. Four fields, no more. That is not minimal effort — that is intentional interface design.

name

The name is the plugin's identifier in every context: the marketplace index, installed_plugins.json, the enabledPlugins setting, and the namespaced command prefix. It must be lowercase, hyphen-separated, and globally unique within a marketplace.

The naming convention matters because of how command namespacing works. When a plugin named code-review ships a command file review.md, the command is accessible as both /review (if no namespace conflict) and /code-review:review (the fully qualified form). The name is the namespace.

description

The description is what users see in marketplace listings and in --help output. It is not a docstring — it is marketing copy for the plugin's primary use case. Write it as a complete sentence. Be specific about what the plugin does and what makes it different from alternatives.

Compare:

// Weak:
"description": "Code review plugin"

// Strong:
"description": "Automated code review for pull requests using multiple specialized agents with confidence-based scoring"

The strong version tells users what the plugin does (automated code review), how it does it (multiple specialized agents), and what makes it notable (confidence-based scoring). That is enough information to decide whether to install it.

version

Versions follow semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. The harness uses the version field to detect when an installed plugin has an available update from the marketplace. When you push a new version to a marketplace repository, users with auto-update enabled will receive the new version.

The installed_plugins.json entry for each plugin stores both version and gitCommitSha. This dual tracking means the harness can detect version mismatches — a case where the marketplace lists a higher version but the local install's SHA matches an older commit.

author

The author object is for attribution and contact. In enterprise settings, the email field is used by security teams to track who is responsible for which plugins. When a plugin causes unexpected behavior or requires security review, the author contact is the first path to resolution.

For enterprise plugins, the name should match the team or service, not an individual:

{
  "author": {
    "name": "Platform Security Team",
    "email": "platform-security@yourorg.com"
  }
}

18.3 Distribution: Marketplaces, Known and Installed

The plugin distribution system has two layers: the marketplace layer (where plugins live) and the install layer (what is on this machine). Understanding both is necessary for enterprise deployment and for publishing your own plugins.

Marketplaces

A marketplace is a GitHub repository with a defined structure. The harness discovers marketplaces through known_marketplaces.json, which lives at ~/.claude/plugins/known_marketplaces.json:

{
  "claude-plugins-official": {
    "source": {
      "source": "github",
      "repo": "anthropics/claude-plugins-official"
    },
    "installLocation": "/Users/user/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/claude-plugins-official",
    "lastUpdated": "2026-03-31T15:52:23.030Z"
  }
}

Each key in this object is a marketplace identifier. The source object describes where the marketplace lives — currently GitHub is the supported source type. The installLocation is where the harness caches the marketplace's plugin index locally. The lastUpdated timestamp drives the refresh cycle.

When you run /plugin install code-review, the harness:

  1. Reads known_marketplaces.json to find registered marketplaces
  2. Checks each marketplace's cached index for a plugin named code-review
  3. Downloads the plugin from GitHub to the local install path
  4. Writes an entry to installed_plugins.json
  5. Activates the plugin for the current scope

The lastUpdated field matters for offline environments. If you set CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_KEEP_MARKETPLACE_ON_FAILURE=true, the harness retains the locally cached marketplace index even when GitHub is unreachable. This means plugin installs from cached data still work in air-gapped or network-constrained environments, but new plugins added to the marketplace since the last cache refresh will not be visible.

installed_plugins.json

Every installed plugin gets an entry in ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json:

{
  "version": 2,
  "plugins": {
    "rust-analyzer-lsp@claude-plugins-official": [{
      "scope": "user",
      "installPath": "...cache/claude-plugins-official/rust-analyzer-lsp/1.0.0",
      "version": "1.0.0",
      "installedAt": "2026-04-10T02:55:43.321Z",
      "gitCommitSha": "52e95f6756e577b6a788c941f994ca44de2cf2d6"
    }]
  }
}

The plugin key is name@marketplace-id. The @marketplace-id suffix matters: the same plugin name could theoretically exist in multiple marketplaces, and the harness needs to distinguish them.

The scope field is "user" for user-level installs and "project" for project-level installs. A project-level install lives in .claude/plugins/ inside the project directory and is only active when Claude Code is run from that project.

The gitCommitSha is the harness's integrity anchor. When verifying a plugin at session start, the harness can confirm the local files match the expected commit. If they do not — because someone manually edited a plugin file — the harness can flag the discrepancy.

Enabling Plugins

Installation and enablement are separate operations. An installed plugin is not active until it appears in the enabledPlugins setting in settings.json:

{
  "enabledPlugins": {
    "code-review@claude-plugins-official": true,
    "hookify@claude-plugins-official": true
  }
}

The /plugin command manages both operations. The full command surface:

/plugin install <name>          # install from marketplace
/plugin enable <name>           # enable an installed plugin
/plugin disable <name>          # disable without uninstalling
/plugin uninstall <name>        # remove entirely
/plugin list                    # show installed and enabled plugins
/plugin update <name>           # update to latest marketplace version

The enable/disable split is useful for plugins you want available but not active in every session. You might have the security-guidance plugin installed but only enable it for sessions involving infrastructure changes.

18.4 Enterprise Control: Governance Without Friction

Enterprise deployments have requirements that consumer use does not: audit trails, allowlists, protection against supply chain attacks, and compliance with internal security policies. Claude Code's enterprise plugin governance is controlled through managed-settings.json, the policy file that administrators push to managed machines.

strictKnownMarketplaces

{
  "strictKnownMarketplaces": true
}

When this is set, users can only install plugins from marketplaces explicitly listed in known_marketplaces.json. Any attempt to install from a marketplace not in the known list fails with a policy error.

This is the primary control for supply chain hygiene. Without it, a user could add any GitHub repository as a marketplace and install arbitrary plugins. With it, the IT or security team controls the full list of approved marketplaces, and that list is the only source of truth.

Typical enterprise configuration:

{
  "claude-plugins-official": {
    "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "anthropics/claude-plugins-official" },
    "installLocation": "/opt/claude/plugins/marketplaces/claude-plugins-official"
  },
  "corp-internal-plugins": {
    "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "yourorg/claude-plugins-internal" },
    "installLocation": "/opt/claude/plugins/marketplaces/corp-internal"
  }
}

Two marketplaces: the official Anthropic one and an internal corporate repository. Nothing else.

allowedChannelPlugins

{
  "allowedChannelPlugins": [
    "code-review@claude-plugins-official",
    "security-guidance@claude-plugins-official",
    "corp-code-standards@corp-internal-plugins"
  ]
}

This is a plugin allowlist. Even if a plugin is available in an approved marketplace, it cannot be installed unless it appears in allowedChannelPlugins. This is the right control when you want to explicitly approve each plugin rather than approve all plugins from approved sources.

The two controls compose: strictKnownMarketplaces limits where plugins come from, allowedChannelPlugins limits which specific plugins from those sources are permitted.

allowManagedHooksOnly

{
  "allowManagedHooksOnly": true
}

This is the most targeted of the three controls. Hooks are powerful — they run automatically, they can intercept tool calls, and they can modify behavior. A malicious hook shipped in an apparently benign plugin is a real attack vector.

When allowManagedHooksOnly is true, only hooks that come from the organization's own managed plugins are allowed to execute. Hooks from user-installed plugins — even from the official marketplace — are silently disabled. This gives organizations the ability to use plugins for commands and agents while retaining full control over the event-driven behavior layer.

Enforcement Behavior

The harness checks policy at install time and at session start. If a policy violation is detected at session start — a plugin was installed before a policy was applied — the harness disables the plugin for that session and logs the reason. Users see a policy notice; they do not see an unexplained failure.

This design is deliberate: enforce early, communicate clearly, never silently succeed with partial behavior. An agent operating with half its expected plugins active because the other half were policy-blocked but not communicated is more dangerous than an agent that refuses to start.

18.5 Plugin Capabilities in Depth

Custom Commands

Commands are the user-facing surface of a plugin. They are markdown files, which means the full power of CLAUDE.md instruction syntax is available: structured task descriptions, tool restrictions, output format specifications, and embedded checklists.

A well-authored command file for a dependency audit command:

---
description: Audit project dependencies for known vulnerabilities and outdated packages
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Write
---

You are running a dependency audit for the current project.

## Steps

1. Detect the package manager (check for package.json, requirements.txt, Cargo.toml, go.mod)
2. Run the appropriate audit command:
   - npm: `npm audit --json`
   - pip: `pip audit --format=json`
   - cargo: `cargo audit --json`
   - go: `govulncheck ./... -json`
3. Parse the JSON output and categorize findings by severity: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW
4. For each CRITICAL or HIGH finding, identify whether a patched version is available
5. Write a report to `audit-report.md` with:
   - Summary table (counts per severity)
   - Detailed findings with CVE IDs and remediation steps
   - Upgrade commands ready to copy-paste

If the audit tool is not installed, output clear installation instructions and stop.

The allowed-tools frontmatter is enforced: Claude cannot use any tool not listed when executing this command, even tools it would normally have access to. This is the command's permission boundary.

Agents

Agent definitions are system prompts for named subagent types. When a parent agent spawns subagent_type: "security-reviewer", the harness looks up the agent definition file and uses it as the subagent's system prompt.

This is how the code-review plugin achieves specialization. Each of its five agents receives a role-specific system prompt — the security reviewer cares about injection flaws, the test coverage reviewer cares about branch coverage, the architecture reviewer cares about coupling metrics. They spawn in parallel and return structured findings that the coordinator synthesizes.

Hooks

Hooks are the event-driven layer. A hook in a plugin fires just like a hook in .claude/hooks/ — the difference is that the plugin author is the one who wrote it, and the enterprise operator can choose to allow or block it via allowManagedHooksOnly.

The security-guidance plugin ships a single PreToolUse hook that monitors for nine patterns:

const DANGEROUS_PATTERNS = [
  { pattern: /rm\s+-rf\s+\//, description: "recursive delete from root" },
  { pattern: />\s*\/etc\/passwd/, description: "write to /etc/passwd" },
  { pattern: /curl.*\|\s*bash/, description: "pipe curl to bash" },
  { pattern: /chmod\s+777/, description: "world-writable permission set" },
  // ... five more
];

When Claude attempts a Bash tool call matching any of these patterns, the hook appends a structured security reminder to the tool result, prompting Claude to reconsider before proceeding.

The explanatory-output-style and learning-output-style plugins both ship SessionStart hooks. These hooks inject behavioral instructions at the beginning of every session where the plugin is active — essentially wrapping the user's CLAUDE.md with additional output formatting rules without requiring the user to edit any files.

MCP Servers

The .mcp.json file lets a plugin declare Model Context Protocol servers. When the plugin is active, those servers are available as additional tool providers. The copilot-mem plugin is the canonical example — its MCP server provides memory read/write/search tools that persist across sessions.

This is how plugins extend the tool surface without modifying the harness itself. An organization that builds an internal knowledge base tool can ship it as an MCP server inside a plugin, and all Claude Code users who have the plugin enabled will see the knowledge base tools in their tool registry.

18.6 Official Plugins: A Practical Survey

The official plugin marketplace ships 14 plugins at the time of writing. Not all of them are equally interesting — some are narrowly scoped utilities, others are architecturally instructive. The ones worth studying closely:

PluginPrimary CapabilityArchitecture
code-reviewMulti-agent PR review1 command, 5 parallel Sonnet agents
feature-dev7-phase feature development1 command, 3 specialized agents
pr-review-toolkitComprehensive PR review1 command, 6 specialized agents
hookifyCreate and manage hooks4 commands, hook pattern matching
plugin-devMeta-plugin for plugin creation1 command, 7 skills
security-guidanceSecurity reminder injection1 hook (PreToolUse, 9 patterns)
copilot-memPersistent memory across sessionsMCP server
explanatory-output-styleEducational output mode1 hook (SessionStart)
learning-output-styleInteractive teaching mode1 hook (SessionStart)
commit-commandsGit workflow shortcuts3 commands
ralph-wiggumSelf-referential iteration loops2 commands
agent-sdk-devSDK scaffolding1 command, 2 verifier agents
frontend-designProduction UI design1 skill
claude-opus-4-5-migrationModel migration automation1 skill

code-review: The Parallel Agent Pattern

The code-review plugin is the reference implementation for parallel agent workflows. Its /code-review command spawns five agents simultaneously:

flowchart TD
    A([/code-review]) --> B[Coordinator Agent]
    B --> C[Security Reviewer<br/>sonnet]
    B --> D[Performance Reviewer<br/>sonnet]
    B --> E[Test Coverage Reviewer<br/>sonnet]
    B --> F[Code Style Reviewer<br/>sonnet]
    B --> G[Architecture Reviewer<br/>sonnet]
    C & D & E & F & G --> H[Synthesize Findings]
    H --> I([Confidence-scored Report])

Each agent returns a structured JSON payload with findings and a confidence score — how certain is the agent that each finding is a real issue, not a false positive. The coordinator synthesizes these into a unified report, weighting findings that multiple agents flagged more heavily.

The confidence scoring is the key innovation. A security finding that only the security reviewer caught gets a base confidence. A security finding that both the security reviewer and the architecture reviewer flagged independently gets boosted confidence. Findings below a configurable threshold are reported but visually de-emphasized.

hookify: The Hook Lifecycle

The hookify plugin ships four commands:

  • /hookify — analyze the current session's patterns and generate a hook
  • /hookify:list — show all active hooks across installed plugins
  • /hookify:edit — modify an existing hook
  • /hookify:delete — remove a hook

The core innovation in hookify is the pattern-to-hook pipeline. When you run /hookify, the agent reviews the current session's conversation history, identifies repeated behaviors (always formatting output as JSON, always checking for secrets before writing files, always running tests after code changes), and generates a hook that automates those behaviors going forward.

This is a plugin that creates hooks. The meta-level is intentional — hookify is how you graduate from manually instructing Claude to do something every session to having it happen automatically.

pr-review-toolkit: Specialization at Scale

Where code-review uses five generalist reviewers, pr-review-toolkit uses six specialists with explicit domain boundaries:

  1. diff-analyzer — structural analysis of what changed
  2. security-scanner — OWASP Top 10 pattern matching
  3. test-quality-reviewer — coverage, edge cases, mock usage
  4. documentation-reviewer — docstrings, README updates, API docs
  5. performance-analyzer — algorithmic complexity, N+1 queries, memory allocations
  6. breaking-change-detector — API contract changes, schema migrations

The breaking-change-detector is the one that gets the most attention in practice. It flags any change that could break downstream consumers of a library or API — changed function signatures, removed fields, altered error codes. In a monorepo with shared libraries, this agent alone justifies installing the plugin.

18.7 The plugin-dev Plugin: Building Plugins With a Plugin

There is a pleasant recursion in the plugin-dev plugin: it is a plugin whose purpose is to help you build plugins. It ships one command, /plugin-dev:create-plugin, and seven skills that command draws on:

  1. plugin-structure — directory layout, required files, optional directories
  2. manifest-authoring — plugin.json fields, versioning, author conventions
  3. command-writing — command markdown format, frontmatter, tool restrictions
  4. agent-design — agent definition structure, role scoping, output format contracts
  5. hook-patterns — event types, TypeScript hook structure, pattern matching
  6. skill-composition — when to use skills vs commands, include syntax
  7. mcp-integration — .mcp.json format, server declaration, tool registration

When you run /plugin-dev:create-plugin, the command gathers information about what you want to build through a structured interview, then draws on the relevant skills to generate a complete plugin scaffold — manifest, directory structure, starter files with inline documentation, and a README explaining how to extend each component.

The plugin-dev plugin is also how Anthropic communicates best practices. When the harness's plugin author guidelines change — new fields in plugin.json, new hook event types, deprecations — the plugin-dev plugin is updated alongside the harness release. Using it to scaffold new plugins means you start from current best practices, not from outdated tutorials.

18.8 Lab: Build a Complete Plugin

The lab builds a plugin called dep-guardian that audits dependencies, enforces a policy against known-bad packages, and hooks into every npm install to warn about newly introduced vulnerabilities. By the end of the lab, the plugin ships a command, an agent, a hook, a skill, and an MCP server.

Step 1: Directory Scaffold

mkdir -p dep-guardian/.claude-plugin
mkdir -p dep-guardian/commands
mkdir -p dep-guardian/agents
mkdir -p dep-guardian/skills
mkdir -p dep-guardian/hooks
mkdir -p dep-guardian/bin

Step 2: The Manifest

Write dep-guardian/.claude-plugin/plugin.json:

{
  "name": "dep-guardian",
  "description": "Dependency audit and policy enforcement with real-time install monitoring",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": {
    "name": "Your Name",
    "email": "you@yourorg.com"
  }
}

Step 3: The Skill — Shared Audit Procedure

Skills are included by multiple commands and agents. Write the audit logic once in dep-guardian/skills/audit-procedure.md:

## Dependency Audit Procedure

Given a project directory, perform the following steps:

1. Detect the primary package manager by checking for:
   - `package.json` → npm/yarn/pnpm
   - `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml` → pip/uv
   - `Cargo.toml` → cargo
   - `go.mod` → go

2. Run the audit command for the detected package manager:
   - npm: `npm audit --json 2>/dev/null`
   - pip: `pip audit --format json 2>/dev/null`
   - cargo: `cargo audit --json 2>/dev/null`
   - go: `govulncheck -json ./... 2>/dev/null`

3. Parse the output. Extract findings with these fields:
   - package_name
   - installed_version
   - vulnerability_id (CVE or GHSA)
   - severity (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW)
   - fixed_in_version (null if no fix available)
   - description (one sentence)

4. Return findings sorted by severity descending, then by package name ascending.

If the audit tool is not available, return an error object:
`{ "error": "audit_tool_missing", "package_manager": "<detected>", "install_command": "<how to install the audit tool>" }`

Step 4: The Agent — Deep Vulnerability Analyst

The skill handles detection. The agent handles interpretation. Write dep-guardian/agents/vuln-analyst.md:

You are a vulnerability analyst specializing in software supply chain security.

You receive the output of a dependency audit as a JSON array of findings. Your task:

1. For each CRITICAL or HIGH finding:
   - Assess whether the vulnerable code path is actually reachable given how this project uses the package
   - Check whether the project version is constrained to a non-vulnerable range
   - Determine the upgrade path: direct upgrade, transitive dependency pin, or no fix available

2. For each package with a CRITICAL finding and no fix available:
   - Research alternative packages that provide equivalent functionality without the vulnerability
   - Provide a concrete migration recommendation with effort estimate (hours)

3. Produce a structured report with three sections:
   - IMMEDIATE ACTION (CRITICAL, fix available)
   - MONITOR (HIGH, fix available or CRITICAL without fix)
   - ACCEPTED RISK (MEDIUM/LOW, or false positives with justification)

Return the report as structured markdown with a summary table at the top.

Step 5: The Command — The User-Facing Entry Point

Write dep-guardian/commands/audit.md:

---
description: Audit project dependencies for vulnerabilities and policy violations
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Write, Agent
---

You are running dep-guardian's full audit workflow.

!include skills/audit-procedure.md

After running the audit procedure:

1. Spawn the vulnerability analyst agent to interpret the findings:
   - subagent_type: "vuln-analyst"
   - Pass the raw audit JSON as the prompt input
   - model: "sonnet"

2. Check the findings against the policy file at `.dep-guardian/blocked-packages.json` if it exists.
   Any installed package appearing in the blocked list is a POLICY VIOLATION regardless of vulnerability status.

3. Write the final report to `dep-guardian-report.md`

4. If any CRITICAL findings exist, exit with a clear summary and the path to the full report.
   If no CRITICAL findings, print a one-line summary: "N findings (H high, M medium, L low). Report: dep-guardian-report.md"

The !include skills/audit-procedure.md directive pulls the skill content inline when the command is assembled. The command stays focused on orchestration; the skill carries the procedure detail.

Step 6: The Hook — Real-Time Install Monitoring

Write dep-guardian/hooks/PreToolUse.ts:

import type { HookContext } from "@anthropic/claude-code";

export async function hook(ctx: HookContext): Promise<void> {
  const { toolName, toolInput } = ctx;

  // Only intercept Bash tool calls
  if (toolName !== "Bash") return;

  const command = toolInput.command as string;

  // Detect npm/pip/cargo install commands
  const isInstall =
    /\bnpm\s+install\b/.test(command) ||
    /\bpip\s+install\b/.test(command) ||
    /\bcargo\s+add\b/.test(command) ||
    /\buv\s+add\b/.test(command);

  if (!isInstall) return;

  // Extract the package name(s) from the install command
  const npmMatch = command.match(/npm\s+install\s+([\w@/.-]+)/);
  const pipMatch = command.match(/pip\s+install\s+([\w-]+)/);
  const cargoMatch = command.match(/cargo\s+add\s+([\w-]+)/);
  const uvMatch = command.match(/uv\s+add\s+([\w-]+)/);

  const packageName =
    (npmMatch?.[1] ?? pipMatch?.[1] ?? cargoMatch?.[1] ?? uvMatch?.[1]);

  if (!packageName) return;

  // Append a security reminder to the tool context
  ctx.appendToToolResult(
    `\n\n[dep-guardian] Package installation detected: ${packageName}\n` +
    `After installation completes, consider running /audit to check for ` +
    `newly introduced vulnerabilities before committing.`
  );
}

This hook fires before every Bash tool call. It checks whether the command is a package install. If it is, it identifies the package name and appends a reminder to the tool result — not blocking the install, just making the reminder visible in the agent's context at the right moment.

Step 7: The MCP Server — Policy API

Write dep-guardian/.mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "dep-guardian-policy": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["./bin/policy-server.js"],
      "description": "Provides tools for reading and updating dep-guardian blocked package policies"
    }
  }
}

The MCP server at bin/policy-server.js exposes two tools:

// policy-server.js (MCP server stub)
import { Server } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/index.js";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js";
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "fs";
import { resolve } from "path";

const POLICY_PATH = resolve(process.cwd(), ".dep-guardian/blocked-packages.json");

const server = new Server({ name: "dep-guardian-policy", version: "1.0.0" }, {
  capabilities: { tools: {} }
});

server.setRequestHandler("tools/list", async () => ({
  tools: [
    {
      name: "get_blocked_packages",
      description: "List all packages blocked by dep-guardian policy",
      inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {} }
    },
    {
      name: "block_package",
      description: "Add a package to the blocked list",
      inputSchema: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
          name: { type: "string", description: "Package name to block" },
          reason: { type: "string", description: "Why this package is blocked" }
        },
        required: ["name", "reason"]
      }
    }
  ]
}));

server.setRequestHandler("tools/call", async (req) => {
  if (req.params.name === "get_blocked_packages") {
    try {
      const policy = JSON.parse(readFileSync(POLICY_PATH, "utf8"));
      return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(policy, null, 2) }] };
    } catch {
      return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "[]" }] };
    }
  }

  if (req.params.name === "block_package") {
    const { name, reason } = req.params.arguments;
    let policy = [];
    try { policy = JSON.parse(readFileSync(POLICY_PATH, "utf8")); } catch {}
    policy.push({ name, reason, blockedAt: new Date().toISOString() });
    writeFileSync(POLICY_PATH, JSON.stringify(policy, null, 2));
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `Blocked ${name}: ${reason}` }] };
  }
});

const transport = new StdioServerTransport();
await server.connect(transport);

With this server active, Claude gains two new tools: get_blocked_packages (read the policy) and block_package (update the policy). When the /audit command finds a CRITICAL vulnerability in a package with no fix available, it can call block_package to add it to the policy — making the block automatic for future installs.

Step 8: Install and Test

# Install the plugin locally (user scope)
/plugin install dep-guardian --local-path ./dep-guardian

# Enable it
/plugin enable dep-guardian

# Run the audit command
/audit

# Verify the hook fires on install
npm install lodash
# Expected: dep-guardian reminder appears in Claude's response

What You Have Built

The completed dep-guardian plugin has:

  • A skill (audit-procedure.md) that encodes audit logic once, reusable anywhere
  • An agent (vuln-analyst.md) with deep domain specialization in vulnerability interpretation
  • A command (audit.md) that orchestrates the skill, agent, and report generation
  • A hook (PreToolUse.ts) that fires automatically on every package install
  • An MCP server (policy-server.js) that extends Claude's tool surface with policy management

This is the full plugin capability surface in one coherent example. Each component earns its place: the skill avoids duplication, the agent handles reasoning-heavy interpretation without bloating the command, the hook is event-driven so users never have to remember to run it, and the MCP server turns policy management into a first-class tool rather than a file-editing exercise.

Distributing the Plugin

To distribute dep-guardian through your organization:

  1. Push the plugin directory to a GitHub repository — either the official marketplace (if you want public distribution) or your internal plugin repository.
  1. Add the repository to known_marketplaces.json in your managed settings:
{
  "your-org-plugins": {
    "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "yourorg/claude-plugins" },
    "installLocation": "/opt/claude/plugins/marketplaces/your-org-plugins"
  }
}
  1. Add dep-guardian@your-org-plugins to allowedChannelPlugins if you are using the allowlist policy.
  1. Users install with /plugin install dep-guardian.

The marketplace model means every developer in your organization gets the same plugin at the same version, with the same policy defaults. When you push a 1.1.0 with an improved hook pattern, users with auto-update enabled get it on their next session start. This is the plugin system's answer to the question of how you maintain consistent tooling across a large engineering organization without asking everyone to manually copy files.

The plugin architecture described in this chapter is the mechanism by which Claude Code evolves beyond what Anthropic ships. Your organization's specific workflows — your code standards, your security policies, your deployment procedures — become first-class capabilities, installable and shareable exactly like the official plugins. The directory structure is simple by design. The manifest is small by design. The distribution system is git-native by design. The complexity lives in what you put in the files, not in the files themselves.

Chapter 19 covers the settings system in full — how user, project, and managed settings layer on top of each other, and how the merge order determines which configuration wins in every conflict.

Chapter 19: MCP Integration — Model Context Protocol

"A harness that talks only to itself is a harness with a ceiling. MCP removes the ceiling."

19.1 MCP Fundamentals

The Model Context Protocol is a standardized wire protocol for connecting AI agents to external capability providers. Where the core tool system — Read, Bash, Edit, Agent — is built directly into Claude Code's runtime, MCP lets any server on the network expose tools and resources to the same interface. The harness calls an MCP tool exactly the same way it calls a built-in tool. The model cannot distinguish between them.

The protocol has three first-class entities:

Tools are callable functions. An MCP server declares a set of tools with names, descriptions, and JSON Schema input specifications. The harness registers these tools alongside its built-ins. When Claude calls one, the harness routes the invocation to the server and passes the result back as a tool result.

Resources are addressable data objects. A resource has a URI (e.g., memory://profiles/db-migrations) and a MIME type. Resources are not tools — they are not called, they are read. A server might expose a database table as a resource, a file in a remote filesystem, or a structured memory record. The harness reads resources on demand; the server streams the content back.

Resource directories are resource containers. A directory entry has mimeType: "inode/directory" and contains child resources or subdirectories. This mirrors the filesystem model: you can list a directory to discover its contents, then read individual resources by URI.

Transports

MCP servers communicate over one of two transports:

stdio — the server is a child process that the harness launches. The harness writes JSON-RPC messages to the process's stdin and reads responses from stdout. This is the default for locally-installed servers. The lifecycle is: harness spawns the process → performs capability handshake → begins exchanging messages → process exits when the harness terminates.

HTTP/SSE — the server is a remote service. The harness connects over HTTP, using Server-Sent Events for streaming server-to-client messages. This is the transport for cloud-hosted MCP servers like mcp.sentry.dev or app.corridor.dev. The handshake is identical to stdio at the protocol level; only the transport layer differs.

graph TD
    H[Claude Code Harness] -->|JSON-RPC via stdin/stdout| S1[Local MCP Server<br/>stdio transport<br/>npx my-mcp-server]
    H -->|JSON-RPC via HTTP/SSE| S2[Remote MCP Server<br/>HTTP transport<br/>mcp.sentry.dev]
    H -->|JSON-RPC via HTTP/SSE| S3[Remote MCP Server<br/>HTTP transport<br/>app.corridor.dev]
    S1 --> T1[tools: db_query, db_schema]
    S1 --> R1[resources: tables/*, views/*]
    S2 --> T2[tools: list_issues, create_comment]
    S3 --> T3[tools: get_context, search_memory]

The MCP Handshake

When the harness connects to an MCP server, regardless of transport, it performs a capability exchange. The server declares what protocol version it supports, what tools it exposes (name, description, input schema), and what resources it can serve (URI patterns, MIME types). The harness registers these into its tool system and resource registry. From this point forward, the server's tools are first-class citizens in every conversation.

The harness caches the capability list at connection time. If a server adds or removes tools while the harness is running, those changes are not visible until an explicit refresh — which is what RefreshMcpTools is for (section 19.5).

19.2 Server Configuration

claude mcp add

The primary command for registering an MCP server:

# stdio server via npx
claude mcp add my-server -e API_KEY=xxx -- npx my-mcp-server

# HTTP server (no auth)
claude mcp add --transport http sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp

# HTTP server with auth header
claude mcp add --transport http corridor https://app.corridor.dev/api/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CORRIDOR_TOKEN}"

# Add from raw JSON spec
claude mcp add-json my-server '{"type":"stdio","command":"npx","args":["my-mcp-server"]}'

# Import servers from Claude Desktop config
claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop

# List registered servers
claude mcp list

# Inspect a specific server
claude mcp get my-server

# Remove a server
claude mcp remove my-server

Server registrations live in your user-level config by default. The harness loads them on every session start.

.mcp.json — Project-Scoped Configuration

For servers that are specific to a project, define them in .mcp.json in the project root. This file is checked into source control, so every engineer who clones the repo gets the same MCP surface:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "project-db": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["./tools/mcp-db-server/index.js"],
      "env": {
        "DATABASE_URL": "${DATABASE_URL}"
      }
    },
    "sentry": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp"
    }
  }
}

The ${DATABASE_URL} syntax performs environment variable interpolation at server launch time. Credentials stay out of the config file while the connection string stays in.

The --mcp-config Flag

For scripted or CI invocations, pass a config file directly:

claude -p "Analyze the error rate spike from yesterday" \
  --mcp-config ./configs/production-mcp.json

The harness connects only to servers in the provided file, ignores user-level config, and enforces a 5-second connection timeout. If a server in the config file is unreachable, the harness logs the failure and continues — it does not abort the session.

--strict-mcp-config

When you want the harness to use only the servers in --mcp-config and ignore everything else — user config, .mcp.json in the project root, all of it:

claude -p "Run security scan" \
  --mcp-config ./scan-servers.json \
  --strict-mcp-config

This is the right pattern for automated pipelines where you need deterministic tool availability. Without --strict-mcp-config, a user's personal MCP servers (memory servers, personal tools, API clients) may show up in an automated run and affect behavior in ways that are hard to reproduce.

enabledMcpjsonServers

In settings.json, you can limit which .mcp.json servers are active:

{
  "enabledMcpjsonServers": ["copilot-mem", "sec-sr-mem", "dt-mem"]
}

Servers not listed are ignored even if they appear in .mcp.json. Use this to opt in explicitly rather than inheriting every server a project defines.

deniedMcpServers

The inverse: list servers that should never be connected regardless of other configuration:

{
  "deniedMcpServers": ["untrusted-experimental-server"]
}

19.3 Tool Passthrough: McpInput and McpOutput

When Claude calls an MCP tool, the harness serializes the call arguments as McpInput and passes them to the server. The server returns McpOutput. These are the two wire types that your server must speak.

export interface McpInput {
  [k: string]: unknown;  // arbitrary JSON passthrough
}

export type McpOutput =
  | string
  | { type: string; [k: string]: unknown }[]
  | { [k: string]: unknown };

McpInput is a plain JSON object. Whatever Claude passes as tool arguments — validated against your tool's JSON Schema — arrives at your server as this object. No special wrapping; the schema is the contract.

McpOutput is deliberately loose. Three forms are valid:

  • Plain string — the most common case. Your tool returns a text result, the harness presents it as a tool result string to Claude.
  • Content block array — for tools that return structured multimedia content (text + images, text + file references). Each element has a type field ("text", "image", "resource").
  • Plain object — for tools that return structured data that Claude should interpret as-is (JSON payloads, key-value results).

In practice, most tools return plain strings. Use content block arrays only when your tool legitimately needs to return mixed content types.

Tool Call Flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Claude (model)
    participant H as Harness
    participant S as MCP Server

    C->>H: tool_use: db_query({"sql": "SELECT ..."})
    H->>H: permission check
    H->>S: JSON-RPC tools/call {name: "db_query", arguments: {...}}
    S->>S: execute query
    S-->>H: {content: [{type: "text", text: "...result..."}]}
    H-->>C: tool_result: "...result..."
    C->>C: incorporate into reasoning

The permission check happens on the harness side before the call reaches the server. If you have configured --allowedTools or an allowList, MCP tool names must appear there to pass through. The naming convention is mcp__<server-name>__<tool-name>:

claude -p "Query the events table" \
  --allowedTools "mcp__project-db__db_query,mcp__project-db__db_schema"

19.4 Resources: ListMcpResources, ReadMcpResource, ReadMcpResourceDir

Resources give MCP servers a way to expose data that does not fit the request-response model of tools. A tool is called; a resource is read. The distinction matters because resources support content negotiation (MIME types), binary data handling, and directory traversal.

Listing Available Resources

export interface ListMcpResourcesInput {
  server?: string;  // filter by server name; omit to list all
}

export type ListMcpResourcesOutput = {
  uri: string;
  name: string;
  mimeType?: string;
  description?: string;
  server: string;
}[];

Calling ListMcpResources with no server argument returns every resource registered across all connected servers. With a server argument, it filters to that server:

// All resources across all servers
const all = await ListMcpResources({});

// Only resources from the memory server
const memResources = await ListMcpResources({ server: "copilot-mem" });
// Returns: [
//   { uri: "memory://profiles/auth-service", name: "Auth Service Profile", mimeType: "application/json", server: "copilot-mem" },
//   { uri: "memory://summaries/daily", name: "Daily Summaries", mimeType: "text/markdown", server: "copilot-mem" },
//   ...
// ]

Reading a Resource

export interface ReadMcpResourceInput {
  server: string;
  uri: string;
}

export interface ReadMcpResourceOutput {
  contents: {
    uri: string;
    mimeType?: string;
    text?: string;
    blobSavedTo?: string;  // binary content saved to file path
  }[];
  error?: string;
}

Text resources come back in the text field. Binary resources — images, PDFs, archives — are saved to a temporary file by the harness and the path appears in blobSavedTo. Your code should check which field is populated:

const result = await ReadMcpResource({
  server: "copilot-mem",
  uri: "memory://profiles/auth-service",
});

if (result.error) {
  throw new Error(`Resource read failed: ${result.error}`);
}

for (const content of result.contents) {
  if (content.text) {
    // Text resource — use directly
    const profile = JSON.parse(content.text);
  } else if (content.blobSavedTo) {
    // Binary resource — file at blobSavedTo path
    const data = await fs.readFile(content.blobSavedTo);
  }
}

Reading a Resource Directory

export interface ReadMcpResourceDirInput {
  server: string;
  uri: string;
}

export interface ReadMcpResourceDirOutput {
  resources: {
    uri: string;
    name: string;
    mimeType?: string;  // "inode/directory" for subdirectories
  }[];
  error?: string;
}

When a resource URI points to a container rather than a leaf, ReadMcpResourceDir returns its children:

const dir = await ReadMcpResourceDir({
  server: "project-db",
  uri: "db://tables",
});

// Returns entries like:
// { uri: "db://tables/users", name: "users", mimeType: "application/json" }
// { uri: "db://tables/events", name: "events", mimeType: "application/json" }
// { uri: "db://tables/archived", name: "archived", mimeType: "inode/directory" }

// Recurse into subdirectory
const archived = await ReadMcpResourceDir({
  server: "project-db",
  uri: "db://tables/archived",
});

The "inode/directory" MIME type signals that an entry is itself a directory. Walk it with another ReadMcpResourceDir call. This recursive pattern is how you traverse a tree of resources programmatically.

19.5 RefreshMcpTools: Hot-Reload Tool Lists

MCP servers can add, remove, or modify their tool definitions while the harness is running. Without a refresh, the harness operates with a stale capability snapshot. RefreshMcpTools forces a re-handshake with one or all servers and updates the tool registry:

export interface RefreshMcpToolsInput {
  server?: string;  // specific server to refresh; omit for all
}

export type RefreshMcpToolsOutput = {
  server: string;
  status: "refreshed" | "error" | "not_connected";
  toolCount?: number;
  added?: string[];
  removed?: string[];
  error?: string;
}[];

The output tells you what changed:

const results = await RefreshMcpTools({});
// Example output:
// [
//   {
//     server: "copilot-mem",
//     status: "refreshed",
//     toolCount: 12,
//     added: ["memory_bulk_import"],
//     removed: [],
//   },
//   {
//     server: "project-db",
//     status: "refreshed",
//     toolCount: 4,
//     added: [],
//     removed: ["db_legacy_query"],
//   },
//   {
//     server: "sentry",
//     status: "error",
//     error: "Connection timeout after 5000ms",
//   }
// ]

When to Refresh

The common case for RefreshMcpTools is during development of an MCP server. You are iterating on tool definitions — adding parameters, changing descriptions, adding new tools — and you want those changes to be visible without restarting the harness.

In production, the scenario is server-side deployments. If your MCP server is a deployed service that receives updates, the harness will not see new tools until a refresh. For long-running harness sessions (daemons, overnight runs), build in periodic refreshes or trigger them when your deployment pipeline signals a server update.

Tracking Added and Removed Tools

The added and removed arrays in the output are the diff since the last refresh. If you are building a harness that needs to adapt to capability changes — for example, a tool router that dispatches tasks differently depending on what capabilities are available — these diffs are how you detect and react:

const refreshResults = await RefreshMcpTools({ server: "my-server" });

const serverResult = refreshResults.find(r => r.server === "my-server");
if (serverResult?.added?.includes("db_bulk_export")) {
  // New bulk export tool available — update routing logic
  routingTable.set("bulk-export", "mcp__my-server__db_bulk_export");
}
if (serverResult?.removed?.includes("db_legacy_query")) {
  // Remove the old fallback path
  routingTable.delete("legacy-query");
}

19.6 OAuth Flow: RFC 9728 Discovery and Step-Up Authorization

HTTP MCP servers that require authentication use OAuth 2.0. The harness implements OAuth client logic including discovery, token acquisition, and refresh. The design follows RFC 9728 for server metadata discovery and the OAuth 2.0 flow for interactive authorization.

Discovery

When the harness connects to an HTTP MCP server, it first fetches the server's OAuth metadata at the well-known endpoint:

GET https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server

The metadata document declares the authorization endpoint, token endpoint, supported scopes, and PKCE requirements. The harness uses this to construct the authorization flow without any server-specific hardcoding.

Initial Authorization

For servers that require auth, claude mcp login initiates the flow:

claude mcp login sentry

The harness opens a browser window to the server's authorization URL with a PKCE code challenge, waits for the redirect, exchanges the code for tokens, and stores the access token and refresh token in the system keychain. On subsequent connections, the harness attaches the access token as a Bearer header automatically.

Step-Up Authorization

Some MCP servers grant minimal-scope tokens on initial login but require additional consent for sensitive operations. This is expressed through HTTP 403 responses with insufficient_scope in the WWW-Authenticate header:

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope",
  scope="memory:read memory:write",
  resource="https://mcp.example.com"

When the harness receives this response, it detects the insufficient_scope error and automatically initiates a step-up authorization. The flow is identical to the initial flow, but the authorization request includes the required scope. The user sees a browser prompt asking for the additional consent. Once granted, the harness retries the original tool call with the upgraded token.

From Claude's perspective, this is invisible. The tool call succeeded, just with a brief delay while the user completed the consent prompt. If the user declines step-up authorization, the tool call returns an error that Claude sees as a standard tool failure.

Token Refresh

Access tokens expire. The harness manages refresh automatically: when an API call returns 401 Unauthorized, the harness uses the stored refresh token to acquire a new access token and retries the call. If the refresh token itself is expired or revoked, the harness falls back to the full authorization flow.

# Logout (clears stored tokens)
claude mcp logout sentry

# Re-login to refresh credentials
claude mcp login sentry

19.7 _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"]: Override the 500K Limit

By default, MCP tool results are capped at a size that prevents runaway context growth. Starting in v2.1.91, tools can override this limit by returning the _meta annotation field with a maxResultSizeChars value up to 500,000 characters:

// In your MCP server, when returning large results:
return {
  content: [
    {
      type: "text",
      text: largeResultString,
    }
  ],
  _meta: {
    "anthropic/maxResultSizeChars": 500000
  }
};

This is an opt-in per-call declaration, not a server-level setting. The server signals "I know this result is large; I am intentionally returning it at this size." Without the annotation, large results are truncated.

When to Use This

The annotation exists for tools that legitimately produce large outputs: a full database dump, a complete log file, a compiled asset. The 500K character limit is approximately 125,000 tokens — well above what most Claude models can effectively process in a single context window. Use this judiciously.

The anti-pattern is using maxResultSizeChars as a workaround for poorly designed tools. If your tool regularly hits the default limit, the better fix is pagination — add a cursor parameter and return results in chunks — rather than raising the cap. A tool that returns 400K characters of log output is probably not serving Claude well; a tool that returns the last 100 lines with a continuation cursor is.

Tool descriptions are also relevant here: v2.1.92 caps tool descriptions at 2KB. If you are writing MCP tool descriptions that approach that limit, you are almost certainly over-explaining. Keep descriptions under 500 characters; the JSON Schema handles the structural specification.

19.8 MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true: Skip Connection Wait in -p Mode

When Claude Code runs in non-interactive mode (-p), it waits for all configured MCP servers to connect before processing the prompt. This is the safe default — you want your tools available when the prompt executes — but it adds latency proportional to the number of configured servers.

For pipelines where you know which servers you need, or where some servers are optional for the current task, set MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true:

MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true claude -p "Summarize the last 24 hours of activity" \
  --mcp-config ./minimal-servers.json

With this flag, the harness starts processing the prompt immediately without waiting for server connections to complete. Servers connect in the background. If a tool call arrives before the target server has connected, the call is queued until the connection is ready, or fails with a timeout error if the server never connects.

This is particularly useful in CI environments where startup latency compounds across many pipeline steps. The combination of --mcp-config (to specify exactly which servers you need), --strict-mcp-config (to ignore everything else), and MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true (to not wait for connections) gives you a tight, fast-starting harness invocation.

The --mcp-config timeout is bounded at 5 seconds — servers that have not connected within 5 seconds of being configured are considered failed connections and their tools are unavailable for that run.

19.9 claude mcp serve: Expose Claude Code as an MCP Server

The harness can expose itself as an MCP server:

# Serve in foreground (useful for development/testing)
claude mcp serve

# Serve as background daemon
claude mcp serve -d

This makes Claude Code's tools — Read, Bash, Edit, Glob, Grep, Agent, and all configured MCP tools — available to any MCP client that connects. The use case is composing Claude Code into larger systems: a parent orchestrator that speaks MCP can delegate to a Claude Code instance as one of its capability providers.

The pattern appears in multi-tier architectures where a lightweight routing agent dispatches work to specialized worker agents, each of which is a Claude Code instance serving MCP. The router does not know or care that it is talking to Claude Code; from its perspective, it is calling MCP tools that happen to be backed by a full agentic harness.

graph TD
    O[Orchestrator Agent<br/>lightweight MCP client] -->|MCP tools/call| W1[Claude Code Worker 1<br/>claude mcp serve<br/>tools: filesystem + shell]
    O -->|MCP tools/call| W2[Claude Code Worker 2<br/>claude mcp serve<br/>tools: web + research]
    O -->|MCP tools/call| W3[Claude Code Worker 3<br/>claude mcp serve<br/>tools: database + analytics]
    W1 --> FS[Filesystem + Git]
    W2 --> WEB[Web APIs]
    W3 --> DB[Database]

In this topology, the orchestrator manages task routing and result synthesis while each Claude Code worker handles a domain-specific subset of the work. The workers are independently restartable, replaceable, and upgradeable without touching the orchestrator.

19.10 Real MCP Servers: copilot-mem at Scale

The copilot-mem memory server is a concrete example of what production MCP looks like at scale. At the time of writing:
