  • 1,035 total memories across three types: episodic (26), procedural (324), semantic (685)
  • By category: fact (350), workflow (228), project (231), preference (30), decision (26), architecture (33), tech_insight (21), workflow_recipe (24), bug_recipe (15), and several smaller categories
  • 14 project profiles — structured summaries of each active project's goals, architecture, and current status
  • 2,627 knowledge links — semantic edges connecting related memories
  • 35MB SQLite database with full-text search
  • 119 daily summaries — auto-generated end-of-day digests

This memory server exposes 12 MCP tools including memory_search, memory_store, memory_recall_context, memory_get_profile, and memory_list_recent. It exposes resources under memory:// URIs: individual memory records, daily summaries, and project profiles.

The scale numbers illustrate why the MCP resource model matters. A memory server with 1,035 entries cannot be loaded into context wholesale — that would consume a significant fraction of a model's context window before any actual work begins. The resource model solves this: the harness can ListMcpResources to see what exists, read specific resources by URI when needed, and search via tool calls to find relevant memories. The data lives in the server; only what is needed flows into context.

Tool Description Quality at Scale

At 12 tools and 35MB of backing data, description quality becomes a navigation problem. Claude uses tool descriptions to decide which tool to call for a given intent. Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause the model to call the wrong tool, waste a round trip, and have to recover. For the memory server, the tool descriptions are tuned to avoid overlap:

  • memory_search — full-text semantic search, returns ranked results
  • memory_recall_context — retrieves memories most relevant to the current task context, no explicit query needed
  • memory_store — creates a new memory record
  • memory_get_profile — retrieves a specific project profile by name

The distinction between memory_search (explicit query) and memory_recall_context (implicit, based on current context) is one that required iteration to get right. The first version described both as "retrieves relevant memories," which caused consistent misrouting. Concrete, specific descriptions at the level of how the tool is invoked — not just what it returns — are what make MCP tools usable at scale.

19.11 Lab: Build an MCP Server Exposing a Database

This lab builds a complete MCP server that exposes a SQLite database as both tools (for querying) and resources (for schema and metadata). The server is written in Node.js using the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk package. By the end, you will be able to point Claude Code at it and have Claude query and analyze the database using natural language.

Setup

mkdir mcp-db-server && cd mcp-db-server
npm init -y
npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk better-sqlite3
npm install --save-dev @types/better-sqlite3 typescript tsx

tsconfig.json:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "outDir": "./dist"
  }
}

The Server

src/index.ts:

import { Server } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/index.js";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js";
import {
  CallToolRequestSchema,
  ListResourcesRequestSchema,
  ListToolsRequestSchema,
  ReadResourceRequestSchema,
} from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/types.js";
import Database from "better-sqlite3";
import { join } from "path";

const DB_PATH = process.env.DATABASE_PATH ?? join(process.cwd(), "data.db");

// Initialize database with sample data if it doesn't exist
function initDb(db: Database.Database): void {
  db.exec(`
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS events (
      id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
      name TEXT NOT NULL,
      occurred_at TEXT NOT NULL,
      severity TEXT CHECK(severity IN ('low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical')),
      payload TEXT
    );

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
      id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
      email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
      created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
      last_seen TEXT
    );
  `);

  const eventCount = (db.prepare("SELECT COUNT(*) as c FROM events").get() as { c: number }).c;
  if (eventCount === 0) {
    const insert = db.prepare(
      "INSERT INTO events (name, occurred_at, severity, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)"
    );
    insert.run("user.login", "2026-07-28T08:00:00Z", "low", '{"user_id": 1}');
    insert.run("auth.failure", "2026-07-28T08:05:00Z", "high", '{"user_id": null, "ip": "10.0.0.1"}');
    insert.run("db.query_slow", "2026-07-28T08:10:00Z", "medium", '{"duration_ms": 4200}');
    insert.run("deploy.complete", "2026-07-28T09:00:00Z", "low", '{"version": "2.1.91"}');
    insert.run("auth.failure", "2026-07-28T09:05:00Z", "critical", '{"user_id": null, "ip": "10.0.0.1", "attempts": 50}');
  }
}

function createServer(db: Database.Database): Server {
  const server = new Server(
    { name: "mcp-db-server", version: "1.0.0" },
    {
      capabilities: {
        tools: {},
        resources: {},
      },
    }
  );

  // ── List tools ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  server.setRequestHandler(ListToolsRequestSchema, async () => ({
    tools: [
      {
        name: "db_query",
        description:
          "Execute a read-only SQL SELECT query against the database. Returns rows as JSON.",
        inputSchema: {
          type: "object",
          properties: {
            sql: {
              type: "string",
              description: "The SQL SELECT query to execute. Only SELECT is permitted.",
            },
            limit: {
              type: "number",
              description: "Maximum rows to return (default 100, max 1000).",
            },
          },
          required: ["sql"],
        },
      },
      {
        name: "db_schema",
        description:
          "Returns the schema (CREATE TABLE statements) for all tables in the database.",
        inputSchema: {
          type: "object",
          properties: {},
        },
      },
      {
        name: "db_table_stats",
        description: "Returns row count and size estimate for each table.",
        inputSchema: {
          type: "object",
          properties: {
            table: {
              type: "string",
              description: "Specific table name (optional — omit for all tables).",
            },
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  }));

  // ── Handle tool calls ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  server.setRequestHandler(CallToolRequestSchema, async (request) => {
    const { name, arguments: args } = request.params;

    if (name === "db_query") {
      const sql = (args?.sql as string) ?? "";
      const limit = Math.min((args?.limit as number) ?? 100, 1000);

      // Enforce read-only: reject anything that isn't SELECT
      const normalized = sql.trim().toUpperCase();
      if (!normalized.startsWith("SELECT")) {
        return {
          content: [{ type: "text", text: "Error: only SELECT queries are permitted." }],
          isError: true,
        };
      }

      try {
        const limitedSql = `SELECT * FROM (${sql}) LIMIT ${limit}`;
        const rows = db.prepare(limitedSql).all();
        return {
          content: [
            {
              type: "text",
              text: JSON.stringify(rows, null, 2),
            },
          ],
        };
      } catch (err) {
        return {
          content: [{ type: "text", text: `Query error: ${(err as Error).message}` }],
          isError: true,
        };
      }
    }

    if (name === "db_schema") {
      const rows = db
        .prepare(
          `SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'`
        )
        .all() as { name: string; sql: string }[];

      const schema = rows.map((r) => r.sql).join("\n\n");
      return {
        content: [{ type: "text", text: schema }],
      };
    }

    if (name === "db_table_stats") {
      const targetTable = args?.table as string | undefined;

      const tables = targetTable
        ? [targetTable]
        : (
            db
              .prepare(
                `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'`
              )
              .all() as { name: string }[]
          ).map((r) => r.name);

      const stats = tables.map((t) => {
        const count = (
          db.prepare(`SELECT COUNT(*) as c FROM "${t}"`).get() as { c: number }
        ).c;
        return { table: t, row_count: count };
      });

      return {
        content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(stats, null, 2) }],
      };
    }

    return {
      content: [{ type: "text", text: `Unknown tool: ${name}` }],
      isError: true,
    };
  });

  // ── List resources ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  server.setRequestHandler(ListResourcesRequestSchema, async () => {
    const tables = (
      db
        .prepare(
          `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'`
        )
        .all() as { name: string }[]
    ).map((r) => r.name);

    const resources = [
      // Schema root directory
      {
        uri: "db://schema",
        name: "Schema Overview",
        mimeType: "application/json",
        description: "Database schema summary with all table definitions.",
      },
      // Per-table resources
      ...tables.map((t) => ({
        uri: `db://tables/${t}`,
        name: `Table: ${t}`,
        mimeType: "application/json",
        description: `Column definitions and sample rows from ${t}.`,
      })),
    ];

    return { resources };
  });

  // ── Read resource ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  server.setRequestHandler(ReadResourceRequestSchema, async (request) => {
    const { uri } = request.params;

    if (uri === "db://schema") {
      const tables = (
        db
          .prepare(
            `SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'`
          )
          .all() as { name: string; sql: string }[]
      );

      const schema: Record<string, unknown> = {};
      for (const t of tables) {
        const cols = db.prepare(`PRAGMA table_info("${t.name}")`).all();
        schema[t.name] = { definition: t.sql, columns: cols };
      }

      return {
        contents: [
          {
            uri,
            mimeType: "application/json",
            text: JSON.stringify(schema, null, 2),
          },
        ],
      };
    }

    const tableMatch = uri.match(/^db:\/\/tables\/(\w+)$/);
    if (tableMatch) {
      const tableName = tableMatch[1];

      const columns = db.prepare(`PRAGMA table_info("${tableName}")`).all();
      const sample = db.prepare(`SELECT * FROM "${tableName}" LIMIT 5`).all();
      const count = (
        db.prepare(`SELECT COUNT(*) as c FROM "${tableName}"`).get() as { c: number }
      ).c;

      const payload = { table: tableName, row_count: count, columns, sample_rows: sample };

      return {
        contents: [
          {
            uri,
            mimeType: "application/json",
            text: JSON.stringify(payload, null, 2),
          },
        ],
      };
    }

    return {
      contents: [],
      error: `Unknown resource URI: ${uri}`,
    };
  });

  return server;
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const db = new Database(DB_PATH);
  initDb(db);

  const server = createServer(db);
  const transport = new StdioServerTransport();

  await server.connect(transport);

  // Keep alive until stdin closes
  process.stdin.resume();
  process.on("SIGINT", () => {
    db.close();
    process.exit(0);
  });
}

main().catch((err) => {
  process.stderr.write(`Fatal: ${err.message}\n`);
  process.exit(1);
});

Register and Test

# Build
npx tsc

# Register with Claude Code
claude mcp add db-server -e DATABASE_PATH="$(pwd)/data.db" -- node dist/index.js

# Verify it registered
claude mcp get db-server

# Open a session and try it
claude

In the session:

> What tables are in the database and how many rows does each have?
> Show me all high and critical severity events from the last hour
> Are there any patterns in the auth failures? Group by IP and count them

Claude will call db_schema to understand the structure, then db_query with appropriate SELECT statements, and db_table_stats for the row counts. The read-only enforcement on the server side means Claude cannot accidentally drop a table or modify data regardless of what the prompt contains.

Verify Resource Access

# List resources (in a harness prompt)
> List all resources available from the db-server MCP server

# Read a specific resource
> Read the resource at db://tables/events from the db-server

The db://tables/events resource returns column definitions and sample rows — useful for Claude to understand the data shape before constructing queries.

Extending the Server

The server above handles the core patterns. From here you can extend it:

Add pagination — add a cursor parameter to db_query that encodes the last-seen id. Return a next_cursor in the result when more rows are available. This is the correct alternative to raising maxResultSizeChars.

Add write tools with confirmation — expose db_execute for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, but require an explain: string parameter that forces the caller to articulate what the change will do. Log all write operations to an audit table.

Add streaming resources — for tables with millions of rows, expose paginated resources: db://tables/events/page/1, db://tables/events/page/2. The ReadMcpResourceDir call on db://tables/events returns the page listing; individual page reads return data in chunks.

Expose views as resources — create SQL views for common analytical queries (daily event counts, top error codes, user activity summaries) and expose them as resources. Claude can read a pre-computed view for summarization tasks instead of constructing ad hoc queries.

Summary

MCP is the integration layer that turns Claude Code from a self-contained harness into a network-connected capability aggregator. The key behaviors to internalize:

  • Tools and resources are two distinct models: tools are called, resources are read. Choose based on whether the data is request-response or addressable content.
  • The _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] annotation is an opt-in, per-call override for large results — not a substitute for pagination.
  • RefreshMcpTools is how you pick up server-side capability changes without restarting the harness. Build refresh into your deployment pipeline.
  • OAuth step-up is transparent to Claude — the harness handles consent prompts and token refresh automatically.
  • --strict-mcp-config + MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true is the production recipe for fast, deterministic pipeline invocations.
  • claude mcp serve exposes Claude Code as an MCP server, enabling multi-tier architectures where Claude Code instances are workers behind a routing orchestrator.
  • At scale (1,000+ memories, 14 project profiles), the resource model's value becomes concrete: data lives in the server, context contains only what is needed.

The database lab is a complete pattern that covers the full MCP lifecycle: capability declaration, tool enforcement (read-only), resource hierarchy, error handling, and server registration. The same structure — tools for operations, resources for schema and data discovery — applies to any backend you want to expose to Claude.

In Chapter 20, we build on this by examining how to manage context growth in long-running harness sessions: when to prune conversation history, how to use MCP resources as an external memory tier, and the patterns that keep a harness sharp through multi-hour agentic runs.

Next: Chapter 20: Context Management in Long-Running Sessions

Part V: Advanced Runtime Mechanics

Chapter 20: Context Window Management

"The context window is not infinite scratch space. It is a finite, metered resource — and every token you waste is a token you cannot use for reasoning."

Every tool call appended to the conversation history, every file read, every subagent prompt injected — it all accumulates. At some point the harness hits a wall: the model can no longer fit the entire conversation into a single API call. How the harness handles that wall — gracefully compressing, preserving critical state, serving from cache, paginating large files — determines whether long-running agents degrade silently or crash loudly.

This chapter is about the economics of context. Tokens cost money in both direct API charges and latency. An agent that burns 800K input tokens on a refactoring task costs four to eight times more than one that achieves the same result in 200K tokens. More importantly, context mismanagement is a source of agent failures that look like model hallucinations but are actually information loss from poor window hygiene.

20.1 Token Budgets

The harness exposes five environment variables that control token allocation:

CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=1000000   # 1M total context window
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=128000     # 128K max output per turn
MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=100000               # 100K for extended thinking
CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_THRESHOLD_MINUTES=180   # idle session timeout
CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_TOKEN_THRESHOLD=500000  # idle threshold at high token usage

These are not suggestions — they are hard caps enforced by the harness before API calls go out.

CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS

The total context window available to the conversation, including system prompt, all prior messages, tool results, and the pending response. The default is 1,000,000 tokens — the maximum supported by claude-sonnet-4-x and claude-opus-4-x as of v2.1.220.

Setting this lower is a deliberate cost-control mechanism. A team running hundreds of parallel CI agents might cap at 200,000 tokens per agent to stay within a daily token budget. The harness respects the cap and triggers compression before the conversation reaches it.

# CI budget: restrict agent context to control spend
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=200000 claude -p "Review this PR diff..."

The relationship between context size and API cost is linear on input tokens but asymmetric on cache behavior — a point covered in section 20.4. Blindly lowering this value without understanding the cache implications can increase costs rather than reduce them.

CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS

The maximum tokens Claude can produce in a single response. The default of 128,000 tokens accommodates large code generation tasks — writing a complete module, generating a migration, producing a detailed report. Most individual turns consume far less.

The practical implication: if you are building a harness that needs deterministic output sizes, this cap is your primary lever. For agents that write to structured output formats (JSON, markdown tables), staying under 128K output tokens is rarely a concern. For agents that generate large files in a single turn, it becomes a real constraint to design around.

MAX_THINKING_TOKENS

Extended thinking — the model's internal reasoning scratchpad before producing its visible response — has its own budget. 100,000 tokens buys significant deliberation before the model commits to output. For tasks like architecture decisions or complex security analysis, this budget is what separates a surface-level answer from one that has actually worked through the edge cases.

Reducing this for routine tasks trades reasoning depth for speed and cost:

# Fast-path for simple tasks — no deep thinking needed
MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=10000 claude -p "Add type hints to this function..."

Idle Thresholds

CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_THRESHOLD_MINUTES triggers session cleanup after 180 minutes of inactivity. CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_TOKEN_THRESHOLD adds a secondary trigger: if the session has accumulated over 500K tokens and is idle, cleanup happens sooner. Both exist to prevent long-lived sessions from holding expensive context indefinitely.

In practice, these thresholds interact with the PreCompact hook (section 20.3). If your agent has critical state that must survive a cleanup event, the hook is your preservation mechanism.

20.2 Automatic Compression

When the conversation approaches CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS, the harness does not crash — it compresses. The compression mechanism is automatic and predictable once you understand it.

How Compression Works

The harness monitors the running token count of the conversation. As it approaches the configured limit (the threshold is roughly 85–90% of the cap), it triggers an autocompact operation:

flowchart TD
    A[Conversation Growing] --> B{Near Token Cap?}
    B -->|No| C[Continue normally]
    B -->|Yes| D[Fire PreCompact hook]
    D --> E[Inject hook output into summary]
    E --> F[Summarize prior messages]
    F --> G[Discard old messages]
    G --> H[Retain: summary + recent N messages]
    H --> I[Continue with compressed context]

The summarization is done by a model call — the harness passes the prior conversation to Claude and asks for a condensed summary that preserves the essential thread: what was asked, what was found, what decisions were made, what state the session is in. This summary replaces the original messages.

The result: the conversation continues carrying forward a compact summary of everything that came before, plus the most recent messages (which are preserved verbatim to maintain coherence around the current task). The model can still reason about prior work through the summary, but the raw detail is gone.

What This Means in Practice

Compression is lossy. A summary of a 100-message investigation preserves the conclusions but discards the intermediate reasoning, the exact file contents that were read, the specific error messages that were encountered. If your agent needs to refer back to something read 80 messages ago, that detail may no longer be in the compressed context.

This has a direct implication for agent design: information that must survive compression must be written to persistent storage, not left in the conversation. The pattern seen in mature harness implementations is to write state files after important discoveries:

# After finding a critical architectural detail, write it out
echo '{"finding": "auth module uses RS256 only in production env", "file": "src/auth/config.py", "line": 47}' \
  >> ~/.claude/projects/myapp/state/session-$(date +%s).json

The PreCompact hook, covered next, is the mechanism for ensuring that state survives the compression boundary.

20.3 The PreCompact Hook

The PreCompact hook fires immediately before the harness executes autocompaction. It is the last moment at which your session's in-memory context is fully intact. The hook's stdout is injected verbatim into the compaction summary — whatever you write to stdout becomes part of the compressed context that carries forward into the next phase of the session.

This is not a convenience feature. For long-running agents — security scanners, codebase refactors, multi-day workflows — the PreCompact hook is what separates graceful continuation from a reset to zero.

Hook Location and Registration

// .claude/settings.json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreCompact": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "~/.claude/hooks/pre-compact.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The matcher is empty — PreCompact fires unconditionally, not based on tool name or content matching.

Real Implementation

Here is a production PreCompact hook for a long-running security audit agent. It reads the current state file, injects its content as critical context, and instructs the model on how to recover after compaction:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

STATE_DIR="${HOME}/.claude/projects/-Users-user-project/state"
MAX_STATE_CHARS=4000
INPUT=$(cat 2>/dev/null || true)

# Find the most recently written state file
LATEST_FILE=$(find "${STATE_DIR}" -name "*.json" -newer /dev/null \
  -exec ls -t {} + 2>/dev/null | head -1)

if [[ -z "${LATEST_FILE}" ]]; then
  # No state file — nothing to preserve
  exit 0
fi

STATE_CONTENT=$(head -c "${MAX_STATE_CHARS}" "${LATEST_FILE}")
DOMAIN=$(grep '"domain"' "${LATEST_FILE}" | head -1 \
  | sed 's/.*"domain"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/')

cat << EOF
CRITICAL — Preserve the following ${DOMAIN} session state verbatim:
${STATE_CONTENT}

After compaction resumes:
1. Read the full state file at ${LATEST_FILE}
2. Verify state freshness (check the "timestamp" field) before acting
3. Resume from the recovered state — do not restart from scratch
4. If the state is stale (>30 minutes), re-verify key findings before continuing
EOF

The MAX_STATE_CHARS=4000 limit is deliberate. The hook output is injected into the compressed summary, and that summary itself has a token budget. Injecting 50,000 characters of state would consume the summary budget and make the compression useless. Four thousand characters — roughly two dense pages of text — is enough to preserve the essential session state: what phase the work is in, what findings have been confirmed, which files have been processed, and where to resume.

Designing State Files for PreCompact

The hook is only as good as the state files it reads. State files should capture:

  • Phase and progress: what stage of the workflow is active, how far it has progressed
  • Confirmed findings: discoveries that took expensive work to reach and should not be discarded
  • Work completed: files already processed, so the agent does not re-process them after compression
  • Decision trail: key choices made during the session that affect subsequent steps
{
  "domain": "security-audit",
  "timestamp": "2026-07-28T14:32:11Z",
  "phase": "deep-analysis",
  "progress": {"files_scanned": 147, "files_total": 312},
  "confirmed_findings": [
    {"file": "src/auth/jwt.py", "line": 84, "severity": "CRITICAL", "cwe": "CWE-347"}
  ],
  "processed_files": ["src/auth/jwt.py", "src/auth/session.py"],
  "next_target": "src/api/middleware.py"
}

The agent writes this file after each completed scan phase. The PreCompact hook reads it and ensures the model knows where it was and what it found, even after all the intermediate conversation messages have been compressed away.

20.4 Prompt Cache

The Anthropic API supports prompt caching: content that appears at the beginning of a request can be stored server-side and served on subsequent requests without re-processing. The harness exploits this aggressively.

Cache Mechanics

Cache entries live for 5 minutes at the ephemeral_5m tier. There is also a longer-lived ephemeral_1h tier for content that benefits from extended reuse. Cached tokens are not re-charged as input tokens — they are served at a fraction of the standard input token rate.

The AgentOutput.usage struct exposes the cache accounting:

usage: {
  input_tokens: number;                    // tokens processed fresh (billed at full rate)
  output_tokens: number;                   // tokens generated
  cache_creation_input_tokens: number | null;  // tokens written to cache (billed at creation rate)
  cache_read_input_tokens: number | null;      // tokens served from cache (billed at cache rate)
  cache_creation: {
    ephemeral_1h_input_tokens: number;     // tokens in 1-hour cache tier
    ephemeral_5m_input_tokens: number;     // tokens in 5-minute cache tier
  } | null;
}

A healthy multi-turn session shows cache_read_input_tokens growing across turns as the system prompt is served from cache repeatedly. A session with poor cache utilization shows input_tokens dominating every turn.

What Gets Cached

The system prompt is the primary cache target. It is static across turns — the base instructions, tool descriptions, CLAUDE.md content, and project context do not change between messages. The harness structures the conversation so that system prompt content appears at the beginning of every request, maximizing cache hit probability.

In a 20-turn session, the system prompt (say, 15,000 tokens) would normally cost 300,000 input tokens across all turns. With cache serving it after the first turn, 19 of those turns serve from cache. At typical pricing, this reduces the system prompt cost by roughly 90%.

Cache Invalidation Pitfalls

The 5-minute TTL means cache entries expire during idle time. Version 2.1.92 added a footer hint to Pro users when the prompt cache expires — a signal that the next turn will be billed at full input token rates.

Two bugs fixed in v2.1.89 are worth understanding because they represent patterns to avoid:

Tool schema byte changes invalidate cache. The system prompt includes tool descriptions serialized as JSON. If any byte in the tool descriptions changes between turns — even formatting — the cache hash changes and the cache misses. In long sessions, if tool schemas are being dynamically rebuilt on every turn (e.g., reading MCP tool schemas from a live server that returns slightly different JSON), the cache will never hit. Keep tool schemas stable across turns.

Nested CLAUDE.md re-injection. Also fixed in v2.1.89: nested CLAUDE.md files (project subdirectories with their own CLAUDE.md) were being re-injected dozens of times in long sessions. Each re-injection produced slightly different assembled system prompts, breaking cache coherence. The fix ensures CLAUDE.md content is assembled once at startup and not reassembled on subsequent turns.

--exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections

This flag shifts dynamic, per-machine content out of the system prompt and into the first user message:

claude --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections ...

By default, the system prompt includes:

  • Current working directory
  • Environment variables
  • Memory file paths
  • Git status

These fields are machine-specific. Two users running the same harness on different machines produce different system prompts, which means their cache entries cannot be shared — each user warms a separate cache. In multi-user deployments, this multiplies the cache warming cost proportionally to the number of users.

With --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections, the system prompt becomes static content that is identical across all users of the same project. Dynamic content moves to the first user message, which is not cached. The tradeoff: the first message is slightly larger, but all subsequent turns hit a shared system prompt cache.

This flag only applies when using the default system prompt. If you pass --system-prompt, the flag is ignored — you are responsible for managing what goes in your custom prompt.

20.5 Read Deduplication

Reading the same file twice in the same session is wasteful — both in token cost and in API call overhead. The harness eliminates redundant reads through a session-level deduplication mechanism.

file_unchanged Response

When the Read tool is called for a file that has already been read in the current session and the file has not been modified since, the harness returns a file_unchanged response type rather than the full content:

{
  "type": "file_unchanged",
  "file_path": "/Users/user/project/src/auth/session.py",
  "source": "session_cache"
}

The model receives a compact acknowledgment rather than thousands of tokens of file content. For a 500-line Python file read three times in a session, deduplication saves roughly 6,000 tokens across the second and third reads.

source: "seeded"

A related variant appears for files injected at session startup — CLAUDE.md files, global memory files, any content the harness seeds into the initial context:

{
  "type": "file_unchanged",
  "file_path": "/Users/user/project/CLAUDE.md",
  "source": "seeded"
}

source: "seeded" means the file matched a startup-seeded entry. The model already has the content from the system prompt injection; the harness does not send it again.

Subagent Deduplication Isolation

Deduplication is session-scoped. Subagents start fresh sessions — they do not inherit the parent's deduplication state. A parent agent that has already read src/auth/session.py and a subagent reading the same file are operating in different sessions; the subagent pays the full token cost.

This is intentional. Subagent isolation means the parent cannot leak file contents to the subagent except through explicit prompt injection. The deduplication boundary is the session boundary.

For harness authors building Agent prompts: if a subagent needs file content that the parent has already read, inject it into the subagent's prompt directly rather than expecting the subagent to re-read and paying the read tool cost again.

20.6 Token Cap Auto-Pagination

Files that exceed the token cap for a single Read call are automatically paginated. The harness returns the first page of content with a signal indicating the response was truncated.

The truncatedByTokenCap Flag

{
  "type": "text",
  "content": "... first N lines of the file ...",
  "truncatedByTokenCap": true
}

truncatedByTokenCap: true is a programmatic signal, not just a display artifact. It means:

  1. The content is the first page only
  2. More content exists that was not returned
  3. A second Read call with offset parameter will return the next page

The harness auto-paginates large files rather than refusing to read them or silently truncating without signaling. For consumers of the Read tool output — whether the model itself or a tool result parser in a custom harness — the flag is the contract that says "this is partial."

Implications for Harness Design

If you are building a custom harness that uses file reading, respect truncatedByTokenCap as a first-class signal:

async function readFullFile(path: string): Promise<string> {
  const chunks: string[] = [];
  let offset = 0;

  while (true) {
    const result = await readTool({ file_path: path, offset, limit: 2000 });
    chunks.push(result.content);

    if (!result.truncatedByTokenCap) {
      break;
    }
    offset += 2000;
  }

  return chunks.join("\n");
}

In the Claude Code harness itself, the model handles pagination organically — it sees the truncatedByTokenCap signal in the tool result and issues a follow-up Read call with the appropriate offset. This is the right behavior; building pagination logic into the model prompt (by noting in the system prompt that large files are paginated and showing offset examples) makes it explicit.

20.7 Autocompact Thrash Loop Prevention

A subtle failure mode was fixed in Claude Code v2.1.89: the autocompact thrash loop. Understanding it is important both for operating existing harnesses and for preventing the same failure in custom implementations.

The Failure Pattern

The thrash loop occurs when:

  1. The conversation approaches the token cap and autocompaction fires
  2. The session resumes, but the combination of system prompt + prior state immediately fills context again
  3. Autocompaction fires again
  4. The session refills again immediately
  5. Repeat indefinitely, burning API calls on compaction overhead with no productive work

This can happen in sessions with very large system prompts (heavy CLAUDE.md, many MCP tool schemas) combined with pre-compaction state injection (large PreCompact hook output). After compression, the static overhead — system prompt + hook injection — may itself consume most of the configured context budget, leaving insufficient space for actual work.

The Fix

From the v2.1.89 CHANGELOG:

"Fixed autocompact thrash loop — now detects when context refills to the limit immediately after compacting three times in a row and stops with an actionable error instead of burning API calls"

The harness now tracks consecutive recompacts. After three consecutive compressions without meaningful productive conversation between them, it halts with an error rather than continuing to compact and refill:

Error: Context window thrash detected — compressed 3 times consecutively without
progress. Reduce system prompt size, lower CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS, or
increase PreCompact hook output selectivity.

Three is the threshold. One recompact is normal. Two is a warning sign. Three is the circuit breaker.

Diagnosing Thrash

If you hit the thrash error, the diagnosis is mechanical:

CauseDiagnosisFix
System prompt too largeSum CLAUDE.md + tool schema tokensUse claudeMdExcludes to reduce discovery scope; trim unused tool descriptions
PreCompact hook output too largeCheck hook stdout byte countReduce MAX_STATE_CHARS; summarize state rather than dumping raw content
Context cap too low for workloadSession productive turn count before first compaction is very lowRaise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS or reduce MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS
Long system prompt + large MCP schemasCount MCP tool descriptionsDisable unused MCP servers for the session

The claudeMdExcludes setting directly addresses CLAUDE.md bloat from large dependency directories:

{
  "claudeMdExcludes": [
    "**/node_modules/**",
    "**/.venv/**",
    "**/vendor/**",
    "**/dist/**"
  ]
}

Without exclusions, the harness walks the entire directory tree looking for CLAUDE.md files. In a monorepo with thousands of node_modules subdirectories, this produces either a very long directory walk or, worse, finds CLAUDE.md files inside dependencies and injects their content into your session.

20.8 --exclude-dynamic-System-prompt-sections for Cache Reuse

Section 20.4 introduced this flag from the cache mechanics side. This section covers the implementation details and when to use it.

The Problem: Per-Machine System Prompts

The default system prompt contains content that varies by machine and session:

Working directory: /Users/alice/project
Git status: M src/auth/session.py
Environment: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-...
Memory paths: /Users/alice/.claude/memory/

Alice's system prompt is different from Bob's. Alice's session on Monday (git status clean) produces a different system prompt than Tuesday (after uncommitted changes). Each variation is a unique cache key — a cache miss.

For a team of 10 engineers all running the same harness against the same codebase, the system prompt is warming 10 separate caches instead of one shared cache. At 15,000 tokens per system prompt, that is 150,000 tokens of warming cost instead of 15,000.

The Solution: Static System Prompt + Dynamic First Message

With --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections, the harness restructures the prompt:

Before:

[system prompt]
Base instructions + tool descriptions + CLAUDE.md + git status + CWD + env info + memory paths

After:

[system prompt — static, shared cache key]
Base instructions + tool descriptions + CLAUDE.md

[first user message — dynamic, not cached]
Working directory: /Users/alice/project
Git status: M src/auth/session.py
Environment context: ...
Memory paths: ...

[actual user prompt]
Fix the authentication timeout in src/auth/session.py

The system prompt is now identical for all users on the same project. The cache entry warms once and serves all of them.

When to Use It

This flag pays off in multi-user team scenarios. For solo use on a single machine, the cache would hit anyway (same user, same CWD, same git status between consecutive calls). For teams, automated CI pipelines, or deployments where multiple users run the same harness, the flag is a significant cost lever.

A caveat: dynamic content in the first user message means the model sees git status, environment info, and memory paths as user-provided context rather than system instructions. For well-written harness prompts, this distinction does not matter — the model interprets the context correctly regardless of which message turn it arrives in. For prompts that rely on the system/user role boundary as a trust signal, review whether the shift changes the expected behavior.

20.9 Lab: Design a Context Strategy for a 200+ File Codebase Agent

This lab is a design exercise, not a code dump. The goal is to produce a context strategy document that a senior engineer could hand to a team implementing a long-running codebase analysis agent.

The Scenario

An agent is tasked with performing a complete security and code quality audit of a Python codebase with 240 source files, 18,000 lines of code, comprehensive test coverage, and an active development team committing daily. The agent must:

  1. Scan all 240 files
  2. Identify security issues, quality issues, and test gaps
  3. Produce a single unified report
  4. Handle interruptions gracefully (the audit may take 45+ minutes of wall clock time)
  5. Run in CI — no interactive user to resolve ambiguities

Context Budget Calculation

Before writing any code, calculate the context budget:

System prompt tokens (estimated):
  Base instructions + tool descriptions:    ~4,000
  CLAUDE.md (project rules):                ~2,000
  Git context + env info:                   ~1,000
  Total system prompt:                      ~7,000

Per-file analysis tokens (estimated):
  Average file size (75 lines):             ~1,500
  Tool result overhead (read + result):     ~500
  Model response (findings JSON):           ~800
  Per-file cost:                            ~2,800

For 240 files:
  Total file analysis tokens:              ~672,000

Synthesis phase:
  All findings aggregated:                  ~20,000
  Synthesis prompt + response:              ~15,000
  Total synthesis:                          ~35,000

Grand total estimate:                      ~714,000 tokens

714,000 tokens is within the 1M cap, but barely. One long source file, verbose model responses, or an extra CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory could push it over. The strategy needs compression headroom.

Decision 1: Use Parallel Subagents

Do not run a single 240-file scan in one agent session. Fan out to parallel subagents, each scanning a bounded slice of the codebase:

Orchestrator (sonnet)
├── Subagent batch 1: files 001-060 (haiku)
├── Subagent batch 2: files 061-120 (haiku)
├── Subagent batch 3: files 121-180 (haiku)
└── Subagent batch 4: files 181-240 (haiku)
         ↓
Synthesizer (sonnet)
         ↓
Report

Each subagent operates in a fresh session — no prior conversation overhead, no compression pressure. 60 files at ~2,800 tokens each = ~168,000 tokens per subagent. Well within a 200K context limit configured for the haiku scanner agents.

As discussed in Chapter 11, subagent prompts must be self-contained. Each batch prompt includes the explicit list of file paths to scan, the output schema, and the complete instructions for what to look for — not a reference to "the project" that the subagent cannot see.

Decision 2: Configure Token Caps Per Agent Role

# Scanner agents: cheap, fast, bounded context
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=200000 \
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=20000 \
MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=5000 \
  claude -p "$(cat scanner-prompt-batch-1.txt)"

# Synthesizer: needs more context to hold all findings
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=400000 \
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=50000 \
MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=20000 \
  claude -p "$(cat synthesis-prompt.txt)"

Scanner agents do not need extended thinking — they are performing structured extraction. Synthesis requires more reasoning to de-duplicate and prioritize across 240 files.

Decision 3: State Files and PreCompact Hook

Even with the parallel architecture, the orchestrator session — which launches all four batches, collects results, and runs the synthesizer — will accumulate substantial context. Configure a PreCompact hook for it:

# ~/.claude/hooks/audit-pre-compact.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

STATE_FILE="${HOME}/.claude/projects/myapp-audit/state/current.json"
[[ -f "${STATE_FILE}" ]] || exit 0

# Report only the completion status, not the full findings
BATCHES_DONE=$(jq '.batches_completed | length' "${STATE_FILE}")
BATCHES_TOTAL=$(jq '.batches_total' "${STATE_FILE}")
FINDINGS_COUNT=$(jq '.findings | length' "${STATE_FILE}")
LAST_BATCH=$(jq -r '.batches_completed[-1] // "none"' "${STATE_FILE}")

cat << EOF
AUDIT STATE: ${BATCHES_DONE}/${BATCHES_TOTAL} batches complete.
${FINDINGS_COUNT} findings accumulated.
Last completed batch: ${LAST_BATCH}
State file: ${STATE_FILE}
On resume: read state file, launch remaining batches, do not re-scan completed batches.
EOF

The hook output is compact — under 200 tokens — but gives the model enough information to resume correctly after compression without re-running completed scans.

Decision 4: Cache Optimization for the CI Environment

In a CI pipeline, the harness runs from a clean environment on each invocation. Use --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections to separate the static project instructions from the per-run git state:

claude --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections \
  -p "Run security audit batches..."

The project's CLAUDE.md, tool descriptions, and base instructions will be cached across CI runs. The commit SHA, current branch, and changed files live in the first user message and vary per run — they should not be in the cached system prompt anyway.

Decision 5: Handle Pagination Explicitly

Scanner prompts must anticipate truncation. Instruct haiku agents to handle it:

If a file read returns truncatedByTokenCap: true, issue a follow-up Read
with offset equal to the number of lines already received. Continue until
truncatedByTokenCap is false. Report findings from all pages.

Without this instruction, a haiku agent that hits truncation may either stop reading the file (missing findings on later pages) or fail to parse the partial content correctly.

The Strategy Document

A context strategy for this workload reduces to five decisions:

DecisionChoiceRationale
Session architecture4 parallel haiku scanners + 1 sonnet synthesizerDistributes context load, exploits parallelism
Context caps200K scanner, 400K synthesizerMatches caps to actual workload size
Thinking budget5K scanner, 20K synthesizerExtraction vs. reasoning distinction
State preservationPreCompact hook writes compact summary of batch progressProtects orchestrator from losing batch status across compressions
Cache optimization--exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections in CIAmortizes system prompt cost across all CI runs

This strategy brings the total cost from ~714,000 tokens in a single session to approximately 4 × 168,000 (scanners) + 200,000 (synthesis + orchestration) = 872,000 tokens — slightly more in raw token count, but distributed across five shorter sessions that each stay well under their caps, with no compression risk and full cache reuse.

More importantly, it is a resilient strategy. If batch 3 fails mid-run, the orchestrator's state file records which batches completed. The PreCompact hook preserves that state across any compression events. Batch 3 can be re-run without re-scanning the 180 files already processed in batches 1, 2, and 4.

Summary

Context window management is an engineering discipline, not an operational afterthought. The six behaviors covered in this chapter form a complete toolkit:

Token budgets (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS, MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS, MAX_THINKING_TOKENS) are explicit resource limits. Set them deliberately per workload rather than leaving them at defaults and hoping for the best.

Automatic compression is lossy. Information not written to persistent state before compression is gone. Long-running agents must write state files — the context window is not a reliable scratchpad across compression boundaries.

The PreCompact hook is your intervention point. It fires before compression and injects critical state into the surviving summary. Keep hook output compact — under 4,000 characters — to avoid consuming the summary budget that compression needs to work correctly.

Prompt cache has a 5-minute TTL and is invalidated by any byte change in the cached prefix. Stable system prompts hit cache reliably. Dynamic content injected into the system prompt (CWD, git status, per-machine env vars) breaks cross-user cache sharing — use --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections in multi-user deployments.

Read deduplication eliminates redundant file reads within a session. Subagents do not inherit the parent's dedup state — they pay the full cost on their first read of any file. For subagents that need file content the parent has already read, inject it into the agent prompt directly.

Pagination via truncatedByTokenCap signals partial file reads programmatically. Handle it explicitly in harness code and scanner agent prompts — a scanner that silently stops at the first page of a long file is producing incomplete findings.

Thrash loop prevention stops the harness after three consecutive compressions without productive progress. Hitting this error means the static overhead (system prompt + hook output) is consuming most of the configured context budget. Reduce system prompt size via claudeMdExcludes, reduce hook output selectivity, or raise the context cap.

The lab's 200-file audit scenario demonstrates how these tools compose: parallel subagents distribute context load, per-role token caps right-size each session, PreCompact hooks protect orchestrator state, and cache optimization amortizes system prompt cost across CI runs.

In Chapter 21, we move to session persistence: how transcript storage, checkpoint files, and the cleanupPeriodDays setting interact to give agents the ability to resume work across process restarts — the full durability layer that context management alone cannot provide.

Next: Chapter 21: Session Persistence and Resumability

Chapter 21: Model Selection and Routing

"Sending every task to Opus is like renting a supercomputer to check your email. The harness should know the difference."

Every request your harness sends to the Claude API carries an implicit model choice. If you have never thought about that choice explicitly, the harness has been making it for you — usually defaulting to whichever model was most capable at install time. This chapter makes that choice explicit, systematic, and cheap.

Model selection is not a one-time decision. It is a runtime routing problem. The right model depends on task complexity, latency requirements, cost budgets, and whether the current primary is overloaded. A harness that treats model selection as a static configuration is leaving performance and money on the table. A harness that treats it as a first-class concern routes intelligently — escalating to Opus when reasoning depth matters, running Haiku for high-volume classification, keeping Sonnet as the workhorse for the median case, and falling back gracefully when a model is unavailable.

This chapter builds the full picture: what each model tier is for, every mechanism the harness exposes to control model selection, how those mechanisms compose, and a working cost-aware routing layer in the lab section.

21.1 Model Tiers

Claude Code exposes four logical tiers, each mapping to one or more concrete model IDs.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      MODEL TIERS                            │
│                                                             │
│  opus   ──── claude-opus-4-8                               │
│               claude-opus-4-7                               │
│               claude-opus-4-6                               │
│                                                             │
│  sonnet ──── claude-sonnet-4-6                             │
│                                                             │
│  haiku  ──── claude-haiku-4-5-20251001                     │
│                                                             │
│  fable  ──── (experimental / specialized routing)         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Opus — Maximum Reasoning Depth

The Opus tier is the highest-capability family. It produces the best output on tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, large-context synthesis, ambiguous problem decomposition, and agentic decisions with high downstream consequence. You pay for this in tokens-per-second and per-call cost.

Use Opus when:

  • The task has a correctness requirement — architecture decisions, security assessments, legal analysis, production code changes where a wrong answer causes an incident
  • The context window is large and the relevant signal is sparse — Opus loses less fidelity when synthesizing a 100K-token codebase into a 3-paragraph summary
  • The task involves non-obvious reasoning chains — "which of these six approaches has the best failure mode under partial network partition" is an Opus question
  • You are orchestrating a workflow and need the conductor to be sharp even if the workers are fast

Within the Opus family, the harness resolves the "opus" alias to the latest available Opus model by default. The concrete IDs — claude-opus-4-8, claude-opus-4-7, claude-opus-4-6 — let you pin a specific generation when you need reproducibility across releases.

Fast mode is Opus-specific. This is a common point of confusion. When you enable fast mode (covered in 21.3), you are not switching to a cheaper model — you are running Opus with a latency-optimized inference profile. The capability ceiling stays the same; the streaming behavior changes. Fast mode is available on Opus 4.8, 4.7, and 4.6.

Sonnet — The Production Workhorse

Sonnet is the default model for most Claude Code workflows. It represents the practical optimum: strong reasoning, solid code generation, large context handling, at roughly half the cost and noticeably better latency than Opus.

Use Sonnet when:

  • The task is well-scoped — "refactor this function", "write tests for this module", "explain what this regex does"
  • You are running an interactive session where latency matters more than maximum depth
  • You are building a multi-agent workflow and need capable-but-fast workers that run in parallel
  • You cannot predict task complexity in advance — Sonnet covers the wide middle of the distribution well

claude-sonnet-4-6 is the current production ID. For most harness deployments, Sonnet is where you start and where you stay until profiling shows you need more.

Haiku — High-Throughput Classification and Screening

Haiku (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001) is the speed and cost tier. It is substantially faster and cheaper than Sonnet at the cost of reasoning depth and reliability on complex tasks.

Use Haiku when:

  • Throughput is the constraint — you are processing thousands of items in a pipeline and can tolerate occasional errors
  • The task is simple and structurally defined — keyword extraction, classification into a fixed taxonomy, format conversion, short summarization
  • You need a fast pre-filter before escalating high-confidence results to Sonnet or Opus
  • You are building a fallback path or a warming step where partial correctness is acceptable

Do not use Haiku for code that goes to production, for security-sensitive analysis, or for tasks where context exceeds a few thousand tokens. Its performance degrades sharply outside its sweet spot.

Fable — Experimental Routing

"fable" is exposed as a valid model alias in the AgentInput type but is not a public production tier in the same sense as Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. It represents experimental or specialized routing that Anthropic may use for specific capabilities or internal testing. Do not build production routing logic that depends on Fable behavior — treat it as a reserved identifier until it is documented as stable.

Cost and Speed Reference

Exact pricing changes, but the order-of-magnitude relationships are stable:

TierRelative costRelative latencyBest for
OpusHighHighestDeep reasoning, high-stakes decisions
SonnetMediumMediumGeneral-purpose, interactive, default
HaikuLowLowestClassification, filtering, high-volume pipelines

When in doubt, start with Sonnet and profile. Escalate to Opus only when you have evidence that Sonnet is producing wrong answers on the task shape you care about. Downgrade to Haiku only when you have evidence that Haiku is right enough on the task shape you care about.

21.2 Selection Mechanisms

The harness exposes four distinct mechanisms for controlling model selection. They form a priority stack that mirrors the configuration cascade from Chapter 2.

The --model CLI Flag

The highest-priority runtime override. Accepts either a logical alias or a concrete model ID:

# Logical alias — resolves to latest in tier
claude --model opus

# Concrete ID — pins to a specific generation
claude --model claude-opus-4-8

# Specific Sonnet
claude --model claude-sonnet-4-6

# Haiku
claude --model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001

The flag is session-scoped. It applies for the duration of the session and overrides everything lower in the stack — the settings file model field, the default model, and (in interactive mode) whatever the /model picker shows as selected. When you exit the session and start a new one without the flag, the lower layers reassert.

Use --model for:

  • One-off experiments ("is Opus actually better on this task class?")
  • CI pipelines where the model should be explicit and auditable in the invocation log
  • Fallback scripting where you need to force a specific tier

The model Settings Field

The settings-layer equivalent of --model. Set it in ~/.claude/settings.json for a personal default, or in .claude/settings.json if you want to enforce a model at the project level:

{
  "model": "sonnet"
}

Valid values are the same as --model: logical aliases ("opus", "sonnet", "haiku", "fable") or concrete IDs. If you omit this field entirely, the harness uses its built-in default, which tracks the current recommended production model.

The practical pattern: set "model": "sonnet" globally if you are on a subscription plan where Sonnet has better rate limits than Opus. Set "model": "opus" if you are doing a focused deep-analysis session and want every query to hit maximum capability without typing --model opus each time.

The /model Interactive Picker

In interactive terminal sessions, /model opens a model picker that lets you switch the active model without leaving the session. The current selection is shown at the top of the picker. Switching is immediate — the next API call uses the new model.

This is useful when you start a session doing quick exploratory work (Sonnet), realize you need deeper analysis on a particular problem (switch to Opus), and then return to exploratory work (switch back to Sonnet). It avoids the latency cost of exiting and restarting a session.

The picker label for each entry is configurable via the ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL_NAME environment variables (covered in 21.7). If you are running against a private deployment with custom model names, this is how you make the picker show your organization's labels instead of the upstream defaults.

Per-Agent Model Override

When spawning subagents, you can specify the model directly in the AgentInput:

await Agent({
  description: "Classify security severity",
  prompt: "Classify each of these 50 findings as critical/high/medium/low: ...",
  model: "haiku",   // fast, cheap, the task is structured
});

The model field accepts the same logical aliases as everywhere else: "sonnet" | "opus" | "haiku" | "fable". The subagent runs on that model regardless of what the parent session is using.

The same override is available in agent frontmatter for custom agents defined in .claude/agents/:

---
name: code-reviewer
model: sonnet
effort: high
---

You are a code reviewer. Your job is to...

This is the right place to set model when the agent's role has a stable model requirement. A security-audit agent that always needs Opus reasoning depth should encode that in its definition, not in every call site. A file-diff summarizer that always runs fine on Haiku should also encode that in its definition.

The precedence stack for per-agent model selection:

1. model field in AgentInput call       (highest)
2. model in agent frontmatter
3. model in settings.json
4. --model CLI flag
5. harness built-in default             (lowest)

21.3 Fast Mode

Fast mode is a latency optimization for the Opus tier. The documentation is precise on this point: fast mode does not downgrade to a smaller model. It runs Claude Opus with a faster output profile. Capability ceiling is unchanged; streaming behavior changes.

Enable it in three ways:

Settings file:

{
  "fastMode": true
}

Interactive toggle:

/fast

Typing /fast in a session toggles fast mode on or off. The current state is reflected in the session status display.

When to use it: Fast mode is appropriate when you need Opus reasoning depth but are latency-sensitive — a developer assistant session where you want near-Sonnet response times without dropping to Sonnet quality. It is specifically useful on tasks where Opus is materially better than Sonnet but where the user is waiting in real time for every token.

When not to use it: Fast mode is Opus-only. If your settings have "model": "sonnet", enabling "fastMode": true has no effect — Sonnet does not have a fast mode variant. Do not enable it if you are cost-sensitive; fast mode does not change the per-token price.

Available on: Opus 4.8, 4.7, 4.6.

21.4 Effort Levels

Effort levels are orthogonal to model selection. They control how hard the model works on a given task — specifically, how much reasoning and internal computation it applies before producing output. This maps roughly to the extended thinking budget.

The five levels, in ascending order of compute:

LevelWhen to use
lowQuick questions, format conversion, lookups — tasks where speed matters and the answer is not ambiguous
mediumThe default. General-purpose tasks where a reasonable answer in reasonable time is the goal
highTasks that benefit from careful consideration — code review, design critique, debugging — where you want more than the first-pass answer
xhighComplex multi-step problems where the model should reason carefully before committing — architecture decisions, security analysis
maxMaximum available compute. Use sparingly — the latency and cost increases are significant. Reserve for tasks where correctness is worth any price

Setting Effort Level

CLI flag — session-scoped:

claude --effort high
claude --effort max

Settings file — default for all sessions:

{
  "effortLevel": "high"
}

Per-agent frontmatter:

---
name: threat-model-agent
model: opus
effort: xhigh
---

The combination of model and effort level defines the compute budget for a task. A Haiku agent at low effort is appropriate for a classification step in a preprocessing pipeline. An Opus agent at xhigh effort is appropriate for the final synthesis step in a security audit. Most tasks sit between those extremes.

Effort and Cost

Higher effort levels consume more tokens — the model runs longer internal reasoning before producing output. The cost increase is non-linear at the upper end. max effort can be 3-5x the cost of medium on the same prompt. This makes effort level the primary cost-control lever after model selection.

Practical rule of thumb: set effortLevel to "high" in your global settings if you are doing engineering work. Use "medium" for interactive assistant sessions. Use "max" explicitly on a per-call basis when a task genuinely requires it — do not set it globally.

21.5 Extended Thinking

Extended thinking is a deeper form of computation than effort level alone. When enabled, the model engages a structured internal reasoning process — working through a problem before producing its output. The output reflects more deliberate analysis than the standard inference path.

Two settings control extended thinking:

{
  "alwaysThinkingEnabled": true,
  "showThinkingSummaries": true
}

alwaysThinkingEnabled — when true, every request goes through the extended thinking path. This is a strong setting: it increases latency on every call, regardless of whether the task benefits from it. The right use case is a dedicated analysis session where every prompt is a hard problem — auditing a codebase, designing a system, debugging an intermittent failure. It is not appropriate for an interactive session mixing hard questions with quick lookups.

showThinkingSummaries — opt-in. When true, the harness surfaces a summary of the model's reasoning chain alongside the response. This is off by default because most users do not want the reasoning surface — they want the answer. Enable it when:

  • You are debugging model outputs and need to understand why it reached a conclusion
  • You are building a system where the reasoning chain is itself an artifact (audit logs, explainability requirements)
  • You are evaluating whether the model is reasoning correctly or pattern-matching incorrectly

Thinking summaries are not the raw internal state — they are a condensed, human-readable representation of the key reasoning steps. They are useful for diagnosis; they are not a substitute for the answer.

Extended Thinking vs. Effort Level

These two controls are related but distinct:

  • Effort level scales the compute budget within the standard inference path
  • Extended thinking engages a qualitatively different reasoning mode

You can combine them: "effortLevel": "xhigh" with "alwaysThinkingEnabled": true is the maximum-depth configuration. Use it for tasks where you would consult a domain expert and want the model to behave like one.

21.6 Fallback Model

The --fallback-model flag addresses overload scenarios: when your primary model is at capacity, the harness can automatically route to a fallback rather than failing the request.

# Single fallback
claude --print --fallback-model sonnet "Analyze the auth module for vulnerabilities"

# Ordered fallback list (comma-separated, tried in order)
claude --print --fallback-model sonnet,haiku "Classify these 100 log entries"

The harness behavior:

  1. Sends the request to the primary model
  2. If the primary is overloaded, tries the first fallback in the comma-separated list
  3. At the start of each new user turn, re-tries the primary model before falling back again

The re-try-primary-per-turn behavior is deliberate. It prevents the fallback from becoming a sticky degraded state — if Opus was overloaded at 2:15pm but recovered by 2:20pm, the next turn's request goes to Opus, not permanently to Sonnet.

Constraint: --fallback-model only works with --print mode. It is designed for non-interactive automation — CI pipelines, background agents, batch processing — where you want resilience without manual intervention.

Typical patterns:

# High-stakes analysis: try Opus, fall back to Sonnet, never Haiku
claude --print --model opus --fallback-model sonnet \
  "Review this PR for security issues: $(cat diff.txt)"

# High-volume pipeline: try Sonnet, fall back to Haiku if overloaded
claude --print --model sonnet --fallback-model haiku \
  "Classify this log entry: ${log_line}"

Do not set a fallback model in settings — it is inherently a session-level concern tied to specific automation scripts. The right place for fallback configuration is in the script that calls Claude, not in shared project settings.

21.7 Third-Party Providers: Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry

When your organization routes Claude traffic through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Azure AI Foundry, the model IDs and available tiers differ from Anthropic direct. The harness provides environment variable overrides to bridge this gap without changing your application code.

Model Support Overrides

Each tier has two override variables:

# Tell the harness that your Bedrock/Vertex deployment supports Opus
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL_SUPPORTS=1

# Tell the harness that your deployment supports Sonnet
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL_SUPPORTS=1

# Tell the harness that your deployment supports Haiku
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL_SUPPORTS=1

These variables are capability declarations, not model IDs. They tell the harness which tiers are available at your endpoint, so the model picker, fallback logic, and per-agent routing work correctly against your deployment.

Model Name and Description Overrides

# Override the label shown in the /model picker
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL_NAME="Enterprise Opus (Bedrock)"
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL_NAME="Sonnet-Prod"
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL_NAME="Haiku-Fast"

# Override the description shown in the picker
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_DESCRIPTION="High-capability model, billed at Enterprise tier"

These are UI-layer overrides. They do not change model behavior — they change what engineers see in the interactive picker and in log output. Useful when your organization has multiple Claude deployments (e.g., a cost-center-separated Bedrock endpoint for engineering and a separate Vertex endpoint for the data team) and you want engineers to see meaningful names rather than opaque model IDs.

Deployment Pattern

Set these variables in the environment your harness runs in — the CI runner, the Docker container, the shell profile for the team's dev machines:

# .env for Bedrock-routed team deployment
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://your-bedrock-endpoint.amazonaws.com/...
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL_SUPPORTS=1
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL_SUPPORTS=1
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL_NAME="Opus (Bedrock/us-east-1)"
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL_NAME="Sonnet (Bedrock/us-east-1)"

Do not commit these variables to version control. They belong in the same secret management layer as your API key.

21.8 Lab: Cost-Aware Routing Layer

This lab builds a routing layer that selects model tier based on task complexity signals. The goal is to run Haiku on simple tasks, Sonnet on medium tasks, and Opus on tasks that signal genuine reasoning depth — automatically, without manual per-call decisions.

The Problem

A naive harness sends every task to the default model. If your default is Opus, you pay Opus rates for every file summarization, every changelog entry, every classification. If your default is Sonnet, complex analysis tasks sometimes produce shallow answers. The fix is a routing layer that infers complexity from the task and dispatches accordingly.

Complexity Signals

For an engineering harness, the following signals correlate with model requirement:

High complexity → Opus
  - Task contains "architect", "design", "tradeoff", "security", "vulnerability"
  - Context window exceeds 50K tokens
  - Task is multi-part (contains enumerated sub-questions)
  - Previous attempt on lower model produced an answer flagged as inadequate

Medium complexity → Sonnet (default)
  - Standard code tasks: review, refactor, test, explain, implement
  - Single-file scope
  - Specific, bounded questions

Low complexity → Haiku
  - Classification into a fixed schema
  - Keyword extraction, tag assignment
  - Format conversion (JSON → YAML, markdown → plain text)
  - Single-fact lookups

Implementation

Create .claude/agents/routing-dispatcher.md:

---
name: routing-dispatcher
model: sonnet
effort: low
---

You are a task classifier. Your only job is to classify the complexity of a task prompt so that it can be routed to the correct model tier.

Given a task description, return a JSON object with:
- tier: "opus" | "sonnet" | "haiku"
- reason: one sentence explaining the classification

Classification rules:
- "haiku": classification tasks, format conversion, simple extraction, single-fact lookup
- "sonnet": code review, refactor, explain, implement, test — bounded, single-concern tasks
- "opus": architecture decisions, security analysis, multi-step reasoning, large-context synthesis

Return only the JSON object. No prose.

Now the routing layer in your workflow script:

export const meta = {
  name: 'cost-aware-dispatch',
  description: 'Route task to optimal model tier'
}

// Classify the task complexity using a cheap Haiku call
const classification = await agent(
  `Classify this task: "${args.task}"`,
  {
    label: 'classify',
    subagent_type: 'routing-dispatcher',
    schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: {
        tier: { type: 'string', enum: ['opus', 'sonnet', 'haiku'] },
        reason: { type: 'string' }
      },
      required: ['tier', 'reason']
    }
  }
)

log(`Routing to ${classification.tier}: ${classification.reason}`)

// Execute the actual task on the classified tier
const result = await agent(args.task, {
  label: 'execute',
  model: classification.tier,
  schema: args.output_schema
})

Escalation on Inadequate Output

A routing layer that only routes on the way in is incomplete. Tasks sometimes start simple and turn out to be complex once the model begins working. Add an escalation path:

// First attempt on classified tier
let result = await agent(args.task, {
  label: 'attempt-1',
  model: classification.tier,
  schema: RESULT_SCHEMA
})

// Check if the model flagged inadequacy
if (result.confidence === 'low' || result.escalate === true) {
  log(`Escalating from ${classification.tier} to opus — low confidence answer`)
  result = await agent(
    `${args.task}\n\nA previous analysis of this task produced a low-confidence result. Please reason carefully.`,
    {
      label: 'attempt-2',
      model: 'opus',
      schema: RESULT_SCHEMA
    }
  )
}

This requires your output schema to include a confidence field that the model can set. Add it to your schema definition:

const RESULT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    answer: { type: 'string' },
    confidence: {
      type: 'string',
      enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'],
      description: 'How confident you are in this answer given the available information'
    },
    escalate: {
      type: 'boolean',
      description: 'Set true if this task would significantly benefit from a more capable model'
    }
  },
  required: ['answer', 'confidence', 'escalate']
}

Cost Tracking with /cost

Since v2.1.92, /cost provides per-model and cache-hit breakdowns for subscription users. Run /cost after a session that uses the routing layer to verify the distribution is what you expect:

Session cost breakdown:
  haiku    (classifier)    12 calls   $0.003
  sonnet   (worker)        31 calls   $0.041
  opus     (escalations)    3 calls   $0.024
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Total                   46 calls   $0.068

If you see Haiku being used for tasks that keep escalating, tighten the classification rules — Haiku is being overconfident about its own tier. If you see Opus being used for tasks that never escalate and produce high-confidence answers, consider whether Sonnet would have been adequate.

Settings for the Lab

The recommended settings configuration for a workflow that uses cost-aware routing:

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "model": "sonnet",
  "effortLevel": "medium",
  "fastMode": false,
  "alwaysThinkingEnabled": false
}

The routing layer overrides model per-agent, so the settings default does not matter much — but set it to "sonnet" as the conservative default for any unrouted calls. Keep effortLevel at "medium" globally; the routing layer can specify effort: high or effort: xhigh in the agent frontmatter for tiers that need it.

Summary

Model selection in the harness is a four-layer composition:

  1. Tier choice (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku) — the primary cost/quality lever. Match to task complexity.
  2. Effort level (low → max) — scales compute within the chosen tier. Match to how carefully you need the answer.
  3. Fast mode — Opus-specific latency optimization. Enable for interactive Opus sessions.
  4. Extended thinking — qualitatively deeper reasoning. Enable per-session for genuinely hard problems; never enable globally.

The mechanisms compose cleanly: --model and --effort at the CLI for session overrides, model and effortLevel in settings for defaults, model and effort in agent frontmatter for stable per-agent requirements, and --fallback-model for resilience in automation pipelines.

The routing lab demonstrates the practical consequence: a workflow that explicitly classifies and dispatches tasks can achieve Opus quality where it matters and Haiku cost where it does not — without manual intervention on every call.

Next: Chapter 22 covers token budgets and context window management — the constraint that shapes every other decision in a long-running harness session.

Chapter 22: Git Worktree Isolation

"Isolation is not paranoia. It is the precondition for running dangerous work at scale."

Parallel agent workflows fail in a specific, predictable way: two agents write to the same file at the same time. The second writer wins, the first agent's context diverges from reality, and both outputs are now wrong in ways that are hard to detect. You can serialize the agents to avoid the collision — but then you have defeated the purpose of running them in parallel.

Git worktrees are the solution the harness provides. Each worktree is an independent checkout of the same repository, living in its own directory, on its own branch. Agents working in different worktrees share the object store but not the working tree. They cannot stomp each other's files. They produce independent branches that you merge, diff, or discard when the work is done.

This chapter covers the full worktree subsystem: the EnterWorktree and ExitWorktree tools, the configuration knobs that control cost and behavior, the CLI integration, the hook system for non-git VCS, and a lab that builds a parallel database migration system that would be fragile without worktrees and robust with them.

22.1 EnterWorktree: Creating and Entering Isolated Environments

EnterWorktree is the boundary tool. Calling it marks the start of an isolated session: the harness creates a new worktree (or enters an existing one), and subsequent tool calls operate inside that isolated directory until ExitWorktree is called.

The interface:

export interface EnterWorktreeInput {
  name?: string;   // optional, max 64 chars, kebab-case segments
  path?: string;   // enter existing worktree (must be in `git worktree list`)
}

export interface EnterWorktreeOutput {
  worktreePath: string;
  worktreeBranch?: string;
  message: string;
}

Creating a new worktree

When you pass name, the harness creates a new worktree under .claude/worktrees/<name>/ on a new branch named worktree/<name>. The branch tip is determined by worktree.baseRef (covered in §22.2).

const result = await EnterWorktree({ name: "migrate-users-table" });
// result.worktreePath: "/repo/.claude/worktrees/migrate-users-table"
// result.worktreeBranch: "worktree/migrate-users-table"
// result.message: "Created worktree at .claude/worktrees/migrate-users-table on branch worktree/migrate-users-table"

Name constraints exist for operational reasons, not aesthetics. The 64-character cap prevents filesystem path lengths from becoming a problem on macOS and Linux. The kebab-case-segments rule (a-z, 0-9, hyphens, no consecutive hyphens, no leading or trailing hyphens) ensures the name can safely become a branch component. A name like feature/my thing would create a branch worktree/feature/my thing with a space — which git allows but tooling downstream of git often does not.

When name is omitted, the harness generates a name from the current timestamp: auto-20260728-143052. You will see this in practice when using the isolation: "worktree" shorthand in the Agent tool, where the agent does not know in advance what the worktree should be called.

Entering an existing worktree

When you pass path instead of name, the harness enters an existing worktree rather than creating one. The path must appear in git worktree list — the harness validates this before proceeding.

const result = await EnterWorktree({
  path: "/repo/.claude/worktrees/migrate-users-table"
});
