This form is used when one agent creates a worktree and a separate agent needs to inspect or continue work in it. The receiving agent calls EnterWorktree with the path returned by the first agent's ExitWorktree output.

Nesting constraint

EnterWorktree can only be called once per session. If a session is already inside a worktree, calling EnterWorktree again returns an error. There is no nesting. This is a deliberate design choice: a worktree session is a scope, not a stack. If you need deeper isolation, spawn a subagent with isolation: "worktree" — the subagent gets its own session and its own worktree scope.

22.2 worktree.baseRef: Where the Branch Starts

Every new worktree branch must start somewhere. The baseRef setting controls that starting point, and the choice has significant consequences for the kind of work you can do in the worktree.

{
  "worktree": {
    "baseRef": "fresh"
  }
}

Two values are supported:

"fresh" — Start from origin/default-branch

origin/main (remote)
     │
     ▼
worktree branch ──── agent makes changes

fresh fetches the current state of the default branch from the remote and branches from that commit. The worktree always starts with the cleanest possible baseline: whatever is currently in origin/main (or origin/master, or whatever the repository's default is).

This is the right choice for:

  • Parallel feature exploration. You want three agents to propose three different refactoring approaches, all starting from the same clean state. If one agent's branch were based on another's in-progress work, the approaches would not be comparable.
  • Security or QA audits. The audit should reflect the authoritative state of the codebase, not some developer's local uncommitted work.
  • Any workflow where you will merge results back. A branch from origin/main creates a clean merge history. A branch from HEAD may include unreviewed local commits in the ancestry.

The cost of fresh is a network round trip on every worktree creation. In high-frequency workflows this adds up. If your agents are creating dozens of worktrees per minute, measure the overhead.

"head" — Start from current local HEAD

local HEAD (may have uncommitted context)
     │
     ▼
worktree branch ──── agent makes changes

head branches from the current HEAD of your local repository. If you have local commits that are not yet pushed, the worktree starts with them included.

This is the right choice for:

  • Explorations on top of in-progress work. You are mid-feature and want an agent to try a risky approach on a throwaway branch while you continue working on the original.
  • Offline operation. No network required; the branch is created from local objects only.
  • Iterative refinement. You accept a worktree's output, commit it to your working branch, and then create a new worktree from that updated HEAD for the next iteration.

The risk of head is that it captures local state that may be inconsistent. An agent that branches from a HEAD with a half-committed refactor may encounter code that does not compile. When in doubt, fresh is safer.

22.3 worktree.symlinkDirectories: Controlling the Cost

A git worktree checkout is not free. The git object store is shared, but the working tree — every tracked file — must exist on disk in the new directory. For a repository with 50,000 source files, a worktree creation takes a few hundred milliseconds and a modest amount of disk space. That is usually fine.

The problem is the untracked directories that sit alongside the source: node_modules, .venv, __pycache__, dist, build. These are not tracked by git and are not created by git worktree add. But many agents need them to run tests, import modules, or execute builds. The naive solution — copy them — is prohibitively expensive: a node_modules directory for a large project can be 400MB. Copying it for each worktree would be both slow and wasteful.

symlinkDirectories solves this by creating symbolic links in the new worktree pointing back to the originals in the main working tree:

{
  "worktree": {
    "symlinkDirectories": ["node_modules", ".venv", "__pycache__", "dist", "build"]
  }
}

When the harness creates a worktree with this configuration, it runs:

ln -s /repo/node_modules /repo/.claude/worktrees/my-task/node_modules
ln -s /repo/.venv /repo/.claude/worktrees/my-task/.venv
# etc.

The worktree's import statements and test runners see the correct dependencies without duplication.

The shared-state hazard

Symlinks mean shared state. If one agent in the worktree installs a new npm package, that change is visible to every other worktree and to the main working tree — because they all point to the same node_modules. This is usually fine for read-only access (running tests against existing dependencies) but breaks for write operations (installing packages, creating Python virtualenvs, writing build artifacts).

The rule of thumb: symlink directories that agents will read but not modify. For everything else, accept the copy cost or restructure the workflow so that dependency installation happens once before agents start.

{
  "worktree": {
    "symlinkDirectories": ["node_modules", ".venv"]
  }
}

Note __pycache__ is absent in this example. Python's __pycache__ entries are keyed by source file path, so two worktrees writing to the same __pycache__ will overwrite each other's cached bytecode. Omit it from symlinkDirectories if your agents run Python code concurrently. The performance cost of not symlinking __pycache__ is minimal — Python regenerates it quickly.

22.4 ExitWorktree: Closing the Isolation Scope

ExitWorktree is the symmetric counterpart to EnterWorktree. It terminates the isolation scope, removes the harness's CWD-dependent caches (system prompt, memory, plans — all assembled assuming the worktree path), and either preserves or removes the worktree branch.

export interface ExitWorktreeInput {
  action: "keep" | "remove";
  discard_changes?: boolean;
}

export interface ExitWorktreeOutput {
  action: "keep" | "remove";
  originalCwd: string;
  worktreePath: string;
  worktreeBranch?: string;
  tmuxSessionName?: string;
  discardedFiles?: number;
  discardedCommits?: number;
  message: string;
}

action: "keep"

The worktree and its branch remain intact. The output returns worktreePath and worktreeBranch so the caller can reference them — pass them to another agent, open a PR, run a diff, or simply log them.

const exit = await ExitWorktree({ action: "keep" });
// exit.worktreeBranch: "worktree/migrate-users-table"
// exit.worktreePath: "/repo/.claude/worktrees/migrate-users-table"
// exit.originalCwd: "/repo"

Use "keep" when the agent produced output worth reviewing: a working implementation, a complete migration script, a refactoring proposal. The branch is the artifact.

action: "remove"

The worktree directory is deleted and the branch is removed. The session returns to the original working directory.

const exit = await ExitWorktree({ action: "remove" });

Use "remove" when the agent's work was exploratory and produced nothing worth keeping — a dead end, a failed approach, a QA run that confirmed no issues.

Dirty worktrees and discard_changes

ExitWorktree with action: "remove" will refuse to proceed if the worktree is dirty — that is, if it has uncommitted changes or commits that are not present in the base branch. The harness is conservative by design: it will not silently delete work.

// This will fail if the worktree has uncommitted changes
await ExitWorktree({ action: "remove" });
// Error: "Worktree has 3 uncommitted files. Set discard_changes: true to remove anyway."

To override, explicitly acknowledge the loss:

await ExitWorktree({
  action: "remove",
  discard_changes: true
});
// exit.discardedFiles: 3
// exit.discardedCommits: 0

The output reports discardedFiles and discardedCommits so you can log what was thrown away. This is an audit trail, not a recycle bin — the data is gone.

No-op behavior

ExitWorktree is a no-op when called outside an EnterWorktree session. It returns a no-op message rather than an error. This lets workflows call ExitWorktree defensively in cleanup paths without needing to track whether an EnterWorktree was called.

22.5 Auto-Cleanup: Worktrees That Cost Nothing to Abandon

The most operationally significant behavior in the worktree subsystem is auto-cleanup: when an agent exits a worktree session without having made any changes, the harness automatically removes the worktree without requiring an explicit ExitWorktree call.

"No changes" is defined precisely: the worktree branch is identical to the base ref (no commits were added, no staged files exist, no unstaged modifications are present). If the agent read files, ran commands, or called web tools — but wrote nothing to the filesystem — the worktree is considered unchanged.

This matters for parallel workflows. Consider a workflow that fans out twenty agents to explore twenty different approaches to a problem:

const results = await parallel(APPROACHES.map(approach => () =>
  agent(`Implement this approach: ${approach.description}`, {
    isolation: "worktree",
    schema: RESULT_SCHEMA
  })
))

Some approaches will produce complete implementations. Others will hit dead ends and exit cleanly after determining the approach is not viable. Without auto-cleanup, every agent that exits with action: "remove" would leave behind a worktree directory. The harness cleans up the no-change cases automatically; only the agents that committed work leave traces.

In practice, expect most "exploration" agents in a fan-out to leave no traces. Expect "implementation" agents — the ones that actually write code — to leave branches that the orchestrator collects and evaluates.

22.6 CLI Integration: --worktree and --tmux

The worktree system is not only accessible via tools. The CLI exposes two flags that enable worktree-isolated sessions from the command line:

-w, --worktree [name]    Create a new git worktree for this session
--tmux                   Create a tmux session for the worktree (requires --worktree)

--worktree

Starting a session with --worktree is equivalent to calling EnterWorktree as the first action in the session. The harness creates the worktree before the model starts executing, and cleans up (or keeps) the worktree when the session ends.

# Start a session in an auto-named worktree
claude --worktree

# Start a session in a named worktree
claude -w migrate-users-table "Write the migration script for the users table"

# Start a session in an existing worktree
claude -w existing-migration "Check the migration for correctness"

When you pass a name that matches an existing worktree under .claude/worktrees/, the harness enters that worktree rather than creating a new one. This is the same path resolution logic as EnterWorktree { path }, but driven by name rather than explicit path.

--tmux: Visual Workflow Integration

--tmux creates a tmux session paired with the worktree. The session name is derived from the worktree name. When you exit the worktree with action: "keep", the tmux session remains running and the ExitWorktreeOutput.tmuxSessionName field tells you how to reattach. When you exit with action: "remove", the tmux session is killed.

claude -w feature-auth --tmux "Implement the OAuth2 token refresh flow"

By default, --tmux integrates with iTerm2 native panes when iTerm2 is detected — the worktree session opens in a new split pane rather than a separate tmux window, which preserves spatial locality with your current work. If you are in a standard terminal or prefer traditional tmux behavior:

claude -w feature-auth --tmux=classic "Implement the OAuth2 token refresh flow"

--tmux=classic forces traditional tmux windows regardless of the detected terminal.

The tmux integration is most valuable for multi-worktree visual workflows. You can run several Claude sessions simultaneously, each in its own named worktree, each visible in a tmux pane. The session names let you identify which pane is handling which task without switching focus. When a session finishes and calls ExitWorktree { action: "keep" }, the pane stays open showing the result and the branch name, so you can review before switching to the next.

22.7 WorktreeCreate and WorktreeRemove Hooks

The hooks system extends worktree operations to repositories that are not using git — or to git repositories that need custom logic during worktree lifecycle events.

Two hooks are available:

{
  "hooks": {
    "WorktreeCreate": [{ "type": "http", "url": "https://ci.internal/worktree/created" }],
    "WorktreeRemove": [{ "type": "http", "url": "https://ci.internal/worktree/removed" }]
  }
}

type: "http" — Non-git VCS and Custom Backends

The most important use of WorktreeCreate is for non-git version control systems. When type: "http" is set, the harness does not call git worktree add itself. Instead, it posts the worktree creation request to your endpoint:

POST https://ci.internal/worktree/created
{
  "name": "migrate-users-table",
  "baseRef": "fresh",
  "sessionId": "sess_abc123"
}

Your endpoint is responsible for creating the isolated workspace — whatever that means in your VCS — and must return the path where the harness should set its CWD:

{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "worktreePath": "/workspaces/migrate-users-table"
  }
}

The harness uses this path as the worktree path going forward. ExitWorktree will still call the WorktreeRemove hook rather than git worktree remove.

This pattern supports Mercurial, Perforce, Plastic SCM, and corporate VCS systems behind HTTP APIs. It also supports custom git workflows where you need the worktree to be created in non-standard locations, registered with an external CI system at creation time, or built from a custom base rather than a git branch.

Changelog note: v2.1.85 and v2.1.84

Two relevant fixes ship in recent versions. In v2.1.85, --worktree was exiting with an error in non-git repositories before the WorktreeCreate hook could run — the harness was failing on git worktree list before it checked for a hook override. This made the HTTP hook unusable for non-git repos when invoked via the CLI flag. The fix in v2.1.85 checks for a WorktreeCreate hook first and bypasses git operations when one is present.

In v2.1.84, type: "http" support for WorktreeCreate was added — so v2.1.84 introduced the feature and v2.1.85 fixed the CLI integration path. If you are on v2.1.83 or earlier, neither hook type is available.

22.8 Lab: Parallel Database Migration System

This lab builds a workflow that runs multiple database migration scripts in parallel, each in its own isolated worktree, validates each migration independently, and collects the results into a single review report. It is the kind of system that is fragile without worktrees and robust with them.

The problem

You have a monorepo with twelve database migrations that need to be tested against a staging database. The migrations touch different tables and should be independent, but you cannot trust that they are — two migrations might both modify the same table in conflicting ways, or a migration might assume a table state that another migration is also modifying. You need to:

  1. Run each migration in isolation, in a clean checkout.
  2. Validate that each migration applies cleanly.
  3. Validate that each migration rolls back cleanly.
  4. Collect the results and flag any conflicts.

The workflow

export const meta = {
  name: 'parallel-migration-validation',
  description: 'Validate all pending database migrations in isolated worktrees'
}

phase('Discover')
log('Scanning for pending migration files...')

const migrations = await agent('List all pending migration files', {
  label: 'discover',
  schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      migrations: {
        type: 'array',
        items: {
          type: 'object',
          properties: {
            filename: { type: 'string' },
            tables: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
            reversible: { type: 'boolean' }
          },
          required: ['filename', 'tables', 'reversible']
        }
      }
    },
    required: ['migrations']
  }
})

log(`Found ${migrations.migrations.length} pending migrations`)

phase('Validate')

const results = await pipeline(
  migrations.migrations,
  migration => agent(
    `Validate migration ${migration.filename} in an isolated worktree.

Steps:
1. Enter a new worktree named: validate-${migration.filename.replace('.sql', '').replace(/_/g, '-')}
2. Copy the migration file to a scratch directory if needed
3. Run: psql $DATABASE_URL -f db/migrations/${migration.filename}
4. Verify the migration applied by checking the schema: \\d ${migration.tables.join(' \\d ')}
5. If reversible, run the rollback: psql $DATABASE_URL -f db/migrations/rollback/${migration.filename}
6. Verify the rollback restored the schema
7. Exit the worktree with action: "keep" if any issues were found, "remove" if clean

Report the outcome.`,
    {
      label: `validate:${migration.filename}`,
      isolation: 'worktree',
      schema: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          filename: { type: 'string' },
          applySuccess: { type: 'boolean' },
          rollbackSuccess: { type: 'boolean' },
          issues: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
          worktreeBranch: { type: 'string' }
        },
        required: ['filename', 'applySuccess', 'rollbackSuccess', 'issues']
      }
    }
  )
)

phase('Conflict Detection')

const cleanResults = results.filter(Boolean)
const failed = cleanResults.filter(r => !r.applySuccess || !r.rollbackSuccess)
const tableConflicts = detectTableConflicts(migrations.migrations, cleanResults)

const report = await agent(
  `Synthesize these migration validation results into a review report.

Results: ${JSON.stringify(cleanResults, null, 2)}
Failed migrations: ${JSON.stringify(failed)}
Table conflicts: ${JSON.stringify(tableConflicts)}

Include: overall pass/fail, per-migration status, conflict analysis, recommended merge order.`,
  {
    label: 'report',
    schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: {
        overallStatus: { type: 'string', enum: ['pass', 'fail', 'warn'] },
        passCount: { type: 'number' },
        failCount: { type: 'number' },
        conflicts: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
        recommendedOrder: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
        summary: { type: 'string' }
      },
      required: ['overallStatus', 'passCount', 'failCount', 'conflicts', 'summary']
    }
  }
)

log(`Migration validation complete`)
log(`Status: ${report.overallStatus.toUpperCase()} — ${report.passCount} passed, ${report.failCount} failed`)
if (report.conflicts.length > 0) {
  log(`Conflicts detected: ${report.conflicts.join(', ')}`)
}
log(report.summary)

function detectTableConflicts(migrations, results) {
  const tableMap = {}
  for (const m of migrations) {
    for (const table of m.tables) {
      if (!tableMap[table]) tableMap[table] = []
      tableMap[table].push(m.filename)
    }
  }
  return Object.entries(tableMap)
    .filter(([, files]) => files.length > 1)
    .map(([table, files]) => ({ table, files }))
}

Why worktrees make this correct

Without worktrees, all twelve validation agents operate in the same working directory. If migration 7 leaves the database schema in a partially-applied state (its apply succeeded but its rollback failed), migration 11 — which touches the same table — now runs against a modified schema rather than the clean baseline. The validation results are no longer independent. You cannot tell from the output whether migration 11 failed because of its own bugs or because migration 7 left the environment dirty.

With isolation: "worktree", each agent operates in a separate checkout. But more importantly, each agent's database operations run against a separate database connection with an isolated transaction — the agent prompt instructs each one to apply and roll back within its own session. The worktree isolation guarantees the filesystem is clean; the database transaction discipline guarantees the schema state is clean.

The two forms of isolation are complementary, not redundant. File isolation prevents agents from interfering with each other's source code. Transaction isolation prevents them from interfering with each other's database state. You need both.

Reading the output

When the workflow completes, failed migrations leave worktrees behind (action: "keep" was set in the agent prompt for failures). You can inspect them:

ls .claude/worktrees/
# validate-add-user-preferences
# validate-rename-order-status

git diff main worktree/validate-add-user-preferences

Clean migrations were removed automatically (either by the agent's explicit action: "remove" or by auto-cleanup if the agent exited without commits). You only see the worktrees you need to look at.

Configuration for this workflow

{
  "worktree": {
    "baseRef": "fresh",
    "symlinkDirectories": ["node_modules", ".venv"]
  }
}

baseRef: "fresh" ensures every migration validates against the current origin/main, not against any local branch that may have other in-progress changes. The symlinks cover the test runner dependencies without duplicating them.

When Worktrees Are Worth Their Cost

Worktrees add overhead: 200-500ms for creation (plus network time if baseRef: "fresh"), disk space for each checkout, and operational complexity in cleanup. That overhead is justified when:

Agents will write to the same files concurrently. Any parallel workflow where agents may touch overlapping paths needs worktree isolation. Without it, file conflicts are silent and results are wrong.

You need to preserve exploratory branches for comparison. A workflow that generates N approaches to a problem needs those approaches to live on separate branches so you can diff them, merge the best one, and discard the rest. Worktrees give you that structure automatically.

Audit and rollback requirements. If you need to demonstrate that an agent's changes are isolated, reversible, and attributable to a specific task, a worktree branch provides the git history to do that. git log worktree/task-name shows exactly what the agent did.

The overhead is not justified when:

Agents run sequentially and share context intentionally. If agent B is building on agent A's output, they should operate in the same working tree. Isolation would break the workflow.

Agents are read-only. Analysis, review, and audit agents that only read files impose no concurrency hazards. Worktree overhead buys nothing.

The task is short-lived and throwaway. A single-shot agent that runs a command and reports the result does not need worktree isolation. The auto-cleanup will remove the worktree anyway, but you have still paid the creation cost.

The isolation: "worktree" shorthand in the Agent tool and the --worktree CLI flag make it low-friction to add worktree isolation when you need it. The discipline is knowing when you actually need it — and when you are just adding ceremony.

As discussed in Chapter 11, the isolation parameter on the Agent tool is the primary way to create worktrees in multi-agent workflows. The tools covered in this chapter — EnterWorktree and ExitWorktree — are what the harness calls under the hood, and are available directly for cases where you need explicit control over the lifecycle.

Chapter 23: REPL, Artifacts, Notifications, and Remote Triggers

"The tools in this chapter are about output that outlives the session — code that executes in a persistent sandbox, pages that live at a URL, alerts that reach a human who isn't watching, and triggers that let the world reach back in."

23.1 REPL — In-Process JavaScript with Persistent State

Every other tool in the harness executes at arm's length: a subprocess, a file system call, an API request. The REPL is different. It runs JavaScript inside the harness process itself, in a sandbox that persists for the lifetime of the session.

The interface:

export interface REPLInput {
  code: string;          // JavaScript, supports top-level await, state persists
  description?: string;  // semantic label
  timeout?: number;      // default 30000ms, max 600000ms
}

export interface REPLOutput {
  code: string;
  result: { [k: string]: unknown };
  stdout: string;       // captured console.log
  stderr: string;       // captured console.error
  error?: string;
  registeredTools?: string[];  // tools registered during execution
  images?: { base64: string; mediaType: string }[];
  documents?: { base64: string }[];
}

What "Persistent State" Actually Means

Variables, functions, and objects assigned in one REPL call remain available in the next call within the same session. This is not a side effect of shared global scope — it is the design. The sandbox is a long-lived JavaScript context, not a fresh Node.js process per call.

// Call 1 — define state
const metrics = new Map();
metrics.set("latency_p99", []);
metrics.set("error_rate", []);
console.log("Metrics tracker initialized");

// Call 2 — same session, same state
metrics.get("latency_p99").push(142);
metrics.get("latency_p99").push(189);
metrics.get("error_rate").push(0.02);
console.log("Recorded:", Object.fromEntries(metrics));
// Outputs: Recorded: { latency_p99: [142, 189], error_rate: [0.02] }

The second call works because metrics persists from the first. This is the property that makes the REPL useful for stateful computations that span multiple steps — aggregating data from multiple Bash calls, building up a data structure incrementally, or maintaining computation state across a long workflow.

Contrast this with Bash: each Bash call is a new subprocess with no memory of prior calls. If you need a variable to survive between Bash calls, you write it to a file. With the REPL, you just keep it in memory.

Top-Level Await

The REPL supports top-level await, which means you can call async operations directly without wrapping them in an async function:

// Fetch and process in one call — no wrapper function needed
const response = await fetch("https://api.github.com/repos/anthropics/claude-code/releases/latest");
const release = await response.json();
console.log(`Latest: ${release.tag_name}, published ${release.published_at}`);

The timeout parameter governs how long the harness will wait for the awaited operation to resolve. The default is 30,000ms (30 seconds). For operations that legitimately need more time — large data processing, paginated API crawls, computationally intensive transforms — you can push this up to 600,000ms (10 minutes).

The maximum is not arbitrary. The REPL runs in-process, and a REPL call that blocks for 10 minutes holds the harness's JavaScript thread for that duration. Design long-running computations as incremental calls with state accumulation rather than a single monolithic call that holds the thread.

Dynamic Tool Registration

The most structurally significant capability of the REPL is the ability to register new tools at runtime. Tools registered during REPL execution become available to the model in the current session without a restart.

// Register a custom tool that wraps an internal service
registerTool({
  name: "QueryMetricsDB",
  description: "Query the internal Prometheus metrics database. Returns time-series data.",
  inputSchema: {
    type: "object",
    properties: {
      metric: { type: "string", description: "Prometheus metric name" },
      range: { type: "string", description: "Time range, e.g. '5m', '1h', '24h'" },
    },
    required: ["metric"],
  },
  handler: async ({ metric, range = "1h" }) => {
    const url = `http://prometheus.internal:9090/api/v1/query_range?query=${encodeURIComponent(metric)}&range=${range}`;
    const res = await fetch(url);
    const data = await res.json();
    return JSON.stringify(data.data, null, 2);
  },
});

console.log("QueryMetricsDB registered");

When this REPL call completes, REPLOutput.registeredTools will include "QueryMetricsDB". The model can now call QueryMetricsDB exactly as it would call any other tool — it appears in tool search results, it can be called by name, and its output arrives in the conversation as a normal tool result.

This is the pattern for environments where you cannot modify the harness configuration files between sessions. A SessionStart hook can execute a REPL call that registers all environment-specific tools, making them available for the entire session without any static configuration.

Image and Document Return

REPL calls can return binary content. If the JavaScript produces base64-encoded image data, it comes back in REPLOutput.images. PDF data comes back in documents. The model receives this content and can reason about it.

// Generate a chart and return it as a PNG
const canvas = createCanvas(800, 400);
const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");

// ... draw chart data ...

const imageData = canvas.toDataURL("image/png").replace("data:image/png;base64,", "");

// Return structure the harness recognizes
({
  images: [{ base64: imageData, mediaType: "image/png" }]
});

The final expression in a REPL call becomes the result field in REPLOutput. Returning the images array in this structure signals to the harness to attach the images to the tool result. The model then receives an image it can describe, interpret, or compare against expected output.

This makes the REPL the right tool for computational tasks where the output is visual: chart generation, diagram rendering, image manipulation, PDF construction.

23.2 Artifact — Publishing to a Hosted URL

The REPL executes ephemeral computation. Artifact is its complement: durable publication. Artifact takes a file — HTML or Markdown — and publishes it to a hosted URL that anyone with the link can visit.

export interface ArtifactInput {
  action?: "publish" | "list";  // default: publish
  file_path?: string;    // .html or .md file
  favicon?: string;      // one or two emoji
  title?: string;        // browser tab title
  description?: string;  // one-sentence subtitle
  label?: string;        // version label, max 60 chars
  url?: string;          // existing artifact URL to update in place
  force?: boolean;       // override 409 conflict
  limit?: number;        // list: max results (default 25)
  scope?: "mine" | "shared" | "all";  // list filter
}

The output varies by action:

// publish result
type ArtifactPublishOutput = {
  url: string;            // the live URL
  path: string;           // storage path
  title?: string;
  version?: string;
  capabilities?: unknown;
  stored?: { contract: string; capabilities?: {} };
  warnings?: string[];
  updated?: boolean;      // true when updating an existing artifact
  liveSubscription?: string;
};

// list result
type ArtifactListOutput = {
  artifacts: {
    title: string;
    url: string;
    updatedAt?: string;
    rel?: "mine" | "shared";
  }[];
  truncated?: boolean;
  scope?: "shared" | "all";
};

First Publish

The minimal publish: provide file_path pointing to an .html or .md file. Everything else has defaults.

// The model generates a report file, then:
await Artifact({
  file_path: "/tmp/coverage-report.html",
  title: "Test Coverage Report — 2026-07-28",
  description: "Per-module coverage for the auth and API packages",
  favicon: "📊",
  label: "v1.0",
});
// Returns { url: "https://claude.ai/artifacts/abc123", ... }

The returned url is the canonical address of this artifact. Share it with the team, link it in a PR description, embed it in a Slack message. The content is static — it reflects the file as it was at publish time. To update it, you publish again.

Versioning and In-Place Updates

When you publish the same artifact again with the url field set to the original artifact's URL, the harness updates the existing artifact in place rather than creating a new one:

// Regenerate the report after more tests ran
await Artifact({
  file_path: "/tmp/coverage-report.html",
  url: "https://claude.ai/artifacts/abc123",  // the original URL
  label: "v1.1 — post hotfix coverage",
  title: "Test Coverage Report — 2026-07-28 (post hotfix)",
});
// Returns { url: "https://claude.ai/artifacts/abc123", updated: true }

The URL does not change. Anyone who bookmarked the original link now sees the updated content. The label field carries semantic version metadata — it appears in the artifact's version history and helps readers understand what changed between versions.

Label constraints: maximum 60 characters. Use them as lightweight changelogs: "v1.0 — initial", "v1.1 — fixed auth module gaps", "v2.0 — full codebase coverage added". The 60-character limit forces brevity.

The 409 Conflict

The 409 status code is the artifact system's concurrency guard. It fires when two conditions are true simultaneously:

  1. You are attempting to publish to an existing artifact URL
  2. Another session published to that same URL between your last read and your current publish

This is not an error to suppress. It is a data race signal. The standard resolution is a three-step process:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Your Session
    participant S as Artifact Store
    participant B as Other Session

    A->>S: Artifact publish (url=X)
    B->>S: Artifact publish (url=X) — arrives first
    S-->>B: 200 OK, version=v2
    S-->>A: 409 Conflict
    A->>S: Artifact list (scope=mine) — find current state
    S-->>A: { url: X, title: "...", updatedAt: "..." }
    Note over A: Read the current version, merge if needed
    A->>S: Artifact publish (url=X, label="v3 — merged")
    S-->>A: 200 OK, updated: true

The harness intentionally does not auto-merge. The model is in the best position to decide whether to overwrite, merge, or skip — it has the context the store does not. The force: true flag bypasses the conflict check entirely, which is appropriate when you are certain your version supersedes the conflicting one (for example, a scheduled regeneration job that always produces the authoritative state):

// Scheduled report refresh — our version is always authoritative
await Artifact({
  file_path: "/tmp/weekly-digest.html",
  url: existingUrl,
  label: `Week of ${weekOf} — scheduled refresh`,
  force: true,  // we own this artifact, don't care about conflicts
});

Reserve force: true for automation that owns a specific artifact. In interactive sessions, prefer the read-merge-republish sequence so you do not clobber another user's edits.

Listing Artifacts

The list action returns artifacts visible to the current session:

const result = await Artifact({
  action: "list",
  scope: "mine",    // "mine" | "shared" | "all"
  limit: 10,
});

// result.artifacts: [{ title, url, updatedAt, rel }]

Use scope: "mine" to find artifacts your current session has published — useful when you have published several artifacts across a session and need to pass their URLs to another tool or embed them in a report. Use scope: "shared" to find artifacts others have shared with you. Use scope: "all" for the full visible set.

The truncated field in the response tells you whether the result was capped at limit. If truncated: true and you need the full list, increase limit or paginate with successive calls narrowed by date or title.

HTML vs Markdown

Both file types are supported. The distinction is in what the hosted page renders:

HTML — The harness serves the file as-is. You control the full page: CSS, JavaScript, inline charts, interactive tables. This is the right format when the artifact is a tool rather than just content — a dashboard the reader interacts with, a report with collapsible sections, a diff viewer, a coverage heatmap.

Markdown — The harness renders the Markdown to HTML using standard rendering (including GitHub Flavored Markdown). You get properly formatted prose, code blocks, tables, and headers. No JavaScript execution. This is the right format when the artifact is a document — a decision record, a runbook, a meeting summary, an architectural specification.

When in doubt: if the reader needs to do something on the page, use HTML. If the reader needs to read the page, use Markdown.

23.3 PushNotification — Reaching a User Who Isn't Watching

The REPL and Artifact tools produce output the user finds when they look. PushNotification is the tool for when the output needs to find the user.

export interface PushNotificationInput {
  message: string;  // ≤200 chars
  status: "proactive";
}

export interface PushNotificationOutput {
  message: string;
  pushSent?: boolean;
  localSent?: boolean;
  disabledReason?: "config_off" | "user_present" | "no_transport";
  sentAt?: string;  // ISO timestamp
}

The status: "proactive" Requirement

The status field has exactly one valid value: "proactive". This is not a placeholder for a richer enum — it is a semantic declaration. You are telling the harness that the agent decided to send this notification based on its own judgment, not in response to a user request.

The distinction matters because the harness's notification routing logic treats proactive notifications differently from reactive ones. A proactive notification fires only when the user is away from the session. Sending one when the user is actively watching would be interruptive and redundant — they can see the output directly. The harness handles this automatically.

Delivery Mechanics

The output fields tell you exactly what happened:

FieldMeaning
pushSent: trueA mobile or desktop push notification was delivered
localSent: trueA local OS notification was shown
disabledReason: "user_present"User is actively in the session — notification skipped (this is correct behavior)
disabledReason: "config_off"Notifications are disabled in user settings — not an error, just configuration
disabledReason: "no_transport"No push backend is configured — nothing was sent
sentAtISO 8601 timestamp of when the notification was dispatched

The user_present reason is not a failure. When you see it, the notification was correctly suppressed — the user does not need a push because they are reading the session output right now. Build logic that treats user_present as success, not as an error to retry.

When to Fire

PushNotification belongs at decision points where the agent has completed a meaningful chunk of work and the user has stepped away. The canonical patterns:

// Long-running task completed
await PushNotification({
  message: "Security audit complete — 3 HIGH findings in src/auth/. Review at: https://claude.ai/artifacts/xyz",
  status: "proactive",
});

// Something requires a decision before proceeding
await PushNotification({
  message: "Deployment plan generated. Requires your approval before I can proceed with the kubectl apply.",
  status: "proactive",
});

// Unexpected condition discovered
await PushNotification({
  message: "Found hardcoded API key in commits/config.py:47. Paused. Need you to confirm remediation plan.",
  status: "proactive",
});

The 200-Character Constraint

Two hundred characters is tight. Mobile lock screens truncate at roughly 100 characters depending on the device and notification style. Write notifications as if they will be read on a phone screen: front-load the important information, cut every filler word.

Too longBetter
"The security audit that you asked me to run has now been completed and there were three findings of HIGH severity that you should probably look at when you get a chance.""Audit done: 3 HIGH findings in src/auth. Artifact: claude.ai/artifacts/xyz"
"I encountered an unexpected error while running the database migration script and I am not sure how to proceed.""Migration failed at step 4/7. Needs manual review. Error: FK constraint on users.org_id"

The constraint forces clarity. If you cannot say what happened in 200 characters, the notification is not specific enough to be actionable.

23.4 RemoteTrigger — Automation From Outside the Session

PushNotification sends a signal out. RemoteTrigger is the mechanism for signals coming in. It exposes a CRUD interface for managing triggers — webhooks, schedule entries, external event subscriptions — that can wake or interact with sessions from outside the harness.

export interface RemoteTriggerInput {
  action: "list" | "get" | "create" | "update" | "run";
  trigger_id?: string;  // required for get, update, run
  body?: { [k: string]: unknown };  // required for create, update
}

export interface RemoteTriggerOutput {
  status: number;
  json: string;
  summary?: string;
}

The response is a thin envelope: HTTP-style status code, raw json string containing the server's response body, and an optional summary that the harness generates as a human-readable interpretation.

The Five Actions

list — Returns all triggers visible to the current session. No trigger_id or body required.

const result = await RemoteTrigger({ action: "list" });
const triggers = JSON.parse(result.json);
// triggers: [{ id, name, type, enabled, lastFiredAt, ... }, ...]

get — Returns the full definition of a specific trigger.

const result = await RemoteTrigger({
  action: "get",
  trigger_id: "trig_abc123",
});
const trigger = JSON.parse(result.json);

create — Defines a new trigger. The body structure depends on the trigger type.

const result = await RemoteTrigger({
  action: "create",
  body: {
    name: "nightly-security-audit",
    type: "schedule",
    schedule: "0 2 * * *",   // 2am daily, cron syntax
    payload: {
      task: "run-security-audit",
      target: "/Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/src",
      notify: true,
    },
  },
});
const { id } = JSON.parse(result.json);

update — Modifies an existing trigger. Provide the trigger_id and a body with the fields to change.

await RemoteTrigger({
  action: "update",
  trigger_id: "trig_abc123",
  body: {
    schedule: "0 3 * * 1",  // change to 3am on Mondays only
    enabled: false,          // temporarily disable
  },
});

run — Fires the trigger immediately, regardless of its schedule or conditions. Useful for testing that a trigger's handler works correctly before relying on it in production.

const result = await RemoteTrigger({
  action: "run",
  trigger_id: "trig_abc123",
  body: {
    dry_run: true,  // most handlers respect this — no side effects
  },
});
console.log(result.summary);

How Triggers Connect to Sessions

The conceptual model: a trigger is a registered entry point. When the trigger fires — because a schedule elapsed, an external system called a webhook, or run was invoked directly — the harness can start a new session, wake a suspended session, or deliver the trigger's payload to a running session.

This makes RemoteTrigger the infrastructure layer beneath ScheduleWakeup (covered in Chapter 14). Where ScheduleWakeup creates one-shot wakeups tied to the current session, RemoteTrigger manages persistent, named triggers that exist beyond any individual session.

flowchart TD
    E[External Event<br/>CI webhook / cron / API] --> T[RemoteTrigger<br/>trig_abc123]
    T -->|fires| H[Harness]
    H -->|new session| S1[New Session<br/>with trigger payload]
    H -->|resume| S2[Suspended Session<br/>awaiting trigger]
    S1 --> P[PushNotification<br/>on completion]
    S2 --> A[Artifact publish<br/>on completion]

The pattern for scheduled automation: create a trigger with a cron schedule and a payload that describes the work. The harness starts a session, Claude reads the payload, executes the work, publishes an artifact, sends a notification, and exits. The trigger fires again at the next scheduled time. You never need to manage the loop manually.

Checking Results

The RemoteTriggerOutput.status mirrors HTTP status semantics:

StatusMeaning
200Success
201Created (for create action)
404trigger_id not found
409Conflict (trigger name already exists, or trigger is already running)
422Invalid body — schema validation failed

Parse status before trusting json. A 404 with a valid JSON error body is a failure, not a success.

const result = await RemoteTrigger({
  action: "get",
  trigger_id: maybeId,
});

if (result.status === 404) {
  // Trigger was deleted or never existed — recreate it
  await RemoteTrigger({
    action: "create",
    body: defaultTriggerDefinition,
  });
} else if (result.status !== 200) {
  throw new Error(`RemoteTrigger get failed: ${result.status} — ${result.json}`);
}

23.5 ReportFindings — Structured Code Review Output

The tools so far produce outputs that go somewhere — a URL, a push, a trigger. ReportFindings produces output that stays in the conversation: a structured list of code review findings that the harness renders as a first-class UI element rather than raw text.

export interface ReportFindingsInput {
  level?: "low" | "medium" | "high" | "xhigh" | "max";
  findings: {
    file: string;           // repo-relative path
    line?: number;          // 1-indexed
    summary: string;        // one-sentence statement of the problem
    short_summary?: string; // ≤60 chars for compact display
    failure_scenario: string;  // concrete inputs/state → wrong output
    category?: string;      // kebab-case slug
    verdict?: "CONFIRMED" | "PLAUSIBLE";
    outcome?: "fixed" | "skipped" | "no_change_needed";
  }[];  // max 32 findings
}

export interface ReportFindingsOutput {
  count: number;
  level?: string;
  findings: [...];  // echoed back
}

Why a Dedicated Tool

You could write code review output as plain text or return it from a REPL call. ReportFindings exists because structure enables tooling. When findings arrive through this interface, the harness can:

  • Render them as a sortable, filterable table in the UI
  • Link each finding to its file and line in the editor
  • Track outcomes across multiple review passes
  • Feed the structured data into downstream workflows (ticket creation, PR comments, metrics)

Returning findings as freeform text forfeits all of this. ReportFindings is the difference between a report that is read and a report that is acted on.

The failure_scenario Field

The most important field in the findings schema is failure_scenario. It is not a description of the problem in the abstract — it is a concrete reproduction case: what specific inputs, state, or conditions trigger the wrong behavior, and what the wrong output is.

Compare:

summaryfailure_scenario
"JWT validation does not check expiry""Call /api/profile with Authorization: Bearer <expired_token_from_2024>. Server returns 200 with user data instead of 401."
"SQL query is not parameterized""POST /api/search with body {\"q\": \"'; DROP TABLE users; --\"}. The query runs as: SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ''; DROP TABLE users; --'"
"Missing null check on user input""Call parseConfig({}) — config.database is undefined. Line 47 calls config.database.host, throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined."

The failure_scenario column is what makes a finding actionable. A developer reading the summary has to figure out if it matters. A developer reading the failure scenario knows immediately: here is the exact input, here is the exact wrong behavior, here is where to look.

Write failure scenarios as if you are writing a failing test case. Concrete state in, specific wrong output out.

Ordering and the Level Ceiling

Findings must be ordered by severity — highest severity first. The level parameter at the top of the input sets the maximum severity level the caller is willing to report. This is a filter, not a label: if you call with level: "medium", only findings at medium severity or below are included in the output. Findings above the ceiling are silently dropped.

In practice, most callers either omit level (no ceiling) or set it to the severity bucket they are acting on now. A CI gate that blocks on high-severity findings might call ReportFindings twice: once with level: "high" to determine whether to block, and once without level to generate the complete report for the PR comment.

The maximum of 32 findings per call is a hard limit. For codebases with more than 32 issues, group by category or severity and make multiple calls. The harness appends findings from successive ReportFindings calls into the same review session, so the total count across calls is not capped at 32 — only the per-call count is.

Verdict and Outcome

The verdict field signals how confident the reviewer is:

  • "CONFIRMED" — the reviewer has verified the finding by reading the code, constructing the failure scenario, and confirming the behavior exists as described. Use this when you have traced the exact execution path.
  • "PLAUSIBLE" — the reviewer believes the finding is likely real based on code patterns, but has not fully traced the execution path. Use this for findings that require more context (runtime behavior, configuration files not in scope, external service behavior) to fully confirm.

The outcome field is for tracking remediation:

  • "fixed" — the issue was addressed in a subsequent edit
  • "skipped" — the issue was reviewed and intentionally not fixed
  • "no_change_needed" — on closer inspection, the issue was not actually present

These fields are optional on initial submission and filled in as the review cycle progresses. A workflow that runs ReportFindings, waits for edits, then re-runs ReportFindings on the same findings with updated outcome values builds a complete audit trail.

23.6 Lab: Report Generator That Publishes Interactive HTML Artifacts

This lab builds a complete code review pipeline. It reads a Python source directory, runs a REPL-based analysis, generates interactive HTML using structured findings, and publishes the result as an artifact. It demonstrates the integration between REPL (computation), ReportFindings (structure), and Artifact (publication).

What We Are Building

flowchart TD
    SRC[Source Files<br/>src/**/*.py] -->|Bash: find + read| RAW[Raw File Content]
    RAW -->|REPL: analyze| METRICS[Complexity Metrics<br/>+ Issue Candidates]
    METRICS -->|ReportFindings| STRUCT[Structured Findings<br/>32 max, severity-ordered]
    STRUCT -->|REPL: build HTML| HTML[Interactive Report<br/>sortable, filterable]
    HTML -->|Artifact: publish| URL[Live URL<br/>shared with team]
    URL -->|PushNotification| NOTIFY[Team Notified]

Step 1: Collect Source Files

// In the harness session
const fileList = await Bash({
  command: `find /Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/src -name "*.py" -not -path "*/.*" | head -100`,
  description: "Enumerate Python source files",
});

const files = fileList.stdout.trim().split("\n").filter(Boolean);

Step 2: Analyze With REPL

The REPL accumulates findings across multiple calls. First call: initialize the state and define the analysis functions.

// REPL call 1 — initialize analysis state
const findings = [];
const fileMetrics = new Map();

function analyzeFile(path, content) {
  const lines = content.split("\n");
  const issues = [];

  // Check: hardcoded credentials pattern
  lines.forEach((line, i) => {
    if (/password\s*=\s*["'][^"']{4,}["']/i.test(line) &&
        !/test|mock|example|sample|fake/i.test(line)) {
      issues.push({
        file: path,
        line: i + 1,
        summary: "Hardcoded password literal assigned to variable",
        short_summary: "Hardcoded password",
        failure_scenario: `Line ${i + 1}: ${line.trim().slice(0, 120)} — credential exposed in source.`,
        category: "security",
        verdict: "CONFIRMED",
      });
    }
  });

  // Check: except bare clause
  lines.forEach((line, i) => {
    if (/^\s*except\s*:/.test(line)) {
      issues.push({
        file: path,
        line: i + 1,
        summary: "Bare except clause swallows all exceptions including KeyboardInterrupt",
        short_summary: "Bare except clause",
        failure_scenario: `except: at line ${i + 1} catches BaseException. Any error in the try block — including syntax errors during reload and KeyboardInterrupt — is silently swallowed.`,
        category: "error-handling",
        verdict: "CONFIRMED",
      });
    }
  });

  // Check: TODO/FIXME markers in security-sensitive files
  const isSecurityFile = /auth|session|token|password|crypt|permission/i.test(path);
  if (isSecurityFile) {
    lines.forEach((line, i) => {
      if (/\b(TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX)\b/i.test(line)) {
        issues.push({
          file: path,
          line: i + 1,
          summary: "Incomplete implementation marker in security-sensitive file",
          short_summary: "TODO in security file",
          failure_scenario: `${path}:${i + 1} — ${line.trim()} — security logic is incomplete or known-broken per the marker.`,
          category: "security",
          verdict: "PLAUSIBLE",
        });
      }
    });
  }

  fileMetrics.set(path, {
    lines: lines.length,
    issues: issues.length,
  });

  return issues;
}

console.log("Analysis functions ready. State initialized.");

Second REPL call: run the analysis over the file content passed from the Bash results.

// REPL call 2 — analyze files (called in a loop per file batch)
// fileContents is passed as a JSON string injected into this call
const batch = JSON.parse(fileContentsJson);

for (const { path, content } of batch) {
  const fileIssues = analyzeFile(path, content);
  findings.push(...fileIssues);
}

console.log(`Batch complete. Total findings so far: ${findings.length}`);

Step 3: Submit Structured Findings

Once analysis is complete, emit findings through ReportFindings. Sort by severity before submission.

const severityOrder = { security: 0, "error-handling": 1 };

const sortedFindings = findings
  .sort((a, b) => (severityOrder[a.category] ?? 99) - (severityOrder[b.category] ?? 99))
  .slice(0, 32);  // enforce the max

await ReportFindings({
  level: "high",
  findings: sortedFindings,
});

Step 4: Build the Interactive HTML Report

Third REPL call: generate the HTML. The findings array is still in scope from calls 1 and 2.

// REPL call 3 — generate HTML report
const totalFiles = fileMetrics.size;
const totalLines = Array.from(fileMetrics.values()).reduce((s, m) => s + m.lines, 0);
const securityFindings = findings.filter(f => f.category === "security").length;
const errorFindings = findings.filter(f => f.category === "error-handling").length;

const rows = findings.map(f => `
  <tr class="finding ${f.category}" data-severity="${f.verdict === 'CONFIRMED' ? 'high' : 'medium'}">
    <td><code>${f.file.replace("/Users/DOANTX26/Documents/2026/", "")}${f.line ? `:${f.line}` : ""}</code></td>
    <td><span class="badge ${f.category}">${f.category}</span></td>
    <td>${f.summary}</td>
    <td class="scenario">${f.failure_scenario}</td>
    <td><span class="verdict ${f.verdict?.toLowerCase() ?? ''}">${f.verdict ?? "—"}</span></td>
  </tr>
`).join("\n");

const html = `<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Code Review Report — ${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
           max-width: 1200px; margin: 40px auto; padding: 0 20px; color: #1a1a1a; }
    h1 { font-size: 1.6rem; font-weight: 600; }
    .summary { display: flex; gap: 24px; margin: 24px 0; flex-wrap: wrap; }
    .stat { background: #f5f5f5; border-radius: 8px; padding: 16px 24px; }
    .stat .value { font-size: 2rem; font-weight: 700; }
    .stat .label { font-size: 0.85rem; color: #666; }
    table { width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; margin-top: 24px; font-size: 0.9rem; }
    th { text-align: left; border-bottom: 2px solid #e0e0e0; padding: 10px 12px;
         position: sticky; top: 0; background: white; }
    td { padding: 10px 12px; border-bottom: 1px solid #f0f0f0; vertical-align: top; }
    tr:hover td { background: #fafafa; }
    .badge { padding: 2px 8px; border-radius: 4px; font-size: 0.78rem; font-weight: 500; }
    .badge.security { background: #fee2e2; color: #b91c1c; }
    .badge.error-handling { background: #fef3c7; color: #92400e; }
    .verdict { font-size: 0.8rem; font-weight: 600; }
    .verdict.confirmed { color: #b91c1c; }
    .verdict.plausible { color: #d97706; }
    .scenario { font-size: 0.82rem; color: #555; max-width: 340px; }
    .filters { margin: 16px 0; display: flex; gap: 12px; }
    button { padding: 6px 14px; border: 1px solid #d0d0d0; border-radius: 6px;
             background: white; cursor: pointer; font-size: 0.85rem; }
    button.active { background: #1a1a1a; color: white; border-color: #1a1a1a; }
    code { font-family: "SF Mono", monospace; font-size: 0.82rem; color: #0f172a; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Code Review Report</h1>
  <p style="color:#666">${new Date().toLocaleString()} — ${totalFiles} files, ${totalLines.toLocaleString()} lines analyzed</p>

  <div class="summary">
    <div class="stat">
      <div class="value">${findings.length}</div>
      <div class="label">Total Findings</div>
    </div>
    <div class="stat">
      <div class="value" style="color:#b91c1c">${securityFindings}</div>
      <div class="label">Security</div>
    </div>
    <div class="stat">
      <div class="value" style="color:#d97706">${errorFindings}</div>
      <div class="label">Error Handling</div>
    </div>
    <div class="stat">
      <div class="value">${totalFiles}</div>
      <div class="label">Files Scanned</div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="filters">
    <button class="active" onclick="filterFindings('all', this)">All</button>
    <button onclick="filterFindings('security', this)">Security</button>
    <button onclick="filterFindings('error-handling', this)">Error Handling</button>
  </div>

  <table id="findings-table">
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th>Location</th>
        <th>Category</th>
        <th>Summary</th>
        <th>Failure Scenario</th>
        <th>Verdict</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      ${rows}
    </tbody>
  </table>

  <script>
    function filterFindings(category, btn) {
      document.querySelectorAll('.filters button').forEach(b => b.classList.remove('active'));
      btn.classList.add('active');
      document.querySelectorAll('#findings-table tbody tr').forEach(row => {
        row.style.display = (category === 'all' || row.classList.contains(category))
          ? '' : 'none';
      });
    }
  </script>
</body>
</html>`;

// Write to disk for Artifact to pick up
const reportPath = "/tmp/code-review-report.html";
// (In practice, use the Write tool to write this — the REPL can return the path)
({ reportPath, html });

Step 5: Publish and Notify

// Write the HTML from the REPL result
await Write({
  file_path: "/tmp/code-review-report.html",
  content: replResult.result.html as string,
});

// Publish as artifact
const artifact = await Artifact({
  file_path: "/tmp/code-review-report.html",
  title: `Code Review — ${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}`,
  description: `${findings.length} findings across ${totalFiles} Python files`,
  favicon: "🔍",
  label: "v1.0 — automated review",
});

// Notify if the user isn't watching
await PushNotification({
  message: `Review done: ${findings.length} findings (${securityFindings} security). ${artifact.url}`,
  status: "proactive",
});

Step 6: Re-run and Version on Fix

After the developer addresses the findings, run the pipeline again with the same artifact URL to produce an updated version:

const updatedArtifact = await Artifact({
  file_path: "/tmp/code-review-report-v2.html",
  url: artifact.url,  // update in place
  label: "v1.1 — post-fix verification",
  title: `Code Review — ${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)} (post-fix)`,
});
// updatedArtifact.updated === true
// URL is unchanged — the PR link still works

What the Lab Demonstrates

REPL state accumulation. The findings array built in REPL call 1 is still live in call 3. No file I/O was needed to pass state between analysis steps. This is the correct pattern for multi-step computations that are logically a single workflow — avoid round-tripping data through files when the REPL can hold it in memory.

ReportFindings as a structural contract. The structured findings drive both the tool output (which the harness renders as a reviewable list) and the HTML generation (which uses the same data to build the interactive table). One data structure, two consumers.

Artifact versioning in practice. The first publish creates the URL. The second publish updates the same URL in place. The PR author bookmarks one URL and always sees the current state of the review. No link rot, no confusion about which report is current.

PushNotification as a non-blocking signal. The notification fires after the artifact is published. If the developer is watching the session, disabledReason: "user_present" comes back and nothing happens — which is correct. If they walked away, a push arrives with the URL embedded in the 200-character message.

Summary

Five tools, each solving a distinct layer of the output problem:

  • REPL executes JavaScript in a persistent in-process sandbox. State survives across calls within a session, top-level await is native, and tools registered during execution extend the session's tool surface. Use it for stateful computation, dynamic data processing, and environments where static tool registration is insufficient.
  • Artifact publishes HTML or Markdown to a hosted URL. The url field makes updates in-place rather than creating a new address. The 409 conflict is the concurrency guard — standard resolution is read, merge, republish. force: true is for automation that owns a specific artifact. list finds artifacts by scope when you need to retrieve URLs across a session.
  • PushNotification reaches users who are not watching. The status: "proactive" value is the declaration that the agent decided to send this. disabledReason: "user_present" is success, not failure. The 200-character limit is a forcing function for clarity.
  • RemoteTrigger manages the automation entry points: create, list, get, update, run. It is the persistent layer beneath ScheduleWakeup — named triggers that survive session boundaries and connect external systems to harness sessions.
  • ReportFindings emits code review findings as structured data. The failure_scenario field is what makes findings actionable — concrete inputs and concrete wrong outputs, not abstract descriptions. Maximum 32 findings per call; multiple calls accumulate. verdict signals confidence; outcome tracks remediation.

The lab integrates all five. The REPL holds computation state, ReportFindings structures the output, Artifact publishes it durably, and PushNotification closes the loop with the human who needs to act on it.

In Chapter 24, we examine the scheduling and wakeup system in depth: how ScheduleWakeup, ScheduleTask, and RemoteTrigger compose into durable automation that survives session boundaries, restarts on schedule, and coordinates work across multiple agents without a continuously running orchestrator.

Next: Chapter 24: Durable Scheduling — Wakeups, Tasks, and Trigger Composition

Chapter 24: CLI Modes and Subcommands

"The CLI is not just a launcher. Every flag you pass reshapes what the harness is."

24.1 Interactive Mode — The Default TUI

When you run claude with no flags and no subcommand, you get interactive mode. This is the full terminal UI: streaming responses, a model picker, a conversation history panel, inline permission prompts, and the complete tool surface. It is the highest-fidelity way to work with the harness because every layer is active.

Interactive mode is not just the default — it is the intended development environment. The session is live, stateful, and designed for back-and-forth work. The harness initializes the full stack in this order:

  1. Read and validate all settings files (global, project, enterprise)
  2. Discover and load CLAUDE.md files from the working directory up to the filesystem root
  3. Register hooks from settings
  4. Initialize the LSP (Language Server Protocol) client for code intelligence
  5. Load plugins
  6. Assemble the system prompt
  7. Present the first prompt to the user

The TUI surfaces the parts of this that matter during use. The model picker (accessible via /model or on session start if unconfigured) lets you switch between claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-opus-4-8, claude-haiku-4-5, and claude-fable without leaving the session. The transcript view (/history) shows the full conversation with tool calls expanded. The /permissions panel shows which tools have been allowed or denied during the session.

For most work — writing code, debugging, interactive refactoring — interactive mode is correct. The other modes exist to make Claude machine-callable.

24.2 Print Mode — --print / -p

Print mode is the foundational CI/CD flag. Pass -p (or --print) and the harness behaves like a command-line tool: read the prompt from the argument or stdin, run the agent loop to completion, write output to stdout, exit.

# simplest form
claude -p "Summarize the changes in the last three commits"

# from a file
claude -p "$(cat prompt.txt)"

# piped input
echo "Explain this error: $(cat build.log)" | claude -p

No TUI. No streaming to the terminal. No interactive prompts. The process exits with code 0 on success, non-zero on failure. This is what makes Claude scriptable.

Output Formats

Print mode accepts --output-format with three values: text, json, and stream-json.

text (default) — The model's final text response, written directly to stdout. Simple to use, simple to pipe.

# grep the model's answer for a specific word
claude -p "List all Python stdlib modules that handle networking" | grep -i socket

json — Wait for the full response, then emit a single JSON object containing the complete run. Useful when you need the full response envelope — tool calls, cost, stop reason — not just the text.

claude -p "Review this function for bugs" --output-format json < func.py | jq '.result'

The JSON object contains:

{
  "result": "The response text",
  "cost_usd": 0.0032,
  "duration_ms": 4120,
  "session_id": "sess_01...",
  "stop_reason": "end_turn",
  "tool_calls": [...]
}

stream-json — Emit newline-delimited JSON events as they arrive. Each event is a self-contained JSON object on a single line. This is the format for real-time CI pipelines that need to process output incrementally rather than waiting for the full response.

claude -p "Run the test suite and report failures" \
  --output-format stream-json \
  --dangerously-skip-permissions 2>/dev/null | \
  jq -r 'select(.type == "text") | .content'

Stream-JSON event types you will encounter:

Event typeDescription
textA text chunk from the model's response
tool_useThe model requested a tool call
tool_resultThe result returned from a tool execution
errorAn execution error
doneTerminal event — the session ended, includes cost and stop reason

Input Format

--input-format mirrors --output-format for the prompt side. The default is text. Set it to stream-json when your upstream is itself a Claude process emitting stream-JSON — this lets you chain Claude instances where one feeds another.

# chain: first claude generates a review prompt, second executes it
claude -p "Generate a security review prompt for this file" --output-format stream-json < auth.py | \
  claude -p --input-format stream-json --output-format text

--fallback-model

Only available in print mode. Accepts a comma-separated list of model names to try if the primary model is unavailable or rate-limited. The harness attempts models in order until one succeeds.

claude -p "Analyze this log" \
  --model claude-opus-4-8 \
  --fallback-model claude-sonnet-4-6,claude-haiku-4-5 \
  --output-format json < system.log

This flag exists specifically for automated pipelines where a model outage should degrade gracefully rather than fail the build. Use it for any critical CI step.

--forward-subagent-text

When a print-mode session spawns subagents (via the Agent tool), those subagents' text output is normally suppressed — only the parent's output reaches stdout. --forward-subagent-text changes this: every subagent's text is forwarded as stream-JSON text events as they occur.

Required in conjunction with --output-format stream-json. Useful when your pipeline needs visibility into what each subagent concluded, not just the coordinator's final summary.

24.3 Background Mode — --bg / --background

Background mode starts a session that runs without an attached terminal. The harness launches, begins processing, and returns control to the calling shell immediately. The session continues running and accumulates output that you can retrieve later.

# start a background session
claude --bg "Run a full security audit of the auth subsystem and write findings to audit-report.md"
# returns: Session started: sess_01AbCd...

# start with a specific model and effort
claude --bg --model claude-opus-4-8 --effort high \
  "Refactor the database layer to use async/await throughout"

The session ID is written to stdout on launch. Store it if you need to track this specific session:

SESSION=$(claude --bg "Audit dependencies for CVEs" --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id')
echo "Audit running as $SESSION"

Background sessions are managed with the claude agents subcommand, covered in section 24.5. The typical pattern is: launch with --bg, record the session ID, poll with claude agents --json until the session appears completed, then retrieve the output.

Background mode is the foundation for multi-agent orchestration from the shell layer rather than from inside a running session. When you need to launch five parallel analysis agents from a CI script and wait for all to finish, --bg is the mechanism.

24.4 Session Continuity — --resume, --continue, --from-pr

The harness persists conversation history to disk after every session. These flags let you re-enter prior sessions or extend them.

--continue / -c

The simplest form: resume the most recent session for the current working directory. No session ID needed.

# start work
claude "Begin refactoring the authentication module"

# later, in the same directory
claude -c "Continue where you left off — now focus on the token validation logic"

The harness finds the most recent session whose working directory matches $PWD and re-enters it with the new message appended to the existing conversation history.

--resume / -r

Two behaviors depending on how it is called:

Without a value — Opens an interactive picker showing all sessions for the current directory, sorted by recency. Select one to re-enter.

claude --resume

With a session ID — Goes directly to that session.

claude --resume sess_01AbCd3EfGh

Session IDs are UUIDs. You can find them in ~/.claude/sessions/ or from the --output-format json output of a prior run. The claude agents --json command also lists active sessions with their IDs.

--from-pr

Links a session to a pull request. The harness fetches the PR's diff, description, and associated comments, injects them into the session context, and optionally pre-populates the initial prompt with the PR content.

# start a session linked to PR 1234
claude --from-pr 1234

# or with a full PR URL
claude --from-pr https://github.com/org/repo/pull/1234

Without a value, it opens a picker to select from open PRs in the current repository. The intended use case is PR review sessions that have access to the full PR context without you having to manually construct a prompt from the diff.

--from-pr and --resume can be combined: claude --resume --from-pr 1234 resumes the most recent session that was originally linked to that PR.

24.5 claude agents — Managing Background Sessions

The claude agents subcommand is the management surface for background sessions. Without flags, it opens the TUI agent view: a live panel showing running sessions, their status, current tool, and elapsed time. You can select a session and attach to it to watch its output in real time.

# open the agent management TUI
claude agents

For scripting, the --json flag is essential:

# list all active sessions as a JSON array
claude agents --json

# include completed sessions
claude agents --json --all

# filter to sessions running in a specific directory
claude agents --json --cwd /path/to/project

The JSON output is an array of session objects:

[
  {
    "session_id": "sess_01AbCd...",
    "status": "running",
    "current_tool": "Bash",
    "started_at": "2026-07-28T14:23:01Z",
    "working_dir": "/Users/tri/projects/myapp",
    "prompt_preview": "Run security audit of auth...",
    "model": "claude-opus-4-8"
  }
]

The status field takes values running, waiting (paused at a permission prompt or tool confirmation), completed, and failed.

Dispatching from the Agent View

The TUI agent view is also a dispatcher. You can send a new background session directly from it without dropping back to the shell. This is the interactive equivalent of --bg — useful when you want to launch several parallel tasks and watch them all from one panel.

Flags that configure dispatched sessions:

--model <model>    Default model for sessions dispatched from this view
--effort <level>   Default effort (low/medium/high/xhigh/max)
--mcp-config       MCP config passed to dispatched sessions
--settings         Settings file passed to dispatched sessions

These are not persistent settings — they configure the specific claude agents invocation, affecting only sessions dispatched during that session.

24.6 claude mcp — Server Management

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the extension mechanism for adding external tools and context sources to the harness. The claude mcp subcommand is the management surface for MCP server configuration.

# list all configured MCP servers
claude mcp list

# add a server
claude mcp add my-server --command "node /path/to/server.js"
claude mcp add remote-server --url https://mcp.example.com/sse

# get details on a specific server
claude mcp get my-server

# remove a server
claude mcp remove my-server

MCP servers registered via claude mcp add are written to ~/.claude/settings.json under the mcpServers key. Project-scoped servers go in .claude/settings.json at the project root.

Authentication

Some MCP servers require authentication — OAuth flows, API keys, or session tokens. The login and logout subcommands handle this:

# authenticate with a server that requires OAuth
claude mcp login my-server

# clear stored credentials
claude mcp logout my-server

Credentials are stored in the system keychain, not in the settings file. This means MCP auth tokens never appear in ~/.claude/settings.json and cannot accidentally be committed to version control.

claude mcp serve

The serve command exposes the local Claude Code instance as an MCP server — making it callable from another harness or tool that understands the MCP protocol.

# expose this claude instance as an MCP server on stdio
claude mcp serve

# on a specific port
claude mcp serve --port 3001

This is the mechanism for using Claude Code as a component inside a larger orchestration layer. If you are building a custom harness that needs to delegate specific tasks to a running Claude Code instance (rather than spawning a new process), claude mcp serve provides the interface.

Runtime MCP Configuration

Two flags bypass the persistent settings and inject MCP configuration directly at session start:

# load MCP servers from a JSON config file at session start
claude --mcp-config ./ci-mcp-config.json -p "Run the audit"

# use ONLY the servers from --mcp-config, ignore all other MCP config
claude --mcp-config ./ci-mcp-config.json --strict-mcp-config -p "Run the audit"

--strict-mcp-config is the isolation flag for CI environments: the pipeline controls exactly which external tools are available, and nothing from the developer's personal MCP setup leaks in. Use it whenever reproducibility matters.

24.7 claude doctor, claude auth, claude update

These three subcommands handle the operational hygiene of a Claude Code installation.

claude doctor

Runs a health check against your installation. It reads settings and validates the environment without triggering the trust prompt that normally appears when a settings file is first loaded.

claude doctor

The check covers:

  • API key validity and auth method
  • Settings file syntax and schema validity
  • MCP server reachability
  • Hook command existence (verifies each hook command is executable)
  • Network connectivity to the Anthropic API
  • Node.js version compatibility

The output is human-readable by default. For CI use, claude doctor --json emits a structured result that you can parse:

claude doctor --json | jq '.checks | map(select(.status != "pass"))'

Run claude doctor when a session fails in an unexpected way before assuming it is a model or prompt issue. Most environment problems — expired tokens, broken hook paths, unreachable MCP servers — surface here.

claude auth

Manages authentication state.

# show current auth status
claude auth status

# log in (opens browser for OAuth or prompts for API key)
claude auth login

# log out
claude auth logout

Claude Code supports two auth paths: Anthropic Console API keys (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable or stored credential) and Claude.ai OAuth sessions. The auth status command shows which path is active and whether the credential is valid.

For automated environments where interactive login is impossible, set the environment variable directly:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
claude -p "Run analysis"

When --bare mode is active, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is the only supported auth path — OAuth sessions are not used in bare mode.

claude update / claude upgrade

Self-update commands. update checks the current installed version against the latest release; upgrade performs the update.

# check for updates
claude update

# install the latest version
claude upgrade

# install a specific version
claude install 2.1.100

# install the latest pre-release (latest channel)
claude install latest

In enterprise environments where the system Claude Code binary is managed centrally, use claude install --target /usr/local/bin/claude stable to pin to the stable channel without installing pre-releases.

24.8 claude ultrareview — Cloud Multi-Agent Code Review

claude ultrareview runs a cloud-hosted multi-agent code review. The description is accurate: it is not a single model pass over the diff. The cloud backend orchestrates multiple review agents across different dimensions — security, correctness, style, test coverage — and synthesizes their findings into a structured report.

# review the current branch against main
claude ultrareview

# review a specific PR by number
claude ultrareview 1234

# review against a specific base branch
claude ultrareview --base develop

Without arguments, it reviews the current branch against the default base branch (usually main). The review runs remotely — your code is sent to Anthropic's infrastructure for processing.

The output is a structured markdown report with severity-ranked findings grouped by category. Each finding includes:

  • File and line reference
  • Severity (CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW / INFO)
  • Category (security, correctness, performance, style, coverage)
  • Explanation and suggested fix

ultrareview is substantially more thorough than a single claude -p "review this diff" because the cloud backend uses models and compute that exceed what a local session can apply. The tradeoff is time — expect two to five minutes for a medium-sized PR — and the requirement that your code leaves your machine.

For pipelines where code confidentiality is a constraint, use local print-mode review instead (see the lab in section 24.11).

24.9 --bare — Minimal Startup

--bare strips the harness down to its minimal configuration. When this flag is set, the harness sets CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE=1 and skips:

  • Hook loading and execution
  • LSP initialization
  • Plugin loading
